title: Learning to Predict Performance-induced Emotion Differences in Classical Piano Music
comment: Accepted by the 27th International Society for Music Information Retrieval (ISMIR)
summary: Music is often used as a medium for communicating emotion, with performers shaping perceived affect through interpretation. This study addresses the challenge of identifying and predicting subtle changes in perceived emotion that are exclusively due to differences in performance. We focus on classical solo piano music, using a set of 6 commercial recordings of Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier Book I, annotated in terms of valence and arousal. By encoding the recordings through performance-specific features only, we isolate performance information from aspects of the composition itself, which tend to dominate the overall perceived emotional category. A preliminary analysis validates that these features vary meaningfully across performers. We then propose a relative regression framework, Delta-VA, to predict deviations in valence-arousal relative to an ``average'' performance, thereby focusing on the changes in emotion brought about by a specific way of playing a piece. In addition to the standard $R^2$ regression score, we introduce geometric evaluation metrics to assess the preservation of pairwise differences between performances. Results indicate high directional consistency with the ground truth, but also a compression in prediction magnitude, indicating that the model tends to underestimate expressive performance effects.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of predicting subtle changes in perceived emotion (valence and arousal) in classical solo piano music that arise purely from performance differences, using 6 commercial recordings of Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier Book I. The authors propose a relative regression framework (Delta-VA) that predicts deviations from an "average" performance using performance-specific features only, and introduce geometric evaluation metrics alongside standard R² to assess pairwise difference preservation. Results show high directional consistency with ground truth but a compression in prediction magnitude, indicating underestimation of expressive performance effects.
AI.motivation: Music performers communicate emotion through interpretation, and there is a need to isolate and predict perceived emotional changes that are exclusively due to performance differences, separate from composition-specific aspects that dominate overall emotional categorization.
AI.method: The method uses 6 commercial recordings of Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier Book I annotated in valence and arousal. Recordings are encoded using performance-specific features only to isolate performance information from compositional aspects. A relative regression framework, Delta-VA, predicts valence-arousal deviations relative to an average performance. In addition to standard R², geometric evaluation metrics are introduced to assess preservation of pairwise differences between performances.
AI.result: Preliminary analysis validates that performance-specific features vary meaningfully across performers. Results show high directional consistency with ground truth, but also a compression in prediction magnitude, indicating the model tends to underestimate expressive performance effects.
AI.conclusion: The Delta-VA framework can effectively predict directional changes in perceived emotion due to performance differences, though it underestimates the magnitude of these expressive effects, suggesting room for improvement in capturing the full extent of performance-based emotional variation.

title: Meshy T2: Fast Native Mesh Generation with Flow Matching
summary: Polygonal meshes are the standard surface representation of modern 3D pipelines, and generating high-quality meshes with artist-style topology is essential for film, gaming, and interactive 3D applications. Mainstream approaches serialize a mesh into a token sequence and decode it autoregressively, which is slow at inference and sensitive to error accumulation, making them impractical for interactive asset creation. We present Meshy T2, a fast native mesh generation framework built on flow matching. At its core is a vertex-set mesh VAE that encodes a mesh into one continuous latent token per vertex and decodes vertices, edge connectivity, and face winding order in a single pass, preserving high-precision geometry and artist-authored topology without vertex quantization or welding. Generation proceeds as a coarse-to-fine cascade of two flow-matching models: an image-conditioned voxel flow first sketches the overall shape as a coarse occupancy scaffold, and a mesh flow then populates the scaffold with per-vertex latent tokens, conditioned on the image, the scaffold, and a requested vertex budget. This design delivers three practical capabilities: interactive generation speed through parallel flow-based synthesis; effective face-count control through the requested vertex budget; and native support for multi-part assets, whose components emerge directly from the generated connectivity. In our experiments, Meshy T2 achieves state-of-the-art geometric fidelity and completes end-to-end image-to-mesh generation within a median of 6 seconds, over an order of magnitude faster than autoregressive baselines. Code and weights will be available at https://github.com/meshy-dev/meshy-t2.

AI.tldr: Meshy T2 is a fast native mesh generation framework built on flow matching, using a vertex-set mesh VAE to encode meshes into continuous latent tokens and a coarse-to-fine cascade of two flow-matching models for image-conditioned mesh generation. It generates high-fidelity meshes with artist-quality topology in a median of 6 seconds, over 10x faster than autoregressive baselines, while supporting interactive generation speed, face-count control, and multi-part assets.
AI.motivation: Existing autoregressive mesh generation approaches serialize meshes into token sequences and decode them autoregressively, which is slow at inference and sensitive to error accumulation. This makes them impractical for interactive 3D asset creation in film, gaming, and interactive applications where fast, high-quality mesh generation with artist-style topology is needed.
AI.method: Meshy T2 uses a vertex-set mesh VAE that encodes each mesh into one continuous latent token per vertex and decodes vertices, edge connectivity, and face winding order in a single pass, avoiding vertex quantization and welding. Generation employs a coarse-to-fine cascade of two flow-matching models: first, an image-conditioned voxel flow sketches the overall shape as a coarse occupancy scaffold; then, a mesh flow populates the scaffold with per-vertex latent tokens, conditioned on the image, the scaffold, and a requested vertex budget.
AI.result: Meshy T2 achieves state-of-the-art geometric fidelity and completes end-to-end image-to-mesh generation within a median of 6 seconds, which is over an order of magnitude faster than autoregressive baselines. It also demonstrates effective face-count control through the requested vertex budget and native support for multi-part assets emerging from generated connectivity.
AI.conclusion: Flow-matching with a vertex-set latent representation provides a practical, fast alternative to autoregressive mesh generation, delivering interactive speed, precise topology control, and multi-part asset support, making it suitable for real-world interactive 3D asset creation workflows.

title: OpenClaw and Ollama in Agentic AI: Toward Fully Autonomous and Scalable AI Agent Systems
summary: The rapid transition from reactive large language models (LLMs) to persistent, action-capable systems has exposed critical gaps in the architectural understanding of Agentic AI, particularly in separating inference, orchestration, and execution layers for autonomous AI agents. Despite recent advances, unified frameworks for designing and evaluating full-stack agentic systems remain limited. This paper presents a comprehensive, layered architecture for Agentic AI, outlining the evolution from reactive LLM interfaces to persistent, goal-driven autonomous AI agents with memory, planning, and continuous execution. We analyze OpenClaw and Ollama as a full-stack Agentic AI system, where Ollama serves as the LLM inference layer and OpenClaw enables agent runtime orchestration, integrating reasoning, tool use, and action execution. A prototype experimental validation of the OpenClaw-Ollama architecture demonstrates that capabilities such as persistent memory, tool utilization, and adaptive decision-making emerge from system-level integration rather than standalone models, with performance improving consistently as architectural complexity increases. The study further examines challenges in scalability, security, privacy, governance, and evaluation of agentic systems, highlighting the need for robust benchmarking and system-level design. Future directions include scalable multi-agent architectures, distributed autonomous systems, and human-aware Agentic AI frameworks for responsible deployment. Overall, this work establishes a unified architectural foundation for Agentic AI, validates the effectiveness of full-stack autonomous AI agents, and provides a roadmap for building scalable, secure, and trustworthy agentic systems. All models, code, and datasets are publicly released to support reproducibility and benchmarking.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a unified layered architecture for Agentic AI, separating inference, orchestration, and execution layers. It validates the architecture using an OpenClaw-Ollama full-stack system, demonstrating that capabilities like persistent memory, tool use, and adaptive decision-making emerge from system-level integration rather than standalone models. The work also addresses challenges in scalability, security, privacy, governance, and evaluation, providing a foundation and roadmap for building scalable, secure, and trustworthy agentic systems.
AI.motivation: The rapid shift from reactive LLMs to persistent, action-capable agentic systems has exposed critical gaps in architectural understanding—particularly around separating inference, orchestration, and execution layers. Despite recent advances, there is a lack of unified frameworks for designing and evaluating full-stack agentic systems.
AI.method: The paper presents a comprehensive layered architecture for Agentic AI, tracing evolution from reactive LLM interfaces to persistent autonomous agents with memory, planning, and continuous execution. It analyzes OpenClaw and Ollama as a full-stack system—Ollama as the LLM inference layer and OpenClaw for agent runtime orchestration—and conducts a prototype experimental validation of this architecture.
AI.result: Experimental validation of the OpenClaw-Ollama architecture shows that capabilities such as persistent memory, tool utilization, and adaptive decision-making emerge from system-level integration rather than standalone models. Performance consistently improves as architectural complexity increases.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a unified architectural foundation for Agentic AI, validates the effectiveness of full-stack autonomous AI agents, and outlines future directions including scalable multi-agent architectures, distributed autonomous systems, and human-aware frameworks. All models, code, and datasets are publicly released for reproducibility and benchmarking.

title: ReLoop-UME: Recurrent Depth with Learnable Retrieval Registers for Universal Multimodal Embedding
summary: Universal multimodal embedding (UME) maps heterogeneous multimodal inputs into a shared embedding space. Existing UME models either form embeddings through single forward encoding or add computation through explicit rationale tokens and latent autoregressive states. Although token expansion can improve complex matching, serial generation increases retrieval latency and makes the final embedding depend on generated intermediate states. This raises a different question: can useful computation be expanded along model depth while keeping the token workspace fixed? We analyze positive-negative similarity separation at every layer of independently trained UME models and observe a shared progression: early layers contextualize multimodal inputs, a contiguous middle-to-late stage forms retrieval-discriminative features, and the final layers map them into the embedding space. Based on this finding, we propose ReLoop-UME, which executes the early layers once, recurrently reuses a parameter-shared retrieval-forming block, and applies the final mapping layers after the last loop. Learnable Retrieval Registers provide persistent retrieval-specific states that accumulate and exchange evidence across loops, with the final register serving as the embedding readout. On MMEB-V2 and MRMR, ReLoop-UME consistently improves retrieval across different backbones while running 44.9x faster than UME-R1 and 1.5x faster than PLUME.

AI.tldr: ReLoop-UME is a universal multimodal embedding model that expands computation along model depth via recurrent reuse of a parameter-shared retrieval-forming block, instead of adding tokens or autoregressive states. It runs 44.9x faster than UME-R1 and 1.5x faster than PLUME while consistently improving retrieval on MMEB-V2 and MRMR.
AI.motivation: Existing UME models either use single forward encoding or expand computation via explicit rationale tokens/latent autoregressive states, where token expansion improves matching but serial generation increases latency and makes embeddings dependent on generated intermediates. The authors ask whether computation can be expanded along model depth while keeping the token workspace fixed.
AI.method: The authors first analyze positive-negative similarity separation at every layer of independently trained UME models, observing a shared three-stage progression: early contextualization, middle-to-late retrieval-discriminative feature formation, and final embedding mapping. Based on this, they propose ReLoop-UME which executes early layers once, recurrently reuses a parameter-shared retrieval-forming block across loops, applies final mapping layers after the last loop, and uses Learnable Retrieval Registers to accumulate and exchange retrieval-specific evidence across loops with the final register as embedding readout.
AI.result: ReLoop-UME consistently improves retrieval across different backbones on MMEB-V2 and MRMR benchmarks while running 44.9x faster than UME-R1 and 1.5x faster than PLUME.
AI.conclusion: Expanding computation along model depth through recurrent looped reuse of a shared block can effectively replace token expansion, achieving both better retrieval performance and significantly lower latency than serial generation-based approaches.

title: Metaphor-Induced Algorithmic Steering: Cross-Domain Procedural Transfer in LLM Code Generation
summary: Large language models benefit from elements in natural language, such as metaphors and analogies in training data and inference input to achieve generalisability across different domains. However, these language elements may also lead to unwanted behaviors when metaphorical expressions implicitly transfer inappropriate procedural patterns into new tasks. In this paper, we show that metaphorical instructions can induce analogical transfer of procedural mechanisms, thus steering code-generation models towards less efficient algorithms. We refer to this metaphor-induced effect as metaphorical algorithmic steering: a skill that is benign and plausible within its source domain transfers an abstract procedural schema into a programming task, causing the model to favor exhaustive search, full scans, or repeated reconstruction without explicitly mentioning the target algorithm. More broadly, this suggests that code-generation models can carry procedures that are appropriate in a task's background domain into the task's programming problem, where they can lead to unwanted outcomes. To study this phenomenon, we develop MASC (Metaphorical Algorithmic Steering for Code Generation), a framework that iteratively metaphorizes and refines benign skills to elicit low-efficiency code while remaining benign and task-relevant. Beyond behavioral evaluation, we study whether this phenomenon is detectable and mechanistically reflected in model representations. Our method achieves high detection rates for metaphorical skills and less-efficient implementations. We also find that metaphorical skills induce a hidden-state shift towards lower-efficiency procedural behavior prototypes. These results suggest that metaphorical algorithmic steering operates through the transfer of procedural patterns associated with metaphorical source scenarios rather than surface level metaphorical language alone.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces and demonstrates "metaphorical algorithmic steering," a phenomenon where metaphorical instructions in prompts cause code-generation LLMs to transfer procedural patterns from a source domain into programming tasks, leading to less efficient algorithm choices (e.g., exhaustive search, full scans). The authors develop MASC, a framework that iteratively metaphorizes benign skills to elicit low-efficiency code, and show the effect is detectable through behavioral evaluation and mechanistic hidden-state analysis.
AI.motivation: While metaphors and analogies are known to help LLMs generalize across domains, they may also inadvertently transfer inappropriate procedural schemes into new tasks. The paper investigates whether metaphorical instructions can steer code-generation models toward suboptimal algorithms, a potentially harmful side effect worth understanding and detecting.
AI.method: The authors propose MASC (Metaphorical Algorithmic Steering for Code Generation), a framework that iteratively metaphorizes and refines benign skills to generate less-efficient code while remaining task-relevant and benign. They combine behavioral evaluation (measuring code efficiency and detection rates) with mechanistic analysis of hidden states to examine whether the steering effect is reflected in model representations.
AI.result: MASC achieves high detection rates for both metaphorical skills and less-efficient implementations. Analysis of model representations reveals that metaphorical skills induce a hidden-state shift toward lower-efficiency procedural behavior prototypes, indicating the effect is mechanism-based rather than driven by surface-level metaphorical language.
AI.conclusion: Metaphorical algorithmic steering operates through the transfer of abstract procedural patterns associated with metaphorical source scenarios into programming tasks. This highlights a subtle risk where benign, domain-appropriate skills can negatively influence code-generation models, and it shows such phenomena are detectable both behaviorally and mechanistically.

title: Learning Manifolds in High-D Point Embedding for Anisotropic Surface Approximation from Unstructured Point Clouds
summary: Dense 3D sensors in various real-world fields produce point clouds that are geometrically redundant for real-time processing. In this paper, we propose an efficient and scalable learning-based anisotropic surface approximation framework, HD-PEA, that operates directly on unstructured point clouds, integrating anisotropic optimization into reconstruction to produce compact, geometry-aligned surface representations with higher fidelity, fewer elements, and improved numerical stability compared to isotropic and adaptive meshes. Firstly, we develop a novel learning-based high-dimensional (high-d) Euclidean point embedding method to map the input point clouds into a high-d manifold embedding space. For handling large-scale point clouds without retraining and fine-tuning, a patch-based meta-embedding scheme is designed during the inference stage. Then, we develop a new tangent subspace estimation for the high-d embedding manifold approximation and anisotropic manifold reconstruction in high-d space. The main contribution of this work is to propose a scalable deep learning framework and a variety of datasets for constructing a high-d Euclidean point embedding space aimed to 3D anisotropic surface mesh approximation and Riemannian curvature tensor estimation from point clouds. We extensively evaluate our method against state-of-the-art surface reconstruction approaches using several datasets, such as Thingi10K dataset, AIM@SHAPE and Stanford 3D Scanning Repository, ScanNet dataset, and further demonstrate its generalization and usability on diverse unseen shapes and applications from these datasets.

AI.tldr: HD-PEA is a scalable deep-learning framework for efficient anisotropic surface approximation directly from unstructured point clouds. It maps input point clouds into a high-dimensional Euclidean manifold embedding space using a novel learned embedding method with a patch-based meta-embedding scheme for large-scale data without retraining, then performs tangent subspace estimation and anisotropic manifold reconstruction in high-d space. The method produces compact, geometry-aligned surface representations with higher fidelity, fewer elements, and improved numerical stability compared to isotropic and adaptive meshes, while also enabling Riemannian curvature tensor estimation.
AI.motivation: Dense 3D sensors produce point clouds that are geometrically redundant for real-time processing, creating a need for compact yet accurate surface representations that preserve geometric fidelity while reducing computational overhead.
AI.method: The framework first maps input point clouds into a high-dimensional Euclidean point embedding space via a novel learning-based approach, using a patch-based meta-embedding scheme at inference to handle large-scale point clouds without retraining. It then develops tangent subspace estimation for the high-d embedding manifold approximation and performs anisotropic manifold reconstruction in the high-d space, enabling both anistropic surface mesh approximation and Riemannian curvature tensor estimation.
AI.result: Extensive evaluation against state-of-the-art surface reconstruction methods on Thingi10K, AIM@SHAPE, Stanford 3D Scanning Repository, and ScanNet datasets demonstrates that HD-PEA achieves higher fidelity, fewer mesh elements, and improved numerical stability compared to isotropic and adaptive meshes, along with strong generalization to unseen shapes and diverse applications.
AI.conclusion: HD-PEA provides a scalable and generalizable deep learning framework for high-dimensional anisotropic surface approximation from point clouds, serving as a versatile tool for compact surface reconstruction and curvature analysis in real-time processing scenarios.

title: Can AI Evaluate AI Scientists? A Benchmarking Study of Autonomous Research Generation Systems Using Automated Multi-Model Review
summary: AI Scientist systems capable of autonomous research have the potential to significantly accelerate scientific discovery. However, evaluating and comparing the quality of AI-generated papers remains an open challenge. We propose and implement a rigorous benchmarking protocol using an automated peer-review system that harnesses frontier large language models to assess scientific papers across four core dimensions: originality, scientific rigor, clarity, and significance. We evaluate four leading AI Scientist frameworks: \textit{Sakana AI (v1 & v2)}, \textit{CycleResearcher}, and \textit{Data-to-Paper}. Each framework was run on a consistent set of 15 research proposals published by a commercial autonomous AI scientist company (FARS), generating 60 papers that we evaluate alongside 15 FARS benchmark papers. Using three independent LLM reviewers (GPT-5.4, Gemini, and Claude), we find that FARS benchmark papers significantly outperform all competing frameworks, achieving mean scores of 2.14--2.47 on a 1--5 scale compared to 1.00--1.87 for other systems. Notably, FARS scores are more than 2$\times$ higher than the next-best systems on Gemini and Claude evaluations. We find strong agreement among Gemini and Claude ($ρ$ = 0.907, $p < 0.001$), and both correlate extremely strongly with the synthesis score ($ρ$ = 0.961, $p < 0.001$), validating the reliability of automated evaluation. However, GPT-5.4 exhibits weaker agreement ($ρ\approx 0.32$), suggesting it evaluates papers using different criteria. These results establish the first quantitative benchmark for AI Scientist systems and demonstrate that multi-model LLM evaluation provides a scalable, consistent framework for assessing autonomous research quality.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an automated peer-review benchmarking protocol using frontier LLMs to evaluate AI Scientist frameworks across four dimensions (originality, rigor, clarity, significance). Testing four AI Scientist systems against FARS benchmark papers on 15 research proposals, the authors find FARS papers significantly outperform all competitors (scores 2.14-2.47 vs 1.00-1.87 on a 1-5 scale). Gemini and Claude show strong review agreement and correlate with synthesis scores, while GPT-5.4 diverges, suggesting different evaluation criteria. This establishes the first quantitative benchmark for AI Scientist systems.
AI.motivation: AI Scientist systems capable of autonomous research could greatly accelerate scientific discovery, but there is currently no rigorous method to evaluate and compare the quality of AI-generated scientific papers. This open challenge motivates the need for a systematic benchmarking protocol.
AI.method: The authors implement an automated peer-review benchmark using frontier LLMs (GPT-5.4, Gemini, Claude) as independent reviewers across four core dimensions: originality, scientific rigor, clarity, and significance. They run four AI Scientist frameworks (Sakana AI v1 & v2, CycleResearcher, Data-to-Paper) on 15 consistent research proposals from FARS, generating 60 papers, then evaluate these alongside 15 FARS benchmark papers, with three independent LLM reviewers scoring each.
AI.result: FARS benchmark papers significantly outperform all competing frameworks, achieving mean scores of 2.14-2.47 on a 1-5 scale compared to 1.00-1.87 for other systems. FARS scores are more than 2x higher than next-best systems on Gemini and Claude evaluations. Gemini and Claude show strong agreement (rho=0.907, p<0.001) and both correlate extremely strongly with the synthesis score (rho=0.961, p<0.001). GPT-5.4 shows weaker agreement (rho~0.32), indicating different evaluation criteria.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes the first quantitative benchmark for AI Scientist systems and demonstrates that multi-model LLM evaluation provides a scalable, consistent framework for assessing autonomous research quality. The validation via inter-reviewer agreement and correlation with synthesis scores supports the reliability of automated evaluation, though the GPT-5.4 discrepancy suggests caution in relying on a single evaluator.

title: TORUS: A Test of Rendering-Understanding Self-Coherence for Unified Audio Models
summary: Unified audio models capable of audio understanding, audio generation and, increasingly, audio editing are proliferating rapidly. Yet a basic question about them remains unanswered: do the two heads of a unified model agree about the same audio? Current practice evaluates each capability in isolation on specialized benchmarks, and never asks whether a model can make sense of its own generations. We present TORUS, the first self-coherence test for audio-native unified models. TORUS comprises 48 three-stage self-coherence tests carrying 432 six-option questions spanning speech, sound and music across five task families. We holistically evaluate five open unified models alongside a Cascaded Baseline that combines state-of-the-art specialized generation, editing and understanding models. The best unified model answers 50.5% of questions against the Cascaded Baseline's 63.2% and a 16.7% chance floor. Models struggle on audio editing. Among the evaluated audio models (specialized and unified), we observe limited self-coherence, and thus position self-coherence as an essential test for future audio systems.

AI.tldr: TORUS is the first self-coherence test for unified audio models, comprising 48 three-stage tests with 432 questions across speech, sound, and music. Evaluating five open unified models against a Cascaded Baseline, the best unified model achieves 50.5% accuracy versus the baseline's 63.2%, revealing limited self-coherence and highlighting it as a critical evaluation dimension.
AI.motivation: Unified audio models with both understanding and generation capabilities are rapidly proliferating, yet no existing evaluation asks whether these models can make sense of their own generations. Current benchmarks evaluate understanding, generation, and editing in isolation, leaving the fundamental question of whether the two "heads" of a unified model agree unaddressed.
AI.method: TORUS comprises 48 three-stage self-coherence tests carrying 432 six-option questions spanning speech, sound, and music across five task families. Five open unified audio models are evaluated alongside a Cascaded Baseline that combines state-of-the-art specialized generation, editing, and understanding models.
AI.result: The best unified model answers 50.5% of questions versus 63.2% for the Cascaded Baseline against a 16.7% chance floor. Models struggle particularly on audio editing, and limited self-coherence is observed across all evaluated models (both specialized and unified).
AI.conclusion: Self-coherence is a fundamentally important but currently unmet property in audio models. The authors position self-coherence as an essential test for future audio systems, suggesting that current unified models do not reliably understand their own outputs.

title: SCMA: Structure-Conditioned and Metal-Aware Flow Matching for CT Metal Artifact Reduction
summary: In X-ray CT, metallic objects cause beam hardening, photon starvation, and scattering, leading to projection inconsistency, streaks, dark bands, and structural distortions that compromise clinical diagnosis and quantitative analysis. Existing metal artifact reduction (MAR) methods remain limited: optimization-based methods may leave residual artifacts or blur structures, regression networks may generalize poorly across scenarios, and generative models without sample-specific structural guidance and physical constraints may produce anatomically inconsistent structures. Flow Matching learns a continuous-time velocity field that deterministically transports a source distribution to a target distribution, providing a flexible MAR prior. However, standard unconditional Flow Matching does not exploit sample-specific structure, spatially nonuniform metal-induced degradation, or measured projections. To address these limitations, we propose SCMA, a structure-conditioned and metal-aware Flow Matching framework. First, a linear-interpolation-corrected image is fed into the velocity network with the intermediate state as a sample-specific structural condition, guiding inference toward artifact-free CT images while preserving anatomy. Second, time-varying spatial weights from the metal mask and its distance transform are incorporated into the Flow Matching loss to emphasize severe degradation within and around metal regions. Finally, conditional Flow Matching updates alternate with projection-consistency correction during inference, allowing reliable measurements outside metal traces to constrain predictions. Experiments on simulated and real CT data demonstrate that SCMA more effectively suppresses metal artifacts, preserves local anatomical structures, and reduces hallucination-like structures inconsistent with projection measurements than representative MAR methods.

AI.tldr: SCMA is a structure-conditioned, metal-aware Flow Matching framework for CT metal artifact reduction that incorporates sample-specific structural guidance, spatially weighted metal-aware loss, and projection-consistency correction to suppress artifacts while preserving anatomy.
AI.motivation: Existing MAR methods (optimization-based, regression networks, generative models) are limited by residual artifacts, poor generalization, or anatomically inconsistent outputs. Standard unconditional Flow Matching fails to exploit sample-specific structure, spatially nonuniform degradation, and measured projections.
AI.method: SCMA integrates three components: (1) a linear-interpolation-corrected image fed into the velocity network with the intermediate state as a sample-specific structural condition; (2) time-varying spatial weights derived from the metal mask and its distance transform applied to the Flow Matching loss to emphasize severe degradation near metal; (3) alternating conditional Flow Matching updates with projection-consistency correction during inference to constrain predictions using reliable measurements outside metal traces.
AI.result: Experiments on simulated and real CT data demonstrate SCMA more effectively suppresses metal artifacts, preserves local anatomical structures, and reduces hallucination-like structures inconsistent with projection measurements compared to representative MAR methods.
AI.conclusion: SCMA provides a principled way to embed sample-specific structural information and physical (projection) constraints into a Flow Matching framework, yielding superior metal artifact suppression and anatomy preservation.

title: Code Is the Body: Agent-Owned Software Bodies for Recursive Evolution and Descent
summary: Personalized AI agents are often configurable without giving users control over the artifacts that determine their future behavior. We present OurArk, an architecture for persistent personal agents centered on an agent-owned software body: an identity-bearing, inspectable, and versioned artifact under human custody. The body contains behavior-defining code, prompts, tools, skills, policies, tests, and evolution mechanisms. Memories and credentials remain private instance state, while model inference is treated as a replaceable external service. OurArk defines governed self-evolution and recursive descent over the same body. Self-evolution produces isolated candidate changes that are validated, reviewed, and merged under human control, enabling human-agent co-development of the agent's software body. Descent creates an independently versioned descendant with a distinct identity, mission, history, and fresh private-state boundary; compatible descendants can themselves source further descent. After divergence, direct-parent changes and peer skills can be inspected for selective local adaptation. We implement the architecture in the open-source Genesis creation engine and Enoch reference agent. A four-agent, three-descent linear lineage and executable regression tests demonstrate recursive creation, inherited validation contracts, isolated body changes, human-controlled review, and failed-update recovery. OurArk provides a concrete substrate for personal agents that people can possess, govern, specialize, and evolve over time.

AI.tldr: This paper presents OurArk, an architecture for persistent personal AI agents built around an agent-owned software body—an identity-bearing, inspectable, versioned artifact under human custody. The architecture supports governed self-evolution and recursive descent (creating versioned descendants with distinct identities). The authors implement it in the open-source Genesis engine and Enoch reference agent, demonstrating recursive creation, inheritance, isolation, human-controlled review, and failed-update recovery through a four-agent lineage.
AI.motivation: Personalized AI agents are typically configurable but do not give users control over the artifacts that determine their future behavior. This lack of user custody and governance over agent behavior-defining artifacts motivates a new architecture.
AI.method: OurArk centers on an agent-owned software body containing behavior-defining code, prompts, tools, skills, policies, tests, and evolution mechanisms. Memories and credentials are kept as private instance state, while model inference is treated as a replaceable external service. It defines two key operations: (1) governed self-evolution, which produces isolated candidate changes validated, reviewed, and merged under human control; and (2) recursive descent, which creates independently versioned descendants with distinct identities, missions, histories, and fresh private-state boundaries. The architecture is implemented in the Genesis engine and Enoch reference agent.
AI.result: A four-agent, three-descent linear lineage and executable regression tests demonstrate recursive creation, inherited validation contracts, isolated body changes, human-controlled review, and failed-update recovery.
AI.conclusion: OurArk provides a concrete substrate for personal agents that people can possess, govern, specialize, and evolve over time.

title: Interactive Generative Motion Editing via Scheduled Inpainting
summary: Motion editing is central to VFX and game development, where it is used extensively to modify and augment existing movements to conform to new environments or changes in artistic direction. While traditional motion editing can do small modifications, it cannot accommodate larger structural edits, resulting in visual warping artifacts that require authoring new motion. Conversely, recent advances in large-scale generative modeling have unlocked newfound capabilities for authoring entire movements by directly manipulating sparse spatial constraints. While impressive at creating new movements, these methods lack the capability to preserve and edit existing motion interactively. In this work, we introduce scheduled inpainting, a method that enables interactive generative motion editing, a novel paradigm unifying motion synthesis and editing by leveraging generative models. Scheduled inpainting is a simple yet powerful inference-based technique that enables fine-grained spatiotemporal control over the balance between preserving the original motion and generating new content. By building atop generative models that support direct manipulation, our system allows artists to interactively refine existing animations while ensuring results remain natural and consistent with the learned motion distribution. Scheduled inpainting is versatile and supports many editing applications, such as extending, stitching, and compositing different clips. Finally, we extensively validate our approach by comparing with four baselines, conducting ablations of our design, and reporting user feedback.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces scheduled inpainting, an inference-based technique for interactive generative motion editing that unifies motion synthesis and editing by leveraging generative models. It enables fine-grained spatiotemporal control over balancing original motion preservation with new content generation, supporting applications like extending, stitching, and compositing motion clips.
AI.motivation: Traditional motion editing handles only small modifications and causes visual warping artifacts for larger structural edits requiring new motion authoring. Conversely, recent large-scale generative models can create entire movements from sparse spatial constraints but lack the ability to preserve and edit existing motion interactively. There is a gap between these two paradigms—no method currently unifies both interactive motion editing and generative motion synthesis.
AI.method: The proposed scheduled inpainting is a simple inference-based technique built atop generative models that support direct manipulation. It provides fine-grained spatiotemporal control over the balance between preserving the original motion and generating new content, thereby unifying motion synthesis and editing in a single framework. The method supports multiple editing applications including extending, stitching, and compositing different motion clips.
AI.result: The authors validate their approach extensively by comparing against four baselines, conducting ablations of their design, and reporting user feedback. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of scheduled inpainting for interactive generative motion editing.
AI.conclusion: Scheduled inpainting bridges the gap between motion synthesis and motion editing by enabling artists to interactively refine existing animations while ensuring results remain natural and consistent with the learned motion distribution. It is a versatile approach supporting a wide range of editing applications.

title: LLM Framework for Discovering Major Mathematical Conjectures: AI's Quest for the Next Riemann Hypothesis
summary: Major mathematical conjectures still depend heavily on expert intuition, so a unified method for the systematic generation and validation of conjectures with substantial mathematical potential remains unavailable. We present a three stage pipeline for major conjecture discovery, with region search from explicit local evidence modules, reflective validation for foundationality, novelty, and potential significance, and formal validation in Lean 4 and Mathlib. The objective is the discovery of mathematical problems with high problem taste, namely problems whose proofs could reorganize the language of a research area and provide durable help to human mathematical research. Experiments on twenty candidates showstable passage from natural language to formal checks, with twenty out of twenty candidates passing Lean parsing and type checking, twenty out of twenty candidates not directly absorbed by exact?,twenty out of twenty candidates not automatically discharged by aesop, and no explicit duplicates or near duplicates.

AI.tldr: A three-stage pipeline for automated mathematical conjecture discovery that combines region search from local evidence, reflective validation of foundationality/novelty/significance, and formal verification in Lean 4, achieving 20/20 candidates passing type checking with no duplicates.
AI.motivation: Major mathematical conjectures still depend heavily on expert intuition; there is no unified method for systematically generating and validating conjectures with substantial mathematical potential.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) region search from explicit local evidence modules, (2) reflective validation assessing foundationality, novelty, and potential significance (problem taste), and (3) formal validation in Lean 4 and Mathlib.
AI.result: On twenty candidates, all twenty passed Lean parsing and type checking, none were directly absorbed by exact?, none automatically discharged by aesop, and no explicit duplicates or near duplicates were found.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline demonstrates stable passage from natural language conjectures to formal checks, suggesting a viable automated route to discovering mathematical problems whose proofs could reorganize the language of a research area.

title: Do Music Foundation Models Embed Pitch in Helical Structure?
summary: This study analyzes the intermediate representations of music foundation models (MFMs) and reports the geometric structures used to represent pitch information. By inputting isolated musical notes into trained MFMs and analyzing their principal components, we reveal that the representations form a helical structure reflecting the octave periodicity of pitch. Furthermore, we show that the clarity and geometry of this helical structure vary not only across models but also with the acoustic properties of the input signals. Our analysis provides a novel approach for clarifying the internal mechanisms of MFMs.

AI.tldr: This study investigates the internal representations of music foundation models (MFMs) by inputting isolated musical notes and analyzing principal components, revealing that pitch information is encoded in a helical geometric structure reflecting octave periodicity. The clarity of this structure varies across models and with input acoustic properties, offering a novel method for interpreting MFM internals.
AI.motivation: The goal is to clarify the internal mechanisms of music foundation models, which remain largely opaque. Understanding how pitch—a fundamental musical attribute—is geometrically represented within these models provides insight into their learned representations and interpretability.
AI.method: The authors input isolated musical notes into trained MFMs, extract intermediate representations, and perform principal component analysis (PCA). They examine the resulting geometric structures to determine how pitch information is organized, specifically looking for helical patterns corresponding to octave periodicity.
AI.result: The representations of pitch form a helical structure that reflects the octave periodicity of pitch. However, the clarity and geometry of this helix vary across different models and depending on the acoustic properties of the input signals.
AI.conclusion: The helix is a novel geometric signature for pitch encoding in MFMs, and the proposed PCA-based approach provides a new avenue for probing and understanding the internal mechanisms of music foundation models.

title: WaiT for the Signal: Simple Frequency-Aware Flow-Matching
summary: As image generation models scale to ever higher resolutions, global coherence, local detail, and texture fidelity become critical axes for generation quality. However, standard flow matching treats all spatial frequencies uniformly, ignoring the natural frequency hierarchy where high-frequency bands become indistinguishable from pure noise far earlier than coarse structures. We introduce WaiT, a Wavelet-aware image Transformer that decomposes generation into coarse and fine bands via lossless wavelets. True to its name, the high-frequency bands wait for the signal: staying pure noise until coarse structure has emerged, then joining the flow for joint refinement. Since standard FID discards fine-grained detail through aggressive downsampling, we introduce a more stringent three-axis evaluation protocol to assess quality at native resolution. On ImageNet 512x512, WaiT achieves a pixel-space FID of 1.43 and is Pareto-optimal across all three axes, reducing sampling compute by up to 50%. With our largest 2B model, we set a new state-of-the-art FID of 1.3 for pixel-space models on ImageNet 512 resolution. Our formulation outperforms even the strongest latent-space models on texture fidelity, and scales seamlessly to high-resolution OpenImages and to video generation, achieving a state-of-the-art FVD of 0.84 on Kinetics-600 with no algorithmic modifications.

AI.tldr: WaiT is a wavelet-aware image Transformer that decomposes image generation into coarse and fine frequency bands via lossless wavelets, where high-frequency bands remain pure noise until coarse structure emerges, then join the flow for joint refinement. It achieves SOTA pixel-space FID of 1.3 on ImageNet 512 with a 2B model, is Pareto-optimal across a new three-axis native-resolution evaluation protocol, reduces sampling compute by up to 50%, and extends to video generation with SOTA FVD of 0.84 on Kinetics-600.
AI.motivation: Standard flow matching treats all spatial frequencies uniformly, ignoring the natural frequency hierarchy where high-frequency bands become indistinguishable from noise far earlier than coarse structures. Additionally, standard FID discards fine-grained detail through aggressive downsampling, making evaluation at native resolution insufficiently stringent.
AI.method: WaiT decomposes generation into coarse and fine bands via lossless wavelets. High-frequency bands remain pure noise until coarse structure has emerged ("waiting" for the signal), then join the flow for joint refinement. A new three-axis evaluation protocol is introduced to assess quality at native resolution.
AI.result: On ImageNet 512x512, WaiT achieves a pixel-space FID of 1.43 and is Pareto-optimal across all three axes, reducing sampling compute by up to 50%. The largest 2B model sets a new SOTA FID of 1.3 for pixel-space models on ImageNet 512. It outperforms latent-space models on texture fidelity, scales to high-resolution OpenImages, and achieves SOTA FVD of 0.84 on Kinetics-600 for video generation.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-ordered generation via wavelets is a principled and scalable approach to flow matching, enabling higher fidelity at native resolution, improved sampling efficiency, and seamless extension to video without algorithmic modifications.

title: DragonCrawl: A Generative, Intent-Based Framework for Scalable Mobile End-to-End Testing
summary: As mobile applications grow in complexity, traditional End-to-End (E2E) testing frameworks struggle with UI volatility, maintenance overhead, and cross-platform scalability. This paper presents DragonCrawl, an AI-driven mobile testing system for continuous regression testing that has evolved from embedding-based similarity matching to generative intent-based reasoning using large language models. Unlike prior LLM-based testing research focused on exploratory testing and crash detection, DragonCrawl validates specific user flows on every code change, blocking commits that break critical functionality. By leveraging GPT-4o's multimodal capabilities, DragonCrawl achieves 91.6% pass rate on iOS and 92.2% on Android across 1,013 automated tests running continuously in CI/CD pipelines. The system reduces test onboarding time from 96-120 hours to under 4 hours and has saved an estimated 27 developer years in test maintenance effort. We present the architectural evolution from V1 (semantic embedding matching) to V2 (generative intent-based reasoning), discuss implementation challenges including token explosion and memory constraints, and report operational experience from production deployment. The integration of multimodal vision for end-state detection and tool calling for backend state transitions enables comprehensive regression testing that bridges UI interactions with system state. Our results demonstrate that AI-driven testing can maintain stability while eliminating the brittleness of traditional automated tests, enabling continuous quality assurance at scale.

AI.tldr: DragonCrawl is an AI-driven mobile regression testing system that evolved from embedding-based similarity matching (V1) to generative intent-based reasoning using LLMs (V2). It validates specific user flows on every code change in CI/CD pipelines, achieving 91.6% pass rate on iOS and 92.2% on Android across 1,013 tests, reducing onboarding time from 96-120 hours to under 4 hours, and saving an estimated 27 developer years in maintenance effort.
AI.motivation: Traditional End-to-End (E2E) mobile testing frameworks suffer from UI volatility, high maintenance overhead, and poor cross-platform scalability as app complexity grows. Prior LLM-based testing research focused on exploratory testing and crash detection rather than continuous regression validation of critical user flows.
AI.method: The paper presents DragonCrawl's two-generation architecture evolution: V1 uses semantic embedding-based similarity matching for UI element identification, while V2 employs GPT-4o's generative intent-based reasoning with multimodal vision for end-state detection and tool calling for backend state transitions. The system integrates into CI/CD pipelines to block commits that break critical functionality.
AI.result: Achieved 91.6% pass rate on iOS and 92.2% on Android across 1,013 automated tests running continuously in CI/CD. Reduced test onboarding time from 96-120 hours to under 4 hours and saved an estimated 27 developer years in test maintenance effort.
AI.conclusion: AI-driven testing can maintain stability while eliminating the brittleness of traditional automated tests, enabling continuous quality assurance at scale. The integration of multimodal vision and tool calling bridges UI interactions with system state for comprehensive regression testing.

title: ThinkReset: Learnable Intermediate Interface Construction for Bounded-Context Long-Horizon Reasoning
summary: Long chain-of-thought reasoning improves performance on complex problems, but it also introduces redundancy accumulation, context overflow, and error anchoring. We argue that under bounded context windows, the core bottleneck is not trajectory compression or test-time control, but the absence of a reusable intermediate interface that can replace discarded history and support continued solving. We further identify a key failure mode of outcome-reward-driven long-chain reinforcement learning: when the model has not solved the task before the window is nearly exhausted, the final-answer reward encourages premature guessing rather than continued careful reasoning. We propose ThinkReset, a text-space instantiation of this view. ThinkReset explicitly constructs reusable intermediate interfaces through interface writeback and reset, and directly optimizes post-reset continuation success. Across multiple long-horizon reasoning benchmarks, this perspective consistently improves success rates under fixed context windows.

AI.tldr: ThinkReset addresses the bottleneck of long chain-of-thought reasoning under bounded context windows by introducing reusable intermediate interfaces that replace discarded history, and directly optimizing post-reset continuation success to prevent premature guessing in outcome-reward-driven RL.
AI.motivation: Long chain-of-thought reasoning suffers from redundancy accumulation, context overflow, and error anchoring under bounded context windows. The core bottleneck is not trajectory compression or test-time control, but the absence of a reusable intermediate interface to replace discarded history and support continued solving. Additionally, outcome-reward-driven long-chain RL encourages premature guessing when the window is nearly exhausted before solving.
AI.method: ThinkReset is a text-space approach that constructs reusable intermediate interfaces through interface writeback and reset, and directly optimizes post-reset continuation success via reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Across multiple long-horizon reasoning benchmarks, ThinkReset consistently improves success rates under fixed context windows.
AI.conclusion: The reusable intermediate interface perspective and ThinkReset's writeback-reset mechanism effectively address the bounded-context bottleneck in long-chain reasoning, outperforming prior approaches on long-horizon benchmarks.

title: DoubleHelix: Structured Cross-Modal Fusion for Audio-Visual Speech Recognition with LLMs
summary: Audio-visual speech recognition (AVSR) relies on effective fusion of audio and visual modalities, yet existing approaches treat cross-modal interaction as a single-step operation without structured iterative refinement. We present DoubleHelix, a multimodal fusion framework that reformulates fusion as an iterative cross-modal interaction process with adaptive degradation-aware enhancement. The framework comprises three components including ReverseParallelHelix for multi-turn structured interaction with learned alignment constraints, QualitySensor for learning degradation-aware gating signals, and HelixReplication for consistency-guided conditional feature enhancement. Experiments on LRS3 demonstrate that DoubleHelix achieves 0.68% WER on clean audio, outperforming previous best results by 5.6% relative improvement under matched backbone settings. Comprehensive ablation studies validate each component contribution, including targeted analysis of design choices such as asymmetric pathway weighting. The framework shows improved robustness under evaluated babble-noise conditions, achieving 11.6% WER at SNR -5dB.

AI.tldr: DoubleHelix is a multimodal fusion framework for audio-visual speech recognition that reformulates fusion as an iterative cross-modal interaction process with adaptive degradation-aware enhancement. It achieves 0.68% WER on LRS3 clean audio (5.6% relative improvement over previous best under matched backbones) and 11.6% WER at SNR -5dB babble-noise conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing AVSR approaches treat cross-modal interaction as a single-step operation without structured iterative refinement, limiting the quality of multimodal fusion for speech recognition.
AI.method: DoubleHelix comprises three components: (1) ReverseParallelHelix for multi-turn structured interaction with learned alignment constraints, (2) QualitySensor for learning degradation-aware gating signals, and (3) HelixReplication for consistency-guided conditional feature enhancement.
AI.result: On LRS3, DoubleHelix achieves 0.68% WER on clean audio, a 5.6% relative improvement over previous best results under matched backbone settings. It achieves 11.6% WER under babble-noise at SNR -5dB. Ablation studies validate each component's contribution, including asymmetric pathway weighting analysis.
AI.conclusion: The iterative cross-modal interaction paradigm with degradation-aware enhancement improves both clean and noisy AVSR performance, with comprehensive ablations confirming the effectiveness of each design component.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Deepfake Detection via Multi-View Structural Learning
summary: Security-critical biometric and forensic applications require accurate predictions and reliable confidence estimates, particularly under distribution shift. This challenge is especially acute for deepfake detection, where foundation-model-based detectors often exhibit overconfident predictions on out-of-distribution manipulations, which limits their suitability for operational deployment. We propose an uncertainty-aware deepfake detection framework that identifies manipulations through inconsistencies across complementary evidence sources. The framework integrates three streams: a visual stream based on an adapted CLIP encoder, a semantic stream that models consistency among facial attributes through differentiable constraints, and a structural stream that captures class-dependent dependency patterns between semantic and forensic features. To effectively combine these signals, we introduce Inter-Branch Disagreement Calibration (IBDC), a disagreement-aware uncertainty modeling mechanism that links predictive uncertainty to conflicts among evidence streams. Extensive cross-dataset experiments using FaceForensics++ as the training source demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art generalization across multiple out-of-distribution benchmarks while consistently improving calibration and selective prediction performance. These results show that combining complementary evidence with disagreement-aware uncertainty provides a robust foundation for trustworthy and well-calibrated deepfake detection under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: An uncertainty-aware deepfake detection framework that fuses visual (CLIP-based), semantic (facial attribute consistency), and structural (feature dependency) streams, using a novel Inter-Branch Disagreement Calibration (IBDC) mechanism to link predictive uncertainty to cross-stream evidence conflicts, achieving SOTA OOD generalization and improved calibration on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Foundation-model-based deepfake detectors are often overconfident on out-of-distribution manipulations, making them unreliable for security-critical deployment. Reliable confidence estimates under distribution shift are essential but lacking in current approaches.
AI.method: A three-stream framework: (1) a visual stream using an adapted CLIP encoder, (2) a semantic stream modeling facial attribute consistency via differentiable constraints, and (3) a structural stream capturing class-dependent dependency patterns between semantic and forensic features. These are combined via Inter-Branch Disagreement Calibration (IBDC), a disagreement-aware uncertainty modeling mechanism that links predictive uncertainty to conflicts among evidence branches.
AI.result: Cross-dataset experiments trained on FaceForensics++ achieve state-of-the-art generalization across multiple OOD benchmarks, with consistently improved calibration and selective prediction performance compared to existing detectors.
AI.conclusion: Combining complementary evidence sources with disagreement-aware uncertainty modeling provides a robust foundation for trustworthy and well-calibrated deepfake detection under distribution shift.

title: Repository-Aware Metamorphic Relation Generation for Augmented Reality Applications using Large Language Models
summary: Metamorphic Testing (MT) provides a promising approach for testing software without defined test oracles by specifying expected relations between inputs and outputs, instead of relying on exact outputs. For example, testing Augmented Reality (AR) applications is challenging due to dynamic interactions between virtual content, physical environments, and code, which make traditional test oracles difficult to define. However, formulating metamorphic relations (MRs) is time-consuming and burdensome. We introduce a context-aware pipeline that generates and refines MRs using repository-level context and reasoning orchestration, evaluated on a dataset of 142 mobile AR system repositories. Across three context configurations generating 14,916 candidate MRs, hierarchical context yielded the broadest coverage (7,004 MRs across 142 repositories and 5,167 class--method pairs) and lower redundancy. An agentic deliberation process then reconciled conflicting candidates---observed in 79.0% of cases---reducing duplication and selecting context-aware relations in 88.2% of outcomes. A manual oracle study shows refined relations (n = 141) are both logically valid and sufficiently concrete to be directly translated into test assertions, and a preliminary case study reveals converting generated MRs (n = 5) into executable tests can detect non-equivalent mutations in real-world code. Overall, our results show that combining repository-aware MR generation with reasoning-based refinement enables scalable construction of reliable, domain-relevant test oracles.

AI.tldr: A context-aware pipeline that generates and refines Metamorphic Relations (MRs) for testing Augmented Reality applications using repository-level context and reasoning orchestration, evaluated on 142 mobile AR repositories with 14,916 candidate MRs, demonstrating scalable construction of reliable test oracles.
AI.motivation: Metamorphic Testing addresses the challenge of testing software without defined oracles by specifying expected input-output relations, but formulating Metamorphic Relations (MRs) is time-consuming and burdensome. AR applications are especially difficult to test due to complex interactions between virtual content, physical environments, and code, motivating the need for automated MR generation.
AI.method: The paper introduces a context-aware pipeline that generates and refines MRs using repository-level context and reasoning orchestration. The pipeline was evaluated across three context configurations on 142 mobile AR system repositories, generating 14,916 candidate MRs. An agentic deliberation process reconciles conflicting candidates, reducing duplication and selecting context-aware relations.
AI.result: Hierarchical context yielded the broadest coverage (7,004 MRs across 142 repositories and 5,167 class-method pairs) with lower redundancy. Agentic deliberation reconciled conflicts in 79.0% of cases and selected context-aware relations in 88.2% of outcomes. A manual oracle study (n=141) showed refined relations are logically valid and translateable into test assertions. A preliminary case study (n=5) showed generated MRs can detect non-equivalent mutations in real-world code.
AI.conclusion: Combining repository-aware MR generation with reasoning-based refinement enables scalable construction of reliable, domain-relevant test oracles for AR applications, addressing the oracle problem in dynamic, interactive software systems.

title: TAPR: Enhancing LLM Performance with a Task-Aware Prompt Rewriter
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often require carefully crafted prompts to unlock their full potential, which can be a barrier for non-expert users. This work addresses the challenge by introducing a Task-Aware Prompt Rewriter (TAPR), a model that reformulates user prompts into task-optimized prompts with the explicit goal of improving downstream LLM performance. We train TAPR using reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), where rewards are derived from LLM-as-judge evaluations of both the reformulated prompt and the corresponding task output. Experimental results on diverse tasks, such as question answering, summarization, and arithmetic reasoning, show that our method yields consistent gains over base models in prompt rewriting ability. Fine-tuning Phi-4-mini-instruct (as the base model for TAPR) produces prompts that contain clearer and more instructive language, leading to higher accuracy on established benchmarks such as Natural Questions and GSM8K. Our code is available at: https://github.com/OliverSavolainen/task-specific-prompt-rewriter

AI.tldr: TAPR is a Task-Aware Prompt Rewriter trained with GRPO that reformulates user prompts into task-optimized prompts to improve downstream LLM performance, yielding consistent gains across QA, summarization, and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLMs often require carefully crafted prompts to perform well, which creates a barrier for non-expert users who may not know how to write effective prompts. This work aims to automate prompt optimization so that users can provide simple prompts and still get strong performance.
AI.method: TAPR is trained using reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rewards are derived from LLM-as-judge evaluations of both the reformulated prompt and the corresponding task output. The base model is Phi-4-mini-instruct.
AI.result: TAPR yields consistent gains over base models in prompt rewriting ability across diverse tasks including QA, summarization, and arithmetic reasoning. It achieves higher accuracy on established benchmarks such as Natural Questions and GSM8K, producing clearer and more instructive prompts.
AI.conclusion: Task-aware prompt rewriting via reinforcement learning is an effective approach to automatically improve prompt quality and downstream LLM performance, making LLMs more accessible to non-expert users.

title: ParaASR: Multi-Token Prediction for Fast and Long-Context LLM-Based Speech Recognition
summary: Audio-encoder-LLM-decoder architectures have become the dominant paradigm for modern automatic speech recognition (ASR), improving transcription quality through large-scale language modeling. However, the cost of autoregressive decoding scales with decoder size, creating a fundamental trade-off between recognition quality and serving latency. We argue this trade-off is not inherent: unlike open-ended text generation, ASR outputs are strongly anchored to the input speech signal, providing a natural inductive bias toward high-parallelism decoding. Building on this, we introduce ParaASR, an ASR system that leverages Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) to let a 4B LLM decoder emit multiple tokens per forward step. Starting from a publicly available audio-language foundation, the model first establishes a robust autoregressive recognizer and then aligns five future-token branches through a staged optimization recipe. At inference, it proposes a six-token continuation per step and admits only the verified prefix into the transcript, preserving the safety of standard autoregressive decoding. The average accepted length reaches 5.0 out of 6 proposed tokens, confirming that the deterministic structure of speech makes ASR an especially natural setting for multi-token decoding. ParaASR further retains a native 32K-context window and transcribes up to 30 minutes of audio in a single pass. Across diverse benchmarks, it attains average error rates of 2.97%, 3.68%, and 3.70% on Chinese, English, and long-form evaluations, respectively, while reaching a real-time factor (RTF) as low as 0.0053. These results show that decoder scaling, low-latency inference, and long-context transcription need not be competing goals when future-token proposals are anchored by the acoustic signal and guarded by autoregressive verification.

AI.tldr: ParaASR is an ASR system with a 4B LLM decoder that uses Multi-Token Prediction to emit six tokens per forward step (with an average of 5.0 accepted), achieving error rates of 2.97% (Chinese), 3.68% (English), and 3.70% (long-form) with an RTF as low as 0.0053, while preserving a native 32K-context window for up to 30 minutes of audio in a single pass.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the premise that autoregressive decoding cost necessarily scales with decoder size in ASR. Since ASR outputs are strongly anchored to the input speech signal (unlike open-ended text generation), there is a natural inductive bias for high-parallelism decoding. The authors aim to break the trade-off between recognition quality and serving latency that plagues large decoder-based ASR systems.
AI.method: ParaASR starts from a publicly available audio-language foundation model and follows a staged optimization recipe: (1) first establishes a robust autoregressive recognizer, then (2) aligns five future-token branches for Multi-Token Prediction. At inference, the model proposes a six-token continuation per step and admits only the verified prefix into the transcript, preserving the safety of standard autoregressive decoding through verification.
AI.result: The average accepted length reaches 5.0 out of 6 proposed tokens. ParaASR attains average error rates of 2.97%, 3.68%, and 3.70% on Chinese, English, and long-form evaluations, respectively, while reaching a real-time factor as low as 0.0053. It also retains a native 32K-context window and can transcribe up to 30 minutes of audio in a single pass.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that decoder scaling, low-latency inference, and long-context transcription need not be competing goals in ASR when future-token proposals are anchored by the acoustic signal and guarded by autoregressive verification, confirming that speech's deterministic structure makes ASR an especially natural fit for multi-token decoding.

title: Do Medical Foundation Models Generalize on the African Brain?
comment: Submitted to the AFRICAI workshop (Held in conjunction with MICCAI 2026, Strasbourg, France)
summary: Medical foundation models (FMs) are increasingly used for brain MRI analysis. However, their evaluation remains dominated by high-resource datasets, leaving generalization to African cohorts underexplored. We assess whether FMs generalize equally to African and non-African brain MRI data across two tasks: dementia classification using a Nigerian dataset and brain tumor segmentation using BraTS-Africa. We evaluate two generalist FMs (BrainIAC, 3DINO) and two segmentation-specific FMs (MedSAM2, Medical-SAM2) against a from-scratch baseline. For classification, FMs provide limited gains (highest ROC-AUC of 0.86 with BrainIAC), whereas for segmentation they consistently improve performance, reaching up to 0.86 Dice with MedSAM2. Performance differences between African and non-African cohorts are inconsistent and appear more related to dataset size than data origin. These results suggest that FMs do not exhibit an inherent bias against African cohorts, and highlight the limited availability and diversity of African neuroimaging datasets as the main barrier to robust evaluation and deployment.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates generalist and segmentation-specific medical foundation models on African brain MRI data (Nigerian dementia dataset and BraTS-Africa tumor segmentation), finding that FMs show limited gains for classification (best ROC-AUC 0.86) but consistent improvements for segmentation (up to 0.86 Dice), with performance differences attributable to dataset size rather than African data origin, indicating no inherent bias against African cohorts.
AI.motivation: Medical foundation models are increasingly used for brain MRI analysis, but their evaluation is dominated by high-resource datasets, leaving generalization to African cohorts largely unexplored. The authors aim to assess whether FMs generalize equally well to African versus non-African brain MRI data.
AI.method: The study evaluates two generalist FMs (BrainIAC, 3DINO) and two segmentation-specific FMs (MedSAM2, Medical-SAM2) against a from-scratch baseline, across two tasks: dementia classification using a Nigerian dataset and brain tumor segmentation using BraTS-Africa.
AI.result: For classification, FMs provide limited gains (highest ROC-AUC of 0.86 with BrainIAC). For segmentation, FMs consistently improve performance, reaching up to 0.86 Dice with MedSAM2. Performance differences between African and non-African cohorts are inconsistent and appear more related to dataset size than data origin.
AI.conclusion: Foundation models do not exhibit an inherent bias against African cohorts. The main barrier to robust evaluation and deployment in African settings is the limited availability and diversity of African neuroimaging datasets, rather than model-level bias.

title: Model-Driven Data Contracts for Digital Twin Services
summary: Digital Twins (DT) integrate data from multiple sources. Models consume data and enable DT services such as simulations, what-if analyses, and ML-driven predictions. To ensure proper DT operation, data-driven services require data to exhibit traits such as reliability and high quality (including, e.g., accuracy, completeness, and timeliness). Yet, there is no systematic way to specify data requirements at the model level, and subsequently enact those specifications at runtime. To address this shortcoming, we propose an approach to contract-based quality management in DTs. We formally define a theory of such contracts, situate them architectually within DTs, and propose a domain-specific language to specify contracts. Our approach enables continuous data quality monitoring, thereby improving the reliability and quality of DT services.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a contract-based approach for managing data quality in Digital Twins, including a formal theory, architectural placement, and a domain-specific language to specify and enact data quality contracts at runtime.
AI.motivation: Digital Twins rely on data-driven services (simulations, what-if analyses, ML predictions) that require reliable, high-quality data. However, there is no systematic way to specify data requirements at the model level and enforce them at runtime, leading to potential degradation of DT services.
AI.method: The authors formally define a theory of data quality contracts, situate these contracts architecturally within the Digital Twin framework, and propose a domain-specific language (DSL) for specifying contracts. This enables continuous monitoring and enactment of data quality requirements at runtime.
AI.result: The approach enables continuous data quality monitoring in Digital Twins, thereby improving the reliability and quality of DT services.
AI.conclusion: Contract-based quality management provides a systematic mechanism to specify data requirements at the model level and enforce them at runtime, ultimately enhancing the reliability and quality of Digital Twin services.

title: Empowering Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Hybrid Tokenization and Serial-Parallel Decoding
summary: Cross-domain sequential recommendation (CDSR) aims to model users' dynamic interest transitions and sequential patterns across multiple domains. Recently, generative recommendation (GR) has emerged. It first learns semantic identifiers (SIDs) from item semantics and formulates recommendation as autoregressive generation. However, existing methods face two critical issues: (1) they ignore collaborative correlations across domains during tokenization, and (2) they adopt inefficient decoding strategies, such as beam search, during generation, which hinders real-time deployment. To address these limitations, we propose GenCDSR, an effective and efficient generative framework for CDSR. Specifically, we design a cross-domain hybrid tokenization mechanism with a multi-tower architecture to jointly capture cross-domain commonalities and domain-specific distinctions through hierarchical shared-specific and fine-grained codebooks. Furthermore, we develop a cross-domain serial-parallel decoding strategy that leverages the hierarchical SID structure to partially parallelize generation, significantly reducing inference latency while preserving generation consistency. Experiments on three public datasets show that GenCDSR achieves an average accuracy improvement of 1.5 percent and an average inference latency reduction of 85.1 percent compared with state-of-the-art baselines. The implementation code and datasets are available online: https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/RecSys2026_GenCDSR.

AI.tldr: GenCDSR is a generative framework for cross-domain sequential recommendation that uses a cross-domain hybrid tokenization mechanism with multi-tower architecture and a cross-domain serial-parallel decoding strategy, achieving 1.5% accuracy improvement and 85.1% inference latency reduction over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing CDSR methods based on generative recommendation face two critical issues: (1) they ignore collaborative correlations across domains during tokenization, and (2) they adopt inefficient decoding strategies like beam search that hinder real-time deployment.
AI.method: GenCDSR introduces (1) a cross-domain hybrid tokenization mechanism with a multi-tower architecture that jointly captures cross-domain commonalities and domain-specific distinctions through hierarchical shared-specific and fine-grained codebooks, and (2) a cross-domain serial-parallel decoding strategy that leverages the hierarchical SID structure to partially parallelize generation, reducing inference latency while preserving generation consistency.
AI.result: Experiments on three public datasets show GenCDSR achieves an average accuracy improvement of 1.5% and an average inference latency reduction of 85.1% compared with state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: GenCDSR effectively and efficiently addresses collaborative correlations and decoding inefficiency in generative CDSR, making it suitable for real-time deployment.

title: Can Synthetic Data Overcome the Generalization Limits of AI-Based Flower and Pod Detection Across Cowpea Breeding Genotypes and Environments?
summary: High-throughput phenotyping requires AI-enabled computer vision models that generalize across genotypes, locations, and growing seasons, yet such models often lose accuracy under new conditions. Annotating real imagery for every genotype-by-environment (G x E) combination a breeding program encounters is prohibitively expensive. We quantify how G x E shifts affect AI-based detection of cowpea flowers and pods across two California locations and two growing seasons. Flower detection mAP@50 fell from 76.3% to as low as 50.6% under unseen shifts, and pod detection was more sensitive. Feature-space and image-quality diagnostics confirmed these losses track measurable distributional shifts. Because closing this gap with real data alone is not practical, we test whether synthetic imagery, rendered from a procedural 3D cowpea model, can substitute for that annotation burden.
