Synthetic supervision alone improved over pretraining but remained limited by a domain gap driven by camera image formation, not scene content. A domain-gap-aware camera-realism augmentation strategy, optimized against measured real-image statistics via Wasserstein distance, narrowed this gap, and a linear HDR representation converted a smaller measured gap into a larger detection gain than an 8-bit representation. Optimized HDR synthetic data combined with as few as five real images matched or exceeded the real-data baseline for spatial generalization, and pod detection benefited most at the lowest shot counts, with more modest gains under temporal shift. These results show that synthetic data can overcome the generalization limits of AI-based flower and pod detection, but only when the domain gap is measured and optimized rather than assumed away.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies how genotype-by-environment (G x E) shifts degrade AI-based detection of cowpea flowers and pods (mAP@50 dropping from 76.3% to 50.6%), and demonstrates that procedurally-rendered 3D synthetic imagery, combined with a domain-gap-aware camera-realism augmentation strategy optimized via Wasserstein distance and linear HDR representation, can match or exceed real-data baselines for spatial generalization when paired with as few as five real images.
AI.motivation: High-throughput phenotyping requires computer vision models that generalize across genotypes, locations, and seasons, but such models lose accuracy under new conditions. Annotating real imagery for every genotype-by-environment combination is prohibitively expensive, so there is a need to find alternatives to closing the domain gap with real data alone.
AI.method: The authors (1) quantify G x E shifts on cowpea flower and pod detection across two California locations and two seasons using feature-space and image-quality diagnostics; (2) build a procedural 3D cowpea model to render synthetic imagery; (3) apply a domain-gap-aware camera-realism augmentation strategy optimized against real-image statistics using Wasserstein distance; (4) compare linear HDR versus 8-bit image representations; and (5) evaluate synthetic data combined with few (as few as five) real images.
AI.result: Flower detection mAP@50 fell from 76.3% to as low as 50.6% under unseen shifts, with pod detection more sensitive. Synthetic supervision alone improved over pretraining but was limited by a camera-related domain gap rather than scene content. HDR representation converted a smaller measured gap into a larger detection gain than 8-bit. Optimized HDR synthetic data with as few as five real images matched or exceeded the real-data baseline for spatial generalization, with pod detection benefiting most at low shot counts and more modest gains under temporal shift.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic data can overcome the generalization limits of AI-based flower and pod detection, but only when the domain gap is measured and optimized rather than assumed away.

title: Preventing Premature Commitment in Coding Agents with an Evidence-Conditioned Execution Layer
summary: LLM-based coding agents often edit source code or submit patches before examining enough repository evidence to justify the change, a failure pattern we call premature commitment. We present ECLoop, an execution layer that interposes between the agent and the repository to enforce evidence-conditioned execution. For each task, ECLoop uses the issue description and repository structure to compile a set of conditions specifying what the agent should observe before each type of code modification or patch submission. During execution, ECLoop tracks which conditions the agent's runtime trajectory has satisfied and postpones any proposed action whose required conditions remain unmet. Evaluated on all 500 instances of SWE-bench Verified with two language models and two agent scaffolds, ECLoop raises Pass@1 by 4.8-11.8 percentage points without model retraining or scaffold changes. Ablation experiments show that each of ECLoop's three operations contributes distinct value and that structured evidence conditions outperform an equivalent natural-language summary. These gains come at no additional inference cost: by redirecting the agent before it pursues unsupported actions, ECLoop lowers average token consumption by up to 12.1%.

AI.tldr: ECLoop is an execution layer for LLM-based coding agents that enforces evidence-conditioned execution, preventing premature code edits or patch submissions before sufficient repository evidence is gathered. It raises Pass@1 by 4.8-11.8 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified while reducing token consumption by up to 12.1%.
AI.motivation: LLM-based coding agents frequently edit source code or submit patches before examining enough repository evidence to justify the change, a failure pattern called "premature commitment" that leads to incorrect or unsupported actions.
AI.method: ECLoop interposes an execution layer between the agent and the repository. It compiles a set of evidence conditions from the issue description and repository structure, specifying what the agent should observe before each type of code modification or patch submission. During execution, ECLoop tracks which conditions the agent's runtime trajectory has satisfied and postpones any proposed action whose required conditions remain unmet.
AI.result: On all 500 instances of SWE-bench Verified with two LLMs and two agent scaffolds, ECLoop raises Pass@1 by 4.8-11.8 percentage points. Ablations show all three operations contribute distinct value, and structured evidence conditions outperform natural-language summaries. ECLoop lowers average token consumption by up to 12.1% with no additional inference cost.
AI.conclusion: ECLoop effectively mitigates premature commitment in coding agents without model retraining or scaffold changes, improving both correctness and efficiency, demonstrating that enforcing evidence-before-action policies at the execution layer is a viable and low-cost intervention.

title: An Ontology-Guided, Deduplication-Aware Extraction Layer for Knowledge Graph Construction from Heterogeneous Documents
summary: Large language models extract entities and relationships from unstructured documents fluently but inconsistently: type vocabularies fracture across documents, the same person surfaces under several name variants, relationships duplicate, and distinct individuals who share a name risk silent conflation. This paper presents the design, implementation, and empirical refinement of a production extraction layer that converts a live document stream into a validated knowledge graph aligned to a formal ontology. The system consumes document metadata from Kafka, routes PDF, spreadsheet, Office, and image content through handlers built for each format, and extracts entities and relationships in two passes using a locally hosted Qwen3.5-9B model tuned on the ontology. Its distinguishing component is ontology-guided extraction: the relevant slice of a curated ontology is retrieved live from a graph database by embedding similarity and injected into the extraction prompt, reducing catalog overhead by about 94 percent relative to static domain slices. Extracted results then pass through a refinement pipeline of five stages: deterministic cleaning, merging across chunks, a second pass for relationships, six deduplication algorithms that require no model inference, and an embedding resolution subsystem whose conflict guard no similarity score can override. Evaluation on intelligence corpora improved search recall from roughly 70 to 95 percent with no false merges, and corrected seven classes of silent quality defect, ranging from a bug that truncated source text by a single character to the systematic duplication of entities that carried title prefixes.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the design, implementation, and empirical refinement of a production knowledge-graph extraction layer that converts a live document stream into an ontology-aligned knowledge graph. It uses ontology-guided extraction via live embedding-based retrieval from a graph database, a two-pass LLM extraction pipeline with locally hosted Qwen3.5-9B, and a five-stage refinement pipeline with six deterministic deduplication algorithms plus an embedding resolution subsystem. Evaluation shows search recall improved from ~70% to 95% with no false merges and corrected seven classes of silent quality defects.
AI.motivation: Large language models extract entities and relationships from unstructured documents fluently but inconsistently—type vocabularies fracture across documents, the same person surfaces under multiple name variants, relationships duplicate, and distinct individuals sharing a name risk silent conflation. These quality defects undermine the reliability of extracted knowledge graphs.
AI.method: The system consumes document metadata from Kafka, routes content through format-specific handlers (PDF, spreadsheet, Office, image), and performs two-pass extraction using a locally hosted Qwen3.5-9B model tuned on the ontology. The key innovation is ontology-guided extraction: the relevant ontology slice is retrieved live from a graph database via embedding similarity and injected into the extraction prompt, reducing catalog overhead by ~94% versus static domain slices. Extracted results then pass through a five-stage refinement pipeline: deterministic cleaning, cross-chunk merging, a second pass for relationships, six model-free deduplication algorithms, and an embedding resolution subsystem with a conflict guard that no similarity score can override.
AI.result: Evaluation on intelligence corpora improved search recall from roughly 70% to 95% with no false merges. The system also corrected seven classes of silent quality defects, including a bug truncating source text by a single character and systematic duplication of entities carrying title prefixes.
AI.conclusion: Ontology-guided extraction combined with a layered deterministic and embedding-based refinement pipeline yields production-grade knowledge graph construction quality, preserving recall gains while eliminating silent conflations and other induced defects from LLM extraction.

title: FocusGS: Spatial Delta Layers for Local Repair and Deterministic Editing of Trained 3D Gaussian Assets
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Ancillary demonstration video included
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is evolving from one-time reconstruction into deliverable, inspectable, and maintainable visual assets. Existing workflows focus on global reconstruction, training-time density control, or open-ended generative editing, leaving trained assets without precise local maintenance. We propose FocusGS, which unifies local repair and deterministic editing as composite spatial deltas. Repair is the purely additive special case: its base-manipulation term is empty, and it adds only local Gaussian bases; deterministic editing uses erase-insert factorization (EIF) to combine old-carrier erasure with new-content insertion. FocusGS addresses spatial gradient starvation: local repair raises target-region PSNR by 7.91 dB over 93 evaluation views. Across all 83 deterministic editing trials, the target ROI improves, with a trial-averaged mean edited ROI PSNR of 21.97 dB and a mean gain of +11.05 dB; across five public editing cases, FocusGS-EIF reaches 33.17 dB Target-mask PSNR and 0.994 Target-delta Correlation, while both text-driven baselines fail to complete the prescribed updates. FocusGS provides a lightweight, verifiable 3DGS maintenance operator.

AI.tldr: FocusGS unifies local repair and deterministic editing for 3D Gaussian Splatting assets as composite spatial deltas, achieving significant PSNR improvements (repair: +7.91 dB over 93 views; editing: 21.97 dB mean ROI PSNR, +11.05 dB mean gain) and outperforming text-driven baselines on public editing cases.
AI.motivation: 3DGS is evolving from one-time reconstruction into deliverable, maintainable visual assets, but existing workflows only support global reconstruction, training-time density control, or open-ended generative editing—leaving trained assets without precise local maintenance capabilities.
AI.method: FocusGS unifies local repair and deterministic editing as composite spatial deltas. Repair is a purely additive special case (empty base-manipulation term, only local Gaussian bases added). Deterministic editing uses erase-insert factorization (EIF) combining old-carrier erasure with new-content insertion. The method addresses spatial gradient starvation.
AI.result: Local repair raises target-region PSNR by 7.91 dB over 93 evaluation views. Across 83 deterministic editing trials, the target ROI improves with 21.97 dB mean edited ROI PSNR and +11.05 dB mean gain. On five public editing cases, FocusGS-EIF reaches 33.17 dB Target-mask PSNR and 0.994 Target-delta Correlation, while text-driven baselines fail to complete prescribed updates.
AI.conclusion: FocusGS provides a lightweight, verifiable 3DGS maintenance operator, enabling precise local repair and deterministic editing of trained 3D Gaussian Splatting assets.

title: Building a Process-Modeling Tool using Agentic AI: An Experience Report on PM4Py-UCM
comment: 17 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables, submitted to a conference
summary: Enterprise-modeling (EM) tools are often complex and hard to extend. Yet, users may want to explore new EM features and capabilities that currently do not exist. AI coding agents can help here by enabling the development of new capabilities and entire tools, but whether we can trust a modeling-language tool an LLM largely wrote remains a question. This paper reports on the AI-assisted construction of PM4Py-UCM, an open-source tool that mines Use Case Map (UCM) models from event logs. PM4Py-UCM's capabilities include some expected from process mining tools (e.g., performance heat-maps and dashboards) and distinctive ones (e.g., mined executable scenarios/variants, and model decomposition). We mined the development record itself, composed of 18 agent sessions (374 human turns and 10,328 tool actions over 65 hours), 151 commits, 20 releases, and a test suite grown from 108 to 691 test functions, in order to characterize, in a single in-depth case, how the tool was built with an agent (Claude Code), complemented by an independent static assessment of the resulting code (coverage, complexity, maintainability, security, architecture). We contribute a reproducible, privacy-preserving toolkit and taxonomy that classify human turns and flag cross-cutting consistency work, agent corrections, and retracted requests. Up to version 0.7.4, fixes outnumber features 2.3:1, with ~18% of turns for correcting agent errors. Feature waves dragged a measurable tail of documentation/test/notebook consistency work, and tests grew lockstep with features. We finally present lessons learned, centered on making model transformations mechanically checkable, and the oracle-based validation strategy that closed the "the agent said it works" gap, for responsibly engineering EM tooling with AI.

AI.tldr: This paper reports on the AI-assisted construction of PM4Py-UCM, an open-source process-mining tool that mines Use Case Map (UCM) models from event logs, built with the Claude Code agent over 18 sessions. The paper characterizes the development process through mining the development record (374 human turns, 10,328 tool actions, 151 commits, 20 releases, test suite growing from 108 to 691 functions) and provides a reproducible, privacy-preserving toolkit/taxonomy to classify human turns, flag consistency work, agent corrections, and retracted requests. Key findings include a 2.3:1 fix-to-feature ratio up to v0.7.4, ~18% of turns correcting agent errors, feature waves dragging documentation/test/notebook consistency work, and lessons on mechanically checkable model transformations and an oracle-based validation strategy to close the "the agent said it works" gap.
AI.motivation: Enterprise-modeling tools are complex and hard to extend, yet users want new capabilities that don't currently exist. While AI coding agents can potentially enable development of new EM capabilities and entire tools, there is uncertainty about whether a modeling-language tool largely written by an LLM can be trusted, motivating this in-depth case study.
AI.method: The authors mined the complete development record of PM4Py-UCM, comprising 18 agent sessions (374 human turns, 10,328 tool actions over 65 hours), 151 commits, 20 releases, and a test suite grown from 108 to 691 test functions. They built a reproducible, privacy-preserving toolkit and taxonomy to classify human turns and flag cross-cutting consistency work, agent corrections, and retracted requests. This was complemented by an independent static assessment of the resulting code covering coverage, complexity, maintainability, security, and architecture.
AI.result: Up to version 0.7.4, fixes outnumber features at a 2.3:1 ratio, with ~18% of human turns used for correcting agent errors. Feature waves consistently dragged a measurable tail of documentation/test/notebook consistency work, and tests grew in lockstep with features. PM4Py-UCM delivers expected process-mining capabilities (performance heat-maps, dashboards) plus distinctive ones (mined executable scenarios/variants, model decomposition).
AI.conclusion: The authors present lessons learned for responsibly engineering EM tooling with AI, centered on making model transformations mechanically checkable and employing an oracle-based validation strategy that closes the "the agent said it works" gap, enabling trustworthy AI-assisted development of modeling-language tools.

title: How Hard Does It Think? Analyzing Step-Aware Reasoning Energy in LLM Chain-of-Thought Trajectories
summary: Understanding how computational effort is allocated across individual chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning steps remains an open challenge: existing interpretability methods rely on output-level signals or collapse processing depth into a single trajectory-level scalar, leaving step-wise effort opaque. We propose Step-Aware Reasoning Energy (SARE), a geometric framework that quantifies effort at the granularity of individual CoT steps via Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) between Gram matrices of token hidden states across adjacent transformer layers, capturing inter-token relational structure without requiring eigenvector alignment or cluster correspondence. SARE further contextualizes this energy within reasoning's semantic progression by modeling CoT trajectories as transitions among latent semantic states. Across six reasoning benchmarks and three open-weight LLMs, we find that reasoning energy is highly non-uniform across step types, exhibiting phase-like transitions invisible to trajectory-level metrics; incorrect trajectories show systematically lower energy at critical reasoning junctions; and SARE-based features match or outperform output-based confidence baselines in most settings, indicating that internal geometric dynamics encode predictive information beyond surface-level signals.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SARE (Step-Aware Reasoning Energy), a geometric framework that quantifies computational effort at individual chain-of-thought reasoning steps using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) between Gram matrices of token hidden states across adjacent transformer layers, revealing non-uniform, phase-like effort distribution across step types, lower energy at critical junctions in incorrect trajectories, and predictive features that match or outperform output-based confidence baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing interpretability methods for chain-of-thought reasoning either rely on output-level signals or collapse processing depth into a single trajectory-level scalar, making step-wise computational effort opaque and unmeasurable.
AI.method: SARE quantifies per-step reasoning effort via Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) between Gram matrices of token hidden states across adjacent transformer layers, capturing inter-token relational structure without needing eigenvector alignment or cluster correspondence. The framework additionally contextualizes this energy within reasoning's semantic progression by modeling CoT trajectories as transitions among latent semantic states.
AI.result: Across six reasoning benchmarks and three open-weight LLMs, reasoning energy is highly non-uniform across step types with phase-like transitions invisible to trajectory-level metrics; incorrect trajectories show systematically lower energy at critical reasoning junctions; and SARE-based features match or outperform output-based confidence baselines in most settings.
AI.conclusion: Internal geometric dynamics (per-step reasoning energy) encode predictive information beyond surface-level output signals, offering a finer-grained lens for interpreting and predicting the reliability of chain-of-thought reasoning.

title: A Unified Benchmark of Deep Learning Models for Multi-task 3D Brain Tumor Segmentation from Magnetic Resonance Imaging
summary: Automatic brain tumor segmentation from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has become a fundamental task in computer-assisted diagnosis, treatment planning, and disease monitoring. Although numerous deep learning architectures have recently been proposed, objective comparisons remain challenging because published studies often employ different datasets, preprocessing strategies, training protocols, and evaluation procedures. This work presents a unified experimental benchmark for comparing representative convolutional neural networks (CNNs), Transformer-based models, and recent State Space Model (SSM) architectures under homogeneous experimental conditions. Five state-of-the-art three-dimensional segmentation models, including 3D U-Net, SegResNet, Swin UNETR, SegMamba, and SegMambaV2, are evaluated on two brain tumor segmentation datasets representing distinct clinical scenarios: intracranial meningioma segmentation (BraTS 2023) and post-treatment glioma segmentation (BraTS 2024). All architectures are trained using identical preprocessing, data augmentation, optimization strategies, and evaluation protocols to ensure a fair comparison. Performance is assessed using segmentation accuracy metrics together with computational cost indicators, including inference time and the size of each model. The results provide practical insights into the trade-offs between segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency, highlighting the suitability of different architectural paradigms for challenging three-dimensional brain tumor segmentation tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified experimental benchmark that fairly compares five state-of-the-art 3D brain tumor segmentation models—3D U-Net, SegResNet, Swin UNETR, SegMamba, and SegMambaV2—under identical preprocessing, training, and evaluation conditions across two clinical scenarios (BraTS 2023 meningioma and BraTS 2024 post-treatment glioma), assessing both segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: Objective comparisons of deep learning architectures for brain tumor segmentation are difficult because published studies use heterogeneous datasets, preprocessing pipelines, training protocols, and evaluation criteria, making it hard to determine which architectural paradigm (CNN, Transformer, or SSM) truly performs best.
AI.method: Five representative 3D segmentation models spanning three architectural families (CNNs: 3D U-Net, SegResNet; Transformers: Swin UNETR; SSMs: SegMamba, SegMambaV2) are trained with identical preprocessing, data augmentation, optimization strategies, and evaluation protocols. Models are evaluated on two datasets: intracranial meningioma (BraTS 2023) and post-treatment glioma (BraTS 2024). Performance is measured using segmentation accuracy metrics alongside computational cost indicators such as inference time and model size.
AI.result: The benchmark yields practical insights into the trade-offs between segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency across different architectural paradigms, highlighting which model families are best suited for challenging 3D brain tumor segmentation tasks in distinct clinical scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The unified benchmark provides reliable, homogeneous comparisons across CNN, Transformer, and SSM architectures for 3D brain tumor segmentation, revealing accuracy-efficiency trade-offs and offering guidance on selecting appropriate architectural paradigms for different clinical settings.

title: From C to Idiomatic Rust: A Ship-of-Theseus Agentic Translation
summary:
C underpins operating systems, embedded platforms, and network infrastructure because its abstractions map directly to machine behaviour. Its explicit memory model, predictable data representations, and minimal runtime allow compilers to generate fast, deterministic code. These properties also leave correctness and memory safety entirely to the programmer, making undefined behaviour, pointer misuse, and lifetime errors persistent sources of defects and security vulnerabilities in long-lived C codebases. Rust eliminates most of failure modes through a static ownership and borrowing model that enforces memory safety and aliasing constraints at compile time. However, mature C systems cannot be translated directly: implicit layout assumptions, aliasing patterns, and undefined behaviour must be reconstructed before safe Rust can be produced.
  This paper presents a migration methodology that first generates a semantics-preserving, non-idiomatic Rust baseline and then incrementally rewrites it into idiomatic Rust using agentic AI, validating each step through compilation and behavioural testing. Applied to iodine (12.5k SLOC), the approach demonstrates that reliable C-to-Rust migration is a structured transformation workflow rather than a single translation step.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a structured C-to-Rust migration methodology that first generates a semantics-preserving, non-idiomatic Rust baseline, then incrementally refactors it into idiomatic Rust using agentic AI, with each step validated via compilation and behavioral testing. Applied to iodine (12.5k SLOC), it demonstrates that reliable migration is a structured transformation workflow rather than a single translation step.
AI.motivation: C underpins critical infrastructure but leaves memory safety and correctness to the programmer, leading to persistent defects and security vulnerabilities. Rust's ownership and borrowing model eliminates most failure modes at compile time; however, mature C systems cannot be directly translated because implicit layout assumptions, aliasing patterns, and undefined behavior must be reconstructed first.
AI.method: The methodology involves two phases: (1) generating a semantics-preserving, non-idiomatic Rust baseline from the C codebase, and (2) incrementally rewriting the baseline into idiomatic Rust using agentic AI, validating each transformation step through compilation and behavioral testing.
AI.result: Applied to iodine (12.5k SLOC), the approach successfully demonstrated that reliable C-to-Rust migration is achievable as a structured transformation workflow rather than a single translation step.
AI.conclusion: C-to-Rust migration is best treated as a structured, multi-step transformation workflow with validation at each stage, rather than expecting a single-pass translation to produce idiomatic and safe Rust code from mature C codebases.

title: Reasoning in Real World Clinical Care: Why Large Language Models Are Not Yet Safe for Autonomous Clinical Decision Support
summary: LLM now pass medical licensing examinations and, in curated cases, can rival physicians at diagnostic reasoning. These developments have accelerated the use of LLMs for symptom assessment and clinical decision support in diagnostic and treatment guidance, administrative documentation, and rules-based alert enhancement. This Perspective concerns the most consequential of these applications: the autonomous triage of self-presenting, undifferentiated patients, with little or no clinician in the loop. For that task, the evidence of safety does not yet exist. The gap is not in medical knowledge but in the fidelity of clinical evaluation: a model optimized to continue the most probable text is not optimized to act safely when the safe answer is the improbable must-not-miss diagnosis. Safe triage is not the selection of the most likely diagnosis; it is a sequential decision under asymmetric cost, in which the single catastrophic miss outweighs many false alarms, and the decisive signal may be one the patient has not volunteered - and that the model has not been trained to seek. The core deficit is therefore one of information gathering under uncertainty. Under incomplete histories, LLM systems may fail to show the behaviors safe triage requires: broadening the differential; seeking the missing red flag; lowering the threshold for escalation; deferring judgement until sufficient information is obtained; and escalating concern where high-harm diagnoses remain unexcluded. These modes of failure for LLMs can be difficult to detect considering that evaluations to date often use complete, well-curated, confidence-gated simulations. The application of LLMs under these conditions may be amplified by assistant-like behaviors and positive bias, including credulity, agreeableness, and miscalibration - when these are not constrained by clinical triage logic.

AI.tldr: This Perspective argues that while LLMs pass medical exams and can rival physicians in curated diagnostic reasoning cases, the evidence for their safety in autonomous triage of self-presenting, undifferentiated patients with minimal clinician oversight does not yet exist. The core gap is not medical knowledge but a mismatch between next-token prediction objectives and the requirements of safe sequential decision-making under asymmetric cost and uncertainty. LLMs may fail to broaden differentials, seek missing red flags, lower escalation thresholds, defer judgment, or escalate concern when high-harm diagnoses remain unexcluded—failures that can be masked by comfortable evaluations using complete history simulations and amplified by assistant-like behaviors such as credulity, agreeableness, and miscalibration.
AI.motivation: As LLMs become increasingly capable on medical knowledge benchmarks and are rapidly deployed for clinical decision support, the most consequential application—autonomous triage of undifferentiated patients—lacks adequate safety evidence. The authors aim to identify the fundamental reasons why performance on licensing examinations does not translate to safe triage behavior and why current evaluation paradigms fail to expose these deficits.
AI.method: The paper is a Perspective piece that performs a conceptual analysis contrasting LLM behavior (optimized for text continuation / most probable sequence) with the requirements of safe clinical triage (sequential decision-making under asymmetric cost). It enumerates specific failure modes in information gathering and escalation behavior, and critiques current evaluation practices (complete, well-curated, confidence-gated simulations) for masking these deficits.
AI.result: The paper identifies that safe triage requires behaviors LLMs may not exhibit under incomplete histories: broadening the differential, actively seeking missing red flags, lowering escalation thresholds, deferring judgment until sufficient information is gathered, and escalating concern when high-harm diagnoses remain unexcluded. It further identifies that these failures can be difficult to detect under current evaluation designs and may be amplified by assistant-like positive biases (credulity, agreeableness, miscalibration) when unconstrained by clinical triage logic.
AI.conclusion: Evidence of safety for autonomous LLM triage does not yet exist. The gap lies not in medical knowledge but in the fidelity of clinical evaluation—specifically in information gathering under uncertainty and sequential decision-making under asymmetric cost. New evaluation paradigms and safety constraints are needed before LLMs can be responsibly deployed for autonomous triage.

title: Physics-Aligned Self-Supervised Learning for Scientific Imaging
summary: Data augmentations define the invariances learned by self-supervised learning (SSL). Standard augmentation pipelines were designed for natural images, yet scientific imaging modalities are governed by physical measurement processes with distinct symmetry and acquisition constraints. Enforcing invariances that contradict these constraints can distort learned representations and limit downstream performance, but practitioners moving from machine learning into a new scientific modality currently have little guidance beyond transferring natural-image pipelines unexamined. We address this gap with a principled, reproducible procedure for augmentation design in scientific SSL: we formalise the physics-aligned augmentation set as a union of measurement-consistent symmetries and acquisition-driven perturbations, and we give a concrete, largely label-free workflow---enumerate candidates, label each by the measurement operator, validate with representation-geometry diagnostics, and confirm by single-factor ablation---for selecting them. We instantiate the procedure for real-space electron microscopy and reciprocal-space 4D-STEM diffraction, and evaluate it across five SSL paradigms (DINOv2, SimCLR, MAE, VICRegL, I-JEPA) on classification and crystal-orientation regression. Physics-aligned augmentations substantially improve downstream performance for objectives relying on cross-view consistency, reduce geodesic error and improve robustness under realistic acquisition variability (detector gain, resolution loss), and systematically reshape representation geometry. While our experiments use electron microscopy, the procedure is modality-agnostic and applies to other measurement-driven domains such as medical and remote-sensing imaging. These results position augmentation design as a primary, and controllable, source of inductive bias in scientific self-supervised learning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a principled, reproducible procedure for designing physics-aligned data augmentations in self-supervised learning (SSL) for scientific imaging. The authors formalize the augmentation set as a union of measurement-consistent symmetries and acquisition-driven perturbations, and provide a largely label-free workflow for selecting them. They validate the approach on real-space electron microscopy and reciprocal-space 4D-STEM diffraction across five SSL paradigms, showing that physics-aligned augmentations substantially improve downstream performance, reduce geodesic error, improve robustness under realistic acquisition variability, and systematically reshape representation geometry.
AI.motivation: Standard SSL augmentation pipelines are designed for natural images, but scientific imaging modalities are governed by physical measurement processes with distinct symmetry and acquisition constraints. Enforcing invariances that contradict these constraints can distort learned representations, yet practitioners moving into new scientific modalities have little guidance beyond transferring natural-image pipelines unexamined.
AI.method: The authors formalize the physics-aligned augmentation set as a union of measurement-consistent symmetries and acquisition-driven perturbations, and give a workflow for selecting them: enumerate candidates, label each by the measurement operator, validate with representation-geometry diagnostics, and confirm by single-factor ablation. They instantiate this for real-space electron microscopy and reciprocal-space 4D-STEM diffraction, evaluating across five SSL paradigms (DINOv2, SimCLR, MAE, VICRegL, I-JEPA) on classification and crystal-orientation regression.
AI.result: Physics-aligned augmentations substantially improve downstream performance for objectives relying on cross-view consistency, reduce geodesic error, and improve robustness under realistic acquisition variability (detector gain, resolution loss), while systematically reshaping representation geometry. The procedure is validated across five SSL paradigms and two scientific imaging modalities.
AI.conclusion: The procedure is modality-agnostic and applies to other measurement-driven domains such as medical and remote-sensing imaging. The results position augmentation design as a primary and controllable source of inductive bias in scientific self-supervised learning.

title: Validation Evidence in LLM Repair Agents: How Much of What Passes Actually Tests the Bug?
summary:
When a repair agent runs a test and sees it pass, the result is treated as evidence about the reported defect. We measure how often that treatment is warranted. BSG-VA (buggy-state/candidate-state/gold-fix validation analysis) captures each validation command at its exact working-tree state, extracts a test-only patch, and replays the command on the original buggy code (B), the candidate state (S), and the developer gold fix (G). The captured outcome and the replay results assign every event an evidence role, from gold-aligned bug-discriminating through regression-only to misleading. Across 3,730 events in 643 rollouts on 110 tasks, 46.0% of positive comparable events carry no bug-discriminating information; 23.8% of baseline rollouts, with no feedback injected, close with a patch whose entire positive evidence base is of this kind. A three-arm experiment tests whether returning the B-replay outcome to the agent changes this pattern. Bug-contrast feedback reduces evidence-inadequate closure by 7.8 percentage points relative to an attention-matched reminder (p = 0.0029) and raises bug-discriminating evidence by 7.4 points (p = 0.011), with no detectable cost to repair success. Both estimates fall below the prespecified 10-percentage-point smallest effect size of interest, so practical magnitude remains uncertain. Roughly a third of the improvement traces to the reminder alone; across two exploratory replications, varying the scaffold and the model, the B-replay content adds a detectable increment only with gpt-5.6-sol under the unconstrained tool-use loop. BSG-VA applies post hoc to any replayable repair trajectory that preserves the required code states and execution environment.
  Keywords: program repair agents, validation evidence, test adequacy, large language models, software quality, controlled experiment.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BSG-VA, a method for analyzing validation commands in automated program repair by replaying each command at the exact working-tree state across three code states (buggy, candidate, gold-fix). Analyzing 3,730 events across 110 tasks, it finds 46% of positive comparable events carry no bug-discriminating information, and 23.8% of baseline rollouts close with evidence-inadequate patches. A three-arm experiment shows bug-contrast feedback reduces evidence-inadequate closures by 7.8 percentage points (p=0.0029) and raises bug-discriminating evidence by 7.4 points, though both fall below the prespecified 10-point smallest effect size of interest.
AI.motivation: Repair agents treat passing tests as evidence about the reported defect, but it is unclear how often this treatment is actually warranted. The paper aims to quantify how frequently validation outcomes provide genuine bug-discriminating information versus merely reflecting regression-only or misleading evidence.
AI.method: BSG-VA captures each validation command at its exact working-tree state, extracts a test-only patch, and replays the command on original buggy code (B), candidate state (S), and developer gold fix (G). Each event is assigned an evidence role. A three-arm experiment tests whether returning the B-replay outcome to the agent changes evidence adequacy, with two exploratory replications varying scaffold and model.
AI.result: Across 3,730 events in 643 rollouts on 110 tasks: 46.0% of positive comparable events carry no bug-discriminating information; 23.8% of baseline rollouts close with evidence-inadequate patches. Bug-contrast feedback reduces evidence-inadequate closure by 7.8 points (p=0.0029) and raises bug-discriminating evidence by 7.4 points (p=0.011) with no cost to repair success. Both estimates fall below the 10-point smallest effect size of interest. Roughly a third of improvement traces to the reminder alone; the B-replay content adds a detectable increment only with gpt-5.6-sol under unconstrained tool-use.
AI.conclusion: Passing tests in repair rollouts frequently lack genuine bug-discriminating evidence. Bug-contrast feedback shows promising but statistically modest effects below the prespecified practical significance threshold. The method BSG-VA is general and applies post hoc to any replayable repair trajectory preserving required code states and execution environment.

title: ViSAGE: Constructing Self-Correcting Memories for Long-Form Video Understanding
summary:
Multimodal agents operating in long-horizon environments must build and continually update multimedia memories to support entity-consistent, temporally grounded reasoning. However, existing agentic memory approaches often discard fine-grained dentity cues under aggressive compression and segment-wise processing. They also rely heavily on vector similarity retrieval, which can surface semantically related yet identity-mismatched evidence, leading to entity confusion, error propagation, and hallucinated answers.
  We propose ViSAGE, a multimodal agentic memory framework that constructs self-correcting, entity-centric memories. Specifically, ViSAGE anchors entity identity via cross-modal binding over long temporal ranges. It then applies bidirectional memory refinement to propagate delayed identity evidence, retroactively unifying historical records and improving future reasoning. We also introduce multi-agent cross-verification to assess retrieved evidence under an identity-evidence alignment onstraint, enabling abstention instead of unsupported answers when evidence is missing. Extensive results demonstrate that ViSAGE consistently outperforms the strongest baseline, achieving 5.9% higher accuracy.

AI.tldr: ViSAGE is a multimodal agentic memory framework that builds self-correcting, entity-centric memories via cross-modal entity binding, bidirectional memory refinement, and multi-agent cross-verification, achieving 5.9% higher accuracy than the strongest baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic memory approaches fail in long-horizon multimodal environments due to aggressive compression losing fine-grained identity cues, segment-wise processing breaking temporal continuity, and heavy reliance on vector similarity retrieval that surfaces semantically related but identity-mismatched evidence—leading to entity confusion, error propagation, and hallucinations.
AI.method: ViSAGE consists of three key components: (1) cross-modal binding to anchor entity identity over long temporal ranges; (2) bidirectional memory refinement to propagate delayed identity evidence bidirectionally, retroactively unifying historical records and improving future reasoning; (3) multi-agent cross-verification that assesses retrieved evidence under an identity-evidence alignment constraint, enabling abstention rather than unsupported answers when evidence is missing.
AI.result: ViSAGE consistently outperforms the strongest baseline, achieving 5.9% higher accuracy across extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: ViSAGE demonstrates that entity-centric, self-correcting memory construction with identity-aware verification effectively addresses entity confusion and hallucinations in multimodal long-horizon agentic reasoning tasks.

title: Group-wise Supervision with Focal-Dice Loss for Long-Tailed Indoor Semantic Occupancy Prediction
summary: Recently, 3D semantic occupancy prediction has garnered increasing attention for understanding the indoor scene. However, unlike structured outdoor environments, indoor scenes feature a high diversity of object categories that exhibit a severe long-tailed distribution, which has become a core bottleneck limiting the performance of existing models. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel method, Group-UFD Occ, based on hierarchical semantic supervision and synergistic loss optimization. At the architectural level, we introduce a fine-grained semantic grouping strategy and design multi-scale, parallel ``main-expert'' prediction heads to guide the model in efficiently learning tail-class features through deep regularization. At the optimization level, we introduce the Unified Focal-Dice (UFD) loss. This synergistic loss function dynamically focuses on hard samples at the per-voxel level. Meanwhile, it simultaneously optimizes the geometric integrity of predicted objects from a region-based perspective. We conducted experiments on the large-scale EmbodiedScan dataset. The results demonstrate that our method yields a relative improvement of 11.38\% over the baseline, with substantial accuracy gains in several critical long-tailed categories.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Group-UFD Occ, a method for 3D semantic occupancy prediction in indoor scenes that addresses the long-tailed distribution of object categories through hierarchical semantic supervision and a synergistic Unified Focal-Dice (UFD) loss, achieving an 11.38% relative improvement over the baseline on the EmbodiedScan dataset.
AI.motivation: Indoor scenes exhibit a high diversity of object categories with a severe long-tailed distribution, unlike structured outdoor environments. This long-tailed nature becomes a core bottleneck limiting the performance of existing 3D semantic occupancy prediction models.
AI.method: The method Group-UFD Occ consists of two key components: (1) At the architectural level, a fine-grained semantic grouping strategy is introduced, along with multi-scale parallel "main-expert" prediction heads to guide efficient learning of tail-class features through deep regularization. (2) At the optimization level, the Unified Focal-Dice (UFD) loss is proposed, which dynamically focuses on hard samples at the per-voxel level while simultaneously optimizing geometric object integrity from a region-based perspective.
AI.result: Experiments on the large-scale EmbodiedScan dataset show a relative improvement of 11.38% over the baseline, with substantial accuracy gains in several critical long-tailed categories.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hierarchical semantic supervision combined with synergistic loss optimization effectively alleviates the long-tailed distribution problem in indoor 3D semantic occupancy prediction, demonstrating significant performance improvements.

title: To Add Is Machine, To Delete Is Human: Measuring and Mitigating Deletion Avoidance in LLM Code Editing
summary: Large language models increasingly write and repair production code, yet evidence is mounting that their test-passing patches leave codebases harder to maintain. We identify one concrete source: deletion avoidance, the systematic tendency to retain code that an intended edit requires removing. Across the five leading models on the official SWE-bench Verified leaderboard, deletion recall against the developer patch reaches at most 71.7% even on tasks all five solve, and models reach the right file for over 92% of required deletions but cut the exact line in under 52% of cases. Instead, 29.0% of passing patches wrap the targeted code in a guard or fallback, a pattern we call Guard-and-Go. Such patches pass because the original tests rarely check removal: when we retrofit 34 Verified tasks with tests that fail if the targeted code remains, four frontier models spanning closed and open weights fall from 63.2% to 41.9%. Because real repairs mix removal with addition, we curate CanItDelete, a benchmark of 200 tasks mined from real commits whose entire required edit is deletion. Even with the addition work gone, the best model still fails one task in five, and smaller open models fall to 18.0%. We then ablate GPT-5.6 Sol under four cumulative prompts; success moves little until we supply the exact lines, which nearly eliminate incomplete deletion yet raise success only to 80.5% because the model then deletes beyond the spans or adds code instead. Finally, through a pilot study we show one potential fix: teaching deletion during post-training reduces deletion avoidance and improves broader code-editing performance, suggesting the behavior is undertrained rather than beyond reach.

AI.tldr: Large language models systematically avoid deleting code when making repairs, a behavior called "deletion avoidance." Across five leading models on SWE-bench Verified, deletion recall tops out at 71.7%, and 29.0% of passing patches wrap targeted code in guards or fallbacks ("Guard-and-Go") instead of removing it. This passes existing tests because they rarely check for removal. The authors curate CanItDelete, a 200-task deletion-only benchmark, showing even the best model fails 1 in 5 tasks. Ablations reveal that supplying exact deletion lines helps but introduces over-deletion, and a pilot post-training study shows deletion can be taught, improving broader code-editing performance.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly write and repair production code, yet their test-passing patches degrade codebase maintainability. The authors aim to identify and characterize the concrete source of this degradation, hypothesizing it stems from deletion avoidance, making maintenance-oriented code repair more reliable.
AI.method: The authors measure deletion recall against developer patches across five leading SWE-bench Verified models, analyze Guard-and-Go patterns in passing patches, retrofit 34 Verified tasks with deletion-checking tests to expose failures, curate CanItDelete (200 deletion-only tasks from real commits), run ablation studies on GPT-5.6 Sol with cumulative prompts, and conduct a pilot post-training study teaching deletion.
AI.result: Deletion recall reaches at most 71.7% among top models; models reach the right file for 92% of deletions but cut the exact line in under 52% of cases. 29.0% of passing patches use Guard-and-Go. With deletion-checking tests, four frontier models drop from 63.2% to 41.9%. On CanItDelete, the best model fails 1 in 5 tasks and smaller models fall to 18.0%. Ablations show exact-line prompts nearly eliminate incomplete deletion but only raise success to 80.5% due to over-deletion. Post-training for deletion reduces avoidance and improves broader editing performance.
AI.conclusion: Deletion avoidance is a systematic, undertrained failure mode in LLM code repair, not an inherent limitation. Teaching deletion during post-training can reduce this behavior and improve overall code-editing performance, suggesting concrete training interventions are a viable path forward.

title: Multi-Agent Planning with Spatio-Temporal and Topological Constraints using STL-GO
comment: Accepted at Formal Methods for Computer-Aided Design 2026
summary: Multi-agent planning problems arise in a variety of engineering applications, such as multi-robot wildfire fighting and unmanned aerial inspection in factories. A particular challenge is the existence of spatio-temporal (i.e., when and/or where an agent should do what) and topological constraints (i.e., how agents should interact), as typically formalized via the notion of graphs. Over the last years, various frameworks have been proposed that can capture such constraints via spatio-temporal logics. We focus here on spatio-temporal logic with graph operators (STL-GO), a recent formalism that supports reasoning about multiple agents and their topologies, such as sensing, communication, and task topologies. In this paper, we consider the problem of planning multi-agent paths that satisfy constraints written in STL-GO. This problem is particularly challenging due to the need of encoding multiple, potentially time-varying graphs via the graph operators inherent to STL-GO. We present two encodings of this problem, one based on mixed-integer programming (MIP) and another based on satisfiability modulo theory (SMT), with soundness guarantees. We provide a unified interface for specifying agent constraints, their graph topologies, and the STL-GO specification, enabling seamless use of both methods and facilitating direct comparison between them. We evaluate both encodings on a multi-UAV search-and-rescue benchmark, ablating over team size and graph complexity, highlighting the expressiveness of the proposed encodings under dynamic multi- graph interactions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents two sound encodings—one based on mixed-integer programming (MIP) and another on satisfiability modulo theory (SMT)—for solving multi-agent path planning problems subject to constraints expressed in Spatio-Temporal Logic with Graph Operators (STL-GO), a formalism capturing spatio-temporal and topological constraints via graphs. A unified interface is provided, and both methods are evaluated on a multi-UAV search-and-rescue benchmark with ablations over team size and graph complexity.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent planning problems (e.g., multi-robot wildfire fighting, UAV inspection) involve complex spatio-temporal and topological constraints formalized via graphs. While spatio-temporal logics like STL-GO can express such constraints, there is a lack of efficient and systematically comparable planning methods that handle the multiple, potentially time-varying graph structures inherent to STL-GO specifications.
AI.method: The authors propose two encodings for the multi-agent path planning problem under STL-GO constraints: (1) a mixed-integer programming (MIP)-based encoding and (2) a satisfiability modulo theory (SMT)-based encoding. Both encodings are proven sound. A unified interface is designed for specifying agent constraints, graph topologies, and STL-GO specifications, allowing seamless use and direct comparison of both methods.
AI.result: Both encodings are evaluated on a multi-UAV search-and-rescue benchmark with ablations over team size and graph complexity, demonstrating the expressiveness of the proposed encodings under dynamic multi-graph interactions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MIP and SMT encodings provide sound and practically viable approaches for STL-GO-constrained multi-agent path planning, offering complementary trade-offs and enabling flexible handling of dynamic multi-graph topologies as evidenced by the benchmark experiments.

title: DiffAttack: Evasion Attacks Against Face Recognition via Latent Diffusion Models
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Joint Conference on Biometrics (IJCB) 2026
summary: Facial biometric identification relies on the distinctiveness of user attributes within a high-dimensional embedding space. However, the decision boundaries of deep face recognition (FR) systems are often sufficiently narrow that they can be conflated, rendering the models vulnerable to adversarial attacks. In such scenarios, the FR system fails to distinguish between an authentic source and a meticulously crafted adversarial face. Existing adversarial methods targeting facial biometrics are limited in both performance and their ability to generate high-quality images that are imperceptible to humans. Moreover, these methods often fail when the source and target images belong to different demographic groups or genders. To address these limitations, we present a novel approach for adversarial face generation via latent-space optimization. We leverage latent diffusion models directly to guide generation toward target identity embeddings, as measured by a face recognition model. Our proposed \textbf{DiffAttack} framework has been evaluated on standard benchmarks, such as the FFHQ and CelebA-HQ datasets. DiffAttack significantly outperforms existing adversarial techniques, achieving a high average attack success rate of 84.86% across multiple face recognition models (e.g., FaceNet). Notably, DiffAttack demonstrates superior transferability, surpassing traditional noise-based methods by over 15.28% and semantic-based approaches by approximately 5.21% on benchmark datasets like FFHQ and CelebA-HQ.

AI.tldr: DiffAttack is a novel adversarial face generation framework that uses latent diffusion models and latent-space optimization to craft imperceptible adversarial faces that fool deep face recognition systems, achieving 84.86% attack success rate and outperforming existing noise-based and semantic-based methods in transferability.
AI.motivation: Deep face recognition systems have narrow decision boundaries that are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, yet existing adversarial methods targeting facial biometrics suffer from limited performance, poor image quality, and frequent failures when source and target images differ across demographic groups or genders.
AI.method: The proposed DiffAttack framework leverages latent diffusion models to guide adversarial face generation toward target identity embeddings measured by a face recognition model, performing optimization directly in the latent space of the diffusion model.
AI.result: DiffAttack achieves a high average attack success rate of 84.86% across multiple face recognition models (e.g., FaceNet) on FFHQ and CelebA-HQ benchmarks. It surpasses traditional noise-based methods by over 15.28% and semantic-based approaches by approximately 5.21% in transferability.
AI.conclusion: Latent-space optimization with diffusion models provides a more effective, transferable, and higher-quality approach to adversarial face generation compared to existing noise-based and semantic-based methods, particularly for cross-demographic and cross-gender attack scenarios.

title: Reducing Data Movement in the Galerkin Product of Block Algebraic Multigrid on GPUs
summary: The Galerkin triple product $A_c = P^T A P$ dominates the recurring per-solve setup cost of algebraic multigrid (AMG). For AMG on systems of PDEs the product is a rectangular-block sparse matrix triple product: for 3D elasticity the fine operator has $3\times3$ blocks, the prolongator $3\times6$, and the coarse operator $6\times6$, a shape no vendor sparse library supports. We map its algorithm space -- classical two-pass, fused-recompute, schedule-reordered, shared-memory-tiled, and inspector-executor variants -- under an explicit DRAM/L2 traffic model, and implement the leading variants in portable Kokkos (CUDA) and native CUDA backends using new PETSc blocked matrix types. Validated on an NVIDIA A100, the model predicts per level which variant moves the fewest bytes. Guided by it, a shared-memory-tiled kernel with a sorted, search-free schedule moves fewer bytes in less than half the time of the portable Kokkos team kernels on the fine-level product (10.5 vs 17.4 GB of DRAM, 45 vs 82 ms), within $2.5\times$ of the model's streaming floor for the full product and $1.9\times$ on its $A\cdot P$ stage. We further present prolongator filtering, a new PETSc GAMG algorithm that drops small blocks from the coarse space under a Frobenius criterion with a kernel-preserving projection; it reduces $P^TAP$ traffic, coarse-operator fill, and memory, and cuts the hot $P^TAP$ time $2.9\times$ on the fine grid with iteration counts unchanged. The driving application is a fully GPU-resident blocked pipeline in PETSc: finite-element assembly writes directly into the blocked device matrix, and the AMG setup, Galerkin products, and solve all operate on primary blocked data with no scalar expansion and no operator-sized device-host transfers in the recurring phases.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the high recurring cost of the Galerkin triple product P^T A P in algebraic multigrid (AMG), specifically for systems of PDEs where these are rectangular-block sparse matrix products. The authors map the algorithmic space of such products under an explicit DRAM/L2 traffic model and implement leading variants in portable Kokkos and native CUDA via new PETSc blocked matrix types. Validated on an NVIDIA A100, a shared-memory-tiled kernel with a sorted, search-free schedule reduces bytes moved and halves the time of portable Kokkos kernels. The paper also introduces prolongator filtering, a new PETSc GAMG algorithm that drops small coarse-space blocks under a Frobenius criterion, cutting P^TAP time 2.9x with unchanged iteration counts.
AI.motivation: The Galerkin triple product P^T A P dominates the per-solve setup cost in AMG. For systems of PDEs (e.g., 3D elasticity), this product involves rectangular blocks (3x3 fine, 3x6 prolongator, 6x6 coarse) that no vendor sparse library supports natively, creating a significant performance bottleneck with no off-the-shelf solution.
AI.method: The authors model the algorithm space of the rectangular-block sparse triple product using an explicit DRAM/L2 traffic model, covering classical two-pass, fused-recompute, schedule-reordered, shared-memory-tiled, and inspector-executor variants. They implement the best variants in portable Kokkos and native CUDA backends using new PETSc blocked matrix types, and validate the model on an NVIDIA A100 to predict per-level optimal variant selection. They also propose prolongator filtering, which drops small coarse-space blocks under a Frobenius norm criterion with a kernel-preserving projection, within a fully GPU-resident PETSc blocked pipeline.
AI.result: The model accurately predicts which variant moves the fewest bytes per level. The shared-memory-tiled kernel with a sorted, search-free schedule moves fewer bytes in less than half the time of portable Kokkos team kernels on the fine-level product (10.5 vs 17.4 GB DRAM; 45 vs 82 ms), within 2.5x of the model's streaming floor for the full product and 1.9x on the A*P stage. Prolongator filtering reduces P^TAP traffic, coarse-operator fill, and memory, cutting hot P^TAP time 2.9x on the fine grid with unchanged iteration counts.
AI.conclusion: The DRAM/L2 traffic model provides a reliable guide for selecting optimal Galerkin product implementations per AMG level. The shared-memory-tiled approach substantially outperforms portable alternatives, and prolongator filtering offers an orthogonal optimization that reduces both traffic and memory footprint. The fully GPU-resident blocked pipeline in PETSc eliminates scalar expansion and operator-sized transfers in recurring phases, enabling efficient AMG for blocked systems on GPUs.

title: Library Reachability in LSR-Synth: How Anti-Memorization Design Changes the Measurement of Symbolic Discovery
summary: Existing benchmarks for scientific equation discovery are largely composed of well-known equations available in the public domain, making it difficult to determine whether a model is discovering laws from data or merely recalling answers from its training corpus. LSR-Synth mitigates this problem by introducing novel synthetic terms into established scientific mechanisms and filtering the resulting tasks for novelty, solvability, and scientific plausibility. This paper examines a narrower measurement question: can these tasks further distinguish scientific priors supplied by language models from conventional operator search that does not access task semantics? We construct a semantics-free baseline using a fixed vocabulary with publicly documented provenance, and assess the role of candidate coverage through semantic blinding, library weakening, and matched operator-family knockouts. Under the current task snapshot, search budget, and scoring protocol, the fixed vocabulary already covers most tasks, while language-model-generated candidates rarely expand the set of solvable instances. Their marginal contribution becomes substantial only when vocabulary coverage is selectively disrupted. Strict out-of-distribution evaluation lowers the absolute success rates of all methods but does not alter this relationship. These findings neither invalidate LSR-Synth's controls against memorization of complete formulas nor imply that language-model priors are generally unhelpful. Rather, they support a more limited conclusion: most current tasks remain suitable for evaluating the fitting and recombination of previously unseen expressions, but are insufficient on their own to identify contributions from priors beyond a fixed search space.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether LSR-Synth's scientific equation discovery tasks can distinguish language-model-driven scientific priors from conventional operator search. Using a semantics-free baseline with fixed vocabulary, the authors find that the fixed vocabulary covers most tasks, while LM-generated candidates rarely expand solvable instances—their contribution only becomes significant when vocabulary coverage is selectively disrupted. The findings support evaluating fitting/recombination of unseen expressions but not identifying prior contributions beyond a fixed search space.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for scientific equation discovery contain well-known public-domain equations, making it unclear whether models genuinely discover laws from data or simply recall answers from training data. The authors want to determine whether LSR-Synth tasks can further differentiate scientific priors from language models versus conventional operator search that lacks task semantics.
AI.method: The authors construct a semantics-free baseline using a fixed vocabulary with publicly documented provenance. They assess the role of candidate coverage through three interventions: semantic blinding, library weakening, and matched operator-family knockouts. They compare this baseline against language-model-generated candidates under current task snapshot, search budget, and scoring protocol.
AI.result: The fixed vocabulary already covers most tasks, while language-model-generated candidates rarely expand the set of solvable instances. The marginal contribution of LM priors becomes substantial only when vocabulary coverage is selectively disrupted. Strict out-of-distribution evaluation lowers absolute success rates for all methods but does not alter the relative relationship between approaches.
AI.conclusion: The findings neither invalidate LSR-Synth's controls against memorization of complete formulas nor imply LM priors are generally unhelpful. Instead, they support a limited conclusion: most current tasks are suitable for evaluating fitting and recombination of previously unseen expressions, but are insufficient on their own to identify contributions from priors beyond a fixed search space.

title: Automated classification method of COVID-19 cases from chest CT volumes using 2D and 3D hybrid CNN for anisotropic volumes
comment: Oral Presentation in SPIE Medical Imaging 2022
summary: This paper proposes an automated classification method of chest CT volumes based on likelihood of COVID-19 cases. Novel coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) spreads over the world, causing a large number of infected patients and deaths. Sudden increase in the number of COVID-19 patients causes a manpower shortage in medical institutions. Computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) system provides quick and quantitative diagnosis results. CAD system for COVID-19 enables efficient diagnosis workflow and contributes to reduce such manpower shortage. This paper proposes an automated classification method of chest CT volumes for COVID-19 diagnosis assistance. We propose a COVID-19 classification convolutional neural network (CNN) that has a 2D/3D hybrid feature extraction flows. The 2D/3D hybrid feature extraction flows are designed to effectively extract image features from anisotropic volumes such as chest CT volumes for diagnosis. The flows extract image features on three mutually perpendicular planes in CT volumes and then combine the features to perform classification. Classification accuracy of the proposed method was evaluated using a dataset that contains 1288 CT volumes. An averaged classification accuracy was 83.3%. The accuracy was higher than that of a classification CNN which does not have 2D and 3D hybrid feature extraction flows.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an automated CNN-based classification method for chest CT volumes to aid COVID-19 diagnosis, using a 2D/3D hybrid feature extraction approach that analyzes three mutually perpendicular planes in CT volumes. The method achieves 83.3% average classification accuracy on a dataset of 1288 CT volumes, outperforming a baseline CNN without the hybrid feature extraction flows.
AI.motivation: The global spread of COVID-19 has caused a surge in infected patients and deaths, leading to manpower shortages in medical institutions. A CAD system that provides quick and quantitative diagnosis would enable efficient diagnosis workflows and help alleviate this shortage.
AI.method: The paper proposes a COVID-19 classification CNN with 2D/3D hybrid feature extraction flows designed to effectively extract image features from anisotropic volumes such as chest CT scans. The flows extract features on three mutually perpendicular planes within the CT volumes and then combine these features for classification.
AI.result: The proposed method was evaluated on a dataset containing 1288 CT volumes, achieving an average classification accuracy of 83.3%, which was higher than that of a classification CNN without the 2D/3D hybrid feature extraction flows.
AI.conclusion: The 2D/3D hybrid feature extraction approach improves COVID-19 classification accuracy on chest CT volumes over a baseline CNN lacking this design, supporting its potential utility in computer-aided COVID-19 diagnosis.

title: Automated Testing and Repair for Verified Compilers Generated by a Coding Agent
summary: We present an agent based automated testing and repair system for verified compilers that contain four kinds of code: verified code, checked code, unverified code, and specification. We present specialized defect detection techniques that exploit the structure present in such compilers. For each surfaced defect the system invokes a coding agent to repair the defect and validate the repair. We evaluate the system on the Axon compiler, a compiler completely generated by a coding agent operating under developer supervision. The compiler was validated during development on a small benchmark set (the Livermore benchmarks), raising the possibility that its coding agent reward hacked the compiler. We also evaluate the possibility that the repair system reward hacked the repairs and find no evidence of reward hacking in either the Axon compiler or the repairs. We present results that characterize the testing and repair effectiveness and discuss repair characteristics.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an agent-based automated testing and repair system specifically designed for verified compilers that contain four types of code (verified, checked, unverified, and specification). The system uses specialized defect detection techniques exploiting compiler structure and invokes a coding agent to repair surfaced defects. It is evaluated on the Axon compiler, which was generated by a coding agent under developer supervision, and the results show no evidence of reward hacking in either the compiler or the repairs.
AI.motivation: Verified compilers contain heterogeneous code types, making them complex to test and maintain. The Axon compiler, being entirely generated by a coding agent, raises the concern that the agent may have reward-hacked the compiler by overfitting to the Livermore benchmark set used during development. The authors aim to develop a system to automatically test and repair such compilers while also investigating whether reward hacking occurred.
AI.method: The system employs an agent-based approach with specialized defect detection techniques that exploit the structural characteristics of the four code types found in verified compilers. For each detected defect, a coding agent is invoked to perform repairs and validate them. The approach evaluates the possibility of reward hacking in both the Axon compiler and the repairs generated by the system.
AI.result: Evaluation on the Axon compiler demonstrates testing and repair effectiveness. The study found no evidence of reward hacking in either the Axon compiler (despite its validation on the small Livermore benchmark set) or in the repairs produced by the system. Results characterize the effectiveness of the testing and repair process, along with repair characteristics.
AI.conclusion: The agent-based automated testing and repair system is effective for verified compilers, and concerns about reward hacking in both the agent-generated Axon compiler and the repair system appear unfounded based on the evaluation. The paper provides a characterization of testing/repair effectiveness and repair behaviors.

title: Safety, or Just Capability? A Validity Audit of Agent-Safety Benchmarks
summary: Agent-safety benchmarks measure different behaviors, and their scores get quoted interchangeably as an agent's safety. We treat four of them (R-Judge, InjecAgent, AgentHarm, AgentDojo) as measurements to be validated, running each under its official implementation and author-provided scorer on up to 22 models, with MMLU and GPQA measured by us under one protocol as a capability composite. The metric is the first problem. On any binary trace-judgment benchmark scored by $F_1$, an ``always positive'' policy attains $F_1 = 2π/(1+π)$; on R-Judge that is $0.690$, above five of the 21 models that actually discriminate. The three broad-coverage benchmarks then rank the same 18 models differently, and the trade-off behind that disagreement is a small-panel artifact: R-Judge specificity against AgentHarm safety correlates $-0.64$ at $n{=}7$ and $+0.02$ at $n{=}18$, and a quarter of random size-7 subsets reach $|ρ| \geq 0.5$ around that near-zero value. Held-out validity turns on which outcome you pick. Capability predicts task success ($ρ{=}{+}0.60$) but correlates negatively with misalignment safety ($ρ{=}{-}0.44$, $n{=}21$). On their paired $n{=}20$ panel, the corresponding contrast is $Δ{=}{-}1.00$ (95% CI $[-1.48, -0.49]$, $p<0.001$), and it survives leave-one-organization-out and organization-clustered bootstrap analyses. On an expanded 41-model panel, the misalignment correlation weakens to $-0.16$ (95% CI $[-0.54, +0.22]$) and jailbreak strengthens to $+0.34$, though neither change is significant. \mbox{AgentHarm} shows the strongest held-out association, $ρ{=}{+}0.72$ with three-template jailbreak safety after controlling capability. But both instruments score harmful compliance, so this is evidence of convergent validity rather than general safety. Naming the benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model panel is the minimum a safety claim needs.

AI.tldr: Agent-safety benchmarks (R-Judge, InjecAgent, AgentHarm, AgentDojo) are validated as measurements across up to 22 models. The metric matters: 'always positive' baselines inflate F1 scores. Benchmarks rank the same models differently due to small-panel artifacts. Held-out validity depends on outcome: capability predicts task success (+0.60) but negatively correlates with misalignment safety (-0.44); this contrast is significant (Δ=-1.00, p<0.001) but weakens on larger panels. AgentHarm shows convergent validity for jailbreak safety but not general safety. Safety claims must name the benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model panel.
AI.motivation: Agent-safety benchmarks are cited interchangeably as a measure of an agent's safety, yet they measure different behaviors. The paper treats these benchmarks as psychometric instruments to be validated, examining whether their scores are reliable, comparable, and predictive of held-out outcomes.
AI.method: Four agent-safety benchmarks (R-Judge, InjecAgent, AgentHarm, AgentDojo) were run under official implementations with author-provided scorers on up to 22 models (expanded to 41 in some analyses). MMLU and GPQA served as a capability composite. Statistical methods include F1 baseline analysis, correlation analysis, leave-one-organization-out and clustered bootstrap analyses, and partial correlations controlling for capability.
AI.result: (1) An 'always positive' policy achieves F1=2π/(1+π) on binary trace-judgment benchmarks, exceeding 5 of 21 discriminating models on R-Judge. (2) Benchmarks rank the same 18 models differently, with the disagreement traceable to small-panel artifacts (r=-0.64 at n=7 vs +0.02 at n=18). (3) Capability positively predicts task success (+0.60) but negatively correlates with misalignment safety (-0.44, n=21), a significant contrast (Δ=-1.00, p<0.001) robust to organization-level analyses but weakening on the 41-model panel. (4) AgentHarm shows strong held-out association (+0.72) with jailbreak safety, indicating convergent validity rather than general safety.
AI.conclusion: Agent-safety benchmark scores are not interchangeable; their validity is domain-specific and depends heavily on metric choice, model panel, and target behavior. Small panels produce unstable rankings. Capability and safety correlate negatively on one panel but this is not robust to expansion. Any safety claim must specify the benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model panel used.

title: Retrieval-Driven Training-Free AI-Generated Video Attribution
summary: AI-generated videos are becoming increasingly realistic and difficult to distinguish from authentic ones, which facilitates malicious misuse and poses growing threats to cybersecurity and social governance. Attributing AI-generated videos to their specific generative sources is therefore of critical importance for forensic investigation and legal regulation. However, most existing visual attribution methods focus on images and particularly rely on the image generation model, thereby lacking the ability to generalize to large-scale AI-generated video data. To address these limitations, we introduce an training-free AI-generated video attribution paradigm. Specifically, we formulates AI-generated video attribution as an instance retrieval task, and design a generative fingerprint-based pipeline. This pipeline consists of an adapted orthogonal color transformation, multi-scale quantized residual generation, and temporal-semantic aggregation, progressively capturing and integrating artifacts introduced by generative models across video frames. Extensive experiments on the GenVidBench benchmark demonstrate that our method achieves strong performance in both AI-generated video detection and attribution, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods with a Rank-1 accuracy of 20.5% and a mean Average Precision of 16.6%. The code is at https://github.com/renxi-seu/Video_Attribution.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a training-free paradigm for AI-generated video attribution, formulated as an instance retrieval task. The method builds a generative fingerprint-based pipeline with adapted orthogonal color transformation, multi-scale quantized residual generation, and temporal-semantic aggregation. On the GenVidBench benchmark, it achieves strong detection and attribution performance, with Rank-1 accuracy of 20.5% and mAP of 16.6%.
AI.motivation: As AI-generated videos become increasingly realistic and difficult to distinguish from authentic content, attributing them to their specific generative sources is critical for forensic investigation and legal regulation. However, existing visual attribution methods focus on images and rely on image generation models, lacking the ability to generalize to large-scale AI-generated video data.
