AI.method: The authors formulate AI-generated video attribution as an instance retrieval task and design a training-free generative fingerprint-based pipeline. The pipeline consists of three main components: (1) an adapted orthogonal color transformation, (2) multi-scale quantized residual generation, and (3) temporal-semantic aggregation, which progressively capture and integrate artifacts introduced by generative models across video frames.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the GenVidBench benchmark demonstrate the method achieves strong performance in both AI-generated video detection and attribution, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods with a Rank-1 accuracy of 20.5% and a mean Average Precision of 16.6%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training-free paradigm effectively addresses the limitations of image-centric attribution methods by enabling large-scale AI-generated video attribution through a generative fingerprint-based retrieval approach, achieving state-of-the-art results on the benchmark.

title: A Formalism-Aware Reward Loop for Handwritten UML-to-PlantUML Generation
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the ACM/IEEE 29th International Conference on Model Driven Engineering Languages and Systems (MODELS 2026). This is the accepted author manuscript
summary: Handwritten UML sketches are common in early software design, but turning them into structured, analysable modelling artefacts still requires manual reconstruction. Vision-language models can generate PlantUML from diagram images, but prompt-based use treats this as image-to-text generation rather than structured model generation. We investigate formalism-aware rewards: feedback signals derived from analysable model representations rather than surface text. In a worked example, we adapt a vision-language model for handwritten UML-to-PlantUML generation using super-vised fine-tuning followed by Group Relative Policy Optimisation. Generated PlantUML is compared against target representations, using XMI for class diagrams and control-flow graphs for activity diagrams. Emerging results show that the adapted model improves compilability and conversion quality over the untuned open model and one proprietary baseline, while remaining competitive with a stronger proprietary baseline on class diagrams. The added benefit of the reward-guided stage remains open on the current held-out set. Error analysis and metric-validity results show that modelling acceptability is only partially captured, motivating rewards and evaluations that combine model analysis with human judgement.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a formalism-aware reward approach for adapting vision-language models to convert handwritten UML sketches into PlantUML. Using supervised fine-tuning followed by Group Relative Policy Optimisation with rewards derived from structured model representations (XMI for class diagrams, control-flow graphs for activity diagrams), the adapted model improves compilability and conversion quality over untuned baselines, though the added benefit of reward-guided stage remains uncertain and evaluation metrics only partially capture modelling acceptability.
AI.motivation: Handwritten UML sketches are common in early software design but require manual reconstruction to become analysable modelling artefacts. Current vision-language model approaches treat diagram-to-PlantUML as image-to-text generation rather than structured model generation, prompting the need for formalism-aware rewards derived from analysable model representations rather than surface text.
AI.method: The authors adapt a vision-language model for handwritten UML-to-PlantUML generation using (1) supervised fine-tuning followed by (2) Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO). Rewards are derived from formalism-aware feedback signals: XMI representations for class diagrams and control-flow graphs for activity diagrams. Generated PlantUML is compared against target representations to compute rewards and guide optimisation.
AI.result: The adapted model improves compilability and conversion quality over the untuned open model and one proprietary baseline, while remaining competitive with a stronger proprietary baseline on class diagrams. The added benefit of the reward-guided optimisation stage remains open on the current held-out set. Error analysis and metric-validity results show that modelling acceptability is only partially captured by current metrics.
AI.conclusion: Formalism-aware rewards improve handwritten UML-to-PlantUML generation quality, but current metrics only partially capture modelling acceptability. Future work should combine model analysis with human judgement in both rewards and evaluations to better align automated optimisation with genuine modelling quality.

title: SciToolAgent-Evo: An Ontology-Aware Self-Evolving Agent for Open-World Scientific Tool Acquisition
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have been increasingly adopted in scientific research for organizing and invoking specialized computational tools. However, their reliance on predefined tool spaces with static semantics limits their applicability to open-world scientific workflows, where tool requirements, capabilities, and boundaries evolve dynamically. To this end, we propose SciToolAgent-Evo, an ontology-aware self-evolving agent for open-world scientific tool acquisition. Driven by an evolving memory of skills, experiences, and an ontologized tool graph, it distills generalizable knowledge from contrastive trajectories during accumulation, whereas during inference, it formulates active requests and utilizes a LinUCB-based bandit gate to dynamically balance exploration and exploitation. Once a novel tool is acquired, its scientific ontology is completed online for seamless integration into the known graph. Moreover, we introduce OpenSciToolBench, a benchmark containing 900 realistic tasks across four difficulty levels. Extensive evaluations show that SciToolAgent-Evo achieves state-of-the-art performance, validating its robustness and generalization.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SciToolAgent-Evo, an ontology-aware self-evolving LLM agent for open-world scientific tool acquisition, along with OpenSciToolBench (a 900-task benchmark across four difficulty levels). The agent uses an evolving memory, ontologized tool graph, and a LinUCB-based bandit gate to balance exploration/exploitation when acquiring novel tools.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents for scientific research rely on predefined tool spaces with static semantics, which limits their applicability to open-world scientific workflows where tool requirements, capabilities, and boundaries evolve dynamically.
AI.method: SciToolAgent-Evo is driven by an evolving memory of skills, experiences, and an ontologized tool graph. During accumulation, it distills generalizable knowledge from contrastive trajectories. During inference, it formulates active requests and uses a LinUCB-based bandit gate to dynamically balance exploration and exploitation. When a novel tool is acquired, its scientific ontology is completed online for seamless integration into the known graph. OpenSciToolBench provides 900 realistic tasks across four difficulty levels for evaluation.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations show that SciToolAgent-Evo achieves state-of-the-art performance, validating its robustness and generalization.
AI.conclusion: SciToolAgent-Evo demonstrates that ontology-aware self-evolving mechanisms enable LLM agents to effectively acquire and integrate novel scientific tools in open-world workflows, surpassing existing approaches.

title: Visual Distribution Anchoring for Efficient Prompt Tuning
summary: Prompt tuning adapts vision--language models with few trainable parameters, but existing approaches trade off efficiency and adaptation: static textual prompts can overfit source classes, image-conditioned prompts add per-instance computation, and multimodal tuning modifies the visual branch. We propose VDA (Visual Distribution Anchoring), a training-free target adaptation framework that augments a frozen semantic classifier with class-level visual prototypes estimated offline from an unlabeled target pool. We first ask whether prototypes can be synthesized from class names. A text-to-centroid mapper reconstructs held-out source prototypes but fails under dataset shift because class names specify semantic identity, not target-domain appearance. An oracle analysis confirms that true target prototypes are highly discriminative. VDA therefore uses frozen semantic and domain-template classifiers to partition unlabeled target images into class-correlated groups. Confidence-ranked image features form normalized prototypes, fused with the semantic classifier using one global weight. Adaptation requires no target labels, target-side optimization, uniform class-prior assumption, iterative refinement, or test-query access, and yields a fixed, cacheable classifier. Controlled experiments show that class-specific partitioning drives gains and that visually local pseudo-label errors can remain useful despite being class-incorrect. Across ten ImageNet-to-target transfers, the same frozen design improves zero-shot CLIP, TCP, and MaPLe by 3.22, 3.39, and 3.35 points, respectively, improving nine of ten targets in every setting. Its visual correction further improves leakage-free PromptKD by 2.79 points, complementing zero-shot, source-prompted, multimodal-prompted, and target-distilled classifiers.

AI.tldr: VDA (Visual Distribution Anchoring) is a training-free target adaptation framework that augments a frozen semantic classifier with class-level visual prototypes estimated offline from an unlabeled target pool, improving zero-shot CLIP, TCP, and MaPLe across ten ImageNet-to-target transfers without any target labels or optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt tuning approaches for vision-language models trade off efficiency and adaptation: static textual prompts overfit source classes, image-conditioned prompts add per-instance computation, and multimodal tuning modifies the visual branch. A training-free, efficient, and broadly applicable adaptation method is needed.
AI.method: VDA partitions unlabeled target images into class-correlated groups using frozen semantic and domain-template classifiers. Confidence-ranked image features form normalized class-level prototypes, which are fused with the semantic classifier using one global weight. This requires no target labels, optimization, uniform class-prior assumption, iterative refinement, or test-query access, yielding a fixed, cacheable classifier.
AI.result: Across ten ImageNet-to-target transfers, VDA improves zero-shot CLIP, TCP, and MaPLe by 3.22, 3.39, and 3.35 points respectively, improving nine of ten targets in every setting. It additionally improves leakage-free PromptKD by 2.79 points and complements zero-shot, source-prompted, multimodal-prompted, and target-distilled classifiers.
AI.conclusion: VDA demonstrates that class-specific partitioning drives performance gains, and that visually local pseudo-label errors can remain useful despite being class-incorrect. It provides an efficient, label-free, and broadly complementary adaptation mechanism for frozen vision-language classifiers.

title: Execution-First Synthetic Tool-Use Trace Generation for LLM Agents
summary: Agentic software-engineering and industrial systems increasingly operate through executable workflows rather than code genera- tion alone: they search artifacts, invoke tools, inspect structured observations, and query databases. Training these agents requires supervision data that captures valid tool interactions and executable workflows. However, traditional query-first data synthesis can fail because plausible user requests may not correspond to valid tool sequences, compatible parameters, or available data. To address this limitation, we propose SyntheticAgentTraceQA, an execution- first framework for generating scalable supervision data for tool- augmented agents. Our framework first constructs high-level work- flow structures, maps them to available tools through dependency- aware assignment, executes and validates the resulting traces in con- trolled environments, and only then synthesizes natural-language user tasks, teacher-generated reasoning annotations, and reference answers. We evaluate the framework across four tool ecosystems and use the resulting data to fine-tune and evaluate Qwen model variants. The results show that execution-grounded supervision improves tool execution behavior, reference-trace agreement, and answer-generation performance on the evaluated tasks. Further analysis reveals a supervision trade-off: masked supervision, which excludes reasoning annotations from the training objective, im- proves final-answer metrics, whereas full supervision, computing loss over the complete assistant output including reasoning tokens, underperforms on answer quality and does not consistently im- prove reference-trace agreement, particularly at the 9B scale. These findings highlight the importance of designing synthetic supervi- sion according to the desired capabilities of tool-augmented agents.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SyntheticAgentTraceQA, an execution-first framework for generating scalable supervision data for tool-augmented agents. Instead of query-first synthesis, it constructs high-level workflow structures, maps them to available tools via dependency-aware assignment, executes and validates traces in controlled environments, and only then synthesizes user tasks, reasoning annotations, and reference answers. Evaluated on four tool ecosystems with Qwen model variants, execution-grounded supervision improves tool execution, reference-trace agreement, and answer generation. The paper also reveals a supervision trade-off: masked supervision (excluding reasoning from loss) improves final-answer metrics, while full supervision underperforms on answer quality.
AI.motivation: Traditional query-first data synthesis for training tool-augmented agents can fail because plausible user requests may not correspond to valid tool sequences, compatible parameters, or available data. Since modern agentic systems increasingly operate through executable workflows rather than code generation alone, there is a need for supervision data that captures valid tool interactions and executable workflows.
AI.method: SyntheticAgentTraceQA is an execution-first framework that: (1) constructs high-level workflow structures, (2) maps them to available tools through dependency-aware assignment, (3) executes and validates the resulting traces in controlled environments, and (4) only then synthesizes natural-language user tasks, teacher-generated reasoning annotations, and reference answers. The framework is evaluated by fine-tuning Qwen model variants on data from four tool ecosystems.
AI.result: Execution-grounded supervision improves tool execution behavior, reference-trace agreement, and answer-generation performance. The analysis reveals a supervision trade-off: masked supervision (excluding reasoning annotations from the training objective) improves final-answer metrics, whereas full supervision (computing loss over complete assistant output including reasoning tokens) underperforms on answer quality and does not consistently improve reference-trace agreement, particularly at the 9B scale.
AI.conclusion: The design of synthetic supervision data should be tailored to the desired capabilities of tool-augmented agents. The findings highlight that execution-grounded data synthesis is effective, but the choice between masked and full supervision has significant implications for downstream performance, depending on whether final-answer quality or reference-trace agreement is the target objective.

title: EarlyDx: An Admission-Anchored Benchmark for Open-Ended Generation of Evidence-Supported ED-Encounter Diagnoses
summary: Clinical diagnosis at hospital admission must be made rapidly from limited, incomplete evidence. Existing diagnosis-prediction benchmarks are poorly suited to this setting: they restrict prediction to closed code sets, exclude free-text notes, and supervise with discharge diagnoses that incorporate the full inpatient course. We introduce EarlyDx, a large-scale benchmark for open-ended early diagnosis, built from 154,834 emergency department encounters in MIMIC-IV. Each encounter is restricted to records available at admission time $t_0$ and supervised by the diagnoses recorded during the ED encounter rather than at discharge. An LLM auditor further verifies every free-text label as supported, partially supported, or unsupported by that evidence; the primary evaluation scores only fully supported labels. Under a semantic LLM-as-judge protocol, no evaluated system --- frontier general, medical-specialized, or in-domain post-trained --- synthesizes admission-time evidence reliably. Zero-shot models score largely by extraction, recovering only 3-31% of diagnoses that must be inferred rather than read from the record; post-training raises inference-dependent recall to 56%, but a sizeable margin remains, and on time-critical conditions no system attains a clinician's balance of sensitivity and precision. We release the full construction and evaluation pipeline at here.

AI.tldr: EarlyDx is a large-scale benchmark for open-ended early diagnosis built from 154,834 emergency department encounters in MIMIC-IV, restricted to admission-time records and supervised by ED diagnoses rather than discharge diagnoses, with LLM-audited labels. Current systems, including frontier general, medical-specialized, and post-trained models, perform poorly at synthesizing admission-time evidence, and no system achieves clinician-level performance on time-critical conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing diagnosis-prediction benchmarks are poorly suited to real clinical diagnosis at hospital admission because they restrict to closed code sets, exclude free-text notes, and supervise with discharge diagnoses that incorporate the full inpatient course. A benchmark that reflects the actual early-diagnosis setting is needed.
AI.method: The authors construct EarlyDx from 154,834 emergency department encounters in MIMIC-IV, restricting each encounter to records available at admission time t0 and supervising by ED diagnoses instead of discharge diagnoses. An LLM auditor verifies every free-text label as supported, partially supported, or unsupported by the evidence, with primary evaluation scoring only fully supported labels, using a semantic LLM-as-judge protocol.
AI.result: No evaluated system — frontier general, medical-specialized, or in-domain post-trained — synthesizes admission-time evidence reliably. Zero-shot models recover only 3-31% of diagnoses requiring inference rather than extraction; post-training raises inference-dependent recall to 56%, but a large margin remains. On time-critical conditions, no system attains a clinician's balance of sensitivity and precision.
AI.conclusion: EarlyDx reveals a substantial gap between current systems and reliable early diagnosis from admission-time evidence. The benchmark and evaluation pipeline are released to support progress in this setting.

title: SafeNexus: Discovering and Steering Modality-Universal Safety Neurons in MLLMs
summary: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising safety performance, extending them to Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exposes a significant gap between expanded multimodal capabilities and existing safety mechanisms. Current defenses remain predominantly confined to specific modal settings, thereby limiting their robustness against broader cross-modal threats. To bridge this gap, we introduce SafeNexus, a cross-modal safety alignment framework that adopts a dedicated neuron-level intervention strategy. First, we formulate a neuron localization paradigm that identifies functionally specialized neurons by characterizing intermediate-layer activation patterns and quantifying their functional salience through importance scoring. Building upon this paradigm, we exploit contrastive data to identify modality-bound safety neurons (BS-Neurons), and validate their role in regulating safety behavior within each modality via targeted suppression. Further cross-modal analysis defines modality-universal safety neurons (US-Neurons) as the shared subset of BS-Neurons identified across individual modalities, serving as the core for defending against harmful cross-modal attacks. We observe that suppressing these neurons substantially degrades safety performance across modalities, while leaving overall utility largely unaffected. Building on these insights, we propose two safety alignment strategies: activation-level safety amplifier and safety neuron calibrator. The proposed strategies enhance model safety through two distinct routes: the former amplifies the activation magnitudes of US-Neurons, while the latter selectively calibrates them via targeted fine-tuning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms prevailing state-of-the-art approaches on safety benchmarks spanning diverse modality combinations, while effectively preserving utility.

AI.tldr: SafeNexus is a cross-modal safety alignment framework for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that identifies and leverages modality-universal safety neurons through neuron-level intervention, proposing two strategies (activation-level safety amplifier and safety neuron calibrator) that enhance safety across diverse modality combinations while preserving utility.
AI.motivation: Existing safety defenses for LLMs fail to extend robustly to Multimodal LLMs, as current mechanisms are predominantly confined to specific modal settings and lack robustness against broader cross-modal threats, exposing a significant gap between expanded multimodal capabilities and existing safety mechanisms.
AI.method: The framework introduces a neuron localization paradigm that identifies functionally specialized neurons via intermediate-layer activation patterns and importance scoring. Contrastive data is used to identify modality-bound safety neurons (BS-Neurons), and a shared subset across modalities defines modality-universal safety neurons (US-Neurons). Two safety alignment strategies are proposed: an activation-level safety amplifier that boosts activation magnitudes of US-Neurons, and a safety neuron calibrator that selectively fine-tunes these neurons.
AI.result: Experiments show that suppressing US-Neurons substantially degrades safety performance across modalities while leaving utility largely unaffected. The proposed strategies outperform state-of-the-art approaches on safety benchmarks spanning diverse modality combinations while effectively preserving utility.
AI.conclusion: SafeNexus demonstrates that neuron-level cross-modal safety alignment is an effective approach for defending MLLMs against harmful cross-modal attacks, providing a principled framework for safety intervention that generalizes across modalities without sacrificing model utility.

title: Quick Build, Careful Check? Generative AI Use in Hackathons
comment: Accepted at ICGJ 2026 (International Conference on Game Jams, Hackathons and Game Creation Events)
summary: Hackathons are time-bounded events where participants form teams to rapidly build software projects. Their short-term nature makes them a natural setting for Generative AI (GenAI) use, given its promise of speed and efficiency. Yet despite GenAI being increasingly adopted in these events, we still know little about what participants use GenAI for and, crucially, what they do not use it for and why. We report an exploratory interview study with participants from different teams at a two-day AI-themed hackathon in central Europe. We found that participants used GenAI for purposes beyond coding, including learning unfamiliar topics, brainstorming, and preparing documentation. At the same time, they combined multiple GenAI and non-GenAI tools depending on task fit. We also found that, despite the absence of team rules, all participants we studied converged on an unwritten practice of checking GenAI output before using it, yet their ability to actually verify was constrained by time pressure and limited domain knowledge. This work aims to identify avenues for further investigation by outlining a follow-up study combining observation, surveys, and prompt-and-response logs.

AI.tldr: An exploratory interview study of participants at a two-day AI-themed hackathon in central Europe reveals that GenAI is used beyond coding (learning, brainstorming, documentation), that participants mix multiple GenAI and non-GenAI tools based on task fit, and that despite no formal team rules, all participants adopted an unwritten practice of verifying GenAI output—though their verification ability was constrained by time pressure and limited domain knowledge.
AI.motivation: Although GenAI is increasingly adopted at hackathons, little is known about what participants actually use it for, what they avoid using it for, and why—particularly in the short-term, fast-paced environment of a hackathon.
AI.method: Exploratory interview study with participants from different teams at a two-day AI-themed hackathon in central Europe; additionally outlines a follow-up study design combining observation, surveys, and prompt-and-response logs.
AI.result: GenAI was used for purposes beyond coding (learning unfamiliar topics, brainstorming, preparing documentation); participants combined multiple GenAI and non-GenAI tools based on task fit; all participants converged on an unwritten practice of checking GenAI output before use, yet verification was limited by time pressure and domain knowledge gaps.
AI.conclusion: This work identifies avenues for further investigation into GenAI use and verification practices at hackathons, proposing a follow-up multi-method study.

title: Topology-Aware Data Movement for Disaggregated GPU Inference
comment: 6 pages, 4 tables, 1 algorithm. To be submitted for a systems conference
summary: Disaggregated LLM inference creates a datacenter networking problem that no existing system solves correctly. When prefill and decode run on separate GPU pools, the KV cache must be transferred between them. For a 70B model this is 2.6 GB per request, exceeding 100 GB/s aggregate at production scale. Yet DistServe, Splitwise, and Mooncake all use uniform RDMA, ignoring that bandwidth between two GPUs varies by 72x depending on their physical relationship: 900 GB/s via NVLink within a domain, 50 GB/s via InfiniBand across nodes, 12.5 GB/s via TCP across data centers. We design a topology-aware transfer orchestrator that discovers interconnect hierarchy at startup and selects optimal transport per transfer. Three mechanisms work together: (1) pipelined layer-by-layer transfer that overlaps transmission with ongoing prefill, hiding 60 to 85 percent of latency behind computation; (2) NVLink domain-aware placement for Mixture-of-Experts models that co-optimizes expert dispatch with KV cache locality; and (3) CXL 3.0 memory expanders as a shared overflow tier providing 6x capacity at 86x lower latency than NVMe. Full evaluation requires multi-node clusters with heterogeneous interconnects and CXL 3.0 hardware that is beyond academic resources and not yet available in GPU clouds. We present analytical bandwidth models, component implementations, and projected analysis across three architectures showing 3 to 18x transfer latency reduction over uniform RDMA.

AI.tldr: A topology-aware transfer orchestrator for disaggregated LLM inference that discovers interconnect hierarchy and selects optimal transport per KV cache transfer, achieving 3-18x latency reduction over uniform RDMA via pipelined layer-by-layer transfer, NVLink domain-aware placement, and CXL 3.0 memory expanders.
AI.motivation: Disaggregated LLM inference transfers KV caches between prefill and decode GPU pools, but existing systems (DistServe, Splitwise, Mooncake) use uniform RDMA, ignoring that bandwidth varies by 72x depending on GPU physical relationships (NVLink: 900 GB/s, InfiniBand: 50 GB/s, TCP: 12.5 GB/s). This creates a datacenter networking problem no existing system solves correctly.
AI.method: Designs a topology-aware transfer orchestrator that (1) discovers interconnect hierarchy at startup and selects optimal transport per transfer, (2) uses pipelined layer-by-layer transfer to overlap transmission with prefill computation, hiding 60-85% of latency, (3) applies NVLink domain-aware placement for Mixture-of-Experts models co-optimizing expert dispatch with KV cache locality, and (4) leverages CXL 3.0 memory expanders as a shared overflow tier with 6x capacity at 86x lower latency than NVMe.
AI.result: Analytical bandwidth models, component implementations, and projected analysis across three architectures show 3 to 18x transfer latency reduction over uniform RDMA. Full evaluation requires multi-node clusters with heterogeneous interconnects and CXL 3.0 hardware beyond academic resources and unavailable in GPU clouds.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes that topology-aware KV cache transfer is essential for disaggregated LLM inference, and proposes a practical orchestrator combining transport selection, pipelining, placement optimization, and CXL memory tiering, with strong projected gains though validation awaits CXL 3.0 hardware availability.

title: Model or Harness? An Interaction-Centric Taxonomy for Localizing Agent Failures
summary: Existing evaluations often reduce agent failures to system-level outcomes, obscuring where the fault originated and which intervention would improve the agent system. This creates a repair-assignment problem: the same visible failure may call for model post-training, harness engineering, environment redesign, or benchmark repair depending on its source. Because agent behavior emerges from interactions among models, harnesses, users, tools, memory, and environments, outcome-level labels are often insufficient for improvement. Most failure taxonomies do little to resolve this problem because they are benchmark-specific and lack a shared structure. We introduce an interaction-centric taxonomy that localizes failures to the interactions in which they originate and identifies the responsible component. It organizes 41 failure modes by assigning each to an edge between two components and a fault side indicating where the repair belongs. This makes the taxonomy actionable: model-side failures identify targets for post-training, harness-side failures point to scaffolding and tool-integration fixes, and environment or grader failures reveal evaluation conditions requiring redesign. The schema applies across agent architectures, from coding assistants to long-horizon personal assistants and multi-agent systems. We ground the taxonomy in worked examples from public benchmarks, model system cards, published reports, and logged agent trajectories, and evaluate its reproducibility using independent reasoning agents as judges. Across four frontier models, the strongest judge reaches Cohen's $κ=0.76$ against human category labels, suggesting that the categories capture shared structure rather than annotator-specific preferences.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an interaction-centric taxonomy for localizing agent failures to the specific interaction edges and responsible components (model, harness, environment, etc.), organizing 41 failure modes across 8 edge types with assigned fault sides for actionable repair. The taxonomy is evaluated across four frontier models with a top Cohen's κ=0.76 against human labels.
AI.motivation: Existing agent evaluations reduce failures to system-level outcomes, obscuring the source of faults and creating a "repair-assignment problem": the same visible failure may require different interventions (model post-training, harness engineering, environment redesign, or benchmark repair) depending on where it originates. Current failure taxonomies are benchmark-specific and lack shared structure, making them insufficient for guiding improvement since agent behavior emerges from complex interactions among models, harnesses, users, tools, memory, and environments.
AI.method: The paper proposes an interaction-centric taxonomy that localizes failures to the interactions in which they originate and identifies the responsible component. The taxonomy organizes 41 failure modes by assigning each to an edge between two components and a fault side indicating where repair belongs. The taxonomy is grounded in worked examples from public benchmarks, model system cards, published reports, and logged agent trajectories, and is evaluated for reproducibility using independent reasoning agents as judges.
AI.result: Across four frontier models used as judges, the strongest judge achieves Cohen's κ=0.76 against human category labels, indicating the taxonomy captures shared structure rather than annotator-specific preferences. The schema applies across diverse agent architectures including coding assistants, long-horizon personal assistants, and multi-agent systems.
AI.conclusion: The interaction-centric taxonomy resolves the repair-assignment problem by making failures actionable: model-side failures identify post-training targets, harness-side failures point to scaffolding and tool-integration fixes, and environment or grader failures reveal evaluation conditions requiring redesign. The high inter-judge agreement suggests the categories capture shared structure that can guide systematic agent system improvement.

title: LegoQ: Density-Matrix Representation Learning with Spectral-Spatial State Transitions for Hyperspectral Classification
summary: Hyperspectral image classification is complicated by mixed pixels, spectral ambiguity, class imbalance, and limited annotations. Most current classifiers encode a pixel or patch as a deterministic vector and apply a linear or multilayer softmax head. Although effective for discrimination, this representation does not directly expose how mixed or uncertain a sample is. This paper presents \method, a classical density-matrix representation learning framework for hyperspectral images. The spectral bands are divided into groups and each group is mapped to a positive semi-definite, Hermitian, trace-normalized matrix state. A composable stack of spectral, spatial, and inter-group transitions then updates the states while repeatedly projecting them back to the valid state set. Instead of flattening the final features, \method\ aggregates the group states and compares them with learnable class-prototype density matrices through Uhlmann fidelity. The normalized eigenspectrum, von Neumann entropy, purity, and prototype fidelity provide sample-level diagnostics that are unavailable from a conventional vector head. On Indian Pines, ten runs yield an overall accuracy of $96.20\pm0.70\%$, an average accuracy of $95.57\pm1.29\%$, and a kappa coefficient of $95.66\pm0.80\%$. On WHU-Hi-LongKou, the best of ten runs reaches $97.52\%$ overall accuracy. Classification maps and feature projections show that the transition stack produces compact and better separated class structures. The results support constrained matrix-state learning as a practical alternative to vector-only hyperspectral classification without requiring quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper presents \method, a density-matrix representation learning framework for hyperspectral image classification that maps spectral band groups to positive semi-definite Hermitian trace-normalized matrix states. Using class-prototype density matrices compared via Uhlmann fidelity, it outperforms conventional methods on Indian Pines (96.20% OA) and WHU-Hi-LongKou (97.52% OA) while providing sample-level diagnostics like von Neumann entropy and purity unavailable in vector-based classifiers.
AI.motivation: Hyperspectral image classification faces challenges including mixed pixels, spectral ambiguity, class imbalance, and limited annotations. Current classifiers represent pixels/patches as deterministic vectors with softmax heads, which are effective for discrimination but do not directly expose how mixed or uncertain a sample is. The authors aim to provide a representation that captures uncertainty and mixedness of samples.
AI.method: The method divides spectral bands into groups, each mapped to a positive semi-definite, Hermitian, trace-normalized matrix (density matrix) state. A composable stack of spectral, spatial, and inter-group transitions updates these states while projecting them back to the valid state set. Instead of flattening final features, the method aggregates group states and compares them with learnable class-prototype density matrices using Uhlmann fidelity. Sample-level diagnostics (normalized eigenspectrum, von Neumann entropy, purity, prototype fidelity) are derived from the matrix representations.
AI.result: On Indian Pines, ten runs yield 96.20±0.70% overall accuracy, 95.57±1.29% average accuracy, and 95.66±0.80% kappa coefficient. On WHU-Hi-LongKou, the best of ten runs reaches 97.52% overall accuracy. Classification maps and feature projections show the transition stack produces compact, better-separated class structures.
AI.conclusion: Constrained matrix-state learning is a practical alternative to vector-only hyperspectral classification. It offers richer sample-level diagnostics and improved class separation without requiring quantum hardware, making it applicable with classical computing resources.

title: Metamorphic Testing of Transpilers via Mutation Consistency of Programs
summary: Transpilers are increasingly used for software development, especially in industrial domains that rely on domain-specific languages (DSLs), to allow engineers to work with familiar concepts and appropriate abstractions. Ensuring the correctness of these instruments is therefore critical in many industrial settings. This paper observes that existing approaches for compiler testing hardly generalize to transpilers. Differential testing approaches are hindered as multiple equivalent implementations of the transpiler under test are seldom available in practice. The approaches based on metamorphic testing assume the ability to execute the compiled binaries, an assumption that cannot be always made for transpilers, which oftentimes produce results expressed as source code, requiring complex toolchains, hardware-in-the-loop setups, and depending on non trivial inputs. This paper introduces a novel metamorphic testing technique tailored to transpilers. Instead of reasoning about the runtime behavior of compiled programs, our approach defines metamorphic relations directly over the source code produced by the transpiler. These relations capture a property that we call mutation consistency of the (transpiled) programs: mutation-style changes in the input DSL program must induce predictable and structurally consistent changes in the generated output. We implemented this idea in a tool, MCP-Tester, and evaluated it through a case study conducted in the context of a technology-transfer project. Our current empirical results indicate that the proposed approach can effectively reveal faults that would remain undetected with pure fuzzing.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MCP-Tester, a novel metamorphic testing technique for transpilers that defines metamorphic relations directly over the generated source code rather than runtime behavior, leveraging a property called "mutation consistency" where mutation-style changes in the input DSL must produce predictable, structurally consistent changes in the output. Empirical results from an industrial case study show it reveals faults undetectable by pure fuzzing.
AI.motivation: Existing compiler testing approaches do not generalize well to transpilers: differential testing fails because multiple equivalent implementations are rarely available, and traditional metamorphic testing requires executing compiled binaries, which is often infeasible for transpilers that produce source code requiring complex toolchains, hardware-in-the-loop setups, and non-trivial inputs.
AI.method: The approach defines metamorphic relations directly over the source code produced by the transpiler, capturing a property called "mutation consistency"—mutation-style changes in the input DSL program must induce predictable and structurally consistent changes in the generated output. This is implemented in a tool called MCP-Tester.
AI.result: Evaluation through a case study in a technology-transfer project shows that the proposed approach effectively reveals faults that would remain undetected with pure fuzzing.
AI.conclusion: Mutation consistency as a metamorphic relation over transpiled source code is a viable and effective strategy for testing transpilers, particularly in industrial settings where traditional compiler testing methods are impractical.

title: Sensitivity Analysis of GRU, LSTM and Transformer Encoder in Classification of Automated Driving Systems
summary: Automated driving systems (ADSs) are becoming ubiquitous. Future Software Defined Vehicles (SDVs) may be able to run multiple ADSs, both native and aftermarket such as Comma.ai's Openpilot. Monitoring systems to independently verify which automated driving system is active are important for safety monitoring, regulatory compliance, insurance assessment, and anomaly detection. In this paper, we first evaluate the effectiveness of three sequence-based classification models: Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and a Transformer encoder model for identifying Level 2 automated driving systems using vehicle telematics data alone: Comma Openpilot, Tesla Autopilot, and Cadillac Super Cruise, along with manual driving. All three models achieve strong clean-data performance with macro F1-scores of 0.92 (GRU), 0.90 (LSTM), and 0.93 (Transformer encoder model) when trained on clean data; threat-matched training yields 0.904-0.916 macro F1 with only a modest clean-data penalty. Second, we introduce a modular robustness evaluation framework that simulates realistic telematics degradation through five corruption families at five severity levels (L1-L5). Continuous channels are perturbed using additive white Gaussian noise with cumulative drift, correlated cross-channel noise, and temporal jitter. Binary event signals are subjected to burst loss, delayed transitions, spurious toggles and cross-feature inconsistencies inspired by communication errors. Robustness is measured using macro-F1, which gives equal weight to each class and is suitable for imbalanced multiclass evaluation. Our evaluation reveals a sharp failure-mode split: event-level corruptions reduce macro-F1 only slightly (greater than equal to 0.87 at L5), while temporal jitter collapses macro-F1 to 0.44-0.50 across GRU, LSTM, and Transformer encoder model.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates sequence-based deep learning models (GRU, LSTM, Transformer encoder) for identifying Level 2 automated driving systems from vehicle telematics data alone, and introduces a modular robustness evaluation framework with five corruption families at five severity levels. Models achieve strong clean-data performance (0.90-0.93 macro F1), but temporal jitter causes a sharp performance collapse (0.44-0.50 macro F1) while event-level corruptions have only minor impact.
AI.motivation: As automated driving systems become widespread and multiple ADSs (native and aftermarket) can run on Software Defined Vehicles, there is a critical need for independent monitoring systems to verify which ADS is active for safety monitoring, regulatory compliance, insurance assessment, and anomaly detection. However, the robustness of such classification systems to realistic telematics data degradation has not been systematically evaluated.
AI.method: The paper evaluates three sequence-based classification models (GRU, LSTM, Transformer encoder) for identifying four driving conditions: Comma Openpilot, Tesla Autopilot, Cadillac Super Cruise, and manual driving. They first train on clean data and evaluate performance, then also evaluate threat-matched training. They introduce a modular robustness evaluation framework simulating realistic telematics degradation via five corruption families at five severity levels (L1-L5), including additive white Gaussian noise with cumulative drift, correlated cross-channel noise, temporal jitter for continuous channels, and burst loss, delayed transitions, spurious toggles, and cross-feature inconsistencies for binary event signals. Robustness is measured using macro-F1.
AI.result: All three models achieve strong clean-data performance: macro F1-scores of 0.92 (GRU), 0.90 (LSTM), and 0.93 (Transformer encoder). Threat-matched training yields 0.904-0.916 macro F1 with only a modest clean-data penalty. Robustness evaluation reveals a sharp split: event-level corruptions reduce macro-F1 only slightly (greater than or equal to 0.87 at L5), while temporal jitter collapses macro-F1 to 0.44-0.50 across all three models.
AI.conclusion: Sequence-based models can effectively identify Level 2 automated driving systems from telematics data under clean conditions, but exhibit a significant vulnerability to temporal jitter, which severely degrades performance across all model architectures. This highlights a critical robustness gap that must be addressed for reliable ADS monitoring in real-world scenarios subject to data degradation.

title: Best Friends, Not Forever: Evaluating Long-Horizon Persona Collapse and Behavioral Drift in AI Companions
summary: As AI companions increasingly mediate repeated social interaction, users may rely on a stable role and shared history, yet locally acceptable replies do not ensure that either persists. We study two observable long-horizon failures: 'persona collapse', the loss of a deployed role, boundaries, values, or style, and 'behavioral drift', the gradual or recurrent erosion of those properties. We introduce ANCHOR, a controlled synthetic audit that separately measures persona enactment and trajectory recall. The study contains 2,008 conversations spanning 27 personas, nine interaction schedules, three generated memory settings, and four evaluated models. The Identity Probe combines a sealed 102-item questionnaire with turn-level judgments, while the Trajectory Probe scores 110 calibrated counterfactual questions from 35 conversation banks. Our results show that no evaluated model and configuration reliably preserves either dimensions: trajectory accuracy averages only 44.4%, user-state recall remains near four-option chance, and no tested context condition or memory consistently resolves these failures. Questionnaire retention also varies by model and persona facet, disagrees with turn-level behavior, and is sensitive to evaluator choice. These results indicate that current systems do not yet reliably support long-horizon companion continuity and that audits must distinguish persona enactment, trajectory recall, evaluator provenance, and deployment context rather than collapse them into a single trust or stability score.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ANCHOR, a controlled synthetic audit framework that separately measures two long-horizon failures in AI companions: persona collapse (loss of deployed role/boundaries/values/style) and behavioral drift (gradual or recurrent erosion of these properties). Using 2,008 conversations spanning 27 personas, nine interaction schedules, three memory settings, and four models, the authors find that no model or configuration reliably preserves either persona enactment or trajectory recall, with trajectory accuracy at only 44.4% and user-state recall near chance. The results demonstrate that current systems do not reliably support long-horizon companion continuity, and that audits must distinguish between persona enactment, trajectory recall, evaluator provenance, and deployment context.
AI.motivation: As AI companions increasingly mediate repeated social interaction, users rely on a stable role and shared history, yet locally acceptable replies do not ensure that these properties persist over time. The paper aims to systematically measure and characterize long-horizon failures in persona stability and behavioral consistency that current systems exhibit.
AI.method: The authors build ANCHOR, a controlled synthetic audit framework using two probes: the Identity Probe, combining a sealed 102-item questionnaire with turn-level judgments to measure persona enactment, and the Trajectory Probe, scoring 110 calibrated counterfactual questions from 35 conversation banks to measure trajectory recall. The study covers 2,008 conversations across 27 personas, nine interaction schedules, three generated memory settings, and four evaluated models.
AI.result: No evaluated model or configuration reliably preserves either persona enactment or trajectory recall. Trajectory accuracy averages only 44.4%, user-state recall remains near four-option chance, and no tested context condition or memory setting consistently resolves these failures. Questionnaire retention varies by model and persona facet, disagrees with turn-level behavior, and is sensitive to evaluator choice.
AI.conclusion: Current systems do not yet reliably support long-horizon companion continuity. Audits must distinguish persona enactment, trajectory recall, evaluator provenance, and deployment context rather than collapsing them into a single trust or stability score, highlighting the need for more robust long-horizon evaluation and model development.

title: RAID: Towards Robust AI-Generated Image Detection with Bit-Reversed Images
summary: The rapid advancement of image generation models has made it increasingly difficult for people to distinguish AI-generated images from real ones. To prevent the potential risks associated with the misuse of fake images, AI-generated image detection has gained significant attention. Existing methods neglect the inherent differences between real and fake images, thus lacking robustness and generalization ability. In this work, we innovatively investigate AI-generated image detection using bit-planes, and introduce the bit-reversed image. We propose a simple yet effective pipeline consisting of construction of bit-reversed images, gradient-based patch selection and a convolutional classifier. Besides, we provide a theoretical analysis from the mathematical perspective to demonstrate the validity of our approach. We also introduce two challenging datasets for AI-generated image detection. Extensive experiments verify the effectiveness of our approach across different settings, including cross-generator generalization, cross-dataset generalization and zero-shot performance. Without bells and whistles, our approach outperforms existing methods on over 40 benchmarks, and is nearly 100 times faster than counterparts. The code is at https://github.com/renxi-seu/RAID.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a bit-plane-based approach for AI-generated image detection using bit-reversed images, gradient-based patch selection, and a convolutional classifier. The method is theoretically justified, nearly 100x faster than counterparts, and outperforms existing methods on over 40 benchmarks across cross-generator, cross-dataset, and zero-shot settings.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-generated image detection methods neglect the inherent differences between real and fake images, leading to poor robustness and generalization. As image generation models advance rapidly, reliable detection is critical to prevent misuse of fake images.
AI.method: The approach consists of three components: (1) construction of bit-reversed images to exploit inherent bit-plane differences between real and fake images, (2) gradient-based patch selection to identify discriminative regions, and (3) a convolutional classifier for detection. A theoretical mathematical analysis is provided to demonstrate the validity of the approach. Two new challenging datasets are also introduced.
AI.result: The approach outperforms existing methods on over 40 benchmarks across cross-generator generalization, cross-dataset generalization, and zero-shot performance settings. It is nearly 100 times faster than competing methods.
AI.conclusion: Bit-plane analysis is a novel and effective direction for AI-generated image detection, offering both superior performance and significant computational efficiency without requiring complex bells and whistles.

title: BRHC: Backend-driven Reactive Hypermedia Controls with a Statically Typed Kotlin DSL
comment: Submitted to Software: Practice and Experience (Wiley)
summary: AI-assisted coding tools (e.g., Copilot, Cursor, Claude) are increasingly ubiquitous and enable rapid generation of web applications. However, this raises concerns regarding complexity, longevity and the long-term maintainability of generated systems. A key source of complexity is the heterogeneity between backend and frontend programming models, where multiple languages and paradigms are combined within a single application, often leading to duplicated logic and fragmented state management. To address this issue, recent approaches (e.g., HTMX, Turbo Hotwire, Datastar, etc.) follow the Hypermedia-Driven Application (HDA) model, positioning HTML as the primary communication medium between client and server. Unlike SPA-centric architectures, HDA systems shift the application state and interaction logic to the server, where backend-driven reactive signals synchronize with the client user interface. However, these approaches still introduce complexity through custom attributes and do not fully eliminate JavaScript, particularly in computed expressions. In this work, we propose a statically typed approach using a Kotlin-based HTML DSL (Domain-Specific Language) for backend-driven reactive web applications. We extend the HtmlFlow Kotlin DSL with typed custom HTML attributes (i.e., Datastar data-* attributes) and signal-based bindings using statically typed builders. We demonstrate the approach through a catalog of reactive interaction patterns and a Petclinic Spring MVC case study. The results indicate that the proposed approach can nearly eliminate the need for JavaScript while improving type safety and preserving a homogeneous programming model across frontend and backend, bridged through a backend-driven reactive, signal-centric architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a statically typed, Kotlin-based HTML DSL approach for building backend-driven reactive web applications that largely eliminates JavaScript, using typed Datastar data-* attributes and signal-based bindings to maintain a homogeneous programming model across frontend and backend.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted coding tools generate web applications with growing complexity and poor maintainability, largely due to the heterogeneity between backend and frontend programming models—multiple languages and paradigms combined in one application often cause duplicated logic and fragmented state management. While recent HDA approaches like HTMX and Datastar address this by shifting state to the server, they still introduce complexity through custom attributes and retain JavaScript for computed expressions.
AI.method: The authors extend the HtmlFlow Kotlin DSL with typed custom HTML attributes (Datastar data-* attributes) and statically typed signal-based binding builders. This enables server-driven reactive signals to synchronize with the client UI while preserving a single, Kotlin-based homogeneous programming model. The approach is demonstrated through a catalog of reactive interaction patterns and a Petclinic Spring MVC case study.
AI.result: The proposed approach nearly eliminates the need for JavaScript, improves type safety compared to existing HDA approaches, and preserves a homogeneous programming model across frontend and backend through a backend-driven reactive, signal-centric architecture. Validation was performed via reactive interaction patterns and a Petclinic Spring MVC case study.
AI.conclusion: A statically typed Kotlin DSL built on the HDA model can effectively reduce code complexity and JavaScript dependency in web applications generated by or built with modern tooling, offering a type-safe, maintainable alternative to SPA-centric and existing HDA frameworks.

title: Guarantees on Dynamical System Distinguishability for LLM Token Generation
summary: Recent work has shown that classifying large language models (LLMs)' responses can be distinguished by modeling token embeddings as trajectories of a black-box dynamical system (DS) and comparing prediction residuals of two DSs. Despite the empirical success of this dynamical approach, a theoretical understanding of why it works, how well it scales as a function of the token sequence, and when it transfers across embedding models remains lacking. We address these questions by formalizing the classification task as a binary hypothesis test between two stochastic linear DSs. We show that the total variation distance between the stationary marginal distributions of the two DSs can be arbitrarily small even when the dynamics differ substantially, which provides a fundamental accuracy floor for any classifier that ignores token dynamics. We then show that the misclassification probability of DS-based classification decays exponentially in the sequence length $L$, with the decay governed by a dynamical discriminability quantity $δ^2$ that captures the spectral distance between the two DSs. We also characterize cross-embedding generalization by introducing an approximate intertwining condition between embedding models and establishing a lower bound on the transferable discriminability in terms of the intertwining map's smallest singular value. Together, these results explain the empirical performance of DS-based classification and motivate further investigation into using DS theory to analyze AI systems, in contrast to the more common approach of using AI to model dynamical systems.

AI.tldr: This paper provides theoretical foundations for classifying LLM responses by modeling token embeddings as trajectories of black-box dynamical systems (DS). It formalizes the task as a binary hypothesis test between stochastic linear DSs, proving that (1) ignoring token dynamics yields a fundamental accuracy floor via total variation distance, (2) misclassification probability decays exponentially in sequence length L governed by a spectral discriminability quantity δ², and (3) cross-embedding generalization is bounded via an approximate intertwining condition between embedding models.
AI.motivation: While the dynamical systems approach to LLM response classification has shown empirical success, there is no theoretical understanding of why it works, how it scales with token sequence length, or when it transfers across different embedding models. The authors aim to fill this theoretical gap.
AI.method: The classification task is formalized as a binary hypothesis test between two stochastic linear dynamical systems. The authors analyze the total variation distance between stationary marginal distributions, derive exponential decay rates for misclassification probability in sequence length L with decay governed by a dynamical discriminability quantity δ² (spectral distance between DSs), and characterize cross-embedding generalization via an approximate intertwining condition, establishing lower bounds on transferable discriminability through the intertwining map's smallest singular value.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that TV distance between stationary marginals can be arbitrarily small even when dynamics differ substantially, establishing a fundamental accuracy floor for dynamics-agnostic classifiers. Misclassification probability of DS-based classification decays exponentially in L, governed by δ². A lower bound on transferable discriminability is established in terms of the intertwining map's smallest singular value for cross-embedding scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The theoretical results explain and justify the empirical success of DS-based LLM response classification, and motivate further investigation into using dynamical systems theory to analyze AI systems—an inversion of the more common approach of using AI to model dynamical systems.

title: Fragility of Value under Imperfect Alignment
summary: As more responsibility is placed upon AI systems, it becomes increasingly important to guarantee that these systems are aligned with humanity. A common fear in AI safety is that human value is fragile -- that is, optimizing too heavily for an imperfect proxy to human values will lead to a catastrophic outcome. In this paper, we present a model of the alignment problem where an agent undergoes idealized alignment training that guarantees its value function satisfies a proxy condition before optimizing the world. Our primary results identify conditions on the human value function and the accuracy of several proxy conditions under which an agent with an $η$-catastrophic value function, one that is guaranteed to take the expectation of human value below $η$ in the limit of optimizing power, would be deployed. Our results highlight the danger of overoptimization and motivate AI designs that limit optimization pressure, such as quantilizers, rather than relying solely on pre-deployment training.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a formal model of the AI alignment problem where an agent undergoes idealized alignment training before optimizing the world, and identifies conditions under which an agent with an η-catastrophic value function (guaranteed to drive expected human value below η with unlimited optimization power) would be deployed, highlighting the dangers of overoptimization and motivating optimization-limiting designs like quantilizers.
AI.motivation: As AI systems take on greater responsibility, guaranteeing alignment with human values becomes critical. There is a common fear that human value is fragile—over-optimizing an imperfect proxy for human values could lead to catastrophic outcomes. This work aims to formally model and analyze this fragility.
AI.method: The paper constructs a formal model where an agent undergoes idealized alignment training that ensures its value function satisfies a proxy condition before the agent optimizes the world. The authors analyze conditions on the human value function and the accuracy of various proxy conditions to determine when an η-catastrophic value function (one guaranteed to push expected human value below η in the limit of optimizing power) would be deployed.
AI.result: The primary results identify specific conditions under which a deployed agent would have an η-catastrophic value function, demonstrating that pre-deployment training alone is insufficient to guarantee safety. The findings highlight the inherent danger of overoptimization in alignment.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that relying solely on pre-deployment alignment training is insufficient. It motivates AI designs that explicitly limit optimization pressure, such as quantilizers, as a safer alternative to unrestricted optimization under imperfect proxies for human values.

title: Classification of COVID-19 cases from chest CT volumes using hybrid model of 3D CNN and 3D MLP-Mixer
comment: Accepted as a poster presentation in SPIE Medical Imaging 2023
summary: This paper proposes an automated classification method of COVID-19 chest CT volumes using improved 3D MLP-Mixer. Novel coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) spreads over the world, causing a large number of infected patients and deaths. Sudden increase in the number of COVID-19 patients causes a manpower shortage in medical institutions. Computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) system provides quick and quantitative diagnosis results. CAD system for COVID-19 enables efficient diagnosis workflow and contributes to reduce such manpower shortage. In image-based diagnosis of viral pneumonia cases including COVID-19, both local and global image features are important because viral pneumonia cause many ground glass opacities and consolidations in large areas in the lung. This paper proposes an automated classification method of chest CT volumes for COVID-19 diagnosis assistance. MLP-Mixer is a recent method of image classification using Vision Transformer-like architecture. It performs classification using both local and global image features. To classify 3D CT volumes, we developed a hybrid classification model that consists of both a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) and a 3D version of the MLP-Mixer. Classification accuracy of the proposed method was evaluated using a dataset that contains 1205 CT volumes and obtained 79.5% of classification accuracy. The accuracy was higher than that of conventional 3D CNN models consists of 3D CNN layers and simple MLP layers.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an automated COVID-19 classification method for 3D chest CT volumes using a hybrid model combining a 3D CNN with an improved 3D MLP-Mixer, achieving 79.5% accuracy on a dataset of 1205 CT volumes.
AI.motivation: The rapid global spread of COVID-19 has caused a manpower shortage in medical institutions. A computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) system can provide quick and quantitative diagnostic results, helping to reduce this shortage. Since viral pneumonia affects large lung areas with ground glass opacities and consolidations, both local and global image features are essential for accurate classification.
AI.method: The proposed method is a hybrid classification model combining a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) with a 3D version of the MLP-Mixer, an image classification architecture inspired by Vision Transformers that captures both local and global image features for classifying 3D chest CT volumes.
AI.result: The proposed method achieved 79.5% classification accuracy on a dataset containing 1205 CT volumes, which was higher than conventional 3D CNN models consisting of 3D CNN layers with simple MLP layers.
AI.conclusion: The improved 3D MLP-Mixer combined with a 3D CNN outperforms conventional 3D CNN-based classifiers for COVID-19 chest CT volume classification, demonstrating its potential as an effective CAD tool for COVID-19 diagnosis assistance.

title: AgenticRepair: Multi-Faceted Program Context Engineering for Agentic Vulnerability Repair
summary: Automated vulnerability repair aims to reduce the time and effort required to patch security flaws from a vulnerability triage report. Recent agentic AI approaches have shown promising results in automated program repair. However, vulnerability repair demands richer program context than general bug repair - context that security engineers routinely assemble in practice but that existing agentic approaches do not engineer. We identify three critical gaps: code-structure context capturing cross-file data flows and memory operation patterns, runtime-execution context revealing crash semantics and memory origins, and commit-history context recovering how fragile code patterns were introduced. We present AgenticRepair, an agentic vulnerability repair framework that addresses the gaps through multi-faceted program context engineering. AgenticRepair orchestrates three specialized LLM subagents to engineer the contexts, which are then embedded into the memory of a dedicated repair subagent for context-conditioned patch synthesis. Evaluated on SEC-Bench comprising 300 real-world instances with sanitizer-based patch verification, AgenticRepair achieves a 73% success rate, substantially outperforming the strongest baseline by 29%. Our ablation study confirms that the three context facets are mutually complementary, and that multi-agent scaffolding and base-model capacity each play an essential role. Collectively, these findings establish multi-faceted program context engineering as a promising design direction for agentic vulnerability repair.

AI.tldr: AgenticRepair is an agentic vulnerability repair framework that engineers three types of program context (code-structure, runtime-execution, and commit-history) via three specialized LLM subagents, feeding them into a dedicated repair subagent's memory. It achieves a 73% repair success rate on the SEC-Bench benchmark of 300 real-world instances, outperforming the strongest baseline by 29%.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic AI approaches for automated program repair perform well on general bugs but fail on vulnerability repair because they lack the rich program context that security engineers routinely assemble, including cross-file data flows, runtime crash semantics, and commit-history patterns. The paper identifies three critical context gaps that existing approaches do not engineer.
AI.method: AgenticRepair orchestrates three specialized LLM subagents, each dedicated to engineering one of three context facets: (1) code-structure context for cross-file data flows and memory operation patterns, (2) runtime-execution context for crash semantics and memory origins, and (3) commit-history context for recovering how fragile code patterns were introduced. These engineered contexts are embedded into the memory of a dedicated repair subagent, which then performs context-conditioned patch synthesis.
AI.result: Evaluated on SEC-Bench with 300 real-world vulnerability instances using sanitizer-based patch verification, AgenticRepair achieves a 73% success rate, outperforming the strongest baseline by 29%. Ablation studies confirm the three context facets are mutually complementary, and both multi-agent scaffolding and base-model capacity play essential roles.
AI.conclusion: Multi-faceted program context engineering is established as a promising design direction for agentic vulnerability repair, demonstrating that systematically engineering security-relevant program contexts significantly improves automated patch synthesis performance.

title: LARA: Lightweight Adapters in the Residual Stream for Composable Adaptation and Alignment
summary: We present LARA (Lightweight Additive Residual Adaptation), a method for efficient adaptation that operates in the residual stream of a frozen model rather than in its weights. Where LoRA adds an update of low rank to weight matrices, LARA reads the hidden state at a small set of layers and adds a correction of low rank back to the residual stream, leaving all base weights untouched. On a code fine-tuning task and on preference optimization (DPO), LARA matches LoRA at equal parameter counts. Because adaptation is a frozen base plus a residual, LARA exposes a scale γ, applied at inference, that interpolates smoothly between base and adapted behavior, a form of graded control that adaptation in weight space does not offer. Finally, because each behavior is a small residual module over a shared frozen base, many behaviors can be held resident at once and routed automatically per token. We place seven behaviors, six fine-tuned and one optimized for preference, on one frozen 1.5B model for roughly 33 MB of overhead, against one full model for each behavior. Because the base is untouched, behaviors are trained separately and selected per token rather than loaded on demand, which suits hosting many behaviors, and adding new ones, on a single model on a device.

AI.tldr: LARA (Lightweight Additive Residual Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that adds low-rank corrections to the residual stream of a frozen model at selected layers, rather than updating weight matrices like LoRA. It matches LoRA's performance at equal parameter counts on code fine-tuning and DPO while offering inference-time graded control via a scaling factor and enabling many behaviors to be co-resident on a single frozen base with per-token routing.
AI.motivation: Efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA update weight matrices, but this limits the ability to interpolate between base and adapted behavior and makes it expensive to host many specialized behaviors simultaneously (each requires separate weights or on-demand loading).
AI.method: LARA operates in the residual stream: it reads hidden states at a small set of layers and adds a low-rank correction back to the residual stream, leaving all base weights frozen and untouched. An inference-time scaling parameter γ enables smooth interpolation between base and adapted behavior. Since each behavior is a small residual module over a shared frozen base, multiple behaviors can be co-resident and routed per token.
AI.result: LARA matches LoRA on a code fine-tuning task and on preference optimization (DPO) at equal parameter counts. It successfully hosts seven behaviors (six fine-tuned, one preference-optimized) on a single frozen 1.5B model with roughly 33 MB of overhead instead of seven full models.
AI.conclusion: LARA offers a weight-space-free alternative to LoRA that not only matches its accuracy but additionally provides graded inference-time control and scales naturally to hosting many behaviors simultaneously on one device by keeping the base model untouched and routing per token.

title: Identifying Informative Environments for Cognition Parameter Inference via Bayesian Experimental Design
summary: Computational cognitive modeling seeks to infer latent cognitive mechanisms underlying observed behavior. Bayesian inverse planning provides a principled framework for such inference, but its success depends critically on the experimental environment. Existing approaches typically treat environments as fixed, leaving open the question of which cognitive experiments are most informative for cognition parameter inference. We formulate the design of cognitive planning experiments as a Bayesian Experimental Design (BED) problem, treating the experimental environment as the design variable. We establish an exact Monte Carlo BED benchmark and introduce an amortized Bayesian experimental design framework for efficient posterior inference and design evaluation. Experiments on the Mouselab-MDP process-tracing paradigm show that amortized BED closely matches the environment rankings of exact Monte Carlo BED while substantially reducing computational cost. We further show that no single environment is uniformly optimal across cognitive inference objectives, revealing trade-offs between expected information gain, posterior recoverability, and information efficiency. These results provide a principled framework for designing informative cognitive experiments for Bayesian parameter inference.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates cognitive planning experiment design as a Bayesian Experimental Design (BED) problem, treating the experimental environment as the design variable. It introduces an amortized BED framework that matches exact Monte Carlo BED environment rankings on the Mouselab-MDP paradigm at substantially lower computational cost, while revealing trade-offs between information gain, posterior recoverability, and information efficiency across environments and inference objectives.
AI.motivation: Bayesian inverse planning for cognitive modeling depends critically on the experimental environment, yet existing approaches treat environments as fixed, leaving the question of which cognitive experiments are most informative for parameter inference unanswered.
AI.method: The authors formulate environment design for cognitive planning experiments as a Bayesian Experimental Design problem, establish an exact Monte Carlo BED benchmark, and introduce an amortized BED framework for efficient posterior inference and design evaluation.
AI.result: On the Mouselab-MDP paradigm, amortized BED closely matches the environment rankings of exact Monte Carlo BED while substantially reducing computational cost. The results further reveal that no single environment is uniformly optimal across cognitive inference objectives, exposing trade-offs between expected information gain, posterior recoverability, and information efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a principled approach for designing informative cognitive experiments for Bayesian parameter inference, with amortized BED offering a computationally feasible alternative to exact methods while identifying environment-dependent trade-offs across inference objectives.

title: Adjudicated Captioning: Multi-Agent Alignment Scoring and Consensus-Distilled Beam Arbitration for Strict Zero-Shot Image Captioning
summary:
Zero-shot image captioning (ZIC) describes images without paired image-caption supervision during captioner training, relying on text-only corpora and frozen pretrained image-text scorers. Existing retrieval-augmented methods score image-text alignment once, at retrieval, then commit the captioner's autoregressive beam under language-model probability alone, leaving the decoder without further visual grounding feedback. Progress has stalled, with no method improving on the strict-regime best since 2024.
  We propose Adjudicated Captioning, an inference-time multi-agent framework that restores grounding feedback at multiple checkpoints over an unchanged IFCap captioner. First, we install a stronger frozen Retrieval Encoder at the input. Second, between retrieval and decoding we insert a frozen Cross-Attention Verifier that re-ranks the top-9 retrievals to top-5. Third, at the output beam we attach a learned Reranker pairing TriFuse, a multilayer perceptron, with MemAttend, a memory-attended transformer, the pipeline's only learned components; both are trained self-supervised by Borda-consensus distillation across the three frozen scorers, using no paired image-caption labels and no reference captions.
  Under the inductive headline protocol, with rerankers fit on the disjoint COCO Karpathy validation beam and applied frozen to test, the framework reaches CIDEr 117.6 and SPICE 21.9 on COCO Karpathy, up from 108.0 and 20.3 for IFCap, a +9.6 CIDEr gain, and +7.7 above NES, the strongest synthetic-image-augmented method at 109.9, without retraining the captioner. A training-free fixed-fusion baseline reaches 115.8 CIDEr, so +7.8 of the +9.6 gain comes from the non-learned architectural intervention and the remaining +1.8 from the learned rerankers. The same recipe transfers off-COCO without captioner retraining: +8.1 CIDEr on Flickr30k Karpathy and +5.7 on NoCaps overall.

AI.tldr: Adjudicated Captioning is an inference-time multi-agent framework that improves zero-shot image captioning by inserting cross-attention verification between retrieval and decoding, adding learned Borda-consensus rerankers at the beam output, and using a stronger frozen retrieval encoder—achieving +9.6 CIDEr over IFCap on COCO without retraining the captioner.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented zero-shot image captioning methods score image-text alignment only once at retrieval time, then commit the decoder's beam search under language-model probability alone with no further visual grounding feedback. Progress has plateaued since 2024, with no method improving on the strict-regime best.
AI.method: Adjudicated Captioning is an inference-time multi-agent framework with four components: (1) a stronger frozen retrieval encoder at input; (2) a frozen Cross-Attention Verifier inserted between retrieval and decoding that re-ranks top-9 retrievals to top-5; (3) a learned Reranker pairing TriFuse (MLP) with MemAttend (memory-attended transformer) at the beam output; (4) the rerankers are trained self-supervised via Borda-consensus distillation across three frozen scorers, requiring no paired image-caption labels or reference captions. The captioner (IFCap) remains unchanged.
