AI.result: Under the inductive headline protocol, the framework reaches CIDEr 117.6 and SPICE 21.9 on COCO Karpathy (up from 108.0/20.3 for IFCap), a +9.6 CIDEr gain, and +7.7 above NES (the strongest synthetic-augmented method at 109.9), without retraining the captioner. A training-free fixed-fusion baseline reaches 115.8 CIDEr, showing +7.8 of the +9.6 gain comes from non-learned architectural changes and +1.8 from learned rerankers. The recipe transfers off-COCO: +8.1 CIDEr on Flickr30k Karpathy and +5.7 on NoCaps overall.
AI.conclusion: Restoring visual grounding feedback at multiple checkpoints over an unchanged captioner yields substantial zero-shot image captioning gains. The bulk of improvement is attributable to non-learned architectural interventions (retrieval encoder upgrade and cross-attention verification), while learned rerankers trained by Borda-consensus distillation provide an additional complementary boost, and the method generalizes off-COCO without captioner retraining.

title: From Code Review to Code Critique: Intent, Drift, and Spotlight for AI-Generated Diffs at Scale
summary: AI coding agents are generating code at volumes that exceed the capacity of traditional peer review. At the same time, existing AI code review tools over-index on low-value suggestions such as style and best practices while under-indexing on the concerns human reviewers prioritize most: correctness, security, and performance. We present ARCTIC, an AI-powered Code Critique system that reframes code review around three capabilities: intent prediction, which infers why a change was made from conversation logs and metadata; drift detection, which measures divergence between the developer's intent and the agent's output via backtranslation; and code spotlight, which ranks the regions of a diff most warranting human scrutiny. We ground these capabilities in a six-theme taxonomy derived from 18,000 code reviews. Offline evaluation shows that intent prediction achieves 0.86 F1, drift detection reaches near-perfect ordinal agreement with human annotators (QWK = 0.907), and spotlight outperforms the baseline AI reviewer by 2.4x on quality estimation at 5x fewer tokens. In the experimental rollout, the drift scores reduces code misalignment by an additional 5.76 points (p = 0.026), intent prediction receives 90.2% approval, and zero defects have been attributed to self-reviewed diffs since launch.

AI.tldr: ARCTIC is an AI-powered Code Critique system that reframes code review around three capabilities—intent prediction, drift detection, and code spotlight—to address the scalability problem of AI-generated code outpacing traditional peer review, prioritizing correctness, security, and performance over low-value style suggestions.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents produce code at volumes exceeding traditional peer review capacity, while existing AI code review tools over-index on low-value suggestions (style, best practices) and under-index on what human reviewers care about most: correctness, security, and performance.
AI.method: ARCTIC is built around three core capabilities: (1) intent prediction—infers why a change was made from conversation logs and metadata; (2) drift detection—measures divergence between developer intent and agent output via backtranslation; (3) code spotlight—ranks diff regions most warranting human scrutiny. These are grounded in a six-theme taxonomy derived from 18,000 code reviews.
AI.result: Offline: intent prediction achieves 0.86 F1, drift detection reaches near-perfect ordinal agreement with human annotators (QWK = 0.907), and spotlight outperforms baseline AI reviewer by 2.4x on quality estimation at 5x fewer tokens. Online: drift scores reduce code misalignment by 5.76 points (p = 0.026), intent prediction receives 90.2% approval, and zero defects attributed to self-reviewed diffs since launch.
AI.conclusion: ARCTIC demonstrates that reframing AI code review around intent, drift, and targeted scrutiny provides a scalable, human-aligned approach to reviewing AI-generated code, achieving both strong offline metrics and real-world deployment success with zero post-launch defects.

title: Hierarchical Copula-Gumbel-Top-\texorpdfstring{$K$}{K} Routing: Two-Sided Dependence Control for Frozen Mixture-of-Experts at Fixed Per-Token Routing Laws
summary: A stochastic Gumbel-Top-$K$ router defines, for every token of a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, a \emph{routing law}: a distribution over ordered expert lists and mixture weights. We ask which \emph{joint} distributions over the routing choices of different tokens are reachable while every individual token's complete routing law is held exactly fixed. We give a two-sided construction, \emph{Hierarchical Copula-Gumbel-Top-$K$} (\CGA{}). Within a group of related tokens, an exchangeable Gaussian copula positively correlates the Gumbel perturbations at each expert coordinate, which can increase within-group expert-set coherence. Across disjoint pairs of groups, a tunable antithetic construction introduces a selectable amount of negative dependence. We prove that both operations leave each token's ordered Top-$K$ sample, mixture weights, and inclusion probabilities identical in distribution to independent routing \emph{at a routing layer conditioned on its pre-routing logits}; conditional expected expert traffic is preserved as a consequence. We characterize the resulting trade-off: positive within-group coupling can only inflate the variance of realized expert loads relative to independent routing, while nonnegative cross-group opposition can only reduce it relative to flat coupling at the same within-group strength. Coherence and load dispersion are thus controlled by two complementary dependence dials on the invariance constraint surface. Because the base model is untouched, the dials can be driven by a small controller over frozen features, trainable with a score-function estimator: the frozen network is evaluated only in the forward direction, and gradients are confined to the controller. An initial small-scale pilot validates the mechanism and the training route, but does not establish task-level fine-tuning gains.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Hierarchical Copula-Gumbel-Top-K (CGA), a two-sided construction that ranges over joint distributions of routing choices across tokens in a Gumbel-Top-K MoE model while keeping each token's marginal routing law exactly fixed—positive within-group coupling via an exchangeable Gaussian copula and tunable cross-group antithetic negative dependence. It proves these operations preserve marginal routing distributions and characterizes a variance trade-off: positive coupling inflates load variance while cross-group opposition reduces it. A trainable controller over frozen features is proposed with score-function estimation.
AI.motivation: The authors ask which joint distributions over routing choices of different tokens are reachable while keeping each token's complete individual routing law (ordered expert list, mixture weights, inclusion probabilities) exactly fixed. This enables controlling expert-load coherence and dispersion in MoE models without modifying the base model.
AI.method: They construct Hierarchical Copula-Gumbel-Top-K (CGA): within a group of related tokens, an exchangeable Gaussian copula positively correlates Gumbel perturbations per expert coordinate; across disjoint pairs of groups, a tunable antithetic construction induces selectable negative dependence. They prove both operations preserve every token's marginal ordered Top-K sample, mixture weights, and inclusion probabilities conditional on pre-routing logits. Dependence is driven by a small controller over frozen features, trained with a score-function estimator.
AI.result: They characterize the trade-off: positive within-group coupling can only inflate variance of realized expert loads relative to independent routing, while nonnegative cross-group opposition can only reduce it relative to flat coupling at the same within-group strength. An initial small-scale pilot validates the mechanism and training route but does not establish task-level fine-tuning gains.
AI.conclusion: Coherence and load dispersion are controlled by two complementary dependence dials on the invariance-constraint surface; the base model remains untouched, and the approach is trainable in a gradient-confined manner, offering a promising direction for controlling expert utilization in MoE routing, pending larger-scale task-level validation.

title: NeSyFS: A Neuro-symbolic Fast-Slow Thinking Framework for LLM Agent under Partial Observability
summary: Recently Large Language Models (LLMs) have been increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in applications such as self-reflection, retrieval-augmented generation, and scientific discovery. In these settings, agents must act based on limited observations rather than full environmental states, leading to partial observability. This introduces several key challenges: belief state inference, task objective misalignment, and planning under uncertainty. Prior approaches typically condition actions on full or summarized action-observation histories whose redundant and irrelevant information can mislead the decision making of LLM agent. Inspired by human cognition, we propose a novel neuro-symbolic fast-slow thinking (NeSyFS) framework for LLM agent, addressing the challenges introduced by partial observability in a unified approach. We use a knowledge graph (KG) to represent the belief state, providing triplets as context for every module of NeSyFS. The fast-thinking module performs reactive action, while slow-thinking conducts a new uncertainty-aware planning by following the high-level structure of twisted sequential Monte Carlo (TSMC) algorithm. To mitigate the misalignment of task objective, a reflection module is used to reflect fast-thinking actions, and also switches to the slow-thinking module whenever reactive actions repeatedly fail. Experiments on three representative benchmarks, i.e. ALFWorld, Webshop, and ScienceWorld, demonstrate significant advantages over previous methods.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces NeSyFS, a neuro-symbolic fast-slow thinking framework for LLM agents operating under partial observability. It uses a knowledge graph to represent belief states, combines a fast-thinking reactive module with a slow-thinking uncertainty-aware planner based on twisted sequential Monte Carlo, and includes a reflection module to handle task-objective misalignment. Experiments on ALFWorld, Webshop, and ScienceWorld show significant improvements over prior methods.
AI.motivation: LLM agents deployed in autonomous settings face partial observability, which introduces challenges including belief state inference, task objective misalignment, and planning under uncertainty. Prior methods condition actions on full or summarized action-observation histories, whose redundant and irrelevant information can mislead the agent's decision making.
AI.method: The proposed NeSyFS framework uses a knowledge graph to represent the belief state, providing triplets as context to every module. It comprises: (1) a fast-thinking module for reactive action execution, (2) a slow-thinking module that performs uncertainty-aware planning using a twisted sequential Monte Carlo (TSMC) algorithm, and (3) a reflection module that corrects fast-thinking actions and triggers switching to slow-thinking when reactive actions repeatedly fail.
AI.result: Experiments on three representative benchmarks—ALFWorld, Webshop, and ScienceWorld—demonstrate significant advantages over previous methods.
AI.conclusion: The NeSyFS framework effectively addresses partial observability in LLM agents in a unified manner by combining knowledge-graph-based belief representation, dual-speed thinking modules, and reflection-based objective alignment, yielding superior performance across multiple benchmark tasks.

title: CAER: Conflict-Aware Evidence Routing with Dual Prefix Experts for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in multimodal understanding and generation. However, when textual inputs conflict with visual evidence, they still suffer from hallucinations and produce responses inconsistent with visual content. Existing approaches mainly rely on decoding strategies, additional training, verification methods, or prompting techniques, but often lack fine-grained conflict localization and conflict-aware generation. In this work, we propose CAER, a backbone-agnostic framework for visual-language conflict detection and conflict-aware generation. CAER introduces a span-grounded evidence router that transforms claim representations into soft textual queries and retrieves corresponding evidence from frozen visual tokens, enabling fine-grained conflict estimation. Furthermore, we design a dual-prefix expert routing mechanism that learns separate experts for visually supported and contradicted inputs, enabling conflict-aware generation through explicit expert selection. Experiments on the public MMMC benchmark and our newly curated AgriConflict dataset demonstrate that CAER effectively detects visual-language conflicts and improves the reliability of open-source MLLMs without updating their backbone parameters.

AI.tldr: CAER is a backbone-agnostic framework for detecting and handling visual-language conflicts in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), using a span-grounded evidence router for fine-grained conflict localization and a dual-prefix expert routing mechanism for conflict-aware generation, all without updating backbone parameters.
AI.motivation: MLLMs still suffer from hallucinations when textual inputs conflict with visual evidence. Existing approaches (decoding strategies, extra training, verification, prompting) lack fine-grained conflict localization and conflict-aware generation capabilities.
AI.method: CAER introduces (1) a span-grounded evidence router that converts claim representations into soft textual queries and retrieves evidence from frozen visual tokens for fine-grained conflict estimation, and (2) a dual-prefix expert routing mechanism that learns separate experts for visually supported versus contradicted inputs, enabling explicit expert selection for conflict-aware generation.
AI.result: Experiments on the public MMMC benchmark and a newly curated AgriConflict dataset demonstrate that CAER effectively detects visual-language conflicts and improves the reliability of open-source MLLMs without updating their backbone parameters.
AI.conclusion: CAER provides an effective, backbone-agnostic solution for conflict-aware generation in MLLMs, improving reliability through fine-grained conflict detection and explicit expert routing without modifying the underlying model parameters.

title: Students' Practices and Skills in the LLM-Era: "You Can't Outsource the Struggle and Still Get the Skill"
summary: Generative AI tools have been rapidly learned in the daily workflow of graduate students in Software Engineering, but little is known about what AI-related skills they actually need for effective use in empirical research. Without this understanding, graduate programs cannot prepare students to conduct rig-orous research in the LLM era, risking creating a generation of researchers who delegate tasks without the necessary expertise. By analyzing 1,383 posts from five research-focused subreddits, we found that students systematically outsource the cognitive effort required to develop research skills and end up with neither the expected results nor the necessary competence. Naming these missing skills is the first step toward curricula that teach graduate students to work \emph{with} LLMs without being replaced by them.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes 1,383 Reddit posts from five research-focused subreddits to identify what AI-related skills graduate students in Software Engineering need when using generative AI in empirical research. The authors find that students systematically outsource cognitive effort needed for skill development, failing to achieve both expected results and necessary competence, and propose that naming these missing skills is the first step toward curricula that teach students to work with LLMs without being replaced by them.
AI.motivation: Generative AI tools are rapidly adopted by graduate students in Software Engineering, yet there is little understanding of what AI-related skills students actually need for effective use in empirical research. Without this knowledge, graduate programs cannot prepare students for rigorous research in the LLM era, risking a generation of researchers who delegate tasks without essential expertise.
AI.method: The study analyzes 1,383 posts from five research-focused subreddits to identify the AI-related skills gap among graduate students in Software Engineering.
AI.result: Students systematically outsource the cognitive effort required to develop research skills, resulting in neither expected outcomes nor the necessary competence. The missing skills are identified and named.
AI.conclusion: Identifying the specific missing AI-related skills is the first step toward designing curricula that teach graduate students to work effectively with LLMs without being replaced by them, ensuring they retain necessary expertise for rigorous empirical research.

title: LAWFUL: Law-Aligned Witness for Faithful Use of Latents
summary: When a neural network predicts a physical system accurately, has it learned the governing law as formal, structured knowledge, and if so, does the network's internal computation actually use that representation throughout the law's domain of validity? We identify four interpretability gaps that limit answering these questions for {\em physics laws over continuous variables}: the absence of a coverage-aware causal-consistency measure over continuous counterfactuals; of a domain-of-validity test for the identified circuit; of a verification of the law's invariants and forbidden behaviors; and of a quantification of how a derived physical quantity flows through the circuit. We develop a foundational framework, LAWFUL, that closes the first two and lays groundwork for the remaining two, and illustrate it on the Mocap2Radar transformer, validating whether it learns and internally uses the Doppler frequency law $f(t) = \frac{2 v(t)}λ$ from motion-capture and radar data in which neither $f(t)$ nor $v(t)$ appears.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LAWFUL, a foundational interpretability framework that addresses four gaps in verifying whether a neural network has learned and internally uses physical laws (defined over continuous variables) as structured knowledge. It is validated on the Mocap2Radar transformer, testing whether it learns and uses the Doppler frequency law f(t)=2v(t)/λ from data where neither variable appears explicitly.
AI.motivation: Even when a neural network predicts a physical system accurately, it is unclear whether it has actually learned the governing law as formal, structured knowledge, and whether its internal computation genuinely employs that representation across the entire domain of validity. Four interpretability gaps hinder answering this: no coverage-aware causal-consistency measure over continuous counterfactuals, no domain-of-validity test for identified circuits, no verification of law invariants and forbidden behaviors, and no quantification of how derived physical quantities flow through the circuit.
AI.method: The paper develops LAWFUL, a foundational framework that closes the first two interpretability gaps (coverage-aware causal-consistency measurement over continuous counterfactuals and domain-of-validity testing for identified circuits) and lays groundwork for the remaining two (verification of law invariants/forbidden behaviors and quantification of physical quantity flow through the circuit). It is illustrated on the Mocap2Radar transformer, which maps motion-capture to radar data in which neither the Doppler frequency f(t) nor the velocity v(t) appears.
AI.result: The framework is applied to the Mocap2Radar transformer to validate whether it learns and internally uses the Doppler frequency law f(t)=2v(t)/λ.
AI.conclusion: LAWFUL provides a principled framework for closing critical interpretability gaps when verifying whether neural networks learn and internally use physical laws over continuous variables, demonstrated on the Doppler frequency law in a transformer model.

title: MerchantBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Long-Term Coherence in E-Commerce Operations
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly evaluated as autonomous tool users, yet most benchmarks focus on bounded tasks with immediate success criteria. Real-world deployments often require Long-Term Coherence, the capacity to preserve purposeful behavior across extended horizons while adapting decisions to accumulated evidence. Evaluating this capacity requires a persistent environment in which actions constrain future choices, feedback arrives at heterogeneous delays, and incoherent behavior produces measurable cumulative effects. Seller-side e-commerce provides a suitable setting for this evaluation through recurrent and interdependent decisions over Product Sourcing, Listing and Pricing Control, Cash-Flow Management, and Mixed-Latency Feedback Adaptation. We introduce MerchantBench, a 365-day order-level simulation grounded in 98,843 real e-commerce product records and equipped with 26 tools for agent interaction. MerchantBench couples promptly observable Upstream Supplier Events with delayed Downstream Order Outcomes, requiring agents to follow individual order lifecycles and revisit earlier decisions. We evaluate eight LLMs under two agent frameworks in 48 runs, each spanning 365 simulated days. Our results reveal a substantial gap between even the latest LLMs and human participants, with the best LLM configuration attaining only 27.3\% of the mean final net assets achieved by human participants.

AI.tldr: MerchantBench is a 365-day order-level e-commerce simulation benchmark with 26 tools, grounded in 98,843 real product records, that evaluates LLM agents on Long-Term Coherence through product sourcing, listing/pricing, cash-flow management, and mixed-latency feedback adaptation. The best LLM configuration achieves only 27.3% of human participants' mean final net assets, revealing a substantial capability gap.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent benchmarks focus on bounded tasks with immediate success criteria, failing to capture Long-Term Coherence—the capacity to preserve purposeful behavior across extended horizons while adapting to accumulated evidence. Real-world deployments require persistent environments where actions constrain future choices, feedback arrives at heterogeneous delays, and incoherent behavior produces measurable cumulative effects.
AI.method: MerchantBench simulates seller-side e-commerce over 365 days using 98,843 real product records, equipped with 26 tools for agent interaction. It couples promptly observable Upstream Supplier Events with delayed Downstream Order Outcomes, requiring agents to follow individual order lifecycles and revisit earlier decisions. The benchmark covers recurrent and interdependent decisions over Product Sourcing, Listing and Pricing Control, Cash-Flow Management, and Mixed-Latency Feedback Adaptation. Eight LLMs were evaluated under two agent frameworks across 48 runs.
AI.result: The best LLM configuration attained only 27.3% of the mean final net assets achieved by human participants, revealing a substantial gap between the latest LLMs and humans on long-horizon, coherence-demanding tasks.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM agents significantly underperform human participants in long-term, coherent decision-making benchmarks such as MerchantBench, indicating that Long-Term Coherence remains a major unsolved challenge for LLM agents and a critical direction for future research.

title: SULAND v2: A Refined RGB Dataset and Deep Learning Object Detection Benchmark for UAV/UGV-Based SUrface LANDmine Detection Under Domain Shift
comment: The manuscript is currently under submission to a journal for peer review
summary: RGB imagery offers a practical, low-cost option for Unmanned Aerial/Ground Vehicle (UAV/UGV) survey support in surface-landmine detection, but object detectors remain underexplored in this safety-critical domain. Limited cross-architecture benchmarking and insufficient out-of-distribution (OOD) analysis obscure whether detectors generalize across deployment conditions. This challenge is amplified by the scarcity of public RGB landmine datasets, making SULAND a key benchmark for PFM-1 and PMA-2 detection. However, inspection reveals missing/false annotations, localization errors, inconsistent visibility criteria, visual artifacts, temporal labeling inconsistencies, and an inverted OOD class-ID convention in SULAND. We present SULAND_v2, a refined RGB surface-landmine dataset and benchmark. Preserving original images and splits, we manually revise annotations to ensure completeness, precise localization, label validity, and class consistency. SULAND_v2 contains 33,771 images and 12,433 bounding boxes. We benchmark 35 detector configurations across nine families. Annotation refinement improves YOLOv8 in-distribution (IID) test mAP@50 by 14.6-19.6 percentage points, while fixing the OOD class-ID convention increases mean YOLOv8 OOD mAP@50 by ~25 percentage points. On SULAND_v2, YOLOv12-Small achieves the highest IID mAP@50 (0.908), while RF-DETR-Large yields the strongest OOD performance (0.799 mAP@50, 0.675 recall). Our results demonstrate that high IID accuracy does not guarantee operational readiness. SULAND_v2 provides a reliable benchmark for evaluating domain-shift robustness in RGB-based mine-action survey support.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SULAND_v2, a refined RGB surface-landmine detection dataset and benchmark. It corrects annotation errors and inconsistent conventions in the original SULAND dataset, benchmarks 35 detector configurations across nine model families, and demonstrates that high in-distribution accuracy does not guarantee out-of-distribution robustness in this safety-critical domain.
AI.motivation: RGB imagery is a practical, low-cost option for UAV/UGV-based surface-landmine detection, but object detectors remain underexplored in this safety-critical domain. Limited cross-architecture benchmarking and insufficient out-of-distribution (OOD) analysis obscure whether detectors generalize across deployment conditions. The original SULAND dataset, a key benchmark for PFM-1 and PMA-2 detection, suffers from annotation errors and inconsistent OOD conventions that undermine reliable evaluation.
AI.method: The authors present SULAND_v2, a manually refined dataset preserving the original images and splits. They revised annotations to ensure completeness, precise localization, label validity, and class consistency. The refinement fixes missing/false annotations, localization errors, inconsistent visibility criteria, visual artifacts, temporal labeling inconsistencies, and an inverted OOD class-ID convention. They then benchmark 35 detector configurations across nine model families on the refined dataset.
AI.result: SULAND_v2 contains 33,771 images and 12,433 bounding boxes. Annotation refinement improves YOLOv8 in-distribution (IID) test mAP@50 by 14.6-19.6 percentage points, while fixing the OOD class-ID convention increases mean YOLOv8 OOD mAP@50 by ~25 percentage points. YOLOv12-Small achieves the highest IID mAP@50 (0.908), while RF-DETR-Large yields the strongest OOD performance (0.799 mAP@50, 0.675 recall).
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that high IID accuracy does not guarantee operational readiness. SULAND_v2 provides a reliable benchmark for evaluating domain-shift robustness in RGB-based mine-action survey support, addressing a critical gap in this safety-critical application domain.

title: AuditCoder: Responsibility-Preserving Task Graphs for Auditable Code Generation and Bounded Repair
comment: Preprint. 37 pages, 5 figures. Code and data are available at the project repository
summary: Code generators return programs, but typically do not preserve the construction record needed to connect a failure to the decision that produced the affected code or to delimit a justified repair. We present AuditCoder, which treats the program and an auditable construction trace as joint outputs. Before code generation, a contract-annotated task graph assigns stable responsibility identities that remain attached to each commitment, its owned implementation, provenance, validation evidence, and intervention history. When validation fails, a conservative locator maps heterogeneous evidence to a node or dependency branch---or abstains---and bounded repair regenerates only that region while reusing the frozen complement. On APPS, \method{} reaches $82.5$--$83.0\%$ \texttt{pass@1}, recovering much of the loss caused by unrepaired graph decomposition but trailing AgentCoder by $7.5$--$8.5$ points. On ClassEval, it reaches $75.0$--$82.0\%$, outperforming CoT + retry while remaining below AgentCoder. A separate audit of 200 APPS records yields $0.9725$ task-macro decision--code trace coverage; the locator identifies an evidence-supported node or branch for 26 of 60 failures, and 17 of those localized repairs pass. For tasks with stable, locally testable boundaries, the graph functions not only as a decomposition structure but also as a persistent index for validation and repair.

AI.tldr: AuditCoder jointly generates programs and an auditable construction trace by using a contract-annotated task graph that assigns stable responsibility identities to code commitments. On validation failure, a conservative locator maps evidence to a specific node or dependency branch and performs bounded repair on only that region. It achieves 82.5–83.0% pass@1 on APPS and 75.0–82.0% on ClassEval, with 0.9725 task-macro decision–code trace coverage on audit records.
AI.motivation: Code generators typically produce programs without preserving the construction record needed to connect failures to the specific decisions that produced affected code, or to delimit a justified repair. This lack of traceability makes debugging and targeted repair difficult.
AI.method: AuditCoder treats the program and an auditable construction trace as joint outputs. Before generation, it constructs a contract-annotated task graph assigning stable responsibility identities to each commitment, its owned implementation, provenance, validation evidence, and intervention history. When validation fails, a conservative locator maps heterogeneous evidence to a node or dependency branch (or abstains), and bounded repair regenerates only the localized region while reusing the frozen complement.
AI.result: On APPS, AuditCoder achieves 82.5–83.0% pass@1, recovering much of the loss from unrepaired graph decomposition but trailing AgentCoder by 7.5–8.5 points. On ClassEval, it reaches 75.0–82.0%, outperforming CoT + retry but remaining below AgentCoder. An audit of 200 APPS records shows 0.9725 task-macro decision–code trace coverage; the locator identifies an evidence-supported node or branch for 26 of 60 failures, and 17 of those localized repairs pass.
AI.conclusion: For tasks with stable, locally testable boundaries, the task graph functions not only as a decomposition structure but also as a persistent index for validation and targeted repair, enabling auditable and localized code generation and repair.

title: MPP-GNN: Subject-Adaptive Community Detection for fMRI-Based Alzheimer's Disease Classification
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging
summary: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is a widely used technique for studying the brain. Recent methods that utilize graph neural networks (GNNs) for analysis of brain functional connectivity have shown great potential for the classification of brain disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, these methods often assume a preset number of functional modules across all subjects, which overlooks inter-subject variability. In addition, the discovered modules are rarely used to directly guide the learned connectivity patterns. Here, to address these issues, we propose a Meta Probabilistic Pooling GNN (MPP-GNN). We frame the model's task as a coupled, bilevel optimization that performs adaptive graph partitioning hierarchically to discover subject-specific modules and then uses the discovered brain modules as an explicit prior to guide edge refinement and representation learning. We validate MPP-GNN on two public datasets for AD classification, achieving the highest AUC in comparison to established baselines for both datasets. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that MPP-GNN shows significant alignment with the canonical functional-network organization defined by the Yeo brain atlas and reveals a network-level dedifferentiation pattern for AD.

AI.tldr: MPP-GNN is a Meta Probabilistic Pooling Graph Neural Network that performs adaptive, subject-specific brain module discovery via coupled bilevel optimization, then uses those modules as explicit priors to guide edge refinement and representation learning for Alzheimer's disease classification from fMRI data, achieving state-of-the-art AUC on two public datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing GNN-based fMRI analysis methods assume a fixed, preset number of functional modules across all subjects, failing to capture inter-subject variability in brain functional connectivity. Additionally, discovered modules are not directly used to guide the learned connectivity patterns, limiting their interpretability and classification power.
AI.method: The proposed MPP-GNN frames the task as a coupled bilevel optimization that hierarchically performs adaptive graph partitioning to discover subject-specific brain modules, which are then used as explicit priors to guide edge refinement and representation learning in the GNN.
AI.result: MPP-GNN achieved the highest AUC compared to established baselines on two public datasets for Alzheimer's disease classification. The discovered modules show significant alignment with the canonical Yeo brain atlas functional-network organization and reveal a network-level dedifferentiation pattern for AD.
AI.conclusion: Subject-specific module discovery coupled with module-guided connectivity learning improves both classification performance and interpretability in fMRI-based brain disorder analysis.

title: Scaling Scientific Discovery Environments for Turn-Level Agentic RL
summary: Large language model agents have shown promising capabilities in data-driven scientific discovery tasks, where an agent interacts with an execution environment and produces a statistical claim. Long-horizon scientific analysis remains constrained by the lack of process supervised environments over real-world scientific data. This paper introduces SciDisco, a scalable framework for training Scientific Discovery agents in process-verifiable environments. SciThèque compiles hypotheses, datasets, hidden evidence graphs, and verifiers into task environments where analytical progress can be checked during interaction. DAG-grounded trajectory synthesis uses these environments to construct verifier-filtered multi-turn demonstrations. DiscoPO then uses the environment as the source of training signal, assigning turn-level credit to actions that produce verifiable analytical evidence. Experiments show that SciDisco-14B reaches state-of-the-art on hypothesis-driven scientific data analysis benchmarks.

AI.tldr: SciDisco is a scalable framework for training scientific discovery agents in process-verifiable environments, comprising SciThèque (task environments with verifiers), DAG-grounded trajectory synthesis for generating filtered demonstrations, and DiscoPO for turn-level credit assignment via the environment as training signal. The resulting SciDisco-14B model achieves state-of-the-art performance on hypothesis-driven scientific data analysis benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon scientific analysis by LLM agents is constrained by the lack of process-supervised environments over real-world scientific data, making it difficult to provide fine-grained training signals during multi-turn interactions with scientific tools.
AI.method: The framework consists of three components: (1) SciThèque, which compiles hypotheses, datasets, hidden evidence graphs, and verifiers into task environments that allow checking analytical progress during interaction; (2) DAG-grounded trajectory synthesis, which constructs verifier-filtered multi-turn demonstrations; and (3) DiscoPO, which uses the environment as the training signal source, assigning turn-level credit to actions that produce verifiable analytical evidence.
AI.result: The trained SciDisco-14B model reaches state-of-the-art performance on hypothesis-driven scientific data analysis benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Process-verifiable environments over real-world scientific data can serve as scalable supervision signals for training scientific discovery agents, improving performance in long-horizon analytical tasks.

title: Evaluation-Verification Reward for Consistent Multi-Reference Image Editing
summary: While recent image editing models have made rapid progress, multi-reference editing remains challenging, particularly in maintaining visual consistency across references and ensuring overall visual harmony. Reinforcement learning has proven highly effective for text-to-image generation and single-image editing, but its extension to multi-reference editing is hindered by the absence of suitable reward models that capture multi-image relational constraints. Moreover, naively using multimodal large language models(MLLMs) as zero-shot evaluators faces a key tension between hallucination-prone long-form reasoning and the limited deductive power of short-form judgments. We address these issues with a Multi-dimensional Evaluation-Verification Reward(EVR). EVR decomposes evaluation into distinct visual criteria; for each criterion, an MLLM Evaluator generates multiple candidate hypotheses, and a Verifier grounds each claim in concrete visual evidence to accept or reject it, producing reliable and fine-grained reward signals. Together with a scalable data pipeline, our method enables RL fine-tuning of off-the-shelf editors without architectural changes. Extensive experiments show substantial gains over the base Qwen-Image-Edit, improving consistency and harmony to match or surpass NanoBanana.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Multi-dimensional Evaluation-Verification Reward (EVR) framework that enables reinforcement learning fine-tuning of off-the-shelf image editors for multi-reference editing. EVR decomposes evaluation into visual criteria, uses MLLM Evaluators to generate candidate hypotheses per criterion, and Verifiers to ground claims in concrete visual evidence, overcoming the tension between hallucination-prone long-form reasoning and limited deductive power of short-form judgments. Combined with a scalable data pipeline, this method improves consistency and harmony to match or surpass NanoBanana without architectural changes.
AI.motivation: Multi-reference image editing remains challenging due to maintaining visual consistency and harmony across references. While RL works well for text-to-image and single-image editing, extending it to multi-reference editing is blocked by the absence of reward models capturing multi-image relational constraints. Naively using MLLMs as zero-shot evaluators faces a fundamental tension between hallucination-prone long-form reasoning and insufficient deductive power of short-form judgments.
AI.method: The proposed EVR (Evaluation-Verification Reward) decomposes evaluation into distinct visual criteria. For each criterion, an MLLM Evaluator generates multiple candidate hypotheses, and a Verifier grounds each claim in concrete visual evidence to accept or reject it, producing reliable and fine-grained reward signals. This is combined with a scalable data pipeline to enable RL fine-tuning of off-the-shelf editors without requiring architectural modifications.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show substantial gains over the base Qwen-Image-Edit model, improving visual consistency and harmony to match or surpass NanoBanana.
AI.conclusion: The multi-dimensional Evaluation-Verification Reward framework effectively addresses the reward modeling challenge for multi-reference editing under RL, demonstrating that reliable and fine-grained reward signals grounded in visual evidence can enable strong performance improvements on off-the-shelf editors without architectural changes.

title: Improving the Understandability of Conceptual Models via Abstract Notation Engineering
summary: Conceptual modeling supports the design, analysis, and communication of the properties of complex systems, yet conceptual models can be difficult to understand when domain-level abstractions must be encoded through low-level constructs required mainly for semantic conformity. Prior work has mainly improved how existing individual constructs are visually represented. We shift the focus from individual constructs to recurring configurations of constructs, and propose abstract notation engineering as a language-agnostic method for replacing such configurations with higher-level, semantically transparent constructs. The method comprises pattern identification, pattern formalization, visual notation design, and empirical validation. We instantiate it for Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, where common workflow patterns require elaborate low-level configurations. The resulting extension, DeCleaR, replaces such configurations with compact pattern-based abstractions. The results of our empirical validation show that DeCleaR improves perceived empirical quality, pragmatic quality, and user preference over standard DCR graphs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes abstract notation engineering, a language-agnostic method for replacing recurring low-level configurations of conceptual modeling constructs with higher-level, semantically transparent abstractions. The method is instantiated for DCR graphs, yielding DeCleaR, which improves perceived empirical quality, pragmatic quality, and user preference.
AI.motivation: Conceptual models are difficult to understand when domain-level abstractions must be encoded through low-level constructs required mainly for semantic conformity. Prior work focused on improving visual representations of individual constructs, not on addressing recurring configurations of constructs.
AI.method: The method, abstract notation engineering, comprises four steps: pattern identification, pattern formalization, visual notation design, and empirical validation. It is instantiated for Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, where common workflow patterns require elaborate low-level configurations, resulting in the DeCleaR extension.
AI.result: Empirical validation shows that DeCleaR improves perceived empirical quality, pragmatic quality, and user preference compared to standard DCR graphs.
AI.conclusion: Shifting focus from individual constructs to recurring configurations of constructs enables the design of more understandable conceptual modeling notations via language-agnostic abstraction engineering.

title: Technological Advances in Detecting and Managing Cognitive Impairment in Older Adults: Trends, Challenges, and Future Directions
summary: As populations age, cognitive decline from mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to dementia is a defining health challenge of the coming decades, yet routine assessment often misses its earliest signs. This article critically synthesizes recent technological advances for detecting and managing cognitive impairment in older adults, spanning neurophysiological signals (chiefly electroencephalography, EEG), structural and molecular neuroimaging (MRI and amyloid/tau PET), blood-based biomarkers, and digital markers, integrated through artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL). Beyond summarizing, it contributes a cross-disciplinary taxonomy, a methodological-rigor lens foregrounding subject- and site-independent validation, an integrative early-detection framework linking tiered screening to intervention, and comparison tables of detection methods, interventions, and risk and protective factors. EEG markers (alpha/theta changes, P300 latency) and deep models (CNNs, LSTM/BiLSTM, transformers, self-supervised EEG foundation models) report strong accuracy, yet many rest on small, single-site datasets unlikely to survive rigorous external validation. Elsewhere, gains are tangible: plasma p-tau217 has reached clinical utility, with the first blood test cleared to aid Alzheimer's diagnosis in 2025; anti-amyloid therapies (lecanemab, donanemab) are approved despite modest, contested benefits; and multidomain lifestyle prevention has matured. Wearable, remote, speech, and virtual-reality tools enable continuous, ecologically valid monitoring, and multimodal fusion improves sensitivity and specificity. Barriers remain: standardization, explainability, data privacy, and equitable, externally validated deployment. The field's near-term promise lies in trustworthy, multimodal, longitudinally validated systems linking early detection to actionable, personalized care.

AI.tldr: A critical review synthesizing recent technological advances (EEG, neuroimaging, blood biomarkers, digital markers, and AI/ML/DL) for detecting and managing cognitive impairment in older adults, proposing a cross-disciplinary taxonomy, a rigor lens emphasizing external validation, and an integrative early-detection framework linking tiered screening to intervention—concluding with the need for trustworthy, multimodal, longitudinally validated systems.
AI.motivation: Aging populations face rising cognitive decline from MCI to dementia, yet routine assessment often misses early signs; a synthesis of emerging detection and management technologies is needed to guide the field toward clinically valid, deployable solutions.
AI.method: Critical synthesis of literature spanning EEG, structural/molecular neuroimaging (MRI, amyloid/tau PET), blood-based biomarkers, digital markers, and AI/ML/DL models; contribution of a taxonomy, a methodological-rigor lens (subject-/site-independent validation), an early-detection framework, and comparison tables.
AI.result: EEG markers and deep models report high accuracy but often rely on small, single-site datasets lacking external validity. Tangible gains exist: plasma p-tau217 reached clinical utility (first blood test cleared for Alzheimer's diagnosis in 2025), anti-amyloid therapies approved, multidomain lifestyle prevention matured, and wearable/remote/speech/VR tools enable continuous monitoring while multimodal fusion improves sensitivity and specificity.
AI.conclusion: The field's near-term promise lies in trustworthy, multimodal, longitudinally validated systems linking early detection to actionable, personalized care; remaining barriers include standardization, explainability, data privacy, and equitable external validation.

title: MMShopBench: A Real-Log Benchmark for Multimodal, Multi-Turn Shopping Agents
summary: Online shoppers increasingly turn to AI shopping assistants, using images and multi-turn dialogue to express and refine product needs that are difficult to articulate in text alone. However, existing benchmarks largely rely on text-only or synthetic requests, underrepresenting complex real-world shopping requirements jointly expressed through images and language. We introduce MMShopBench, the first real-log benchmark for multimodal, multi-turn shopping agents. Built from carefully cleaned and manually annotated shopping logs, MMShopBench provides ground-truth annotations of each request's purchase intent and mandatory product requirements. Agents must infer these requirements jointly from user images and multi-turn dialogue, retrieve candidate products through image and text search, and verify that each candidate satisfies all requirements using its product images and structured attributes. We evaluate representative open-source and proprietary models using an evidence-grounded multimodal protocol and construct a companion training set for fine-tuning an open-source model. To ensure reproducible experimentation, we build an offline shopping sandbox, where fine-tuning substantially narrows the performance gap between our open-source model and leading proprietary models, demonstrating the effectiveness of our training data.

AI.tldr: MMShopBench is the first real-log benchmark for multimodal, multi-turn shopping agents, built from manually annotated shopping logs with ground-truth purchase intent and mandatory product requirements. Evaluation of open-source and proprietary models using an evidence-grounded multimodal protocol shows that fine-tuning on a companion training set substantially narrows the performance gap between open-source and leading proprietary models.
AI.motivation: Existing shopping benchmarks rely on text-only or synthetic requests, underrepresenting complex real-world shopping needs that are jointly expressed through images and multi-turn dialogue, which are increasingly common with AI shopping assistants.
AI.method: MMShopBench is constructed from carefully cleaned and manually annotated real shopping logs, providing ground-truth annotations of purchase intent and mandatory product requirements. Agents must infer requirements jointly from user images and multi-turn dialogue, retrieve candidates via image and text search, and verify each candidate against all requirements using product images and structured attributes. A companion training set is built and an offline shopping sandbox is constructed for reproducible experimentation.
AI.result: Evaluation of representative open-source and proprietary models using an evidence-grounded multimodal protocol shows that fine-tuning on the companion training set substantially narrows the performance gap between the open-source model and leading proprietary models.
AI.conclusion: The companion training set is effective, demonstrating that fine-tuning can significantly close the performance gap to proprietary models, and MMShopBench provides a realistic and reproducible benchmark for multimodal multi-turn shopping agents.

title: SAM+D: Parameter-Efficient Dimensional Lifting of SAM-Family Models via Depth-Routed LoRA and Depth Shifting
summary: Existing methods for adapting 2D foundation models such as SAM to 3D volumes either process slices independently---ignoring inter-slice context---or require substantial architectural changes and retraining. In this paper, we present \textbf{SAM+D}, a parameter-efficient framework that lifts SAM-family models by one spatial dimension---enabling 3D volumetric segmentation from 2D SAM and, for the first time via parameter-efficient fine-tuning, end-to-end 4D (3D+T) spatiotemporal segmentation from video-based SAM2---while keeping the vast majority of pre-trained parameters frozen. SAM+D introduces two lightweight, model-agnostic modules into frozen transformer blocks: (1)~\textbf{Depth-Routed LoRA (DRLoRA)} experts with learned routing for spatially adaptive low-rank updates, and (2)~\textbf{Depth Shift Modules (DSM)} for cross-slice feature exchange at zero additional parameter cost. Together, they provide volume-level context while tuning only ${\sim}$2.8\% of parameters for SAM and ${\sim}$3.7\% for SAM2. We evaluate SAM+D in two distinct settings, each lifting the base model by one spatial dimension: 3D segmentation, where SAM(2D$\,\to\,$3D) is evaluated on four CT benchmarks (KiTS, Pancreas, LiTS, Colon), and 4D segmentation, where SAM2 (2D+T$\,\to\,$3D+T) is evaluated on a cell tracking challenge (CTC) dataset (Fluo-N3DH-SIM+). In both settings SAM+D achieves competitive or superior results under the single-point prompt setting while using fewer trainable parameters than existing methods, demonstrating that SAM+D generalizes across SAM-family architectures, target dimensionalities (3D, 4D), and domains spanning medical imaging and bio-scene understanding. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/JerrySongCST/SAM-Plus-D.

AI.tldr: SAM+D is a parameter-efficient framework that lifts 2D/foundation segmentation models (SAM and SAM2) by one spatial dimension using two lightweight modules (Depth-Routed LoRA experts and Depth Shift Modules). It achieves competitive 3D volumetric segmentation on four CT benchmarks and 4D spatiotemporal segmentation on a cell tracking dataset while tuning only ~2.8% (SAM) and ~3.7% (SAM2) of parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for adapting 2D foundation models like SAM to 3D volumes either ignore inter-slice context by processing slices independently, or require substantial architectural changes and retraining. There is a need for a parameter-efficient approach that preserves the pre-trained model while adding volume-level context.
AI.method: SAM+D inserts two model-agnostic lightweight modules into frozen transformer blocks: (1) Depth-Routed LoRA (DRLoRA) experts with learned routing for spatially adaptive low-rank updates, and (2) Depth Shift Modules (DSM) for cross-slice feature exchange at zero additional parameter cost. This allows lifting SAM by one spatial dimension (2D→3D) and SAM2 (2D+T→3D+T) for 4D segmentation, tuning only ~2.8% of SAM and ~3.7% of SAM2 parameters.
AI.result: Evaluated in two settings: 3D segmentation on four CT benchmarks (KiTS, Pancreas, LiTS, Colon) using SAM, and 4D segmentation on a cell tracking challenge dataset (Fluo-N3DH-SIM+) using SAM2. SAM+D achieves competitive or superior results under single-point prompt setting while using fewer trainable parameters than existing methods, generalizing across architectures, dimensionalities (3D, 4D), and domains (medical imaging and bio-scene understanding).
AI.conclusion: SAM+D demonstrates that 2D foundation models can be efficiently lifted to higher-dimensional segmentation tasks via parameter-efficient fine-tuning, achieving strong performance across 3D and 4D settings while keeping the vast majority of pre-trained parameters frozen.

title: Alteron: A Tool for Behavioral Regression Testing Across NLP Classifier Versions
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME), Tool Demonstration and Data Showcase Track
summary: Evaluating evolving Natural Language Processing (NLP) models is important for ensuring reliable behavior across updates, but standard benchmark metrics do not fully capture how model behavior changes across versions. Existing work has focused mainly on testing models in isolation rather than comparing successive versions in continuous integration workflows. We present Alteron, a tool for detecting behavioral regressions across NLP model versions with metamorphic testing. Alteron constructs a test corpus from labeled source examples and compares model versions on metamorphically transformed inputs. In an evaluation spanning 10 metamorphic relations (MRs), 4 model versions, and 3 model-update transitions, Alteron identified 16 behavioral regressions, 11 of which were release-blocking. The results show that common model updates can preserve overall task performance while still introducing undesirable behavior changes, and that behavioral checks across model versions can reveal failures that aggregate benchmark metrics alone do not capture. The tool is open-source and available at https://github.com/shazzad5709/alteron. A screencast demonstration is available at https://youtu.be/szwiWW5O4do.

AI.tldr: Alteron is an open-source tool that detects behavioral regressions across NLP model versions using metamorphic testing. It constructs test corpora from labeled examples and compares model versions on transformed inputs across 10 metamorphic relations. In evaluation with 4 model versions and 3 update transitions, it identified 16 behavioral regressions (11 release-blocking), demonstrating that aggregate benchmark metrics miss behavioral failures that cross-version comparison can reveal.
AI.motivation: Standard benchmark metrics do not fully capture how NLP model behavior changes across versions, and existing work focuses on testing models in isolation rather than comparing successive versions in continuous integration workflows. This gap means behavioral regressions introduced by model updates can go undetected even when overall task performance remains stable.
AI.method: Alteron constructs a test corpus from labeled source examples and applies metamorphic testing by comparing successive model versions on metamorphically transformed inputs. It uses 10 metamorphic relations across 4 model versions and 3 model-update transitions to systematically detect behavioral differences between versions.
AI.result: Alteron identified 16 behavioral regressions across the evaluated model transitions, 11 of which were release-blocking. The evaluation showed that common model updates can preserve overall task performance while still introducing undesirable behavior changes, and that cross-version behavioral checks reveal failures not captured by aggregate benchmark metrics.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral checks across model versions are essential for reliable NLP system evolution; metamorphic testing provides an effective mechanism to detect regressions that standard benchmark metrics miss. Alteron is released as an open-source tool with a demonstration screencast.

title: SEDR-Seq2P: A Lightweight Dilated Residual Sequence-to-Point Network for Multi-Task Industrial NILM
summary: Industrial NILM remains challenging because measurement noise and widespread concurrent machine operation reduce the generalization of models tuned on residential data. This work adopts a one-to-many, multi-task disaggregation setting, in which a single network estimates multiple industrial machine loads from aggregate power. Under a unified evaluation protocol on IMDELD, we benchmark Seq2Seq, Seq2SubSeq, Seq2Point, GRU, and WaveNet using energy-estimation metrics and the accuracy-delay criterion. While Seq2Point offers a stronger accuracy-delay balance than Seq2Seq/Seq2SubSeq, GRU and WaveNet achieve higher accuracy at markedly higher computational cost. To close this gap, we propose SEDR-Seq2P, a lightweight Seq2Point extension with dilated residual blocks and squeeze-and-excitation attention. Relative to the Seq2Point baseline, SEDR-Seq2P reduces MAE by approximately 7%, improves the coefficient of determination by approximately 1%, and increases the match rate by approximately 0.8%. In addition, compared to WaveNet, SEDR-Seq2P reduces inference latency by approximately 58%, yielding a favorable accuracy-delay trade-off for scalable industrial deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses industrial non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM) in a one-to-many multi-task setting, benchmarked on IMDELD. It proposes SEDR-Seq2P, a lightweight Seq2Point extension with dilated residual blocks and squeeze-and-excitation attention, which reduces MAE by ~7%, improves R² by ~1%, increases match rate by ~0.8%, and cuts inference latency by ~58% versus WaveNet.
AI.motivation: Industrial NILM is challenging due to measurement noise and concurrent machine operation, which reduce generalization of residential-tuned models. There is a need for efficient disaggregation models that balance accuracy and computational cost for industrial deployment.
AI.method: Adopts a one-to-many multi-task disaggregation setting and introduces SEDR-Seq2P, a lightweight extension of Seq2Point incorporating dilated residual blocks and squeeze-and-excitation attention. Benchmarking is performed on IMDELD under a unified evaluation protocol using energy-estimation metrics and the accuracy-delay criterion, comparing Seq2Seq, Seq2SubSeq, Seq2Point, GRU, and WaveNet.
AI.result: Seq2Point achieves a stronger accuracy-delay balance than Seq2Seq/Seq2SubSeq, while GRU and WaveNet achieve higher accuracy at higher computational cost. SEDR-Seq2P reduces MAE by ~7%, improves R² by ~1%, and increases match rate by ~0.8% relative to Seq2Point, and reduces inference latency by ~58% compared to WaveNet.
AI.conclusion: SEDR-Seq2P provides a favorable accuracy-delay trade-off, making it suitable for scalable industrial NILM deployment.

title: Evidence-Grounded Constraint Checking in Construction Documents
summary: Professional-document review is a constraint-checking problem in which decisions depend on relations among text, geometry, pages, and document revisions. We present an evidence-grounded pipeline that normalizes extracted facts, executes four-state rules deterministically, retains source spans, and escalates unresolved cases. We evaluate its PDF evidence allocator on 160 reference-based tasks from 29 construction projects using a repeated four-system test and a disjoint two-system breadth extension. In the repeated test, reallocating a four-image budget from retrieved page overviews to one overview and three overlapping tiles improves project-family standardized decision accuracy by 10.6 percentage points (95% project-cluster bootstrap CI: 4.3 to 18.0; exact p = 0.031). This effect does not persist in the broader block: Region-RAG changes accuracy by -4.1 points (95% CI: -10.2 to 1.9; exact p = 0.209), while an equal-image sensitivity favors page breadth. Exact finding-set recovery remains low, false passes remain common, and repeated-run agreement is poorly calibrated. The results identify a resolution-breadth trade-off rather than a universal advantage for region-focused evidence, motivating rule-aware evidence routing and expert review.

AI.tldr: A professional-document review pipeline using evidence-grounded, rule-based constraint checking with four-state rules is evaluated on construction project PDFs. Reallocating image budgets from page overviews to overlapping tile regions improves decision accuracy by 10.6 points in a repeated internal test but not in a broader disjoint extension, revealing a resolution-breadth trade-off rather than universal benefit of region-focused evidence.
AI.motivation: Professional document review is a constraint-checking problem where decisions depend on relations among text, geometry, pages, and revisions. The authors aim to determine whether region-focused (tiled) evidence allocation improves decision accuracy over broad page-level evidence.
AI.method: A four-stage pipeline normalizes extracted facts, executes deterministic four-state rules, retains source spans, and escalates unresolved cases. The PDF evidence allocator is evaluated on 160 reference-based tasks from 29 construction projects using both a repeated four-system test and a disjoint two-system breadth extension, with project-cluster bootstrap CIs and exact permutation tests.
AI.result: In the repeated test, reallocating a four-image budget from page overviews to one overview plus three overlapping tiles improved project-family standardized decision accuracy by 10.6 percentage points (95% CI: 4.3-18.0; p=0.031). However, in the broader disjoint block, Region-RAG changed accuracy by -4.1 points (95% CI: -10.2 to 1.9; p=0.209), and equal-image sensitivity favored page breadth. Exact finding-set recovery remained low, false passes were common, and repeated-run agreement was poorly calibrated.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a resolution-breadth trade-off rather than a universal advantage for region-focused evidence allocation. The work motivates rule-aware evidence routing and expert review for professional-document constraint checking.

title: GO-PRE: Goal-Oriented Next-Best-View Selection via Predictive Rendering Entropy for Active 3D Reconstruction
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Active 3D reconstruction relies on active view selection to maximize reconstruction fidelity under limited capture budgets. However, most existing methods rely on surrogate signals such as parameter uncertainty or geometric heuristics, but these signals are often misaligned with the ultimate goal: the fidelity of rendered predictions. We propose GO-PRE, a goal-oriented next-best-view selection framework that explicitly targets information gain in the prediction space. Specifically, we formulate the objective as maximizing the reduction of the average marginal predictive entropy over a user-specified target view manifold. GO-PRE supports interactive goal specification and yields an efficient acquisition rule that enables real-time computation of information gain. Extensive experiments across benchmarks demonstrate that GO-PRE consistently improves active reconstruction performance and provides more reliable uncertainty quantification compared to state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: GO-PRE is a goal-oriented next-best-view selection framework for active 3D reconstruction that directly maximizes information gain in prediction space by reducing average marginal predictive entropy over a user-specified target view manifold, improving reconstruction fidelity and uncertainty quantification over state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Most existing active 3D reconstruction methods rely on surrogate signals like parameter uncertainty or geometric heuristics for view selection, which are often misaligned with the actual goal of maximizing the fidelity of rendered predictions. This misalignment limits reconstruction performance under limited capture budgets.
AI.method: GO-PRE formulates the next-best-view selection objective as maximizing the reduction of average marginal predictive entropy over a user-specified target view manifold. It supports interactive goal specification and derives an efficient acquisition rule enabling real-time computation of information gain.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across benchmarks show GO-PRE consistently improves active reconstruction performance and provides more reliable uncertainty quantification compared to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: Directly targeting information gain in the prediction space, rather than relying on surrogate signals, is a more effective and reliable approach for active 3D reconstruction, and goal-oriented view selection yields measurable performance gains.

title: Educating the Agentic Engineer: Curricula, Collaboration, and Continuous Learning in the AI Era
summary: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) are reconfiguring software and systems engineering from a discipline centered on human authorship of artifacts to one focused on directing, verifying, and governing autonomous systems. This transition demands a new professional archetype, the \emph{agentic engineer}, whose enduring value lies in intent specification, orchestration of multi-agent workflows, critical evaluation of machine-generated outputs, and ethical judgment. This article presents an integrative conceptual synthesis across engineering education, computing education, human--AI interaction, human factors, and the learning sciences to derive an evidence-grounded educational architecture for this archetype. We introduce the ACCEL framework (Agentic Competencies through Curricula, Collaboration, and Enduring Learning), which organizes five competency pillars and maps them to three delivery vectors: curricula, collaboration, and continuous learning. Drawing on agency theory, trust-in-automation research, and empirical studies of AI-assisted programming, including evidence that AI benefits are unevenly realized and often misperceived, we propose a scaffolded curriculum, a delegation--verification pedagogical loop for human--AI teaming, redesigned assessment, governance-literate ethics integration, and alignment with current curricular guidelines and international AI competency frameworks. We identify key risks, including automation bias, deskilling, superficial engagement, and diffuse accountability, and conclude that educating the agentic engineer requires systemic transformation rather than incremental curricular change: instruction must shift from producing artifacts to exercising judgment over increasingly autonomous socio-technical systems.

AI.tldr: This article proposes the ACCEL framework for educating a new professional archetype—the "agentic engineer"—who directs, verifies, and governs autonomous AI systems. It synthesizes evidence across multiple disciplines to derive an educational architecture comprising five competency pillars delivered through curricula, collaboration, and continuous learning, arguing that systemic educational transformation is required.
AI.motivation: Generative and agentic AI are shifting software/systems engineering from human authorship of artifacts to directing and governing autonomous systems, requiring a new professional identity and corresponding educational paradigm that current curricula do not address.
AI.method: Integrative conceptual synthesis across engineering education, computing education, human-AI interaction, human factors, and learning sciences; introduces ACCEL framework organizing five competency pillars mapped to three delivery vectors (curricula, collaboration, continuous learning), grounded in agency theory, trust-in-automation research, and empirical studies of AI-assisted programming.
AI.result: Proposes a scaffolded curriculum, a delegation-verification pedagogical loop for human-AI teaming, redesigned assessment, governance-literate ethics integration, and alignment with curricular guidelines and international AI competency frameworks; identifies key risks including automation bias, deskilling, superficial engagement, and diffuse accountability.
AI.conclusion: Educating the agentic engineer requires systemic rather than incremental curricular transformation—shifting instruction from artifact production to exercising judgment over increasingly autonomous socio-technical systems.

title: Predicting Steel Fatigue Life from Micrographs Using Physics-Informed Deep Learning
summary: Here is the plain text version optimized for arXiv's submission form. Custom macros (like \CV and \SI) have been converted to standard text/math so they render correctly on the webpage: Evaluating the fatigue life of structural steels conventionally requires mechanical testing lasting tens to hundreds of hours, making it impractical for rapid quality control. We present CV, a computer vision framework that estimates the fatigue life ($\log N_f$) of lightweight alloy steels directly from optical micrographs without physical testing.The pipeline features a seven-stage OpenCV preprocessing routine to remove artifacts, a 28-dimensional physics-informed feature extractor (quantifying crack morphology, grain structure, porosity, and texture), and a CNN regression model trained with a Gaussian negative log-likelihood (GNLL) loss to jointly predict $\log N_f$ and sample-specific uncertainty $\hatσ$.Evaluating three architectures (SE-CNN, ResNet-50, VGG-16) on a synthetic micrograph benchmark, ResNet-50 achieves $R^2 = 0.93$, RMSE = 0.18 log-cycles, and macro-F1 = 0.91. The GNLL objective reduces Expected Calibration Error by 76% compared to a mean-squared-error baseline (ECE: $0.089 \rightarrow 0.021$). Grad-CAM maps confirm the network attends to metallurgically meaningful microstructural features.Running in under 65 ms per image, the pipeline and synthetic dataset generator are open-sourced. Because validation relies entirely on synthetic micrographs, these results demonstrate methodological soundness under simulated conditions; a domain-transfer study on real field samples is the immediate next step.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a computer vision framework (CV) that estimates the fatigue life (log Nf) of lightweight alloy steels directly from optical micrographs, bypassing time-consuming mechanical testing. The pipeline combines a seven-stage OpenCV preprocessing routine, a 28-dimensional physics-informed feature extractor, and a CNN regression model trained with Gaussian negative log-likelihood loss. ResNet-50 achieves R²=0.93, RMSE=0.18 log-cycles, and macro-F1=0.91 on a synthetic benchmark, with GNLL reducing ECE by 76%. Validation is exclusively on synthetic data; real-sample domain transfer is planned.
AI.motivation: Conventional fatigue life testing of structural steels requires mechanical testing over tens to hundreds of hours, which is impractical for rapid quality control in industrial settings. A fast, non-destructive method to estimate fatigue life from micrographs is needed.
AI.method: The framework comprises: (1) a seven-stage OpenCV preprocessing routine to remove imaging artifacts, (2) a 28-dimensional physics-informed feature extractor quantifying crack morphology, grain structure, porosity, and texture, and (3) a CNN regression model trained with Gaussian negative log-likelihood (GNLL) loss to jointly predict log Nf and sample-specific uncertainty. Three architectures (SE-CNN, ResNet-50, VGG-16) are evaluated, with Grad-CAM used for interpretability.
AI.result: On a synthetic micrograph benchmark, ResNet-50 achieves R²=0.93, RMSE=0.18 log-cycles, and macro-F1=0.91. The GNLL objective lowers Expected Calibration Error by 76% versus MSE baseline (ECE: 0.089→0.021). Inference runs in under 65 ms per image. Grad-CAM confirms attention on metallurgically meaningful features.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CV framework demonstrates methodological soundness for rapid, non-destructive fatigue life estimation from micrographs under simulated conditions. Results are promising but require validation on real field samples; a domain-transfer study is identified as the immediate next step before industrial deployment.

title: On the Generalization of Steering Vectors for Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness
summary: Model capabilities have improved in large part due to scaling chain of thought. This has been a promising development for AI safety--where models verbalize their reasoning, it is possible to monitor it. However, in some cases, models do not verbalize important steps in their reasoning process. For example, models prompted with a cue suggesting the incorrect answer may fail to acknowledge that cue, even when it appears instrumental to their conclusion. When chain of thought (CoT) fails to disclose instrumental reasoning steps, we describe it as unfaithful. Prior work has shown that activation steering can be a useful method to improve faithfulness in CoT. We extend this line of work by studying how well steering for faithfulness generalizes across cue types, datasets, and methods of constructing the steering vector for three models (Gemma-3 4B, Qwen-3.5 9B, Gemma-3 12B) in a cued question-answering setting. While steering reliably increases cue acknowledgment for only the largest model (Gemma-3 12B), we find that when steering is effective, its effect generalizes broadly across cue types and datasets--in cross-cue and cross-dataset analyses, effect size is determined primarily by the evaluation setting, rather than the vector's train setting. How the vector is built also matters little--four construction methods, including one whose optimization target mentions no specific cue, yield similar effect sizes. Finally, we consider the possibility that steering promotes the salience of the cue and causes greater cue use, rather than targeting verbalization behaviors. However, we find no evidence for this--steering leaves the rate of cue use roughly unchanged while reducing hidden cue use, i.e., cue use that is not acknowledged.

AI.tldr: This paper studies whether activation steering can improve the faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning by prompting models to acknowledge instrumental cues they would otherwise fail to verbalize. Across three models, steering reliably improves cue acknowledgment only for the largest model (Gemma-3 12B), but when effective, the effect generalizes across cue types, datasets, and vector construction methods. Steering does not increase actual cue use—it reduces hidden (unacknowledged) cue use, supporting the hypothesis that steering targets verbalization behavior rather than promoting greater cue reliance.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought scaling has advanced model capabilities and offers a monitoring surface for AI safety, but models sometimes omit instrumental reasoning steps, making CoT unfaithful. Prior work suggested activation steering could improve faithfulness; this work extends that investigation to understand how well such steering generalizes across cue types, datasets, models, and steering-vector construction methods, and to test whether steering works by changing verbalization behavior or by altering actual cue use.
AI.method: The authors use activation steering in a cued question-answering setting across three models (Gemma-3 4B, Qwen-3.5 9B, Gemma-3 12B). They construct steering vectors using four different methods (including one whose optimization target mentions no specific cue) and evaluate faithfulness improvements via cue acknowledgment. They perform cross-cue and cross-dataset analyses and measure both cue acknowledgment and hidden cue use to distinguish verbalization effects from changes in actual cue reliance.
AI.result: Steering reliably increases cue acknowledgment only for Gemma-3 12B, the largest model. When effective, the effect generalizes broadly across cue types and datasets—effect size is determined primarily by the evaluation setting, not the vector's training setting. Vector construction method has little impact; all four methods yield similar effect sizes. Steering leaves the rate of actual cue use roughly unchanged while reducing hidden cue use, indicating it targets verbalization rather than increasing cue use.
AI.conclusion: Activation steering for faithfulness can be an effective intervention, but its reliability is model-dependent. When it works, it generalizes well across settings and is robust to vector construction choices. The mechanism appears to be about making hidden (unacknowledged) cue use overt rather than changing the model's actual reliance on the cue.

title: ReMoE: Report-Guided Mixture-of-Experts for Multimodal OCT/OCTA Anomaly Detection
summary: Multimodal medical anomaly detection identifies samples deviating from normal patterns, where scarce abnormal cases make normality modeling from normal data practical. In retinal Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) and OCT Angiography (OCTA) anomaly detection, existing unsupervised methods rely on visual feature distributions, reconstruction residuals, or encoder-decoder discrepancies, making anomaly scores depend on appearance-level deviations, while multimodal normality also contains semantic organization described in normal medical reports. To this end, we propose Report-Guided Mixture-of-Experts (ReMoE), which distills normal report semantics into an image-to-text prior student, builds modality-aware priors, and uses Report-Guided Modality Modulation (RMM) to modulate features through mixture-of-experts routing. Experiments on a private OCT/OCTA dataset with paired normal reports and a public OCTA500-3MM setting using a fixed normal report demonstrate state-of-the-art performance.
