AI.tldr: The paper proposes ReMoE (Report-Guided Mixture-of-Experts), a multimodal anomaly detection method for retinal OCT/OCTA images that distills semantic information from normal medical reports into an image-to-text prior student, builds modality-aware priors, and uses Report-Guided Modality Modulation (RMM) with mixture-of-experts routing to modulate features, achieving state-of-the-art performance on private OCT/OCTA and public OCTA500 datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing unsupervised multimodal anomaly detection methods for retinal OCT/OCTA rely solely on appearance-level deviations (visual features, reconstruction residuals, encoder-decoder discrepancies) and ignore the semantic organization present in normal medical reports, limiting their ability to detect anomalies grounded in normal data semantics.
AI.method: ReMoE distills normal report semantics into an image-to-text prior student to build modality-aware priors, then applies Report-Guided Modality Modulation (RMM) which uses mixture-of-experts routing to modulate image features guided by the report-derived priors.
AI.result: ReMoE achieves state-of-the-art performance on a private OCT/OCTA dataset with paired normal reports and on the public OCTA500-3MM setting using a fixed normal report.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating semantic information from normal medical reports into multimodal anomaly detection significantly improves performance compared to appearance-only approaches, demonstrating the value of report-guided semantic priors for retinal OCT/OCTA anomaly detection.

title: Reusing Past Repairs Through Hierarchical Trajectory Abstraction for Coding Agents
summary: Although LLM-driven repair agents can tackle complex, repository-level issues, they treat every issue independently and discard the procedural knowledge accumulated from previous repairs. We introduce STAIR, a framework that converts historical repair trajectories into hierarchical, reusable plans that can be adapted to steer future repairs. Each past trajectory is transformed into a multi-level tree that ranges from fine-grained diagnostic actions to high-level repair strategies, encoding experience at several granularities. When a new issue arrives, STAIR selects relevant plan nodes from multiple abstraction levels, tailors them into executable, issue-specific plans, and supplies them to the agent through its prompt. On SWE-bench Verified, STAIR integrated with Lingxi reaches 81.2% Pass@1 using MiniMax M2.5 and 79.2% using GPT-5. The generated plans also generalize across agents: without any code change, they lift the Pass@1 of a structurally different agent, mini-SWE-agent v2, from 75.8% to 81.0%. Ablation experiments further show that mixing multiple abstraction levels surpasses any single level and that raw, unabstracted trajectories transfer substantially worse.

AI.tldr: STAIR is a framework that converts historical LLM-driven repair trajectories into hierarchical, multi-level reusable plans to steer future repository-level bug fixes. On SWE-bench Verified, it boosts Lingxi to 81.2% Pass@1 with MiniMax M2.5 and 79.2% with GPT-5, and transfers across agents, lifting mini-SWE-agent v2 from 75.8% to 81.0% without code changes.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-driven repair agents handle complex repository-level issues but treat each issue independently, discarding procedural knowledge accumulated from previous repairs. This lack of learning from prior trajectories limits efficiency and effectiveness.
AI.method: STAIR converts each past repair trajectory into a multi-level tree spanning fine-grained diagnostic actions to high-level repair strategies. When a new issue arrives, it selects relevant plan nodes from multiple abstraction levels, tailors them into executable, issue-specific plans, and injects them into the agent's prompt.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified, STAIR with Lingxi achieves 81.2% Pass@1 using MiniMax M2.5 and 79.2% using GPT-5. Plans generalize across agents: they lift mini-SWE-agent v2 from 75.8% to 81.0% Pass@1 with no code changes. Ablations show mixing multiple abstraction levels outperforms any single level, and raw unabstracted trajectories transfer substantially worse.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchically abstracted repair trajectories serve as reusable, cross-agent transferable procedural knowledge that substantially improves repository-level repair performance compared to both single-level abstractions and raw trajectory transfer.

title: Mitigating Class-Tail Undercoverage in Medical Vision-Language Models under Clinical Shift
summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) can retain high observed marginal coverage after clinical shift while substantially under-covering an individual disease class. The affected class varies with acquisition protocol and backbone geometry, so source prevalence does not reliably reveal the failure. Existing localized and tail-aware conformal methods respectively adapt to test neighborhoods and source-frequency tails, leaving held-out class-wise coverage failure unmodeled. We introduce Class-Tail Adaptive Localized Conformal Deferral (CALCoDe), a post-hoc reliability layer for frozen medical VLMs. Cross-fitted validation predictions identify classes at risk of undercoverage, and a disjoint calibration split estimates their class-conditional tail thresholds. CALCoDe combines each protected threshold with a localized conformal threshold using a one-sided maximum. The resulting set contains every label admitted by the localized rule, with additional protection confined to validation-identified classes. An independently calibrated support audit defers cases with insufficient inlier support. Under exchangeability among accepted examples within each protected class, CALCoDe provides finite-sample coverage at the prespecified guard level and contains the corresponding localized conformal sets; coverage on shifted external cohorts is evaluated empirically. Among standard conformal baselines and recent VLM-specific conformal methods evaluated across two dermatology shifts (HAM10000 to ISIC 2019 and HAM10000 to PAD-UFES-20) and four frozen VLM backbones (BiomedCLIP, OpenAI CLIP ViT-B/32, PubMedCLIP ViT-B/32, and MedSigLIP-448), CALCoDe is the only approach whose observed marginal and worst-class accepted coverage both reach 0.95 in all eight settings. On HAM10000 to ISIC 2019, its average worst-class accepted coverage is 0.970, compared with 0.926 for sTACP and 0.864 for LCP-VLM.

AI.tldr: CALCoDe is a post-hoc reliability layer for frozen medical vision-language models that combines class-tail adaptive thresholds with localized conformal prediction to maintain both marginal and worst-class coverage under clinical distribution shift.
AI.motivation: Medical VLMs retain high average coverage after clinical shift but severely under-cover individual disease classes, and the failing class varies unpredictably with acquisition protocol and backbone geometry, making source prevalence unreliable for detection. Neither localized nor tail-aware conformal methods model this held-out class-wise coverage failure.
AI.method: CALCoDe uses cross-fitted validation to identify at-risk classes, estimates class-conditional tail thresholds from a disjoint calibration split, and combines each protected threshold with a localized conformal threshold via a one-sided maximum. An independently calibrated support audit defers low-support cases; the method provides finite-sample coverage guarantees under within-class exchangeability and empirical coverage evaluation on shifted cohorts.
AI.result: Across two dermatology shifts (HAM10000 to ISIC 2019 and HAM10000 to PAD-UFES-20) and four frozen VLM backbones, CALCoDe is the only method achieving both 0.95 marginal and worst-class accepted coverage in all eight settings. On HAM10000 to ISIC 2019, its average worst-class accepted coverage is 0.970 vs 0.926 for sTACP and 0.864 for LCP-VLM.
AI.conclusion: CALCoDe is the only conformal deferral method that simultaneously preserves marginal coverage and protects at-risk classes against undercoverage in shifted medical VLM settings, while retaining localized conformal set containment and finite-sample guarantees under exchangeability.

title: A Generalized-Bayes Perspective on Counterfactual Explanations: Posterior-Based Decision-Making and Evaluation
summary: Counterfactual explanations (CEs) enhance the interpretability of machine learning models by identifying the smallest change to an input required to obtain a desired output. Although CEs are conventionally formulated as a distance-minimization problem, the theoretical basis of this formulation has received limited attention. We show that a distance-minimization-based CE is mathematically equivalent to the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate of a Gibbs posterior within the generalized Bayes framework, specifically when a distance-based prior is used. We call this formulation the Distance-Prior Generalized Bayes CE (DP-GBCE). Building on this posterior perspective, we introduce two decision rules beyond MAP within a unified framework: a Bayes decision that minimizes expected decision loss and CVaR-CE, a risk-averse decision rule. We also propose an extension that uses Bayesian model weights to mix the posterior distributions of multiple models, thereby accounting for model multiplicity, where several models have comparable predictive performance. Finally, we define metrics for evaluating both individual CEs and the posterior distribution as a whole, and use experiments on simulated data and Google Trends data to quantify the trade-offs among the decision rules.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes that distance-minimization-based counterfactual explanations (CEs) are mathematically equivalent to MAP estimates of a Gibbs posterior under a generalized Bayes framework, and introduces new decision rules (Bayes decision and CVaR-CE) and model-mixing extensions within this unified posterior perspective.
AI.motivation: Although CEs are conventionally formulated as a distance-minimization problem, the theoretical foundation of this formulation has received limited attention. The authors aim to provide a rigorous theoretical basis for CEs by connecting them to the generalized Bayes framework.
AI.method: The authors show that a distance-minimization-based CE is equivalent to a MAP estimate of a Gibbs posterior under a distance-based prior, calling this DP-GBCE. They then introduce two additional decision rules within the unified framework: a Bayes decision rule minimizing expected decision loss, and CVaR-CE as a risk-averse rule. They also extend the framework to mix posterior distributions of multiple models via Bayesian model weights to handle model multiplicity. Metrics are defined to evaluate individual CEs and the posterior distribution as a whole.
AI.result: Experiments on simulated data and Google Trends data quantify trade-offs among the decision rules (MAP, Bayes decision, and CVaR-CE), demonstrating the practical utility of the proposed metrics and decision rules.
AI.conclusion: The generalized Bayes perspective provides a principled theoretical foundation for counterfactual explanations, enabling richer decision rules, model multiplicity handling, and systematic evaluation metrics that go beyond the conventional distance-minimization formulation.

title: Rethinking Detection Calibration: A Coordinate and Direction Perspective
summary: Deep learning based object detectors require trustworthiness beyond competitive detection performance, but deep neural networks are prone to overconfident predictions, assigning high confidence scores to predictions that are likely to be inaccurate. To improve the alignment between confidence scores and prediction accuracy, existing methods calibrate confidence scores based on box-level localization, such as precision or intersection over union with the ground truth bounding box. However, box-level localization reflects only a measure of agreement between the predicted box and the ground truth, resulting in calibrated confidence scores for box-level accuracy failing to capture the localization accuracy of coordinates of box. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel post-hoc calibration framework, rethinking detection calibration (ReDC), which provides reliable coordinate-level confidence scores, including directional information. The proposed framework defines coordinate-wise alignment and deviation direction between predictions and ground truth. Based on the alignment measure, confidence re-encoding produces reliable coordinate-level confidence scores, while directional displacement estimation predicts coordinate-wise deviation directions. Extensive experiments under in-domain and out-domain scenarios demonstrate that the proposed approach expresses the coordinate-wise localization of detected objects more precisely than existing methods. Furthermore, our method covers the representational scope of prior calibration approaches by aggregating coordinate-level confidence scores into box-level localization.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ReDC, a post-hoc calibration framework for object detection that provides reliable coordinate-level confidence scores (including directional information) that go beyond existing box-level calibration approaches, and demonstrates superior performance in both in-domain and out-domain scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing detection calibration methods only calibrate confidence scores based on box-level localization (e.g., IoU with ground truth), which fails to capture the localization accuracy of individual box coordinates. Deep neural network detectors are prone to overconfident predictions, so better confidence calibration is needed for trustworthy object detection.
AI.method: ReDC (rethinking detection calibration) is a post-hoc calibration framework that: (1) defines coordinate-wise alignment and deviation direction between predictions and ground truth, (2) uses confidence re-encoding based on alignment measures to produce reliable coordinate-level confidence scores, and (3) performs directional displacement estimation to predict coordinate-wise deviation directions. It can also aggregate coordinate-level confidence scores into box-level localization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments in both in-domain and out-domain scenarios show that ReDC expresses coordinate-wise localization of detected objects more precisely than existing methods, and covers the representational scope of prior box-level calibration approaches.
AI.conclusion: Coordinate-level confidence calibration with directional information provides a more granular and trustworthy representation of detection uncertainty than existing box-level calibration methods, serving as a more general and expressive framework for detector calibration.

title: Mining Verdict Boundaries for Neural Network Verification
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Published in the proceedings of the 27th International Symposium on Formal Methods (FM 2026)
summary: Branch and Bound (BaB) aims to achieve complete verification of neural networks by adaptively partitioning the problem and applying off-the-shelf verifiers to subproblems. Its problem-splitting history can be represented as a tree, where each subproblem corresponds to a child node. A key problem of BaB lies in searching for the verdict boundaries across all the paths that divide the verified and unverified subproblems. We observe that the existing BaB approach tackles this problem by solving each expensive subproblem sequentially along the tree path as its depth increases, requiring costly bounds propagation at every visited BaB tree node (i.e., subproblem), which is inefficient. To address this issue, we propose effective search approaches that leverage the monotonicity of each path to efficiently and precisely locate the verdict boundary by simultaneously splitting multiple activation functions (e.g., ReLU), rather than processing them one at a time as in the classical approach. Our approach performs an effective exponential search along each path, allowing us to skip many boundary-unrelated subproblems when identifying the verdict boundary. The enhanced version further improves this process by estimating the boundary's position using quantitative information obtained from subproblem solving. We perform experimental evaluation on commonly-used benchmarks to assess our proposed techniques, and compare them with recent BaB-based approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes efficient search strategies for Branch and Bound verification of neural networks, leveraging path monotonicity to locate verdict boundaries by simultaneously splitting multiple activation functions and using exponential search to skip boundary-unrelated subproblems.
AI.motivation: Existing BaB-based neural network verification approaches are inefficient because they sequentially solve subproblems along tree paths, requiring costly bounds propagation at every visited tree node. This leads to unnecessary computation when searching for the verdict boundary between verified and unverified subproblems.
AI.method: The approach exploits the monotonicity of each BaB search path to efficiently locate the verdict boundary. Instead of splitting activation functions (e.g., ReLU) one at a time as in classical BaB, the method simultaneously splits multiple activation functions and performs an exponential search along each path, skipping boundary-unrelated subproblems. An enhanced version uses quantitative information from subproblem solving to estimate the boundary's position.
AI.result: The proposed techniques were experimentally evaluated on commonly-used benchmarks and compared against recent BaB-based approaches, demonstrating their effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting path monotonicity and performing exponential search with simultaneous multi-activation splitting can significantly improve the efficiency of finding verdict boundaries in BaB-based neural network verification.

title: Flow Matching with Missing Data
summary: Flow matching assumes fully observed training data, which many real-world applications rarely provide. We propose Missing-Data Flow Matching, which treats the missing coordinates of training samples as latent variables and averages the flow matching loss over the values they could take. We first prove the correction is exact rather than approximate. Under missing completely at random with true completions, the incomplete-data objective equals the complete-data objective, so missingness changes nothing about what flow matching learns and the entire difficulty relocates to the completion model. Our finite-sample analysis then answers design questions that the algorithm leaves open, and the answers are not the ones intuition suggests. Missingness transfers estimator variance rather than adding it, one completion per example already matches complete-data variance exactly, and under a fixed evaluation budget one completion is optimal. A learned completion model contributes a single irreducible bias, which we bound by its expected conditional Wasserstein distance to the true completion law. Experiments numerically validate the theoretical predictions, show that deterministic rather than frozen imputation is what collapses the generated distribution, and place our method alongside strong classical and deep imputation baselines on real tabular data.

AI.tldr: We propose Missing-Data Flow Matching (MDFM), a method that treats missing coordinates in training samples as latent variables and averages the flow matching loss over possible completions. We prove the correction is exact under missing completely at random, show that missingness transfers rather than adds estimator variance, and demonstrate that one completion per example is optimal under a fixed evaluation budget.
AI.motivation: Flow matching assumes fully observed training data, but many real-world applications involve missing data. Standard flow matching cannot directly handle incomplete observations, creating a gap between the method's assumptions and practical needs.
AI.method: The method treats missing coordinates as latent variables and averages the flow matching loss over all possible values they could take. It includes a theoretical analysis covering exactness proofs under missing completely at random, finite-sample analysis of variance properties, and a learned completion model whose bias is bounded by the expected conditional Wasserstein distance to the true completion law.
AI.result: The incomplete-data objective equals the complete-data objective under MCAR with true completions. Missingness transfers estimator variance rather than adding it; one completion per example matches complete-data variance exactly and is optimal under a fixed evaluation budget. A learned completion model introduces a single irreducible bias bounded by conditional Wasserstein distance. Numerical experiments validate the theory and show deterministic imputation (rather than frozen imputation) is what collapses the generated distribution. The method performs competitively against strong classical and deep imputation baselines on real tabular data.
AI.conclusion: Missing-data flow matching is theoretically exact under MCAR, the design choices differ from intuition (one completion is optimal), and the method achieves strong empirical performance on both synthetic and real tabular data, offering a principled approach to flow matching with incomplete observations.

title: Harnessing the Wisdom of LLM Crowds through Complementarity-Driven Iterative Collaboration
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in enterprise settings, yet individual models remain bounded by model-specific capability limitations. These heterogeneous boundaries pose a deployment challenge, but also create an opportunity: strategically coordinating multiple LLMs may unlock collective intelligence exceeding any single model. Existing approaches fix how models are combined in advance, overlooking the dynamic, state-dependent role of complementarity in complex problem solving. Drawing on the wisdom-of-crowds paradigm, we reconceptualize collective LLM intelligence as relay-style complementarity: a sequential process in which each successor model is selected to address the specific bottleneck identified in its predecessor's output. To operationalize this, we propose WILC (Wisdom Integration of LLM Crowds), a framework grounded in two design principles. First, iterative reflection-and-refinement establishes a state-preserving workflow through which models diagnose and refine prior outputs. Second, complementarity-driven model selection governs transitions via a dual-gate mechanism: prospective complementarity fit (PCF) identifies the worker most suited to the current bottleneck, while posterior complementarity gain (PCG) evaluates whether the selected transition improves the evolving solution. Experiments across four diverse benchmarks show that WILC outperforms existing approaches, including single-model self-refinement, ensemble methods, and query-routing methods. Under standardized pricing assumptions, WILC matches the average benchmark performance of GPT-5.2 at roughly 7 times lower estimated per-query cost, while facilitating data sovereignty through self-hosted deployment. This study extends wisdom-of-crowds theory from static aggregation to sequential AI complementarity and provides transferable design principles for multi-AI coordination.

AI.tldr: WILC (Wisdom Integration of LLM Crowds) is a framework for coordinating multiple LLMs via relay-style complementarity, where each successor model is dynamically selected to address the bottleneck identified in its predecessor's output. It uses reflection-and-refinement workflows and a dual-gate mechanism (PCF for prospective fit, PCG for posterior gain). Experiments across four benchmarks show it outperforms single-model self-refinement, ensembles, and query-routing methods, matching GPT-5.2 performance at roughly 7x lower estimated cost while enabling self-hosted deployment.
AI.motivation: Individual LLMs have heterogeneous capability boundaries that limit their standalone performance in enterprise deployments. Existing approaches fix model combinations in advance, failing to exploit the dynamic, state-dependent complementarity among models. The authors seek to unlock collective intelligence that exceeds any single model by treating LLM coordination as a sequential, bottleneck-driven process rather than static aggregation.
AI.method: WILC reconceptualizes collective LLM intelligence as relay-style complementarity. It is built on two design principles: (1) iterative reflection-and-refinement, a state-preserving workflow where models diagnose and refine prior outputs; and (2) complementarity-driven model selection controlled by a dual-gate mechanism—Prospective Complementarity Fit (PCF) selects the worker best suited to the current bottleneck, and Posterior Complementarity Gain (PCG) evaluates whether the transition improved the evolving solution.
AI.result: Across four diverse benchmarks, WILC outperforms single-model self-refinement, ensemble methods, and query-routing approaches. Under standardized pricing assumptions, WILC matches the average benchmark performance of GPT-5.2 at roughly 7 times lower estimated per-query cost, and facilitates data sovereignty via self-hosted deployment.
AI.conclusion: The study extends wisdom-of-crowds theory from static aggregation to sequential AI complementarity, providing transferable design principles for multi-AI coordination. The framework demonstrates that strategically sequencing heterogeneous LLMs can yield performance exceeding any single model while reducing cost and supporting data sovereignty.

title: Adaptive Emotional Video Captioning via Affective Heterogeneous Graph Reasoning and Multi-task Joint Learning
summary: Emotional video captioning (EVC) aims to describe a video with both factual correctness and affective expressiveness. It requires a model to perceive subtle, ambiguous, and temporally varying emotional cues and translate them into natural language without weakening objective visual content. Existing methods have progressively introduced contextual attention, emotion interpretation, emotion priors, dynamic emotion perception and emotion-cause reasoning. Nevertheless, most of them still depend on either global emotion vectors or rigid hierarchical priors. In recent methods, the tree-structured emotion prior establishes a coarse-to-fine connection between psychological emotion categories and daily emotion words, but its hard subordinate masking may irreversibly suppress correct lexical emotions once the coarse category prediction is inaccurate. It is also limited in representing mixed or overlapping emotions that frequently occur in real videos. To address the issues, we propose SAGML, an adaptive EVC framework via affective heterogeneous graph and multi-task language modeling. Instead of treating the emotion prior as a discrete tree, SAGML constructs a soft affective heterogeneous graph containing catalog-level emotion nodes and lexical-level emotion word nodes. The soft gate is injected into video-to-emotion graph attention as a continuous bias, allowing visually supported lexical emotions to remain recoverable rather than being removed by a hard mask. The resulting affective representation is fed together with visual tokens into a causal language decoder, while dual catalog and lexical heads impose explicit emotion distribution learning on the prompt hidden states. The overall model is trained with a joint objective that combines autoregressive caption generation and emotion distribution supervision. SAGML provides an error-resilient and multi-emotion-aware baseline for EVC.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SAGML, an adaptive emotional video captioning framework that replaces discrete tree-structured emotion priors with a soft affective heterogeneous graph comprising catalog-level and lexical-level emotion nodes, using soft-gated graph attention and multi-task language modeling to enable error-resilient and multi-emotion-aware video captioning.
AI.motivation: Existing emotional video captioning (EVC) methods rely on either global emotion vectors or rigid hierarchical priors. Tree-structured emotion priors use hard subordinate masking that irreversibly suppresses correct lexical emotions when coarse category predictions are inaccurate, and cannot represent mixed or overlapping emotions present in real videos.
AI.method: SAGML constructs a soft affective heterogeneous graph containing catalog-level emotion nodes and lexical-level emotion word nodes. A soft gate is injected into video-to-emotion graph attention as a continuous bias, preventing hard masking of lexical emotions. The affective representation is combined with visual tokens and fed into a causal language decoder, while dual catalog and lexical heads impose explicit emotion distribution learning on prompt hidden states. Training uses a joint objective combining autoregressive caption generation and emotion distribution supervision.
AI.result: SAGML provides an error-resilient and multi-emotion-aware baseline for EVC, overcoming the limitations of hard masking in tree-structured emotion priors and improving representation of mixed or overlapping emotions.
AI.conclusion: The soft affective heterogeneous graph with continuous gating offers a more robust approach to emotion perception in video captioning, allowing visually supported lexical emotions to remain recoverable even when coarse emotion category predictions are inaccurate.

title: Exploring Block Anomaly Detection In HDFS Log Data Analysis
summary: In recent years, with the development of big data technology, increasingly more companies use HDFS for data processing and storage. As a result, the maintenance of distributed file systems has become an extremely important part of data management. As the function of server systems is becoming increasingly diversified and their services are becoming complex, the logs, recording real-time events make it easier for system operators to locate the failures and errors that happened in the server systems to make server always available. HDFS, a distributed file system, which contains large data sets, will record a large number of logs. Moreover, the logs are not always structured data, they are not stable as well. However, to detect the problems that occur in the system by checking one log by one log, it's complicated and boring work for the system operators. Using machine learning techniques and natural language processing techniques to detect the HDFS block anomaly will help the system operators to locate and fix the anomaly rapidly and accurately. This paper proposes a streaming HDFS log block anomaly workflow. It helps maintenance practitioners to use parallel computing network in processing historical log, and construct LLM-BiLSTM hybrid deep learning model to detect anomaly block in HDFS, then build streaming log pipeline based on Kafka to give one real-time HDFS log block anomaly detection solution.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a streaming HDFS log block anomaly detection workflow that uses parallel computing for historical log processing, an LLM-BiLSTM hybrid deep learning model for anomaly detection, and a Kafka-based streaming pipeline for real-time monitoring of HDFS log blocks.
AI.motivation: As HDFS is widely used for big data storage, the volume and complexity of logs make manual anomaly detection impractical and error-prone. System operators need automated, accurate, and real-time solutions to identify failures in distributed file systems.
AI.method: The approach combines: (1) parallel computing networks to process historical logs, (2) an LLM-BiLSTM hybrid deep learning model to detect anomalous blocks in HDFS, and (3) a Kafka-based streaming log pipeline for real-time anomaly detection.
AI.result: The paper presents a complete workflow enabling rapid and accurate detection of HDFS block anomalies, supporting both historical batch processing and real-time streaming scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The proposed streaming HDFS log block anomaly workflow integrates machine learning and natural language processing to automate anomaly detection, significantly reducing the burden on system operators while improving detection accuracy and speed.

title: MMFGU: Multimodal Federated Graph Unlearning
summary: Multimodal federated graph learning enables clients to collaboratively train graph models over structural, textual, and visual signals without sharing private local data. However, the presence of heterogeneous multimodal content also makes unlearning requests more frequent and fine-grained: users may delete accounts or interactions, remove a particular image or text while retaining the associated entity, or revoke the learned correspondence between retained modalities or graph attributes. Existing federated graph unlearning mainly handles entity/relation or client removal and cannot directly satisfy these multimodal requests. They introduce three challenges: removing only the requested information without damaging retained content, preventing the target from being recovered through remaining modalities or graph neighborhoods, and stopping related traces on other clients from re-entering the global model after aggregation. To address them, we propose \textsc{\textbf{MMFGU}}, a multimodal federated graph unlearning framework built around target-specific representation decoupling. \textsc{MMFGU} maps heterogeneous requests into unified target carriers, decouples requested representations while anchoring retained semantics, exposes and repairs propagated residuals with lightweight probes, and selectively purges affected clients through compact prototype and response signals. Experiments show that \textsc{MMFGU} effectively removes requested information, preserves retained graph utility, and achieves a $\boldsymbol{41.5\times}$ speedup over full retraining.

AI.tldr: MMFGU is a multimodal federated graph unlearning framework that uses target-specific representation decoupling to handle fine-grained unlearning requests (entity/relation, image/text removal, modality/graph attribute correspondence revocation) without retraining from scratch, achieving 41.5x speedup over full retraining while preserving retained graph utility.
AI.motivation: Existing federated graph unlearning methods only handle entity/relation or client removal and cannot satisfy the more frequent and fine-grained multimodal unlearning requests (e.g., deleting a specific image/text while retaining the entity, or revoking learned cross-modal correspondences). This creates three challenges: removing only the requested information without damaging retained content, preventing target recovery through remaining modalities or graph neighborhoods, and stopping related traces on other clients from re-entering the global model after aggregation.
AI.method: MMFGU is built around target-specific representation decoupling. It maps heterogeneous unlearning requests into unified target carriers, decouples requested representations while anchoring retained semantics, exposes and repairs propagated residuals using lightweight probes, and selectively purges affected clients through compact prototype and response signals.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that MMFGU effectively removes requested information, preserves retained graph utility, and achieves a 41.5x speedup over full retraining.
AI.conclusion: MMFGU provides a general, efficient solution for multimodal federated graph unlearning that handles diverse fine-grained requests while maintaining model utility and significantly reducing computational cost compared to full retraining.

title: CAGE: Certified Authorization under Typed-Return Uncertainty for Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool-using LLM agents act on typed tool returns, records pairing provenance and categorical fields with numerical values. Runtime permission gates generally authorize the observed return and action, leaving the decision unprotected against small errors in how the return was bound to its source. We ask whether a candidate action stays authorized over a declared neighborhood of plausible correctly bound returns: one admissible binding fault plus bounded numerical drift. We prove that certifying the categorical and numerical channels separately does not compose: perturbations that are safe on each channel alone can jointly turn the same action unsafe. CAGE certifies this joint neighborhood directly, enumerating the discrete branches exactly and certifying the continuous perturbation within each branch. Across synthetic, policy-as-code, regulatory, and real-transaction settings, CAGE removes the in-budget false allows that accurate pointwise gates admit, while keeping a useful fraction of decisions autonomous. When the policy is executable, CAGE-Exact certifies the policy itself; otherwise CAGE-Lip and CAGE-RS certify a learned gate under an explicit, measured fidelity assumption.

AI.tldr: CAGE is a certification framework for tool-using LLM agents that verifies whether an action remains authorized not just at the observed tool return but across a neighborhood of plausible correctly-bound returns (one binding fault plus bounded numerical drift), thereby eliminating in-budget false allows that pointwise permission gates admit.
AI.motivation: Runtime permission gates for LLM agents typically authorize only the observed tool return, leaving decisions unprotected against small errors in how the return was bound to its source. Certifying categorical and numerical channels separately is insufficient because perturbations that are individually safe can jointly turn an action unsafe.
AI.method: CAGE certifies the joint neighborhood of admissible binding faults (discrete) and bounded numerical drift (continuous). It enumerates the discrete branches exactly and certifies the continuous perturbation within each branch. Three variants exist: CAGE-Exact certifies the policy itself when it is executable; otherwise CAGE-Lip and CAGE-RS certify a learned gate under an explicit, measured fidelity assumption.
AI.result: Across synthetic, policy-as-code, regulatory, and real-transaction settings, CAGE removes the in-budget false allows that accurate pointwise gates admit while keeping a useful fraction of decisions autonomous.
AI.conclusion: Certifying a joint neighborhood (rather than separate channels) of tool returns is both necessary and practically achievable, providing robustness guarantees for autonomous decisions made by tool-using LLM agents under binding and numerical perturbation.

title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Spiking Point Cloud Models
summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer energy-efficient solutions for point cloud analysis on resource-constrained devices through event-driven computation. However, existing pre-trained spiking point cloud models rely on full fine-tuning for downstream task adaptation, incurring substantial parameter and storage overhead. Furthermore, binary spike propagation suppresses task-relevant sub-threshold information. To address these issues, we propose SpikePEFT, the first parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework for spiking point cloud models. Specifically, Intrinsic Dynamics Tuning (IDT) adaptively modulates membrane decay and firing thresholds, enabling efficient neuron-intrinsic adaptation while keeping the pre-trained synaptic transformations frozen. Moreover, Silent-State Disambiguation Adaptation (SSDA) recovers task-relevant information from informative silent states, thereby providing richer evidence for downstream adaptation. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of SpikePEFT. In particular, our method achieves 92.4% accuracy on ModelNet40 and 85.6\% on the most challenging classification split ScanObjectNN(PB\_T50\_RS) while updating only about 5% of the trainable parameters and preserving the energy efficiency of SNNs. This work provides a promising step toward parameter-efficient adaptation of neuromorphic vision models.

AI.tldr: SpikePEFT is the first parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework for spiking point cloud models, using Intrinsic Dynamics Tuning (IDT) to modulate membrane decay and firing thresholds, and Silent-State Disambiguation Adaptation (SSDA) to recover task-relevant information from silent states. It achieves 92.4% accuracy on ModelNet40 and 85.6% on ScanObjectNN while updating only ~5% of trainable parameters, preserving SNN energy efficiency.
AI.motivation: Pre-trained spiking point cloud models rely on full fine-tuning for downstream tasks, causing substantial parameter and storage overhead. Additionally, binary spike propagation suppresses task-relevant sub-threshold information, limiting adaptation effectiveness.
AI.method: Two components: (1) Intrinsic Dynamics Tuning (IDT) adaptively modulates membrane decay and firing thresholds for efficient neuron-intrinsic adaptation while keeping pre-trained synaptic transformations frozen; (2) Silent-State Disambiguation Adaptation (SSDA) recovers task-relevant information from informative silent states to provide richer evidence for downstream adaptation.
AI.result: 92.4% accuracy on ModelNet40 and 85.6% on ScanObjectNN(PB_T50_RS) while updating only about 5% of trainable parameters and preserving SNN energy efficiency.
AI.conclusion: SpikePEFT provides a promising step toward parameter-efficient adaptation of neuromorphic vision models, addressing both parameter overhead and information loss in spiking point cloud fine-tuning.

title: Simulation Code Generation for Fluid Systems using Large Language Models: Benchmarking Models and Prompting Strategies
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated a strong ability to generate syntactically correct code from natural-language specifications. In this study, we explore how LLMs can be harnessed to automatically translate a neutral graph representation of fluid system models into executable code for two widely adopted simulation environments: the Python library WNTR and the Modelica Standard Library. We conduct a systematic comparison of ten state-of-the-art LLMs and six prompting strategies that differ in the contextual information supplied (e.g., code or documentation). For each configuration we assess the generated code using a suite of software-quality metrics and we validate the functional fidelity of the resulting simulation models by reproducing benchmark fluid system scenarios. Our findings offer concrete guidance for researchers and engineers seeking to integrate LLM-driven code synthesis into model-based design pipelines. While the best-performing configurations achieve acceptable syntactic quality, we observe substantial gaps remain in simulation fidelity.

AI.tldr: This paper explores using LLMs to automatically translate neutral graph representations of fluid system models into executable code for WNTR (Python) and Modelica. Ten state-of-the-art LLMs and six prompting strategies are systematically compared using software-quality metrics and functional fidelity validation against benchmark scenarios. Best configurations achieve acceptable syntactic quality, but significant gaps remain in simulation fidelity.
AI.motivation: To investigate how LLMs can be harnessed to automate the translation of neutral graph representations of fluid system models into executable code for two simulation environments (WNTR and Modelica), providing guidance for integrating LLM-driven code synthesis into model-based design pipelines.
AI.method: Ten state-of-the-art LLMs and six prompting strategies differing in contextual information (e.g., code or documentation) are systematically compared. Generated code is assessed using software-quality metrics, and functional fidelity is validated by reproducing benchmark fluid system scenarios.
AI.result: Best-performing configurations achieve acceptable syntactic quality, but substantial gaps remain in simulation fidelity.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can generate syntactically correct code for fluid system simulations, yet simulation fidelity remains a major challenge, offering concrete guidance for researchers and engineers using LLM-driven code synthesis in model-based design.

title: Mirror Learning
summary: We investigate imitation learning through the lens of third-person observation and propose a framework for mirror learning: acquiring actionable policies from passive observation. While behavior cloning (BC) excels under dense, well-aligned first-person data, it fundamentally fails to leverage the rich observational signals arising from third-person demonstrations that humans and animals routinely exploit. We introduce a method that composes (i) a learned perspective transformation that places learners in demonstrators' shoes using a fine-tuned video diffusion model and (ii) an inverse dynamics model that infers action trajectories in the learners' control space. This enables the synthesis of mirror data, pseudo first-person expert data generated from third-person observations of demonstrator behavior. Empirically, we show that mirror data alone can train effective policies, and that augmenting first-person BC training with mirror data further improves downstream policy performance. Our results suggest that modern generative world models implicitly encode sufficient structure to enable a scalable and safe alternative to teleoperation-heavy data collection.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework for "mirror learning" that extracts actionable policies from third-person demonstrations by composing a learned perspective transformation (using a fine-tuned video diffusion model) with an inverse dynamics model, generating pseudo first-person expert data (mirror data) that can train or augment imitation learning policies effectively.
AI.motivation: Behavior cloning excels under dense, well-aligned first-person data but fails to exploit rich observational signals from third-person demonstrations that humans and animals routinely use. This limits scalability and safety, as teleoperation-heavy data collection is expensive and restrictive.
AI.method: The method composes (i) a learned perspective transformation using a fine-tuned video diffusion model to place learners in demonstrators' perspective, and (ii) an inverse dynamics model that infers action trajectories in the learner's control space, synthesizing pseudo first-person expert data (mirror data) from third-person observations.
AI.result: Mirror data alone can train effective policies, and augmenting first-person BC training with mirror data further improves downstream policy performance, demonstrating that modern generative world models encode sufficient structure for scalable imitation from passive observation.
AI.conclusion: Generative world models implicitly encode enough structure to enable a scalable and safe alternative to teleoperation-heavy data collection for imitation learning.

title: MirrorCraft: Paired Evaluation under Hidden Rule Changes in Minecraft
summary: With the prosperity of the large language models (LLMs), it has become an interesting topic: how do LLM-based agents work in Minecraft? Unfortunately, most existing benchmarks evaluate them under fixed game mechanics. High performance in these settings does not show whether an agent can continue making progress when familiar recipes, drops, and other rules change. In this paper, we introduce MirrorCraft, a paired benchmark for evaluating agents under hidden rule changes in Minecraft. Each Mirror world is a copy of its paired Vanilla world, with selected server-side rules modified by the corresponding datapack. Terrain, spawn, resource placement, objective, interface, and action budget remain matched within every Vanilla-Mirror pair. MirrorCraft includes five controlled biomes, six rule suites, three progression objectives, two model families, and six agent configurations under a shared Mineflayer interface. We evaluate task progress with deterministic advancement milestones and success rate and use the Rule Intervention Effect (RIE) to measure the performance change between matched Vanilla and Mirror worlds. The experiments show that hidden rule changes have strongly different effects across suites. Among the configurations evaluated without rule descriptions, ReAct achieves the highest pooled Mirror score. Providing the exact rules yields modest gains in average progress and completion across all three objectives. MirrorCraft extends Minecraft evaluation beyond fixed mechanics and provides a controlled setting for studying how agents use gameplay outcomes when the rules of the current world differ from familiar ones.

AI.tldr: MirrorCraft is a paired benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agents in Minecraft under hidden server-side rule changes, using matched Vanilla-Mirror world pairs with controlled datapacks that modify recipes, drops, and other mechanics. It includes five biomes, six rule suites, three objectives, and six agent configurations, measuring success via deterministic milestones and a Rule Intervention Effect metric.
AI.motivation: Existing Minecraft benchmarks evaluate LLM agents under fixed game mechanics, which does not reveal whether agents can adapt when familiar recipes, drops, and rules change—a critical gap for assessing real-world robustness.
AI.method: MirrorCraft pairs each Mirror world with a Vanilla world, modifying selected server-side rules via datapacks while keeping terrain, spawn, resources, objectives, interface, and action budgets matched. It spans five controlled biomes, six rule suites, three progression objectives, two model families, and six agent configurations under a shared Mineflayer interface. Performance is measured using deterministic advancement milestones, success rates, and the Rule Intervention Effect (RIE).
AI.result: Hidden rule changes have strongly different effects across rule suites. ReAct achieves the highest pooled Mirror score among configurations evaluated without rule descriptions, and providing exact rules yields only modest gains in average progress and completion across all three objectives.
AI.conclusion: MirrorCraft extends Minecraft evaluation beyond fixed mechanics and provides a controlled setting for studying how agents utilize gameplay outcomes when world rules diverge from familiar ones.

title: Learning from Adversity: Semantic-Aware Mask Refinement through Adversarial Perturbation
summary: Despite significant advances in image segmentation, even state-of-the-art models produce masks with imperfect boundaries, semantic inconsistencies, and structural errors. Mask refinement addresses these limitations, yet current approaches rely on simplistic synthetic noise that fails to capture the complex error patterns of real segmentation models. We introduce Phoenix, a novel framework that leverages adversarial learning to generate semantically meaningful noise patterns and contrastive learning to model refinement relationships. Our approach consists of two key innovations: (1) Adversarial Mask Perturbation, which employs embedding attacks to create semantic-aware noise that mimics real segmentation errors, and (2) Contrastive Mask Refinement Learning, which establishes a tri-directional framework that ensures feature consistency within semantic regions while maintaining separation between classes. Experiments demonstrate that Phoenix significantly outperforms existing methods across diverse tasks, while consistently enhancing state-of-the-art segmentation models with substantial improvements. Our code and project page are publicly available at https://phoenix-eccv26.github.io.

AI.tldr: Phoenix is a novel mask refinement framework that uses adversarial learning to generate semantically meaningful noise patterns that mimic real segmentation errors and contrastive learning to model refinement relationships, significantly outperforming existing methods across diverse segmentation tasks while enhancing state-of-the-art models.
AI.motivation: Current mask refinement methods rely on simplistic synthetic noise that fails to capture the complex error patterns of real segmentation models, which produce masks with imperfect boundaries, semantic inconsistencies, and structural errors.
AI.method: Phoenix consists of two key innovations: (1) Adversarial Mask Perturbation, which employs embedding attacks to create semantic-aware noise that mimics real segmentation errors, and (2) Contrastive Mask Refinement Learning, a tri-directional framework that ensures feature consistency within semantic regions while maintaining separation between classes.
AI.result: Experiments show Phoenix significantly outperforms existing methods across diverse tasks and consistently enhances state-of-the-art segmentation models with substantial improvements.
AI.conclusion: Phoenix demonstrates that adversarial learning for realistic noise generation combined with contrastive refinement learning provides an effective solution for mask refinement, with code and project page publicly available.

title: Beyond Component Testing: Validating Agentic AI Systems
comment: 61 pages, 3 figures, to be submitted to Springer Artificial Intelligence Review
summary: Agentic AI systems act through multi-step trajectories that combine planning, tool use, memory, interaction, and adaptation. This behavior stretches validation practice beyond component testing and one-shot input--output evaluation, because acceptable system behavior now depends on how decisions unfold over time and under changing environmental conditions. This survey synthesizes 257 papers spanning agent evaluation, software assurance, cyber-physical systems, runtime monitoring, and regulatory guidance in order to characterize the validation problem for agentic systems. The review is organized around a five-dimension taxonomy covering behavioral, safety, temporal, regulatory, and multi-agent concerns, and uses that taxonomy to map current approaches and expose recurrent coverage gaps. The analysis shows that behavioral evaluation is comparatively mature, while temporal validity, runtime evidence maintenance, regulatory legibility, and open-ended multi-agent systems assurance remain under-developed. Three cross-domain case studies (medical care, industrial operations, smart-mobility systems) provide operational illustrations of how the five taxonomy dimensions recur in safety-critical settings, grounded in the failure patterns documented in the reviewed literature. The paper concludes with a lifecycle-oriented research agenda centered on bounded-autonomy specifications, adversarial trajectory generation, runtime monitoring, and audit-ready evidence structures. The central claim is that trustworthy deployment of agentic AI depends on validating trajectories in context rather than assessing isolated components alone.

AI.tldr: This survey synthesizes 257 papers across agent evaluation, software assurance, cyber-physical systems, runtime monitoring, and regulatory guidance to characterize validation challenges for agentic AI systems, organizing findings around a five-dimension taxonomy (behavioral, safety, temporal, regulatory, multi-agent) and proposing a lifecycle-oriented research agenda.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems operate through multi-step trajectories combining planning, tool use, memory, interaction, and adaptation, stretching validation practice beyond component testing and one-shot input-output evaluation. Acceptable behavior now depends on how decisions unfold over time under changing conditions, yet existing validation approaches are fragmented across disciplines.
AI.method: The authors synthesize 257 papers spanning five related fields (agent evaluation, software assurance, cyber-physical systems, runtime monitoring, regulatory guidance), organize approaches using a five-dimension taxonomy (behavioral, safety, temporal, regulatory, multi-agent), and use the taxonomy to map current approaches and expose coverage gaps. Three cross-domain case studies (medical care, industrial operations, smart-mobility systems) ground the findings in safety-critical failure patterns from the literature.
AI.result: Behavioral evaluation is comparatively mature, while temporal validity, runtime evidence maintenance, regulatory legibility, and open-ended multi-agent systems assurance remain under-developed. The analysis exposes recurrent coverage gaps across the five taxonomy dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy deployment of agentic AI depends on validating trajectories in context rather than assessing isolated components alone. The paper proposes a research agenda centered on bounded-autonomy specifications, adversarial trajectory generation, runtime monitoring, and audit-ready evidence structures.

title: TAGTorch: A PyTorch Library for Geometry, Topology, and Symmetry-Aware Machine Learning
summary: Over the last decade, neural networks have been applied to an increasingly diverse range of applications, including data with rich geometric, topological, or symmetry-related structure. As a result, researchers have increasingly drawn inspiration from topology, algebra, and geometry. Despite this rich algorithmic development, the supporting software ecosystem remains fragmented. Many important methods exist only as research prototypes in unmaintained repositories. We address this by introducing Topology, Algebra, and Geometry Torch (TAGTorch), an open-source, PyTorch-based library that unifies tools inspired by topology, algebra, and geometry, including data-preprocessing methods, architectures, training techniques, and model analysis tools. We describe the design philosophy of TAGTorch and then discuss its current architecture and capabilities, highlighting areas where it can fill gaps in the current software ecosystem. We conclude with a discussion of our future development priorities for the library.

AI.tldr: TAGTorch is an open-source, PyTorch-based library that unifies tools inspired by topology, algebra, and geometry, providing data preprocessing, architectures, training techniques, and model analysis tools to address the fragmented software ecosystem in this emerging field.
AI.motivation: Despite rich algorithmic development in neural networks for data with geometric, topological, or symmetry-related structure, the supporting software ecosystem remains fragmented, with many important methods existing only as research prototypes in unmaintained repositories.
AI.method: The authors introduce TAGTorch, an open-source PyTorch-based library that unifies topology-, algebra-, and geometry-inspired tools, covering data-preprocessing methods, architectures, training techniques, and model analysis tools. They describe its design philosophy, current architecture, and capabilities.
AI.result: TAGTorch provides a unified library that fills gaps in the current software ecosystem by consolidating fragmented topological, algebraic, and geometric methods into a single maintainable PyTorch-based framework.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude with a discussion of future development priorities for the library, indicating ongoing plans to expand TAGTorch's capabilities.

title: Don't Mix Rewards, Mix Policies: Policy Decomposition and Optimization for Multi-Reward RL
summary: Modern large language models (LLMs) are expected not just to answer correctly, but to adapt their behavior to different human values and use cases. As a result, multi-reward reinforcement learning (RL) has become an increasingly important problem for LLMs, where each reward captures a different aspect of desired behavior. However, optimizing with multiple rewards suffers from a more severe alignment tax issue, where different optimization objectives can trade off or even conflict with each other, leading to unstable and inefficient post-training. In this work, we propose PRISM, a new multi-reward RL framework built upon the idea of policy-space decomposition and composition. Instead of compositing different rewards, PRISM optimizes a set of standalone positive policies and a global negative policy. This alleviates the potential conflict during multi-reward policy optimization, while enabling controllability during inference by flexible policy composition. Experiments on scientific reasoning, tool-use reasoning, and helpfulness-safety alignment show that PRISM consistently outperforms existing multi-reward RL baselines, with extra controllability for inference-time preference control.

AI.tldr: PRISM is a multi-reward RL framework for LLMs that decomposes the policy space into standalone positive policies and a global negative policy, then composes them during inference. This avoids reward conflicts during training and enables controllable behavior at inference time, outperforming existing multi-reward RL baselines on scientific reasoning, tool-use reasoning, and helpfulness-safety alignment.
AI.motivation: Multi-reward RL for LLMs suffers from a severe alignment tax, where different optimization objectives trade off or conflict with each other, leading to unstable and inefficient post-training. Existing approaches composite rewards directly, which exacerbates these conflicts.
AI.method: PRISM decomposes the multi-reward optimization problem into policy-space decomposition and composition. It trains a set of standalone positive policies (each specialized for one reward) and a global negative policy, then enables controllability during inference through flexible policy composition of these decomposed components.
AI.result: PRISM consistently outperforms existing multi-reward RL baselines across scientific reasoning, tool-use reasoning, and helpfulness-safety alignment tasks, while providing extra controllability for inference-time preference control.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing rewards into standalone policies with a global negative policy mitigates reward conflicts in multi-reward RL and offers a practical path toward controllable LLM alignment with multiple human values and use cases.

title: MHRGait: Gait Recognition from Momentum Human Rig Pose
summary: Gait recognition is shaped by its input representation. Silhouettes encode projected body shape, skeletons encode sparse joint coordinates, and 3D meshes encode dense surface geometry. In each case, identity-bearing articulation is observed through geometric carriers that also vary with clothing, skeletal scale, or body shape. We investigate whether gait can instead be recognized from compact articulated controls. We introduce Momentum Human Rig (MHR) pose as a gait representation, describing each frame using 184 semantically organized body and hand parameters estimated from monocular video. MHRGait groups these heterogeneous controls by anatomy, models their intra-frame coordination and temporal evolution, and produces compact body and hand descriptors. We further introduce MHRGait++, which combines MHR pose with silhouettes through modality-balanced distance fusion, preventing descriptor count from determining modality importance. Experiments on four benchmarks show that MHRGait attains the best overall performance among compared model-based methods on CCPG and SUSTech1K and transfers effectively across datasets, while its recognition network requires only 2.76M parameters and 0.69 GFLOPs for a 30-frame input. MHRGait++ consistently improves silhouette recognizers with a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. These results establish rig-space articulation as an effective standalone gait representation and a complementary cue to projected body shape. Our code is available at https://github.com/duanhuiran/MHRGait.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MHR (Momentum Human Rig) pose as a new gait recognition representation, using 184 semantically organized body and hand parameters per frame. MHRGait groups these controls by anatomy with intra-frame coordination and temporal modeling, and MHRGait++ fuses MHR pose with silhouettes via modality-balanced distance fusion. The methods achieve state-of-the-art performance on four benchmarks with a lightweight 2.76M-parameter recognition network.
AI.motivation: Existing gait representations (silhouettes, skeletons, 3D meshes) carry identity information through geometric carriers that are confounded by clothing, skeletal scale, and body shape. The authors ask whether gait can be recognized from compact articulated controls instead, decoupling identity-bearing articulation from these nuisance factors.
AI.method: Introduces MHR pose, a gait representation with 184 semantically organized body and hand parameters per frame derived from monocular video. MHRGait groups these parameters by anatomy, models intra-frame coordination and temporal evolution, and produces compact body and hand descriptors. MHRGait++ combines MHR pose with silhouettes through modality-balanced distance fusion so that descriptor count does not dominate modality importance.
AI.result: On four benchmarks, MHRGait achieves the best overall performance among model-based methods on CCPG and SUSTech1K, transfers effectively across datasets, and uses only 2.76M parameters and 0.69 GFLOPs for 30-frame input. MHRGait++ consistently improves silhouette recognizers with a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Rig-space articulation proves effective as a standalone gait representation and as a complementary cue to projected body shape, establishing articulated controls as a viable alternative to geometric carrier-based representations.

title: CodeShrink: Adaptive Visual Compression for Efficient Multimodal Code Understanding
summary: Rendering source code as images offers a promising way to reduce the input costs of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Adjusting image resolution can trade visual token cost against content fidelity. However, resolution scaling alone overlooks two sources of inefficiency: blank regions created by line breaks and indentation, and code regions irrelevant to the current instruction. Moreover, the best compression setting varies across inputs, tasks, and models, limiting fixed-ratio strategies. We propose CodeShrink, an adaptive visual compression framework with three components. Blank-Free Rendering replaces whitespace-dependent layouts with compact layouts and explicit structural markers, removing layout-induced tokens. Adaptive Compression Configuration uses a lightweight agent trained with reinforcement learning to predict a per-input setting that balances token efficiency and readability. Dominant Token Selection jointly analyzes the instruction and code image to prune task-irrelevant visual tokens during inference. We evaluate CodeShrink on code question answering, clone detection, and code completion. CodeShrink reduces visual token use by up to 71.2\% while matching or exceeding uncompressed text-only inputs, and consistently outperforms text-based and visual compression baselines across all three tasks. These results show that combining layout compaction, adaptive configuration, and instruction-aware pruning can make multimodal code understanding more efficient. Our code is available at https://github.com/vinsontang1/CodeShrink.

AI.tldr: CodeShrink is an adaptive visual compression framework for MLLMs that reduces visual token usage by up to 71.2% in code understanding tasks through blank-free rendering, RL-trained adaptive compression configuration, and instruction-aware dominant token selection.
AI.motivation: Rendering source code as images for MLLMs is promising but suffers from token inefficiency. Resolution scaling alone overlooks two sources of waste: blank regions from line breaks/indentation and task-irrelevant code regions. Additionally, the optimal compression setting varies across inputs, tasks, and models, making fixed-ratio strategies inadequate.
AI.method: CodeShrink consists of three components: (1) Blank-Free Rendering, which replaces whitespace-dependent layouts with compact layouts and explicit structural markers to remove layout-induced tokens; (2) Adaptive Compression Configuration, which uses a lightweight agent trained with reinforcement learning to predict per-input settings balancing token efficiency and readability; (3) Dominant Token Selection, which jointly analyzes the instruction and code image to prune task-irrelevant visual tokens during inference.
AI.result: Evaluated on code question answering, clone detection, and code completion. CodeShrink reduces visual token usage by up to 71.2% while matching or exceeding uncompressed text-only inputs, and consistently outperforms both text-based and visual compression baselines across all three tasks.
AI.conclusion: Combining layout compaction, adaptive configuration, and instruction-aware pruning makes multimodal code understanding significantly more efficient, achieving substantial token reduction without sacrificing performance.

title: Feature Interaction Modeling for Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Neural Operators
summary: This work embeds feature interaction modules derived from factorization machines (FMs) into physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and neural operator learning, to enhance model expressiveness for solution manifolds of parameterized partial differential equations (PDEs). Motivated by the second-order Taylor expansion of multivariate functions to characterize variable couplings, we first propose FM-PINN. It explicitly captures spatio-temporal variable interactions and improves the approximation accuracy for smooth high-order PDEs. We further group spatial coordinates, time, physical parameters, and initial and boundary conditions into independent feature sets and model their cross-group interactions. Based on this strategy, we develop FM-Operator and FM-DeepONet, which are particularly effective for nonlinear conservation laws and problems with sharp gradients or discontinuities, while offering no consistent advantage on smooth operator learning benchmarks. Numerical tests demonstrate that the proposed mechanism delivers substantial accuracy gains on challenging shock-dominated equations, indicating a promising direction for physics-consistent modeling of parameterized PDEs with strong cross-field dependencies.

AI.tldr: The paper embeds factorization machine (FM) feature interaction modules into PINNs and neural operators to capture spatio-temporal variable couplings via second-order Taylor expansion-like interactions, yielding FM-PINN, FM-Operator, and FM-DeepONet. These methods significantly improve accuracy for nonlinear conservation laws and shock-dominated problems with sharp gradients, though they offer no consistent advantage on smooth operator learning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard PINNs and neural operators lack explicit mechanisms to model interactions between input variables (space, time, parameters, IC/BCs), limiting their expressiveness for solution manifolds of parameterized PDEs, especially those with strong cross-field dependencies and discontinuities.
AI.method: The authors leverage second-order Taylor expansion of multivariate functions to characterize variable couplings. They propose FM-PINN to explicitly capture spatio-temporal variable interactions for smooth high-order PDEs. They group inputs (spatial coordinates, time, physical parameters, IC/BCs) into independent feature sets and model cross-group interactions, leading to FM-Operator and FM-DeepONet for operator learning.
AI.result: Numerical tests show the FM-based mechanism delivers substantial accuracy gains on challenging shock-dominated equations and nonlinear conservation laws, while providing no consistent advantage on smooth operator learning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The FM feature interaction mechanism is a promising direction for physics-consistent modeling of parameterized PDEs with strong cross-field dependencies, particularly effective for problems with sharp gradients or discontinuities.

title: Tool Specifications Matter: Uncovering and Mitigating Safety Risks in AI Agents
summary: AI agents extend large language models (LLMs) with external tools, enabling them to perform complex tasks and translate model outputs into consequential real-world actions. Yet LLMs often become substantially less safe when deployed as agents, and the source of this degradation remains poorly understood. In this paper, we identify schema-formatted tool specifications as a primary source of agent safety degradation and show, through white-box representation analysis, that they weaken the model's internal refusal signals and contribute to unsafe tool execution. Building on this finding, we propose SafeKeep, an inference-time safeguard that decouples safety judgment from tool execution: it assesses requests using flattened textual tool specifications while retaining the original schema-formatted specifications for execution. Across two representative benchmarks and four LLMs, including both white-box and black-box models, SafeKeep increases the average refusal rate for harmful requests from 23.8% to 70.6% and reduces the average attack success rate under observation-level prompt injection from 25.6% to 2.5%. It also outperforms existing safeguards and preserves task-handling capability. We release the code and data at https://github.com/snowcatsmoking/SafeKeep .

AI.tldr: This paper identifies schema-formatted tool specifications as the primary cause of safety degradation in LLM agents, and proposes SafeKeep, an inference-time safeguard that decouples safety judgment from tool execution by using flattened textual tool specifications for safety assessment while retaining schema-formatted specs for execution. SafeKeep increases refusal rates for harmful requests from 23.8% to 70.6% and reduces attack success rates under prompt injection from 25.6% to 2.5% across two benchmarks and four LLMs.
AI.motivation: LLMs become substantially less safe when deployed as agents, but the source of this safety degradation is poorly understood. The authors aim to identify the root cause and develop an effective mitigation strategy.
AI.method: Through white-box representation analysis, the authors identify schema-formatted tool specifications as the primary source of agent safety degradation, as they weaken the model's internal refusal signals. They propose SafeKeep, an inference-time safeguard that decouples safety judgment from tool execution: it assesses requests using flattened textual tool specifications while retaining the original schema-formatted specifications for execution.
AI.result: Across two representative benchmarks and four LLMs (including white-box and black-box models), SafeKeep increases the average refusal rate for harmful requests from 23.8% to 70.6% and reduces the average attack success rate under observation-level prompt injection from 25.6% to 2.5%. It also outperforms existing safeguards and preserves task-handling capability.
AI.conclusion: Schema-formatted tool specifications are the primary cause of agent safety degradation, and decoupling safety assessment from tool execution using flattened textual specifications effectively restores safety while maintaining task-handling capability. The code and data are publicly released.

title: Forwardrobe: Garment-Aware Gaussian Avatars from a Single Image
summary: Reconstructing animatable 3D human avatars from a single image remains particularly challenging for loose garments, whose geometry and motion cannot be adequately represented by body-aligned topology and skinning. We present Forwardrobe, a feed-forward framework for reconstructing garment-aware Gaussian avatars from a single image. Forwardrobe explicitly separates clothing from the body in canonical Gaussian space and equips the garment layer with continuity-aware geometry and skinning initialization, pose-conditioned non-rigid deformation, and appearance adaptation. These designs improve garment reconstruction and visual quality during animation, particularly for skirts and dresses. The separated garment layer additionally forms an independently controllable 3D asset, enabling garment editing, transfer, and 3D virtual try-on. Experiments demonstrate improved garment reconstruction quality and greater flexibility in garment manipulation compared with existing single-image avatar reconstruction methods.

AI.tldr: Forwardrobe is a feed-forward framework that reconstructs animatable 3D human avatars with loose garments from a single image by explicitly separating clothing from the body in canonical Gaussian space, using continuity-aware geometry and skinning initialization, pose-conditioned non-rigid deformation, and appearance adaptation.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing animatable 3D human avatars from a single image is challenging for loose garments (e.g., skirts, dresses) because their geometry and motion cannot be adequately represented by body-aligned topology and skinning approaches.
AI.method: Forwardrobe explicitly separates the garment layer from the body in canonical Gaussian space and equips the garment layer with three key components: continuity-aware geometry and skinning initialization, pose-conditioned non-rigid deformation, and appearance adaptation.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate improved garment reconstruction quality and greater flexibility in garment manipulation compared with existing single-image avatar reconstruction methods. The separated garment layer also enables garment editing, transfer, and 3D virtual try-on.
AI.conclusion: The explicit garment-body separation in Gaussian space not only improves loose garment reconstruction and animation quality, but also provides an independently controllable 3D garment asset for downstream applications such as editing, transfer, and virtual try-on.

title: Representations from Pretrained Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials as Coarse Coordinates for Material Generation and Evaluation
summary: Generative machine learning is increasingly used for inorganic crystal structure generation. Most models and the corresponding evaluation approaches rely on simple forms of crystal structure representation. In this paper, we showcase the power of atom-averaged features from pretrained Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs), such as MACE, for such tasks. We first introduce a distance measure that assesses the output of material generative models by capturing both quality and novelty in a single distribution-based evaluation framework. In particular, we introduce the Coarse-Fine Transport Distance (CFTD) using two different featurizers, where the quality component is based on coarse MACE features. We showcase CFTD's versatility in capturing crystal-structure quality while also detecting memorization, and compare it with the recently introduced continuous SUN metrics. We further show that coarse MACE features can be used as guidance for a material generative model.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Coarse-Fine Transport Distance (CFTD), a distribution-based evaluation metric for inorganic crystal structure generative models, built on atom-averaged MACE interatomic potential features. CFTD simultaneously captures quality and novelty, detects memorization, and the coarse MACE features are also shown to be useful as guidance for generative models.
AI.motivation: Most crystal structure generation models rely on simple structure representations, and existing evaluation approaches are limited. There is a need for a more powerful representation and a unified evaluation framework that captures both quality and novelty of generated materials, while also detecting memorization.
AI.method: The paper leverages atom-averaged features from pretrained MLIPs (specifically MACE) as a representation.
