It introduces CFTD, a distribution-based distance measure composed of a quality component using coarse MACE features and a novelty component, evaluated via optimal transport across the distributions of generated vs. reference structures. It compares against continuous SUN metrics and also demonstrates the use of coarse MACE features as guidance signals for a generative model.
AI.result: CFTD is shown to be versatile in capturing crystal-structure quality and detecting memorization in generated structures. It is compared favorably against continuous SUN metrics. Additionally, coarse MACE features provide effective conditioning/guidance for material generative models.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained MLIP features (MACE) significantly enhance both the evaluation and generation of inorganic crystal structures, and CFTD offers a unified distribution-based metric for assessing quality and novelty simultaneously.

title: MAGA: Multi-Platform Self-Fusion of GUI Agents via Structured Action Distillation
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents based on large language models are increasingly deployed across mobile, web, and desktop environments. However, existing agents are typically domain-specific, limiting the deployment and user experience. This motivates the consolidation of specialized models into a single cross-environment policy. Weight merging directly merges domain-specific experts but can corrupt executable actions under expert disagreement, while on-policy distillation (OPD) avoids conflicting teacher supervision yet still treats all response tokens equally during distillation, ignoring that action tokens are the only interface between the environment and the agent. To address this, We introduce MAGA that re-allocates training signal according to the structured action. Based on the correctness of the generated action, it suppresses unnecessary or invalid distillation signals and focuses learning on erroneous actions. Besides, a training-only hint optimizes the supervision signal provided by domain-specific teachers without changing the student input. Across two model scales, MAGA achieves the highest mean success rate, outperforming the strongest baseline by 2.0% at 8B and achieves almost the same average performance with teachers.

AI.tldr: MAGA is a method for training cross-environment GUI agents by distilling knowledge from domain-specific expert models. It re-allocates training signals based on structured action correctness, suppressing unnecessary or invalid distillation signals and focusing learning on erroneous actions, plus a training-only hint to optimize teacher supervision. It outperforms strong baselines by 2.0% at 8B scale and nearly matches teacher performance.
AI.motivation: Existing GUI agents are domain-specific (mobile, web, desktop), limiting deployment and user experience. Prior approaches for consolidating them—weight merging can corrupt executable actions under expert disagreement, and on-policy distillation treats all response tokens equally, ignoring that action tokens are the only interface between the environment and the agent.
AI.method: MAGA re-allocates distillation training signals based on the correctness of generated structured actions. It suppresses unnecessary or invalid distillation signals and concentrates learning on erroneous actions. Additionally, a training-only hint mechanism optimizes the supervision signal from domain-specific teachers without modifying student input.
AI.result: Across two model scales, MAGA achieves the highest mean success rate. At 8B scale, it outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.0%, and it achieves almost the same average performance as the domain-specific teachers.
AI.conclusion: By focusing distillation on erroneous structured actions and enhancing teacher supervision with a training-only hint, MAGA effectively consolidates domain-specific GUI agents into a single cross-environment policy, achieving state-of-the-art results.

title: A Frozen Pixel-Space Diffusion Model Can Guide Itself with Its Own Samples
summary: Pixel-space diffusion models aim to learn an end-to-end generator directly over raw pixels. This is challenging because a single model must capture both global structure and local texture in the same high-dimensional space. While recent work improves pixel diffusion through alternative prediction targets, training objectives, and architectures, these advances typically require training a new model from scratch. We show there is a cheaper, complementary strategy: \textbf{a frozen, pretrained pixel diffusion model can guide itself}. Our key observation is that intermediate layers of a pretrained pixel diffusion transformer can be decoded into coarse predictions that capture the main low-frequency structure, while the final layers progressively refine local, high-frequency details. We therefore attach a lightweight prediction head to an intermediate layer, keep the backbone frozen, and use the discrepancy between the intermediate and final predictions as a self-guidance direction during sampling. To train this head, we further find that real images are not necessary. Instead, model-generated samples suffice and even outperform real images for training the head, especially in enhancing the high-frequency components that pixel diffusion tends to underfit. Across multiple pixel diffusion models on ImageNet, our \textbf{Synthetic Self-Guidance (SSG)} consistently improves generation while adapter training requires less than 1$\%$ of full-model training compute: it reduces FID by over 50$\%$ across the evaluated JiT variants without classifier-free guidance (CFG) and further improves strong baselines with CFG, e.g., JiT-H/16 from 1.86 to 1.67 and PixelREPA-H/16 from 1.81 to 1.59. Our code is available at https://github.com/zfu006/SSG.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Synthetic Self-Guidance (SSG), a method where a frozen pretrained pixel-space diffusion model guides itself during sampling. By attaching a lightweight head to an intermediate layer and using the discrepancy between intermediate and final predictions as a guidance direction, SSG improves generation quality using only model-generated synthetic samples for adapter training (requiring <1% of full-model compute). It reduces FID by over 50% across JiT variants and improves strong CFG baselines (e.g., JiT-H/16 from 1.86 to 1.67, PixelREPA-H/16 from 1.81 to 1.59).
AI.motivation: Pixel-space diffusion models must simultaneously capture global structure and local texture in a single high-dimensional space, which is challenging. Existing improvements (alternative prediction targets, objectives, architectures) require training new models from scratch. The authors aim to find a cheaper, complementary strategy that improves frozen pretrained pixel diffusion models without retraining the backbone.
AI.method: The key observation is that intermediate layers of a pretrained pixel diffusion transformer decode into coarse predictions capturing low-frequency structure, while final layers refine high-frequency details. SSG attaches a lightweight prediction head to a frozen intermediate layer, and uses the discrepancy between intermediate and final predictions as a self-guidance direction during sampling. Notably, the head is trained on model-generated samples (synthetic data) rather than real images, which the authors find performs better and enhances high-frequency components that pixel diffusion tends to underfit.
AI.result: SSG consistently improves generation quality across multiple pixel diffusion models on ImageNet. It reduces FID by over 50% across evaluated JiT variants without CFG and further improves strong CFG baselines: JiT-H/16 from 1.86 to 1.67 and PixelREPA-H/16 from 1.81 to 1.59. Adapter training requires less than 1% of full-model training compute.
AI.conclusion: A frozen pretrained pixel diffusion model can guide itself via intermediate-to-final layer prediction discrepancies. Training the lightweight guidance head on synthetic data suffices and even outperforms real-image training. SSG offers a highly compute-efficient plug-in method that improves frozen pixel diffusion models without retraining, with code publicly available.

title: Distilling Knowledge from Large Language Models into Lightweight Reinforcement Learning Agents for Autonomous Cyber Operations
summary:
Autonomous Cyber Operations (ACO) are increasingly important for defending enterprise networks as cyber threats continue to evolve in sophistication. ACO applications commonly employ Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents to learn defensive behaviors through interaction with environments. However, RL agents typically require extensive exploration during training, often resulting in unstable behavior and poor initial decision-making before converging toward effective defense strategies.
  In this work, we investigate the use of a Large Language Model (LLM) to improve autonomous defensive decision-making within an ACO environment. Through prompt engineering rather than fine-tuning, we demonstrate that an 8-billion parameter LLM pretrained on cybersecurity data can outperform a baseline RL agent in a modified CybORG CAGE Challenge 2 environment. We then propose an online policy distillation framework that transfers the LLM's defensive policy into a lightweight RL agent containing only 64,910 parameters, reducing model size by several orders of magnitude while maintaining effective defensive capabilities. This provides a pathway toward operationalizing frontier cybersecurity models within lightweight, deployable agents.
  To evaluate transferability, we construct CybORG scenarios ranging from 4 to 12 hosts and assess the approach across varying network configurations. We also evaluate teacher-guided RL stabilization strategies and observe that none consistently surpass the optimized teacher policy, suggesting policy-alignment limitations between reward-driven RL optimization and teacher-guided defense strategies.
  Our results demonstrate the potential of cybersecurity-focused LLMs as sources of expertise for autonomous cyber defense, while policy distillation provides a practical path toward operationalizing frontier cybersecurity models within efficient, scalable agents.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using a cybersecurity-pretrained 8B-parameter LLM to improve autonomous cyber defense decision-making in a CybORG CAGE Challenge 2 environment. Through prompt engineering (not fine-tuning), the LLM outperforms a baseline RL agent, and an online policy distillation framework transfers the LLM's defensive policy into a lightweight 64,910-parameter RL agent—a reduction of several orders of magnitude—while maintaining effective defense. Transferability is evaluated across CybORG scenarios with 4 to 12 hosts, and teacher-guided RL stabilization strategies are found not to consistently surpass the optimized teacher policy, suggesting policy-alignment limitations between reward-driven RL optimization and teacher-guided strategies.
AI.motivation: RL agents used for autonomous cyber operations require extensive exploration during training, resulting in unstable behavior and poor initial decision-making. The authors seek to leverage LLMs as knowledgeable teachers to improve defensive decision-making without the instability of pure RL exploration, and to make such expertise practical via distillation into lightweight deployable agents.
AI.method: The approach uses an 8-billion parameter LLM pretrained on cybersecurity data with prompt engineering (no fine-tuning) to make defensive decisions in a modified CybORG CAGE Challenge 2 environment. An online policy distillation framework transfers the LLM's defensive policy into a lightweight RL agent with only 64,910 parameters. Experiments evaluate transferability across CybORG scenarios ranging from 4 to 12 hosts and assess teacher-guided RL stabilization strategies across varying network configurations.
AI.result: The cybersecurity-pretrained LLM outperforms a baseline RL agent in the CybORG environment via prompt engineering alone. The distilled lightweight RL agent maintains effective defensive capabilities despite being reduced by several orders of magnitude in size. Teacher-guided RL stabilization strategies do not consistently outperform the optimized teacher policy across scenarios, indicating policy-alignment limitations between reward-driven RL optimization and teacher-guided defense strategies.
AI.conclusion: Cybersecurity-focused LLMs can serve as effective sources of expertise for autonomous cyber defense, and policy distillation offers a practical pathway toward operationalizing frontier-scale model knowledge within efficient, scalable, lightweight agents suitable for real-world deployment.

title: SciFigPlag-Bench: A Benchmark for Provenance-Aware Scientific Figure Plagiarism Detection
summary: Scientific figures often encode the visual evidence behind scientific findings, yet figure plagiarism remains underexplored as a benchmarked multimodal evaluation problem. We present SciFigPlag-Bench, a benchmark for provenance-aware reasoning over scientific figures in scholarly documents. Unlike general image-similarity or image-forensics benchmarks, SciFigPlag-Bench evaluates whether a suspicious figure reuses evidence from a specific source figure, how the reused content has been transformed, and where the reused evidence appears. We introduce a factorized taxonomy that separates what is reused from how it is transformed, covering material-preserving reuse, such as full-figure and subfigure reuse, as well as abstract-content reuse, such as data re-expression and structural redraw. Guided by this taxonomy, we construct a hybrid benchmark with 2,582 positive pairs and 2,541 negative pairs, combining documented real-world cases, taxonomy-guided synthetic examples, and visually similar negatives. The benchmark supports four diagnostic tasks: pairwise detection, source attribution, hierarchical reuse-type classification, and reuse correspondence localization. Experiments with diverse vision-language models establish initial baselines and reveal persistent challenges in fine-grained provenance reasoning, reuse-type understanding, and spatial evidence grounding.

AI.tldr: SciFigPlag-Bench is a benchmark for provenance-aware reasoning over scientific figures, evaluating whether a suspicious figure reuses evidence from a specific source figure via four diagnostic tasks across 2,582 positive and 2,541 negative pairs.
AI.motivation: Scientific figures encode visual evidence behind findings, yet figure plagiarism remains underexplored as a benchmarked multimodal evaluation problem, unlike general image-similarity or image-forensics tasks.
AI.method: The paper introduces a factorized taxonomy separating what is reused from how it is transformed (material-preserving reuse like full-figure/subfigure reuse vs. abstract-content reuse like data re-expression and structural redraw), and constructs a hybrid benchmark combining documented real-world cases, taxonomy-guided synthetic examples, and visually similar negatives.
AI.result: The benchmark supports four diagnostic tasks—pairwise detection, source attribution, hierarchical reuse-type classification, and reuse correspondence localization—and experiments with diverse VLMs establish baselines revealing persistent challenges in fine-grained provenance reasoning, reuse-type understanding, and spatial evidence grounding.
AI.conclusion: Current vision-language models exhibit significant limitations in scientific figure provenance reasoning, indicating a need for more robust multimodal approaches to detect and characterize figure reuse in scholarly documents.

title: Hypergradient-based Bilevel Reinforcement Learning with Improved Sample Complexity
summary: Bilevel reinforcement learning (RL) is an important framework within the literature of RL that can be used to formalize various categories of problems, such as meta-learning, hierarchical task decomposition, and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RL-HF). Most of the bilevel RL algorithms are either not scalable because of using hypergradient with Hessian, or they suffer from high sample complexity because of using penalty-based approximation methods. In this work, we propose a hypergradient-based bilevel RL algorithm using the optimality of the Boltzmann policy for the entropy regularized discounted RL objective function. Our proposed algorithm is Hessian-free and obtains an iteration complexity of $O(ε^{-1})$ and state-of-the-art sample complexity of $\tilde{O}(ε^{-2})$ under mild regularity conditions. Further, in our convergence analysis, we are able to remove the assumption of the Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition on the outer-level objective function present in the prior state-of-the-art sample complexity work.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hypergradient-based bilevel reinforcement learning algorithm that leverages the optimality of Boltzmann policies in entropy-regularized discounted RL. The algorithm is Hessian-free, achieves O(ε⁻¹) iteration complexity and Õ(ε⁻²) sample complexity under mild regularity conditions, and removes the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition assumption on the outer-level objective.
AI.motivation: Existing bilevel RL algorithms suffer from either scalability issues due to Hessian-based hypergradient computation or high sample complexity due to penalty-based approximation methods. The goal is to design an algorithm that is both scalable (Hessian-free) and sample-efficient.
AI.method: The proposed algorithm computes hypergradients using the optimality structure of Boltzmann policies within an entropy-regularized discounted RL framework, making it Hessian-free. It avoids penalty-based approximations and eliminates the need for the Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition on the outer-level objective in the convergence analysis.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves O(ε⁻¹) iteration complexity and state-of-the-art Õ(ε⁻²) sample complexity under mild regularity conditions, while removing the PL condition assumption that was required in prior state-of-the-art work.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method offers a scalable and sample-efficient approach to bilevel RL, applicable to problems such as meta-learning, hierarchical task decomposition, and RL-HF, with stronger theoretical guarantees than prior work.

title: ModelEquivBench: Certifying Multi-Relational Evaluation of LLM-Generated Optimization Models
summary: Large language models increasingly generate optimization models from natural language, but existing evaluation often reduces a generated model and its ground truth to a single equivalent/not-equivalent verdict or an execution-success rate--labels that are neither independently checkable nor faithful to the multiple distinct senses in which two formulations can agree. We present ModelEquivBench, a certifying, multi-relational evaluation system that reports a per-pair semantic profile E0--E6: model construction and exact ingestion (E0), verified representation alignment (E1), same-space and projected feasible-set relations (E2, E3), objective-order equivalence (E4), optimal-value equality (E5), and optimizer-set equivalence (E6). Each decided entry carries relation-appropriate, independently re-checkable evidence: replayable traces or explicit maps for E0--E1, exact-rational certificates for positive E2--E6 conclusions, and explicit witnesses for supported negatives. Incomplete mapping search, unsupported structure, and resource limits produce typed UNKNOWN or N/A outcomes rather than guesses, while unmet prerequisites are reported as ABSENT. Using ModelEquivBench to evaluate three model snapshots--GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B--on the same frozen cohort of 173 base problems (346 cells per model) under a no-repair protocol, the resulting profiles expose distinctions that coarse baselines do not represent: 49, 35, and 25 cells contain executable candidates that are nevertheless certified negative on at least one supported relation, and 25, 8, and 18 structural rejections occur on pairs for which E2 certifies mapped feasible-set equality under a verified map. The three model snapshots fail at different stages of the profile and therefore cannot be meaningfully reduced to a single accuracy score.

AI.tldr: ModelEquivBench is a certifying, multi-relational evaluation system that reports per-pair semantic profiles (E0–E6) for comparing LLM-generated optimization models against ground truth, providing independently re-checkable evidence (traces, exact-rational certificates, witnesses) and typed UNKNOWN/N/A outcomes. When used to evaluate three model snapshots on 173 frozen optimization problems, it reveals stage-specific failures that coarse baselines cannot capture, showing the models cannot be reduced to a single accuracy score.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-generated optimization models reduce comparison to a single equivalent/not-equivalent verdict or execution-success rate, which are neither independently checkable nor faithful to the multiple distinct senses in which two formulations may agree.
AI.method: ModelEquivBench defines a hierarchy of semantic relations E0–E6 (ingestion/construction, representation alignment, feasible-set relations in same/projected spaces, objective-order equivalence, optimal-value equality, optimizer-set equivalence). Each relation produces certifying evidence: replayable traces or explicit maps for E0–E1, exact-rational certificates for positive E2–E6, explicit witnesses for supported negatives, and typed UNKNOWN/N/A/ABSENT outcomes for undecidable or unsupported cases. Models were evaluated on 173 base problems (346 cells per model) under a no-repair protocol.
AI.result: Across three model snapshots (GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B): 49, 35, and 25 cells contain executable candidates certified negative on at least one supported relation; 25, 8, and 18 structural rejections occur on pairs where E2 certifies mapped feasible-set equality. The models fail at different stages of the profile, so they cannot be meaningfully reduced to a single accuracy score.
AI.conclusion: Multi-relational, certifying evaluation is necessary to faithfully assess and compare LLM-generated optimization models; coarse single-label baselines obscure stage-specific differences in model capability.

title: First Investigation of Deep Learning for Intraoperative Gauze Segmentation in Minimally Invasive Abdominal Surgery
comment: Paper already published in IEEE DSAA conference. The purpose here is to make it open-access
summary: Surgical gauze is an essential part of surgical procedures, primarily used for controlling bleeding and absorbing bodily fluids. The post-surgical retention of gauze can lead to serious complications and necessitate additional surgery for its removal. Despite the clinical significance, research on gauze segmentation using real-world surgical data remains underexplored, owing in part to the scarcity of annotated datasets. In this work, we investigate the use of deep learning methods for gauze segmentation in robot-assisted minimally invasive abdominal surgeries, utilizing an in-house surgical dataset prepared at a university hospital. The training data reflects realistic surgical settings and captures extensive diversity in spatial, morphological, and visual attributes across three different gauze categories. We evaluate several widely used segmentation architectures, including CNN-based, transformer-based, and hybrid architectures, to establish a proof-of-concept for gauze segmentation in a realistic clinical setting. In addition, we investigate the influence of sub-optimally annotated, auto-tracked segmentation masks as a strategy to address data scarcity and improve performance. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of real-world training data in countering the main challenge reported by prior works, the trade-off between blood presence and gauze detection. The incorporation of auto-tracked annotations yields performance enhancements, particularly in generic surgical scenarios. The integration of effective segmentation approaches can benefit robot-guided surgical procedures and various downstream applications by providing precise delineation of foreign objects, thereby enhancing patient safety and surgical outcomes.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates deep learning-based segmentation of surgical gauze in robot-assisted minimally invasive abdominal surgeries using an in-house annotated dataset from a university hospital. The authors evaluate CNN, transformer, and hybrid segmentation architectures, and explore auto-tracked (noisily annotated) segmentation masks to address data scarcity. Results show real-world training data mitigates the blood-vs-gauze detection trade-off, and auto-tracked annotations improve performance in generic surgical scenarios.
AI.motivation: Retained surgical gauze after surgery leads to serious complications and requires additional operations. Despite clinical importance, gauze segmentation from real-world surgical data is underexplored due to a scarcity of annotated datasets, motivating the need for feasible segmentation approaches tested in realistic clinical settings.
AI.method: The authors prepared an in-house surgical dataset from robot-assisted minimally invasive abdominal procedures spanning three gauze categories with diverse spatial, morphological, and visual attributes. They benchmarked CNN-based, transformer-based, and hybrid segmentation architectures, and additionally studied the use of sub-optimally annotated, auto-tracked segmentation masks as a data-augmentation strategy to mitigate annotation scarcity.
AI.result: Real-world training data effectively addresses the trade-off between blood presence and gauze detection, a key limitation identified in prior works. Incorporating auto-tracked annotations improved performance, especially in generic surgical scenarios. The study establishes a proof-of-concept for gauze segmentation across multiple architecture families.
AI.conclusion: Effective deep learning segmentation approaches can provide precise delineation of surgical gauze and other foreign objects, benefiting robot-guided surgical procedures and downstream applications, thereby enhancing patient safety and surgical outcomes.

title: An analysis of machine learning approaches for enhancing decision-making in complex discrete choice tasks
comment: Published in Decision Analytics Journal, Dec 16 2025
summary: Discrete choice modeling is a common tool used for preference elicitation during policy-making, but this is typically done through parametric models. Machine learning can push the boundaries of discrete choice modeling for policy-based preference elicitation by adopting a data-driven approach or learning individual preferences. However, there is limited knowledge of how well machine learning methods can estimate individual discrete choice rules under individual heterogeneity, especially in the context of challenges often experienced during preference elicitation. This study evaluates four machine learning models (multinomial logistic regression, generalized additive model, twinned neural network, and Gaussian process) with respect to their capacity to learn and predict five choice rules that are important in the behavioral and social sciences (linear strong utility, monotonic strong utility, ideal point, lexicographic semiorder, and multiattribute linear ballistic accumulator). Monte Carlo experiments were performed to assess model performance when increasing a) the number of attributes in the choice alternatives, b) the number of training choice sets, and c) the choice rule's determinism. The simulation results demonstrated that semi-parametric and non-parametric models generally outperform parametric models across all choice rules and experimental contexts. Model performance also generally improves by 6% to 96% and 0% to 55%, respectively, with an increase in training choice sets and choice rule determinism. A case study using real energy policy preference data was also conducted, where TNN performed best with a BIC of 13.351. This work demonstrated the viability and limitations of semi-parametric and non-parametric models in the context of policy-centric discrete choice modeling and showed how the choice task context should drive model selection.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates four machine learning models (multinomial logistic regression, generalized additive model, twinned neural network, and Gaussian process) for learning individual discrete choice rules under heterogeneity, using Monte Carlo experiments and a real energy policy case study. Semi-parametric and non-parametric models generally outperform parametric models across all choice rules and experimental contexts.
AI.motivation: Discrete choice modeling is important for policy preference elicitation but is typically limited to parametric models. There is limited knowledge of how well machine learning methods can estimate individual discrete choice rules under heterogeneity, particularly under challenges common in preference elicitation.
AI.method: Four machine learning models (multinomial logistic regression, generalized additive model, twinned neural network, and Gaussian process) were evaluated against five choice rules (linear strong utility, monotonic strong utility, ideal point, lexicographic semiorder, and multiattribute linear ballistic accumulator). Monte Carlo experiments varied the number of attributes, number of training choice sets, and choice rule determinism. A real energy policy preference case study was also conducted.
AI.result: Semi-parametric and non-parametric models generally outperform parametric models across all choice rules and experimental contexts. Model performance improves by 6% to 96% with more training choice sets and 0% to 55% with increased choice rule determinism. In the energy policy case study, the twinned neural network performed best with a BIC of 13.351.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the viability and limitations of semi-parametric and non-parametric models for policy-centric discrete choice modeling, and shows that the choice task context should drive model selection.

title: Beyond Retrieval: Analytic Memory for Multimodal Agents
summary: Long-term multimodal memory must support not only retrieving relevant information but also computing over observations accumulated across interactions. Existing systems largely emphasize \emph{retrieval memory}, organizing interaction histories through summaries and indexes to return query-relevant information at multiple granularities, from high-level abstractions to underlying records. In this paper, we formulate \emph{analytic memory} as a complementary abstraction that organizes recurring multimodal observations into queryable structures supporting filtering, aggregation, ranking, and temporal comparison. We present AdaMM, a framework that jointly supports retrieval and analytic memory. Rather than relying on application-defined schemas, AdaMM extracts provenance-linked attribute-value observations from dialogue, images, and contextual metadata, discovers recurring field structures, and materializes them for analytical access. At inference time, a memory-aware planner decomposes queries into retrieval and analytic operations and routes each operation to the appropriate tools. Experiments on two long-term multimodal memory benchmarks, MemEye and MemGallery, show that AdaMM improves performance by up to 11.3\% and 7.3\%, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AdaMM, a framework that augments traditional retrieval-based multimodal memory with "analytic memory"—queryable structures derived from recurring multimodal observations that support filtering, aggregation, ranking, and temporal comparison. AdaMM extracts provenance-linked attribute-value observations from dialogue, images, and metadata, discovers recurring field structures, and uses a memory-aware planner to decompose queries into retrieval and analytic operations. Experiments on MemEye and MemGallery benchmarks show improvements of up to 11.3% and 7.3% respectively.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term multimodal memory systems focus primarily on retrieval memory—organizing interaction histories via summaries and indexes to return query-relevant information. However, many real-world queries require computing over accumulated observations (e.g., filtering, aggregation, ranking, temporal comparison), which retrieval-only approaches cannot directly support.
AI.method: AdaMM jointly supports retrieval and analytic memory. It extracts provenance-linked attribute-value observations from dialogue, images, and contextual metadata without relying on application-defined schemas. It discovers recurring field structures and materializes them for analytical access. At inference time, a memory-aware planner decomposes user queries into retrieval and analytic operations, routing each to appropriate tools.
AI.result: On two long-term multimodal memory benchmarks, AdaMM improves performance by up to 11.3% on MemEye and 7.3% on MemGallery compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Analytic memory is a valuable complementary abstraction to retrieval memory for long-term multimodal interaction systems. AdaMM demonstrates that automatically discovering and materializing recurring observation structures—without application-defined schemas—enables effective analytical query answering alongside retrieval, advancing the capability of memory systems to support computation over accumulated multimodal histories.

title: On the Efficacy of Self-Supervised Point Cloud Encoders for Efficient 3D Large Language Models
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures. This work has been previously released as a preprint on ChinaXiv (No. ChinaXiv:202607.00167, DOI: 10.12074/202607.00167)
summary:
3D point cloud-language models (3D-LLMs) enable 3D understanding by pairing point cloud encoders with large language models, but existing methods rely on costly multi-modal encoders (e.g., ULIP-2) that require image-text-point cloud alignment on 8x A100-scale compute, creating high barriers for research and deployment. In this work, we systematically investigate whether low-cost self-supervised point cloud encoders, specifically PCP-MAE and Point-MAE, can serve as effective alternatives.
  Using MiniGPT-3D as our testbed, we evaluate 7 encoder initialization/pre-training setups (1 multi-modal baseline, 5 self-supervised, 1 random init) under frozen and unfrozen fine-tuning (12 total groups), across 2 architectures (MaskTransformer, PointTransformer), 3 objectives (PCP-MAE, Point-MAE, random init), and 2 datasets (Objaverse 660K, ShapeNet55-34 approximately 50K).
  Our experiments reveal three key findings: (1) The four-stage MiniGPT-3D pipeline can effectively train a 3D encoder from random initialization: an end-to-end trained random init encoder reaches 52.50% open-vocabulary accuracy and 44.45 captioning score, approaching top pre-trained variants; (2) Architecture and pre-training objective show strong crossover interaction: PCP-MAE + MaskTransformer achieves 59.00% accuracy (best self-supervised), while Point-MAE + MaskTransformer drops to 46.50%, with the pattern reversed for PointTransformer; (3) Closed-set ModelNet40 classification remains a core weakness of purely geometric encoders, reaching only ~13-18% accuracy vs. ~62% for the multi-modal baseline, even after end-to-end fine-tuning.
  Our results offer practical guidelines for cost-effective 3D-LLM design and reveal interaction patterns between self-supervised objectives and encoder architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether low-cost self-supervised point cloud encoders (PCP-MAE, Point-MAE) can replace costly multi-modal encoders (e.g., ULIP-2) in 3D point cloud-language models. Using MiniGPT-3D as a testbed across 12 experimental groups, 2 architectures, 3 objectives, and 2 datasets, the authors find that (1) a randomly initialized encoder can be effectively trained end-to-end, approaching top pre-trained performance; (2) there is a strong crossover interaction between architecture and pre-training objective; and (3) purely geometric encoders remain significantly weak at closed-set ModelNet40 classification compared to multi-modal baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D-LLMs depend on costly multi-modal encoders requiring image-text-point cloud alignment on 8x A100-scale compute, creating significant barriers for research and deployment. The authors aim to determine whether low-cost self-supervised point cloud encoders can serve as effective practical alternatives.
AI.method: Using MiniGPT-3D as a testbed, the authors systematically evaluate 7 encoder initialization/pre-training setups (1 multi-modal baseline, 5 self-supervised, 1 random init) under frozen and unfrozen fine-tuning (12 total groups). They test across 2 architectures (MaskTransformer, PointTransformer), 3 objectives (PCP-MAE, Point-MAE, random init), and 2 datasets (Objaverse 660K, ShapeNet55-34 ~50K). The four-stage MiniGPT-3D pipeline is employed for end-to-end 3D encoder training from various initializations.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) The four-stage MiniGPT-3D pipeline can train a 3D encoder from random initialization, reaching 52.50% open-vocabulary accuracy and 44.45 captioning score, approaching top pre-trained variants; (2) Architecture and pre-training objective exhibit strong crossover interaction: PCP-MAE + MaskTransformer achieves 59.00% accuracy (best self-supervised), while Point-MAE + MaskTransformer drops to 46.50%, with the pattern reversed for PointTransformer; (3) Closed-set ModelNet40 classification remains a core weakness of purely geometric encoders, achieving only ~13-18% accuracy versus ~62% for the multi-modal baseline, even after end-to-end fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The results provide practical guidelines for cost-effective 3D-LLM design, demonstrating that random initialization with end-to-end training via the MiniGPT-3D pipeline is a viable low-cost alternative, while highlighting critical architecture-objective interaction patterns and the persistent limitation of purely geometric encoders in closed-set classification tasks.

title: Fast Rates for Swap-Agnostic Learning of Proper Losses
summary: Swap-agnostic learning strengthens classical agnostic learning by allowing the comparator to select a different hypothesis on each level set of the learner's predictions. This benchmark captures prediction-dependent postprocessing, but appears to require solving a separate agnostic-learning problem for every possible prediction value. We show that, for proper losses, these prediction-level comparisons can instead be controlled jointly. Our main result is an offline swap-agnostic learner for any fixed proper loss. For a finite hypothesis class $H$ and any fixed smooth proper loss, the excess risk from $m$ i.i.d. samples is $\widetilde{O}((\log |H|/m)^{2/3})$, with a corresponding online swap-regret bound of $\widetilde{O}(T^{1/3}(\log |H|)^{2/3})$. We also give algorithms whose predictions are simultaneously swap-agnostic for entire families of losses. For all proper losses bounded in $[-1,1]$, we obtain online and offline rates of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T\log |H|})$ and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\log |H|/m})$, respectively. For convex, $1$-Lipschitz proper losses, these rates improve to $\widetilde{O}(T^{1/3}(\log |H|)^{2/3})$ online and $\widetilde{O}((\log |H|/m)^{2/3})$ offline. These bounds are tight up to logarithmic factors and improve upon the $\widetilde{O}(T^{2/3}(\log |H|)^{1/3})$ rate implied by the swap-omniprediction guarantee of Luo et al. (2025). Our main technical contribution is a reduction from swap-agnostic learning to a second-order form of multicalibration, obtained via Blackwell approachability with a Bernstein-style variance correction.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces efficient offline and online swap-agnostic learners for proper losses. For any fixed smooth proper loss, it achieves offline excess risk of O((log|H|/m)^(2/3)) and online swap-regret of O(T^(1/3)(log|H|)^(2/3)). For families of all bounded proper losses and convex 1-Lipschitz proper losses, it provides simultaneous swap-agnostic guarantees with matching or improved rates. The key technical contribution is a reduction from swap-agnostic learning to second-order multicalibration via Blackwell approachability with Bernstein-style variance correction.
AI.motivation: Classical swap-agnostic learning requires solving a separate agnostic-learning problem for every possible prediction value, making it computationally prohibitive. The goal is to show that for proper losses, these prediction-level comparisons can be jointly controlled, yielding efficient algorithms with tight rates.
AI.method: The paper develops a reduction from swap-agnostic learning to a second-order form of multicalibration, achieved through Blackwell approachability with a Bernstein-style variance correction. This allows joint control of prediction-level comparisons for proper losses, yielding both offline and online learners with rates depending on the loss family.
AI.result: For a fixed smooth proper loss: offline excess risk O((log|H|/m)^(2/3)) and online swap-regret O(T^(1/3)(log|H|)^(2/3)). For all proper losses bounded in [-1,1]: O(sqrt(log|H|/m)) offline and O(sqrt(T log|H|)) online. For convex 1-Lipschitz proper losses: O((log|H|/m)^(2/3)) offline and O(T^(1/3)(log|H|)^(2/3)) online. All bounds are tight up to logarithmic factors and improve upon the O(T^(2/3)(log|H|)^(1/3)) rate from swap-omniprediction.
AI.conclusion: Swap-agnostic learning for proper losses can be solved efficiently via a reduction to second-order multicalibration using Blackwell approachability with Bernstein-style variance correction. The obtained rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors for both fixed and families of proper losses.

title: Self-Play Meets Skill Evolution: Self-Evolving Search Agents that Pose, Solve, and Remember
summary: Self-play agents can generate training problems without questions from target benchmarks, but their curricula lack persistent state: failures affect gradients yet do not explicitly shape future practice. External skill memories preserve procedural experience but are typically learned from fixed task distributions. We introduce \textbf{SESA} (Self-Evolving Skill-Augmented Agent), which makes procedural memory an evolving state of tool-augmented search self-play. A challenger poses problems, while a separately parameterized solver alone retrieves skills. Informative failures are distilled into reusable skills and written back to memory. The updated memory changes solver behavior and success, which changes the challenger's reward and the distribution of future problems; the resulting frontier produces new failures that rewrite memory. This bidirectional loop makes task generation and skill memory co-evolve. Because retrieved skills shape on-policy training trajectories, their benefits can enter the model parameters as well as remain in the external bank, enabling memory-free deployment and optional inference-time retrieval. Across seven open-domain and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, SESA improves average accuracy over SSP by 1.2--3.2 points across multiple backbones and surpasses the skill-augmented SkillRL baseline by 0.9 points under a unified evaluation protocol. On Qwen3 models, SESA-Off retains 1.8--2.2 points of improvement over SSP, while the final skill bank adds a further 0.5--1.0 points. These results show that evolving skill memory is not merely an inference-time plug-in: it changes policy learning and the future training distribution while retaining value as optional external memory. Our code is available at https://github.com/Zenghuang-Fu/SESA-Self-Evolving-Search-Agents.

AI.tldr: SESA (Self-Evolving Skill-Augmented Agent) makes procedural memory an evolving state of tool-augmented search self-play, where a challenger poses problems and a solver retrieves skills. Informative failures are distilled into reusable skills and written to memory, creating a bidirectional loop where task generation and skill memory co-evolve. Across seven QA benchmarks, SESA improves accuracy by 1.2-3.2 points over SSP and 0.9 over SkillRL, with deployment without memory retention.
AI.motivation: Self-play agents generate training problems without relying on target benchmark questions, but their curricula lack persistent state—failures affect gradients but do not explicitly shape future practice. External skill memories preserve procedural experience but are typically learned from fixed task distributions, limiting their adaptability.
AI.method: SESA uses a challenger to pose problems and a separately parameterized solver that alone retrieves skills. Informative failures are distilled into reusable skills and written back to memory. The updated memory changes solver behavior and success, which changes the challenger's reward and the distribution of future problems; this bidirectional loop makes task generation and skill memory co-evolve. Retrieved skills shape on-policy training trajectories, allowing benefits to enter model parameters as well as remain in the external bank, enabling both memory-free deployment and optional inference-time retrieval.
AI.result: Across seven open-domain and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, SESA improves average accuracy over SSP by 1.2-3.2 points across multiple backbones and surpasses the skill-augmented SkillRL baseline by 0.9 points. On Qwen3 models, SESA-Off retains 1.8-2.2 points of improvement over SSP, while the final skill bank adds a further 0.5-1.0 points.
AI.conclusion: Evolving skill memory is not merely an inference-time plug-in: it changes policy learning and the future training distribution while retaining value as optional external memory. This demonstrates that making procedural memory an evolving state of self-play significantly improves agent performance in complex reasoning tasks.

title: Have I Seen You? Embedding Behavior Signals Synthetic Face Dataset Membership
summary: Synthetic face datasets are increasingly used to reduce privacy exposure and data access constraints in biometric recognition. Yet the generators that produce these datasets are trained on real faces, so synthetic data may still reveal their real source data. We study this risk through a dataset-level membership inference attack that first identifies the synthetic dataset used to train a face recognizer and then infers the real dataset used to train the generator. Across 11 face recognition models, 11 synthetic datasets, and 7 real datasets, the attack recovers the synthetic training dataset in 100% of cases and identifies the generator's source dataset in 54.5% of cases. These results show that synthetic data can retain dataset-level traces of real training data and that privacy-preserving deployment requires stronger leakage mitigation.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates dataset-level membership inference attacks against synthetic face datasets used in biometric recognition. The attack first identifies which synthetic dataset trained a face recognizer, then infers the real dataset used to train the synthetic data generator. Across 11 face recognition models, 11 synthetic datasets, and 7 real datasets, the attack achieves 100% success in recovering the synthetic training dataset and 54.5% in identifying the generator's source real dataset, demonstrating that synthetic face data retains traces of real training data.
AI.motivation: Synthetic face datasets are used to reduce privacy exposure, but since generators are trained on real faces, synthetic data may still leak information about real source data. The paper aims to quantify this leakage risk at the dataset level, which has not been thoroughly studied.
AI.method: A two-stage dataset-level membership inference attack: first, identify which synthetic dataset was used to train a given face recognition model; second, infer which real dataset was the source for the synthetic data generator. Evaluated across a broad matrix of 11 face recognition models, 11 synthetic datasets, and 7 real datasets.
AI.result: The attack recovers the synthetic training dataset in 100% of cases and identifies the generator's source real dataset in 54.5% of cases, demonstrating that synthetic face data can retain dataset-level traces of real training data.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic face data does not fully eliminate privacy risks—dataset-level traces of real training data persist through the generator. Privacy-preserving deployment of synthetic face datasets requires stronger leakage mitigation strategies.

title: Adaptivity via a Parallel Architecture for Stochastic Gradient Methods Adaptivity via a Parallel Architecture for Stochastic Gradient Methods Adaptivity via a Parallel Architecture for Stochastic Gradient Methods
summary: We develop a parallel framework that assembles static gradient methods to achieve better adaptivity. A static gradient method, denoted by $\mathrm{GD}(x_0,T)$, takes as input an initial point $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and $T\in \mathbb{R}^+$ specifying the number $\floor{T}$ of iterations. The step size is chosen as $s=S(T)$, where $S(\cdot)$ is a predetermined function of $T$. The method then performs the iterations $ x_{i+1}=x_i-\fracη{s}\cdot g_i,$ where $g_i$ is a stochastic gradient evaluated at $x_i$, and $η$ is a scaling factor. For an integer $p\ge1$, the $p$ processors in the proposed parallel framework search for an appropriate value of $T$ according to a geometric sequence so that the resulting gradient descent satisfies the desired convergence conditions. Each processor executes an infinite sequence of stages indexed by $i=1,2,\ldots$. At stage $i$, processor $j$ is assigned $ T_{j,i}=h(j,i),$ where $h:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N} \rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{+}$ is a prescribed function. Processor $j$ $(j=0,1,\ldots,p-1)$ executes $\mathrm{GD}(x_0, T_{j,i})$ at stage $i$.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a parallel framework that assembles static gradient methods to achieve better adaptivity. The framework uses p processors, each executing a static gradient descent method GD(x0,T) with step size determined by a function of T, searching over a geometric sequence of T values across stages. Each processor at stage i executes GD(x0, h(j,i)) where h is a prescribed function, allowing parallel exploration of different iteration counts and step sizes to satisfy desired convergence conditions.
AI.motivation: Static gradient methods require predetermined iteration counts and step sizes, which limits their adaptivity. The authors aim to develop a parallel framework that can automatically find appropriate parameters (T and step size) during execution, achieving better adaptivity without sacrificing the simplicity of static methods.
AI.method: The framework assigns p processors, each running an infinite sequence of stages. At stage i, processor j is assigned T_{j,i} = h(j,i) where h is a prescribed function, and executes the static gradient method GD(x0, T_{j,i}) with step size s = S(T). The processors search for appropriate T values according to a geometric sequence so that the resulting gradient descent satisfies desired convergence conditions.
AI.result: The paper presents a parallel framework that assembles static gradient methods to achieve better adaptivity, though specific numerical or theoretical results are not detailed in the abstract provided.
AI.conclusion: The proposed parallel framework enables better adaptivity for gradient-based optimization by leveraging multiple processors to search over iteration counts systematically, potentially achieving convergence conditions that would be difficult to guarantee with a single static gradient method.

title: AMTFV: Agentic Mathematical Tool-Flow Verification for LLM Self-Correction
summary: Large language models have demonstrated strong mathematical problem-solving capabilities, yet reliably verifying their candidate answers remains challenging. Existing representative methods mainly revise outputs through natural-language reflection or assist verification by directly generating verification programs; the former may not reliably support exact computation, whereas the latter prematurely couples mathematical modeling with low-level implementation. We propose AMTFV (Agentic Mathematical Tool-Flow Verification). By introducing Mathematical Tool Flow (MTF) as an interrupt--execute--resume interface, AMTFV decouples verification modeling from concrete execution and supports exact computation through a mathematical toolbox. Specifically, the verification agent first constructs a verification workflow, encodes the mathematical objects and computational intent requiring reliable execution in an MTF request, and sends it to the mathematical toolbox agent. The latter parses the request, generates executable calls, and dispatches them to the backend for exact computation. Tool outputs then support candidate-answer adjudication, answer revision, and verification-workflow revision. We evaluate AMTFV on five challenging mathematical reasoning datasets with seven model configurations from DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini. Experimental results show that AMTFV outperforms the representative baselines evaluated in this study overall; under an individual model configuration, it improves average accuracy over the strongest baseline by up to 8.3 percentage points, with larger gains on samples of medium and high verification complexity.

AI.tldr: AMTFV introduces an Agentic Mathematical Tool-Flow Verification framework that decouples verification modeling from execution via an interrupt-execute-resume Mathematical Tool Flow interface, achieving up to 8.3 percentage points accuracy improvement over the strongest baseline across five datasets and seven model configurations.
AI.motivation: Large language models show strong mathematical problem-solving capabilities but reliably verifying candidate answers remains difficult. Existing approaches either use natural-language reflection (which may not support exact computation reliably) or directly generate verification programs (which prematurely couples mathematical modeling with low-level implementation).
AI.method: AMTFV introduces Mathematical Tool Flow (MTF) as an interrupt-execute-resume interface. The verification agent constructs a verification workflow, encodes mathematical objects and computational intent in an MTF request, and sends it to a mathematical toolbox agent. The latter parses the request, generates executable calls, dispatches them to a backend for exact computation, and returns tool outputs to support candidate-answer adjudication, answer revision, and verification-workflow revision.
AI.result: AMTFV was evaluated on five challenging mathematical reasoning datasets with seven model configurations from DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini. It outperforms representative baselines overall, improving average accuracy over the strongest baseline by up to 8.3 percentage points under an individual model configuration, with larger gains on samples of medium and high verification complexity.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling mathematical verification modeling from concrete execution through a tool-flow interface (MTF) improves accuracy and reliability compared to existing reflection-based and program-generation-based verification approaches, especially on more complex verification tasks.

title: Progressive Decision-Making for Localizing Open-Ended AI-Generated Image Forgeries
summary: AI-generated image forgeries are becoming increasingly realistic and difficult to characterize with fixed manipulation patterns. As generative models continue to evolve, it is impractical to expect a localization model to exhaustively learn all possible forgery appearances from large-scale training data alone. Nevertheless, many AI-generated forgeries still leave subtle forensic traces, although these cues are often weak and unevenly reliable across regions. Therefore, robust localization requires not only extracting informative forensic traces, but also making reliable decisions from incomplete and ambiguous evidence. In this paper, we move beyond static one-shot prediction and reformulate final forgery localization as an adaptive sequential decision-updating process, where the localization map is treated as an intermediate state rather than a fixed output. Rather than producing the final mask via one-shot pixel-wise prediction, our method progressively updates the localization state guided by available evidence, uncertainty, and boundary conditions. Specifically, we first transform mesoscopic traces into compact decision evidence via a lightweight decision evidence projector, and then introduce Evidence-Guided Mamba (EG-Mamba) to perform uncertainty- and boundary-aware state updating. This design allows reliable manipulated and background regions to be preserved, while ambiguous regions are cautiously revised according to the available evidence. Extensive experiments on both conventional and AI-generated manipulation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Notably, even when trained only on conventional manipulation data, our method brings larger gains on unseen AI-generated forgeries, indicating that progressive decision-updating is especially useful for heterogeneous and hard-to-exhaustively-learn manipulation traces.

AI.tldr: This paper reformulates AI-generated image forgery localization as an adaptive sequential decision-updating process rather than one-shot prediction. Using an Evidence-Guided Mamba (EG-Mamba) architecture, the method progressively updates localization maps based on available evidence, uncertainty, and boundary conditions, showing notable gains on unseen AI-generated forgeries even when trained only on conventional manipulation data.
AI.motivation: AI-generated image forgeries are becoming increasingly realistic and cannot be exhaustively covered by fixed manipulation patterns learned from large-scale training data. While subtle forensic traces exist in many AI-generated forgeries, they are often weak and unevenly reliable across regions, making it difficult to extract informative traces and make reliable decisions from incomplete and ambiguous evidence using static one-shot prediction.
AI.method: The method treats final forgery localization as an adaptive sequential decision-updating process with the localization map as an intermediate state. It first transforms mesoscopic traces into compact decision evidence via a lightweight Decision Evidence Projector, then introduces Evidence-Guided Mamba (EG-Mamba) to perform uncertainty- and boundary-aware state updating. This design preserves reliable manipulated and background regions while cautiously revising ambiguous regions based on available evidence.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on both conventional and AI-generated manipulation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of the method. Notably, even when trained only on conventional manipulation data, the method achieves larger gains on unseen AI-generated forgeries, demonstrating that progressive decision-updating is especially useful for heterogeneous and hard-to-exhaustively-learn manipulation traces.
AI.conclusion: Progressive decision-updating with evidence guidance is more robust for AI-generated forgery localization than static one-shot prediction, particularly for handling weak, uneven, and heterogeneous forensic traces that are difficult to exhaustively learn from training data alone.

title: Reflection or Re-Generation? Why LLM Revision Fails Where Human Revision Succeeds
summary: Reflection, the ability to revisit and revise prior reasoning, is central to how humans improve their answers. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly prompted to "reflect," yet whether this resembles human revision remains unclear. We introduce the Human-LLM Reflection Framework (HRF), a controlled two-pass protocol comparing human and LLM revision under identical conditions across self-, peer-, and cross-agent settings. Using an information-theoretic analysis based on per-iteration cross-entropy reduction, we find two failure modes of LLM reflection. On objective tasks with finite answer spaces, reflection yields near-zero information gain (Delta I approx 0), behaving as neutral re-generation indistinguishable from re-sampling. On subjective tasks, it yields significant negative gain (Delta I < 0), moving predictions away from the target. Human revision, by contrast, yields positive gain in both settings. Cross-agent experiments localize the failure to the revision step, not input quality: LLMs degrade even high-quality human responses. Diagnostic analyses (revision conditioned on first-pass correctness, and oracle-guided revision against a random-reshuffle baseline) show that which sub-step dominates varies by task and by model rather than reducing to a single mechanism: self-error detection is present on objective multiple-choice tasks but weak on subjective ones, and recovery under an oracle error signal exceeds the baseline for some models and falls below it for others. The unifying account is structural: without external information, self-conditioned revision cannot reduce uncertainty about the target, so LLM reflection is better understood as conditioned re-generation than as genuine error-driven revision.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Human-LLM Reflection Framework (HRF), a controlled two-pass protocol comparing human and LLM revision under identical conditions. Using information-theoretic analysis based on per-iteration cross-entropy reduction, the authors find that LLM reflection fails on both objective tasks (near-zero information gain, equivalent to neutral re-generation) and subjective tasks (negative information gain, moving predictions away from target), whereas human revision yields positive gain in both settings. The failure is localized to the revision step itself—LLMs degrade even high-quality human inputs. The unifying account is structural: without external information, self-conditioned revision cannot reduce target uncertainty, so LLM reflection is better understood as conditioned re-generation than genuine error-driven revision.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly prompted to "reflect" and revise their prior reasoning, but it is unclear whether this process resembles genuine human revision or merely re-generation. The authors aim to rigorously establish whether LLM reflection actually improves answers and how it compares to human revision under controlled conditions.
AI.method: The authors introduce HRF, a controlled two-pass protocol comparing human and LLM revision across self-, peer-, and cross-agent settings under identical conditions. They employ an information-theoretic analysis based on per-iteration cross-entropy reduction (ΔI) to quantify information gain. They also conduct diagnostic analyses: revision conditioned on first-pass correctness, and oracle-guided revision against a random-reshuffle baseline, to decompose which sub-step (error detection vs. recovery) dominates.
AI.result: LLM reflection exhibits two failure modes: near-zero information gain (ΔI ≈ 0) on objective tasks, behaving as neutral re-generation indistinguishable from re-sampling; and significant negative gain (ΔI < 0) on subjective tasks, moving away from the target. Human revision achieves positive gain in both settings. Cross-agent experiments localize the failure to the revision step, as LLMs degrade even high-quality human responses. Diagnostic analyses reveal that self-error detection is present on objective multiple-choice tasks but weak on subjective ones, and oracle-guided recovery varies by model relative to baseline.
AI.conclusion: Without external information, self-conditioned revision cannot reduce uncertainty about the target. LLM reflection is therefore better understood as conditioned re-generation rather than genuine error-driven revision, providing a structural explanation for its failure modes across task types.

title: COntExt: Towards Context-Aware Ontology Extension from Operational Metrics
summary: Organizations increasingly define operational metrics in structured, machine-readable formats to monitor systems, processes, and compliance. These metric definitions implicitly encode domain knowledge, such as referencing concepts, properties, and relationships, that often extends what is captured in formal ontologies. Yet the connection between operational metric catalogues and ontological knowledge remains manual, ad-hoc, and labor-intensive. We present COntExt, a framework for context-aware ontology extension that takes structured metric definitions as input and suggests how referenced concepts and properties should be integrated into an existing ontology, utilizing the context of these metrics. The framework defines the extension problem as three sub-tasks: parent class prediction, relation type prediction, and data property assignment. Across four cybersecurity ontologies, we evaluate different algorithms for each task. Our results show that metric-derived context improves the suggestions over ontology-context baselines for relation type prediction and data property assignment. Our work demonstrates that operational metric catalogues are a practical and underexploited source for ontology extension. This work enables organizations to maintain their ontologies at a significantly lower cost than manual engineering.

AI.tldr: COntExt is a framework that automatically extends ontologies using context derived from operational metric definitions, framing the task as three sub-problems (parent class prediction, relation type prediction, data property assignment) and showing that metric-derived context outperforms ontology-context baselines across four cybersecurity ontologies.
AI.motivation: Operational metric definitions implicitly encode domain knowledge that often extends beyond formal ontologies, but connecting metric catalogues to ontological knowledge is currently manual, ad-hoc, and labor-intensive, driving up ontology maintenance costs.
AI.method: COntExt takes structured metric definitions as input and formulates ontology extension as three sub-tasks: parent class prediction, relation type prediction, and data property assignment. It uses the context of the metrics (rather than ontology context alone) to suggest how referenced concepts and properties should be integrated into an existing ontology, with different algorithms evaluated for each sub-task.
AI.result: Across four cybersecurity ontologies, metric-derived context improves suggestion quality over ontology-context baselines for relation type prediction and data property assignment tasks.
AI.conclusion: Operational metric catalogues are a practical and underexploited source for ontology extension, enabling organizations to maintain their ontologies at significantly lower cost than manual engineering.

title: MoRAE: Flow-Friendly Self-Supervised Latents for Text-to-Motion Generation
summary: Text-to-motion generation must produce motions that are semantically correct, temporally coherent, and physically plausible. A natural approach is to first project motion data into a structured semantic space and then train a generative model within that space. Such a paradigm has been highly successful in image generation through Representation Autoencoders (RAEs), where a frozen self-supervised encoder provides semantic features for diffusion or flow models to learn from. However, direct transfer of such a paradigm to motion space using Motion-JEPA as the frozen encoder fails dramatically. We diagnose this failure geometrically and identify two motion-specific bottlenecks: (1) the JEPA feature space is spectrally ill-conditioned, making the Gaussian-to-data transport unstable; and (2) even with a well-conditioned spectrum, flow residuals tend to align with decoder-sensitive directions, where small latent errors are amplified into large motion artifacts after decoding. Based on these insights, we propose MoRAE. MoRAE addresses the two bottlenecks separately. A compact bottleneck distills the structured JEPA representation while removing weak and redundant directions, bringing the latent spectrum into a transport-stable regime. Motion-coupled training then aligns the retained latent geometry with the decoder, making characteristic flow errors less costly after decoding. With this flow-friendly latent, a standard non-autoregressive Flow-Matching DiT achieves state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: MoRAE is a motion generation framework that fixes the failure of directly transferring Representation Autoencoder (RAE) paradigms from images to motion. It addresses two motion-specific bottlenecks—spectrally ill-conditioned JEPA feature spaces and flow residuals aligning with decoder-sensitive directions—via a compact bottleneck and motion-coupled training, achieving SOTA performance with a standard Flow-Matching DiT.
AI.motivation: Text-to-motion generation requires motions that are semantically correct, temporally coherent, and physically plausible. The authors explore projecting motion into a structured semantic space (via Motion-JEPA) before training a generative model, following the successful RAE paradigm in image generation. However, direct transfer fails dramatically, and the authors seek to diagnose and overcome this failure geometrically.
AI.method: MoRAE addresses two diagnosed bottlenecks: (1) a compact bottleneck that distills the structured JEPA representation while removing weak and redundant directions to make the latent spectrum transport-stable, and (2) motion-coupled training that aligns the retained latent geometry with the decoder so characteristic flow errors are less costly after decoding. The resulting flow-friendly latent is used with a standard non-autoregressive Flow-Matching DiT.
AI.result: With the flow-friendly latent space, a standard non-autoregressive Flow-Matching DiT achieves state-of-the-art performance in text-to-motion generation.
AI.conclusion: MoRAE demonstrates that the RAE paradigm can be effectively transferred to motion generation when motion-specific spectral conditioning and latent-decoder alignment issues are properly handled, achieving SOTA results with a standard generative architecture.

title: Gated Q-learning: Add Off-Policy Bias to Taste
comment: 18 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Published in the Reinforcement Learning Journal (RLJ); presented at the Reinforcement Learning Conference (RLC 2026)
summary: Multistep credit assignment is critical for sample-efficient reinforcement learning, yet managing off-policy bias in Q-learning remains a fundamental challenge. For 30 years, practitioners have been limited to a binary choice: eliminate the bias at the cost of severely truncated eligibility traces (Watkins' Q($λ$)), or ignore the bias to learn faster while injecting detrimental errors into the value estimates (Peng's Q($λ$)). Modern off-policy estimators fail to resolve this tension, as importance-sampling ratios collapse under Q-learning's greedy target policy. We introduce Gated Q-learning, a novel algorithmic framework that ends this dilemma by smoothly interpolating between the two historical extremes. Rather than relying on importance sampling, our approach employs a continuous, state-action-dependent gating mechanism to selectively attenuate eligibility traces in an exploration-aware manner. We provide a rigorous theoretical foundation for this mechanism, proving that the expected operator remains a contraction mapping and deriving its exact fixed point. Empirical evaluations verify that intermediate gating safely enables longer credit-assignment horizons, yielding faster initial learning than either extreme. Gated Q-learning offers a simple alternative to importance sampling while enabling customization of the effective multistep horizon and the amount of off-policy bias in Q-learning agents.

AI.tldr: Gated Q-learning is a new algorithmic framework that resolves the multistep credit assignment dilemma in Q-learning by using a continuous, state-action-dependent gating mechanism to smoothly interpolate between Watkins' Q(λ) (bias-free but truncated) and Peng's Q(λ) (fast but biased). It avoids importance sampling, provides contraction and fixed-point guarantees, and empirically enables longer credit-assignment horizons with faster initial learning.
AI.motivation: Traditional multistep Q-learning forces a binary choice: Watkins' Q(λ) eliminates off-policy bias by severely truncating eligibility traces, while Peng's Q(λ) ignores bias for faster learning but injects detrimental errors into value estimates. Modern off-policy estimators fail to resolve this because importance-sampling ratios collapse under Q-learning's greedy target policy. There is a need for a method that can tune the trade-off between bias and credit-assignment horizon.
AI.method: The paper introduces Gated Q-learning, which replaces importance sampling with a continuous, state-action-dependent gating mechanism that selectively attenuates eligibility traces in an exploration-aware manner. This allows smooth interpolation between the two historical extremes (Watkins' and Peng's Q(λ)). The authors prove the expected operator remains a contraction mapping and derive its exact fixed point.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show that intermediate gating safely enables longer credit-assignment horizons, yielding faster initial learning than either extreme. The framework proves theoretically sound (contraction and fixed-point guarantees) and offers a simple, customizable alternative to importance sampling.
AI.conclusion: Gated Q-learning provides a principled resolution to the bias-versus-horizon trade-off in multistep reinforcement learning, allowing practitioners to customize the effective multistep horizon and the amount of off-policy bias in Q-learning agents without relying on importance sampling.

title: LEMUR: Learning to Align with Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning from Preference Feedback
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) systems are typically trained using a single, well-specified scalar reward function. However, real-world decision-making tasks often involve multiple, competing objectives, such as performance versus efficiency, where ground-truth reward functions are difficult to specify or inaccessible. While Multi-Objective RL (MORL) addresses such trade-offs by modeling rewards as vectors, existing approaches typically assume access to a well-specified reward function for each objective, inheriting the same challenges faced by single-objective RL. Meanwhile, Preference-based RL (PbRL) has shown great potential in solving complex tasks without access to a pre-defined reward function through reward learning from human feedback, yet has largely been studied in single-objective settings. In this work, we bridge this gap with LEMUR: Learning to Align with Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Preference feedback, a novel framework where an agent interactively learns from the preferences of multiple humans to learn optimal multi-objective policies. Our approach jointly learns policies and multiple objective-specific reward models from human feedback, enabling agents to effectively balance competing objectives during learning. We evaluate LEMUR on a variety of benchmark multi-objective tasks, and empirical results demonstrate its superior performance over baseline methods. Our method presents a promising direction for solving multi-objective decision-making tasks without pre-defined reward functions.

AI.tldr: LEMUR is a novel framework that combines Preference-based RL with Multi-Objective RL, allowing agents to learn optimal multi-objective policies from multiple human preference feedback without pre-defined reward functions.
AI.motivation: Real-world decision-making tasks involve multiple competing objectives, but existing MORL methods require well-specified reward functions for each objective, inheriting the same specification challenges as single-objective RL. PbRL avoids reward specification but has largely been limited to single-objective settings. This gap motivates the need for a framework that learns multi-objective policies from human preference feedback.
AI.method: LEMUR jointly learns policies and multiple objective-specific reward models from human feedback. The agent interactively learns from preferences provided by multiple humans, using these preferences to simultaneously estimate reward models for each objective and optimize multi-objective policies that balance competing objectives during learning.
AI.result: LEMUR was evaluated on a variety of benchmark multi-objective tasks, with empirical results demonstrating superior performance over baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: LEMUR presents a promising direction for solving multi-objective decision-making tasks without requiring pre-defined reward functions, effectively bridging the gap between MORL and PbRL.

title: Locally Consistent Transductive Information Maximization for Few-Shot Remote Sensing Scene Classification
summary: Remote sensing scene classification is increasingly relying on foundation models pre-trained on large-scale Earth-observation data. Moreover, transductive inference, which exploits the collective statistical structure of the entire unlabeled query set, appears to naturally match remote sensing pipelines where large images are routinely split into patches and inferred as a batch. In this work, we introduce LC-TIM (Locally Consistent Transductive Information Maximization), which extends the state-of-the-art Transductive Information Maximization for Few-Shot CLIP (TIM++) objective with a local consistency regularizer that enforces prediction agreement between each query sample and its $κ$ nearest feature-space neighbors. The regularizer enters as a single multiplicative factor in the closed-form $q$-update, adding negligible computational overhead. We further propose a multi-source extension that fuses the affinity graph from multiple remote sensing foundation model, further boosting classification accuracy. To assess these methods, we establish the first comprehensive, open-source benchmark for transductive few-shot RS scene classification, evaluating LP++, TransCLIP, TIM++, and LC-TIM across ten diverse datasets, two remote sensing vision-language models, and across various few-shot settings. Our experiments show that transductive methods consistently outperform zero-shot baselines, and that LC-TIM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, with the largest gains in the low-shot regime where neighborhood cues are most informative. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/elkhouryk/LC-TIM

AI.tldr: LC-TIM (Locally Consistent Transductive Information Maximization) extends the TIM++ transductive few-shot CLIP objective with a local consistency regularizer that enforces prediction agreement between each query sample and its k nearest feature-space neighbors, plus a multi-source extension fusing affinity graphs from multiple remote sensing foundation models. It establishes the first comprehensive open-source benchmark for transductive few-shot RS scene classification across ten datasets and two vision-language models, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with largest gains in low-shot regimes.
AI.motivation: Remote sensing scene classification increasingly relies on foundation models, and transductive inference naturally matches RS pipelines where large images are split into patches and inferred as batches. The authors aim to improve state-of-the-art transductive few-shot classification for remote sensing by adding local neighborhood consistency and establishing a standardized benchmark.
