AI.method: LC-TIM extends the TIM++ objective with a local consistency regularizer enforcing prediction agreement between each query sample and its k nearest neighbors in feature space. The regularizer enters as a single multiplicative factor in the closed-form q-update, adding negligible computational overhead. A multi-source extension fuses affinity graphs from multiple remote sensing foundation models. A comprehensive benchmark compares LP++, TransCLIP, TIM++, and LC-TIM.
AI.result: Transductive methods consistently outperform zero-shot baselines; LC-TIM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across ten datasets and various few-shot settings, with the largest gains in the low-shot regime where neighborhood cues are most informative.
AI.conclusion: LC-TIM provides a computationally efficient, state-of-the-art transductive few-shot classification method for remote sensing scene classification, validated on a new comprehensive open-source benchmark, with code publicly available.

title: Learning Optimal Dynamic Matching via Graph Neural Networks
summary: Dynamic matching markets require decisions about whom to match and when: matching now yields value but removes participants who may create better future opportunities. We develop a value-based reinforcement-learning framework for this problem on finite, evolving weighted graphs. We study an infinite-horizon continuous-time model with stochastic arrivals, node-type transitions, edge realizations, and exogenous exits. We prove an event-time reduction: without loss of optimality, the planner acts immediately after each exogenous event and then waits for the next one. We further show that the optimal edge-wise $Q$-function is characterized by a single continuation-value function on post-decision residual graphs, reducing the learned object from state-action values to graph values. Exact action selection still requires combinatorial matching optimization; we approximate the value with a graph neural network, train it by temporal-difference learning, and use it in a forward-greedy matching heuristic. In a binary-type benchmark, the learned policy substantially outperforms immediate and threshold-greedy rules by preserving common nodes for rare arrivals of valuable matches while forming lower-value matches only in thick pools. In a kidney paired donation benchmark, it performs similarly to immediate greedy when exits are unpredictable, recovers the logic of patient matching when warnings are reliable, and outperforms the better of Immediate Greedy and Patient Greedy across intermediate warning probabilities. These results show that residual-graph value learning yields state-dependent dynamic matching policies that adapt to realized connectivity and exit information.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a value-based reinforcement learning framework for dynamic matching on finite, evolving weighted graphs. It proves an event-time reduction (acting only after exogenous events is optimal), shows the optimal edge-wise Q-function reduces to a single continuation-value function on post-decision residual graphs, and approximates this value with a graph neural network trained via temporal-difference learning combined with a forward-greedy matching heuristic. Experiments on binary-type and kidney paired donation benchmarks show the learned policy adaptively balances immediate matching versus waiting for better future opportunities.
AI.motivation: Dynamic matching markets face a fundamental trade-off: matching now yields immediate value but removes participants who might create greater future opportunities. Existing approaches lack a principled framework for learning state-dependent policies that account for evolving connectivity, arrivals, type transitions, and exits.
AI.method: The paper formulates the problem as an infinite-horizon continuous-time model with stochastic arrivals, node-type transitions, edge realizations, and exogenous exits on weighted graphs. It proves an event-time reduction showing optimality is preserved by acting only after each exogenous event. It then shows the optimal edge-wise Q-function is characterized by a single continuation-value function on post-decision residual graphs, reducing the learning target from state-action values to graph values. The value function is approximated with a graph neural network trained via temporal-difference learning, and used within a forward-greedy matching heuristic.
AI.result: In a binary-type benchmark, the learned policy outperforms immediate and threshold-greedy rules by preserving common nodes for rare valuable matches while forming lower-value matches only in thick pools. In a kidney paired donation benchmark, it performs comparably to immediate greedy when exits are unpredictable, recovers patient-matching logic when warnings are reliable, and outperforms both Immediate Greedy and Patient Greedy across intermediate warning probabilities.
AI.conclusion: Residual-graph value learning yields state-dependent dynamic matching policies that adapt to realized connectivity and exit information, providing a flexible and effective approach to dynamic matching in evolving weighted graphs.

title: DungeonBench: A Benchmark for Rules-Rich Tactical Reasoning in Dungeons & Dragons Combat
summary: Games and simulators make valuable benchmarks by turning decisions into measurable outcomes, but many current suites under-test rules-rich tactical reasoning: the ability to choose well when geometry, timing, resources, objectives, and rule interactions all matter at once. We introduce DungeonBench, a benchmark for tactical reasoning in Dungeons & Dragons combat, built to cover the vast majority of combat-relevant 2014 System Reference Document content whose effects can be resolved by the simulator while retaining mechanics that simplified combat simulators often abstract away. At each step, DungeonBench exposes a complete tactical observation, a pending decision, and an indexed list of executable options spanning movement, attacks, spells, reactions, objectives, preparation, and scarce resources. The task is to value legal choices whose consequences depend on action economy, creature traits, battlefield geometry, timing windows, and future encounters. DungeonBench has two tracks: Encounter, which evaluates local tactical play in single fights, and Day, which links encounters through persistent hit points, spell slots, consumables, preparation, and short-rest timing, forcing policies to trade off immediate tactical advantage against future survivability. The same engine-generated decision stream supports heuristic controllers, language-model policies, learned option rankers, and masked-action reinforcement-learning agents. We evaluate frontier language-model policies on this shared decision stream. Results show that full tactical observations do not saturate the benchmark: frontier policies often win direct encounters, but linked encounter days expose failures in resource budgeting, rest timing, and rule-aware tactical discipline.

AI.tldr: DungeonBench is a benchmark for tactical reasoning in Dungeons & Dragons combat, covering combat-relevant 2014 SRD content in a simulator that preserves complex mechanics. It provides complete tactical observations, pending decisions, and indexed executable options at each step across two tracks (Encounter for single fights, Day for linked encounters with resource persistence). Evaluations of frontier LM policies show they often win direct fights but fail at resource budgeting, rest timing, and rule-aware tactics in linked-encounter settings.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmark suites under-test rules-rich tactical reasoning—the ability to make good decisions when geometry, timing, resources, objectives, and rule interactions jointly matter—because simplified combat simulators abstract away key mechanics.
AI.method: DungeonBench is built on a simulator preserving combat-relevant 2014 SRD mechanics (action economy, creature traits, battlefield geometry, timing, resources). It exposes per-step complete tactical observations, pending decisions, and indexed executable options. Two tracks: Encounter (single fights) and Day (linked encounters with persistent HP, spell slots, consumables, preparation, short-rest timing). The engine-generated decision stream supports heuristic controllers, LM policies, learned rankers, and masked-action RL agents.
AI.result: Frontier LM policies often win direct encounters, but full tactical observations do not saturate the benchmark: linked-encounter Day track exposes failures in resource budgeting, rest timing, and rule-aware tactical discipline.
AI.conclusion: DungeonBench demonstrates that current frontier language-model policies lack robust rule-aware tactical reasoning and resource management over extended decision horizons, indicating the benchmark is not saturated and remains a useful testbed.

title: UltraSAM3: A Concept-Driven Foundation Model for Universal Ultrasound Image Segmentation
summary: Ultrasound imaging has become increasingly widespread in clinical practice due to its portability, low cost and real-time capability, making ultrasound image segmentation important. However, ultrasound images differ substantially from CT, MRI, and other medical imaging modalities, as they are often affected by speckle noise, low contrast, acoustic shadows and ambiguous boundaries. Existing ultrasound segmentation methods are still mainly limited to task-specific models or visual-prompt-based foundation models, which are either tailored to particular tasks or require expert-provided visual prompts, making them inconvenient for flexible clinical use. To address these challenges, we propose UltraSAM3, a concept-driven foundation model for universal ultrasound image segmentation. Unlike conventional models, UltraSAM3 enables text-based target specification by adapting SAM3 to ultrasound-specific image--mask--concept triplets. The model is trained on a large-scale ultrasound segmentation corpus covering 37 public datasets and 13 anatomical categories, allowing it to align ultrasound visual patterns with clinically meaningful concepts across diverse organs and lesions. To further improve usability under realistic clinical interaction, we propose an instruction-guided agent that parses complex natural language queries into concise ultrasound concept prompts for UltraSAM3. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UltraSAM3 consistently outperforms representative concept- and text-driven biomedical segmentation models on multi-organ ultrasound benchmarks, external datasets, and visual-prompt-enhanced settings. Moreover, the agent improves segmentation robustness for complex user instructions. These results indicate that ultrasound-specific concept adaptation is effective for building generalizable and interactive ultrasound segmentation foundation models.

AI.tldr: UltraSAM3 is a concept-driven foundation model for universal ultrasound image segmentation that adapts SAM3 to ultrasound-specific image-mask-concept triplets, is trained on 37 public datasets and 13 anatomical categories, and pairs with an instruction-guided agent that parses natural language queries into concise ultrasound concept prompts. It consistently outperforms representative concept- and text-driven biomedical segmentation models on multi-organ benchmarks, external datasets, and visual-prompt-enhanced settings.
AI.motivation: Ultrasound images are widely used clinically due to portability, low cost, and real-time capability, but existing ultrasound segmentation methods are limited to either task-specific models or visual-prompt-based foundation models that require expert-provided visual prompts, making them inflexible for practical clinical use. Additionally, ultrasound images suffer from speckle noise, low contrast, acoustic shadows, and ambiguous boundaries, making segmentation particularly challenging.
AI.method: UltraSAM3 adapts SAM3 to ultrasound-specific image-mask-concept triplets, enabling text-based target specification. The model is trained on a large-scale ultrasound segmentation corpus covering 37 public datasets and 13 anatomical categories to align ultrasound visual patterns with clinically meaningful concepts. An instruction-guided agent is also proposed to parse complex natural language queries into concise ultrasound concept prompts for enhanced clinical usability.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show UltraSAM3 consistently outperforms representative concept- and text-driven biomedical segmentation models on multi-organ ultrasound benchmarks, external datasets, and visual-prompt-enhanced settings. The instruction-guided agent also improves segmentation robustness for complex user instructions.
AI.conclusion: Ultrasound-specific concept adaptation is effective for building generalizable and interactive ultrasound segmentation foundation models, suggesting this approach can support flexible clinical use without requiring expert visual prompts or task-specific model designs.

title: Latent Lie-Poisson Neural Networks (LLPNNs): Discovering the motion of Lie-Poisson systems through observable data and latent dynamics
summary:
Structure-preserving neural networks are essential for the long-term prediction of Hamiltonian systems from data. Many important Hamiltonian systems in mechanics and control admit symmetry reduction to Lie--Poisson systems, including rigid bodies, underwater vehicles, fluids, plasmas, and optimal control problems. A fundamental challenge in learning such systems is that their dynamics evolve in momentum variables that are typically unobservable, while available data consist only of observable quantities such as configurations and velocities. In optimal control applications, the situation is further complicated because the latent variables contain unobservable co-states and the Hamiltonian may be degenerate, preventing the existence of a corresponding Lagrangian and rendering the encoder-decoder approaches inapplicable.
  We introduce Latent Lie--Poisson Neural Networks (LLPNNs), a structure-preserving framework for learning Lie--Poisson dynamics directly from observable data. The proposed approach exploits three geometric ingredients: (i) learning either a Hamiltonian decoder or a pseudo-Lagrangian encoder on the active variables, (ii) constructing latent trajectories through a universal Noether invariant arising from Lie--Poisson symmetry reduction, and (iii) reconstructing observable and latent dynamics through Lie--Poisson flows combined with Magnus-based Lie-group updates. The resulting method preserves the geometric structure and is applicable to both regular and degenerate Hamiltonian systems.
  We demonstrate the method on three examples: a generalized rigid body on SO(3), Kirchhoff's underwater vehicle on SE(3), and an optimal-control problem for interacting vehicles on $SE(2)^N$. Numerical experiments show excellent long-term predictive accuracy, strong robustness to noise, and competitive performance using only modest datasets and lightweight neural-network architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Latent Lie-Poisson Neural Networks (LLPNNs), a structure-preserving framework for learning Lie-Poisson dynamics from observable data only, applicable to both regular and degenerate Hamiltonian systems including optimal control problems.
AI.motivation: Many Hamiltonian systems (rigid bodies, underwater vehicles, fluids, plasmas, optimal control) admit symmetry reduction to Lie-Poisson systems, but their dynamics evolve in latent momentum variables that are unobservable. Available data only contains observable quantities like configurations and velocities. In optimal control, latent co-states are unobservable and the Hamiltonian may be degenerate, preventing a corresponding Lagrangian and rendering encoder-decoder approaches inapplicable.
AI.method: LLPNNs exploit three geometric ingredients: (i) learning either a Hamiltonian decoder or a pseudo-Lagrangian encoder on active variables, (ii) constructing latent trajectories through a universal Noether invariant from Lie-Poisson symmetry reduction, and (iii) reconstructing observable and latent dynamics via Lie-Poisson flows combined with Magnus-based Lie-group updates.
AI.result: Demonstrated on three examples: a generalized rigid body on SO(3), Kirchhoff's underwater vehicle on SE(3), and an optimal-control problem for interacting vehicles on SE(2)^N. Experiments show excellent long-term predictive accuracy, strong noise robustness, and competitive performance with modest datasets and lightweight neural architectures.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method preserves geometric structure and is applicable to both regular and degenerate Hamiltonian systems, enabling accurate long-term prediction of latent Lie-Poisson dynamics directly from observable data.

title: AgentHPOBench: A Benchmark For Evaluating LLM Agents as Sequential Hyperparameter Optimizers
summary: As LLMs evolve from code completion systems into autonomous scientific agents, evaluating their ability to conduct experiments has become increasingly important. Existing benchmarks typically focus on static code generation, paper replication, or final answer correctness, but do not directly assess whether agents can interpret experimental evidence and use it to guide subsequent hyperparameter decisions. To address this gap, we introduce AgentHPOBench, a sequential benchmark comprising 30 executable machine learning tasks across seven research categories. Each task begins with a validated baseline run, after which an agent performs several sequential interventions. At each step, the agent observes the accumulated configurations, metrics, and logs before proposing the next valid configuration. We evaluate 12 widely used agents and conventional HPO baselines under a unified protocol. The results show that current agents exhibit measurable experimental optimization ability across domains, but still face clear limitations in sustained iterative refinement, complex log diagnosis, and consistent progress toward reported reference performance.

AI.tldr: AgentHPOBench is a sequential benchmark with 30 executable ML tasks across seven research categories, designed to evaluate whether LLM-based agents can interpret experimental evidence and use it to guide hyperparameter decisions in iterative experimental workflows.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-based scientific agents focus on static code generation, paper replication, or final answer correctness, but fail to directly assess whether agents can interpret experimental evidence and use it to inform subsequent hyperparameter decisions—a critical capability as LLMs evolve from code completion systems into autonomous scientific agents.
AI.method: The benchmark comprises 30 executable machine learning tasks across seven research categories. Each task starts with a validated baseline run, after which an agent performs multiple sequential interventions. At each step, the agent observes accumulated configurations, metrics, and logs before proposing the next valid configuration. Twelve widely used agents and conventional HPO baselines are evaluated under a unified protocol.
AI.result: Current agents exhibit measurable experimental optimization ability across domains, but still face clear limitations in sustained iterative refinement, complex log diagnosis, and consistent progress toward reported reference performance.
AI.conclusion: AgentHPOBench fills a gap in agent evaluation by directly testing iterative experimental reasoning and hyperparameter optimization in a sequential setting, revealing both the strengths and persistent weaknesses of current LLM-based agents in autonomous scientific experimentation.

title: Domain-Division based Progressive Learning for Source-Free Domain Adaptation
comment: Accepted by IEEE Transactions on Multimedia 2025
summary: With growing privacy and portability concerns, source-free domain adaptation requires only a source pre-trained model and an unlabeled target domain, allowing for effective adaptation to the target data. Most existing self-training methods focus on selecting and exploiting samples with reliable predictions, often neglecting others. Inspired by the finding that deep models learn clean samples faster than noisy ones, we propose a domain-division based progressive learning method named DPL. Specifically, our approach consists of two alternating stages, each beginning with the division of the target domain into easy-to-adapt and hard-to-adapt subdomains based on adaptation difficulty, followed by neighborhood-based pseudo label assignment. In stage one, we enhance classification accuracy through uncertainty-aware self-training and alignment of corresponding classes between subdomains. Stage two then applies tailored learning strategies to each subdomain, starting with consistency learning on the easy-to-adapt samples and progressing to utilizing local structural information for the more challenging ones, thereby mining the intrinsic properties of the target data. Extensive experiments on several widely used benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/iamjingli/DPL.

AI.tldr: DPL is a source-free domain adaptation method that divides the target domain into easy-to-adapt and hard-to-adapt subdomains based on adaptation difficulty, then applies progressive learning strategies—from uncertainty-aware self-training and class alignment to consistency learning and local structural information mining—to achieve superior performance over state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Most existing self-training methods in source-free domain adaptation focus only on samples with reliable predictions while neglecting others. The authors leverage the finding that deep models learn clean samples faster than noisy ones to propose a domain-division based progressive learning approach that systematically handles both easy and hard samples.
AI.method: The method (DPL) consists of two alternating stages. Each stage begins by dividing the target domain into easy-to-adapt and hard-to-adapt subdomains based on adaptation difficulty, followed by neighborhood-based pseudo label assignment. Stage one enhances classification accuracy through uncertainty-aware self-training and alignment of corresponding classes between subdomains. Stage two applies tailored learning strategies per subdomain: consistency learning on easy samples and local structural information utilization for hard samples, thereby mining intrinsic properties of the target data.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on several widely used benchmarks validate the effectiveness of DPL, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The code is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: The domain-division based progressive learning approach effectively addresses the limitations of existing self-training methods by progressively adapting from easy to hard samples, achieving state-of-the-art performance in source-free domain adaptation.

title: FairDiffuseVQVAE: Sampling-Time Fairness in Tabular Diffusion via Conditional Refinement of Vector-Quantized Latents
summary: Synthetic tabular data is increasingly used in privacy-preserving data sharing, data augmentation, and to mitigate downstream classifier bias. State-of-the-art tabular diffusion models such as TabDDPM and TabSyn achieve excellent distributional fidelity but offer no mechanism for fairness; conversely, fairness-aware tabular generators (DECAF, FairTGAN, FairTabDDPM) impose explicit fairness penalties at training time, yielding modest fairness gains at substantial cost to either sample quality or downstream utility. We introduce FairDiffuseVQVAE, a two-stage architecture that decouples fidelity from fairness: a vector-quantized autoencoder with a row-level discriminator (Stage~1, no fairness terms) is followed by a DiffuseVAE-style continuous diffusion refiner that conditions on both the Stage-1 reconstruction and the protected attribute via classifier-free guidance (Stage~2). Fairness emerges as a property of the sampling distribution -- uniform sampling of the protected attribute at inference time enforces demographic parity by construction, rather than from competing loss terms. On the Adult, Bank and COMPAS datasets, FairDiffuseVQVAE achieves the highest mean Demographic Parity Ratio ($0.702$, $+47\%$ over FairTabDDPM) and Equalized Odds Ratio ($0.686$, $+100\%$). It also attains the lowest mean pair-wise correlation error ($0.034$) of any published method, while explicitly trading $\sim$$15$ AUC points for these fairness gains.

AI.tldr: FairDiffuseVQVAE is a two-stage architecture for fair synthetic tabular data generation that decouples fidelity from fairness: a vector-quantized autoencoder with a row-level discriminator (Stage 1) followed by a DiffuseVAE-style continuous diffusion refiner using classifier-free guidance on the protected attribute (Stage 2). Fairness is enforced by construction through uniform sampling of the protected attribute at inference, achieving state-of-the-art Demographic Parity Ratio (0.702, +47% over FairTabDDPM) and Equalized Odds Ratio (0.686, +100%), while trading ~15 AUC points.
AI.motivation: Existing state-of-the-art tabular diffusion models (TabDDPM, TabSyn) offer excellent distributional fidelity but no fairness mechanism, while fairness-aware generators (DECAF, FairTGAN, FairTabDDPM) impose explicit fairness penalties that yield modest fairness gains at substantial cost to sample quality and downstream utility. There is a need for an approach that achieves both high fidelity and strong fairness without competing loss terms.
AI.method: A two-stage architecture: (1) a vector-quantized autoencoder with a row-level discriminator trained without fairness terms; (2) a DiffuseVAE-style continuous diffusion refiner that conditions on both the Stage-1 reconstruction and the protected attribute via classifier-free guidance. Fairness is achieved by uniformly sampling the protected attribute at inference time, enforcing demographic parity by construction rather than through loss penalties.
AI.result: On Adult, Bank, and COMPAS datasets, FairDiffuseVQVAE achieves the highest mean Demographic Parity Ratio (0.702, +47% over FairTabDDPM) and Equalized Odds Ratio (0.686, +100%). It also achieves the lowest mean pair-wise correlation error (0.034) of any published method, while trading roughly 15 AUC points for these fairness gains.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling fidelity from fairness via a two-stage architecture enables fairness to emerge as a property of the sampling distribution rather than competing with fidelity objectives. This yields superior fairness metrics and correlation fidelity simultaneously, at a tunable cost in downstream utility (AUC).

title: Development of FDD-ON: an Ontology for VAV HVAC System Fault Detection and Diagnostics
summary: Fault detection and diagnosis (FDD) technology is essential for improving HVAC system reliability, energy efficiency, and maintenance effectiveness. However, effective deployment of FDD solutions in buildings requires structured domain knowledge that can bridge heterogeneous data sources, diverse equipment types, and varied diagnostic outputs. Limited data interpretability and interoperability within the FDD domain have led to fragmented information silos, hindering the implementation of FDD and related applications, such as the digital twin-enabled FDD frameworks and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven maintenance decision-making systems. This paper presents an FDD Ontology (FDD-ON), a modular and extensible ontology to formally represent variable air volume (VAV) HVAC system components, fault types, symptom statuses, fault impacts and associated attributes. FDD-ON integrates HVAC system FDD semantics to provide comprehensive representations of fault and symptom attributes, supported by the well-defined controlled vocabulary. Additionally, FDD-ON offers comprehensive fault, symptom, and impact libraries to capture a broad spectrum of operational abnormalities and their consequences in VAV HVAC systems. Through explicit contributing cause-fault-symptom-impact relations, FDD-ON serves as a machine-interpretable basis for querying diagnostic knowledge, mapping heterogeneous FDD outputs, and developing interoperable FDD-related applications. FDD-ON is evaluated using publicly available VAV HVAC system datasets and demonstrated through FDD development applications. Results indicate that FDD-ON provides a foundational semantic framework for advancing scalable, transparent, and interoperable FDD solutions across various applications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents FDD-ON, a modular and extensible ontology for formally representing VAV HVAC system components, fault types, symptom statuses, fault impacts, and associated attributes, aimed at overcoming data interpretability and interoperability challenges in fault detection and diagnosis (FDD). FDD-ON integrates FDD semantics with controlled vocabularies and comprehensive fault/symptom/impact libraries, and is evaluated using public VAV HVAC datasets and demonstrated through FDD development applications.
AI.motivation: Effective deployment of FDD solutions in buildings requires structured domain knowledge to bridge heterogeneous data sources, diverse equipment types, and varied diagnostic outputs. However, limited data interpretability and interoperability within the FDD domain have led to fragmented information silos, hindering the implementation of FDD and related applications such as digital twin-enabled FDD frameworks and AI-driven maintenance decision-making systems.
AI.method: The paper develops FDD-ON, a modular and extensible ontology that formally represents VAV HVAC system components, fault types, symptom statuses, fault impacts and associated attributes. It integrates HVAC system FDD semantics with well-defined controlled vocabulary and provides comprehensive fault, symptom, and impact libraries. The ontology establishes explicit contributing cause-fault-symptom-impact relations to serve as a machine-interpretable basis for querying diagnostic knowledge, mapping heterogeneous FDD outputs, and developing interoperable FDD-related applications.
AI.result: FDD-ON was evaluated using publicly available VAV HVAC system datasets and demonstrated through FDD development applications. Results indicate that FDD-ON provides a foundational semantic framework for advancing scalable, transparent, and interoperable FDD solutions across various applications.
AI.conclusion: FDD-ON serves as a foundational semantic framework that enhances interoperability and scalability of FDD solutions, enabling transparent and interoperable fault detection and diagnosis across diverse HVAC applications.

title: Multi-Modal Object Re-Identification with Dual Semantic Guidance and Global-Local Mutual Modulation
comment: Accepted by IEEE TCSVT 2026. The version of record may differ slightly
summary: Multi-modal object Re-Identification (ReID) aims to retrieve target instances by leveraging complementary information across modalities. However, existing methods suffer from two challenges. First, they often fail to exploit well-aligned and reliable semantic priors, making them vulnerable to background clutter and cross-modal misalignment. On the other hand, they typically rely on holistic feature modeling, overlooking the synergy between global and local representations. To overcome these limitations, we propose a robust multi-modal ReID framework with dual semantic guidance and global-local mutual modulation, which mainly consists of three key components, namely the Text-Semantic Injector (TSI), the Masked Global-Local Modulator (MGLM), and the Hierarchical MoE Fusion (HMF). The TSI enhances semantic awareness by integrating clean and coherent textual features into visual tokens. The MGLM enables part-aware cross-modal interaction through joint guidance from soft masks and global context, improving fine-grained feature alignment. Finally, the HMF adaptively aggregates multi-spectral features under local semantic supervision, yielding discriminative and robust representations. Extensive experiments on three multi-modal ReID benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/zw-absin/DSGM upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a robust multi-modal ReID framework called DSGM (Dual Semantic Guidance and global-local Mutual modulation) to address two key challenges in multi-modal object re-identification: lack of well-aligned semantic priors (vulnerable to background clutter and cross-modal misalignment) and reliance on holistic feature modeling (overlooking global-local synergy). The framework consists of three components: Text-Semantic Injector (TSI) for integrating textual features into visual tokens, Masked Global-Local Modulator (MGLM) for part-aware cross-modal interaction, and Hierarchical MoE Fusion (HMF) for adaptive multi-spectral feature aggregation with local semantic supervision. Experiments on three multi-modal ReID benchmarks demonstrate effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-modal ReID methods fail to exploit well-aligned semantic priors, making them vulnerable to background clutter and cross-modal misalignment. They also rely on holistic feature modeling, neglecting the synergy between global and local representations, which limits fine-grained discrimination.
AI.method: The proposed framework includes three key components: (1) Text-Semantic Injector (TSI) injects clean and coherent textual features into visual tokens for enhanced semantic awareness; (2) Masked Global-Local Modulator (MGLM) performs part-aware cross-modal interaction using joint guidance from soft masks and global context for fine-grained feature alignment; (3) Hierarchical MoE Fusion (HMF) adaptively aggregates multi-spectral features under local semantic supervision to produce discriminative and robust representations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three multi-modal ReID benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method over existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: The DSGM framework with dual semantic guidance and global-local mutual modulation effectively addresses semantic prior exploitation and global-local feature synergy challenges in multi-modal ReID, achieving strong performance across benchmarks. Code will be released publicly.

title: Shapley-Value-Based Feature Attribution for Data Masking
summary: Despite its many benefits, widespread access to individuals' personal data also causes severe privacy concerns for consumers, companies, and policymakers. This study proposes a novel framework that adapts the Shapley-value-based feature attribution approach to the problem domain of data privacy by capturing the two crucial dimensions of data privacy---disclosure risk and data utility. Our proposed framework takes a holistic view of data masking through a fair feature attribution approach based on Shapley values. Different from the existing literature that mostly focuses on the risk-utility tradeoff at the dataset level, the proposed framework addresses the tradeoff at the feature level. Furthermore, the proposed framework is agnostic to data masking methods, statistical and machine learning methods, and data utility and disclosure risk evaluation metrics. Experimental results show that our proposed method can effectively reduce disclosure risk while preserving data utility.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel framework that adapts Shapley-value-based feature attribution to data privacy, capturing both disclosure risk and data utility at the feature level to balance the privacy-utility tradeoff.
AI.motivation: Widespread access to personal data raises severe privacy concerns, and existing literature mostly addresses the risk-utility tradeoff at the dataset level rather than identifying which features contribute most to disclosure risk versus data utility at a finer granularity.
AI.method: The proposed framework applies Shapley-value-based feature attribution to quantify each feature's contribution to both disclosure risk and data utility, enabling a holistic view of data masking. It is agnostic to data masking methods, statistical/machine learning models, and evaluation metrics for both utility and risk.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively reduces disclosure risk while preserving data utility.
AI.conclusion: The feature-level Shapley-based attribution framework provides a flexible and model-agnostic approach to balancing privacy and utility in data masking, outperforming dataset-level tradeoff strategies.

title: ExtractBench: A Benchmark for Schema-Guided Enterprise Document Extraction
summary: Enterprise workflows increasingly rely on agents for \emph{schema-guided extraction}: given a document and a user-defined schema, the agent faithfully follows the schema to produce the correct output with source evidence as grounding metadata. We present ExtractBench, a benchmark for schema-guided extraction and, to our knowledge, the first to score value accuracy, record completeness at scale, grounding, and measured cost together. The evaluation system contains 4,869 pages across 370 enterprise documents, 8 business domains, and 67 document types, with clear tags differentiating their challenge scenarios. The scalable schema and ground-truth curation pipeline combines independent-system agreement for real documents, known values for synthetic lists, and human verification for forms. We report order-insensitive value F1 for value accuracy, plus two grounding metrics for source traceability: word- and page-level F1. Commercial VLMs perform well on short documents but often truncate record lists on long ones, while coding agents retain higher accuracy at much higher cost. LlamaExtract Agentic Plus ranks first on all three metrics, with accuracy comparable to coding agents at a fraction of the cost. Dataset and evaluation code are available on \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/llamaindex/ExtractBench}{HuggingFace} and \href{https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench}{GitHub}.

AI.tldr: ExtractBench is a benchmark for schema-guided extraction from enterprise documents, the first to jointly score value accuracy, record completeness at scale, grounding, and cost. It contains 4,869 pages across 370 documents from 8 business domains and 67 document types, with a scalable curation pipeline combining independent-system agreement, synthetic known values, and human verification. Commercial VLMs struggle with long documents by truncating record lists, while coding agents are more accurate but costly; LlamaExtract Agentic Plus ranks first across all metrics with coding-agent-level accuracy at a fraction of the cost.
AI.motivation: Enterprise workflows increasingly use agents for schema-guided extraction, yet no existing benchmark comprehensively evaluates value accuracy, record completeness at scale, grounding, and measured cost together. Prior benchmarks fail to capture the full demands of real-world enterprise extraction tasks.
AI.method: The authors construct ExtractBench with 4,869 pages across 370 enterprise documents spanning 8 business domains and 67 document types, tagged with challenge scenarios. A scalable ground-truth curation pipeline combines independent-system agreement for real documents, known values from synthetic lists, and human verification for forms. Evaluation uses order-insensitive value F1 for accuracy plus word- and page-level F1 for grounding (source traceability).
AI.result: Commercial VLMs perform well on short documents but frequently truncate record lists on long ones. Coding agents retain higher accuracy at much higher cost. LlamaExtract Agentic Plus ranks first on all three metrics, achieving accuracy comparable to coding agents at a fraction of the cost.
AI.conclusion: ExtractBench provides a comprehensive, multi-metric benchmark for schema-guided extraction, revealing that general VLMs struggle with long-document record completeness while agentic systems with coding capabilities offer better accuracy-cost trade-offs.

title: Is It Time for the Renaissance of Salient Object Detection in the Era of MLLMs?
summary: The zero-shot capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are pushing salient object detection (SOD) beyond task-specific supervision. To disentangle MLLMs beyond conventional mask-based evaluation, we decompose SOD into localization and segmentation, and re-engineer datasets with phrases, boxes, and attributes, establishing a diagnostic benchmark for MLLM saliency perception (SaliLLM). SaliLLM uncovers a striking capability mismatch: MLLMs outperform state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in localization, yet remain substantially weaker in segmentation. Further analyses attribute this gap primarily to mismatches between MLLMs and annotations over foreground cardinality, granularity, and extent. Motivated by this diagnosis, we recast zero-shot SOD as protocol-aligned Foreground Organization and introduce the first training-free framework that leverages Gestalt-inspired Collaborative attention for Unified SOD (FOCUS). FOCUS couples top-down Bayesian-surprise calibration of protocol-conditioned foreground granularity with bottom-up propagation of MLLMs evidence over entity-centric perceptual manifolds induced by self-supervised features, yielding coherent object extents as prompts for a general segmenter. Across 13 RGB, RGB-D, and RGB-T SOD benchmarks, FOCUS generally surpasses SOTA methods without training, reducing mean absolute error by 11\%, 34\%, and 48\% compared with fully, weakly, and self-supervised methods, respectively. Our findings signal the renaissance of SOD: from task-specific supervision to zero-shot foreground organization. Code is available in the supplementary material.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SaliLLM, a diagnostic benchmark decomposing salient object detection (SOD) into localization and segmentation for zero-shot evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). It reveals that MLLMs excel at localization but lag in segmentation, attributed to mismatches in foreground cardinality, granularity, and extent. Motivated by this, the authors propose FOCUS, a training-free framework that uses Gestalt-inspired collaborative attention to organize foregrounds via Bayesian-surprise calibration and self-supervised perceptual manifolds, achieving SOTA results across 13 RGB, RGB-D, and RGB-T benchmarks with MAE reductions of 11%, 34%, and 48% over fully, weakly, and self-supervised methods.
AI.motivation: To move beyond conventional mask-based evaluation and understand the true zero-shot saliency perception capabilities of MLLMs by disentangling SOD into localization and segmentation, thereby diagnosing the capability mismatch between MLLMs and traditional task-specific methods.
AI.method: The paper (1) decomposes SOD into localization and segmentation and re-engineers datasets with phrases, boxes, and attributes to build the SaliLLM diagnostic benchmark; (2) analyzes MLLM-annotation mismatches in foreground cardinality, granularity, and extent; (3) introduces FOCUS, a training-free framework combining top-down Bayesian-surprise calibration with bottom-up collaborative attention propagation over entity-centric perceptual manifolds derived from self-supervised features, using the resulting coherent object extents as prompts for a general segmenter.
AI.result: Across 13 RGB, RGB-D, and RGB-T SOD benchmarks, FOCUS surpasses state-of-the-art methods without any training, reducing mean absolute error by 11% vs fully supervised, 34% vs weakly supervised, and 48% vs self-supervised methods.
AI.conclusion: The findings signal a paradigm shift in SOD from task-specific supervision to zero-shot foreground organization, demonstrating that protocol-aligned foreground organization leveraging MLLM evidence and self-supervised perceptual structure can outperform supervised approaches.

title: Overcoming the Weakest-Link Effect in LLM-Driven Program Optimization via Heterogeneous Edit Recombination
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to solve complex problems by searching over program space, offering a general paradigm for scientific problems that can be naturally represented and solved as programs. Despite recent progress, identifying effective optimization directions for a candidate program remains challenging. By analogy with automatic differentiation, existing methods typically guide the search using a textual ``gradient'': a first-order update direction expressed as textual edits. Such gradients are inferred either from previously evaluated programs or from LLM-generated feedback on the implicit program-score mapping. However, these estimates become increasingly unreliable as the program--score mapping grows more complex, limiting their practical utility. We argue that explicit gradients are not essential for effective program optimization. Leveraging their prior knowledge, LLMs can propose plausible atomic edits directly from the current program, thereby enabling a zeroth-order optimization strategy. However, zeroth-order search suffers from a \textit{weakest-link effect}: when a bundle of edits is accepted or rejected as a whole, a single harmful edit can negate the benefits of all remaining edits. To address this issue, we introduce HERO, a program optimizer that prompts an LLM to generate diverse, non-overlapping atomic edits and then systematically selects and composes them into coherent program improvements using evaluator scores. We evaluate HERO across algorithmic problems, strategy games, the design of LLM-based agentic systems, and robotic path planning. Across these domains, HERO consistently discovers higher-scoring programs and converges substantially faster than prior LLM-based optimizers, while consuming fewer tokens.

AI.tldr: HERO is a zeroth-order LLM-based program optimizer that proposes diverse atomic edits directly from the current program and systematically selects/composes them using evaluator scores, overcoming the "weakest-link effect" of bundle-based edit rejection.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based program optimizers rely on textual "gradients" (first-order update directions) to guide search, but these estimates become unreliable as the program-score mapping becomes complex. The authors argue explicit gradients are not essential; however, zeroth-order search suffers from a weakest-link effect where a single harmful edit in a bundled set can negate all other beneficial edits.
AI.method: HERO prompts an LLM to generate diverse, non-overlapping atomic edits from the current program, then systematically selects and composes them into coherent program improvements using evaluator scores—a zeroth-order optimization strategy without explicit gradient signals.
AI.result: Across algorithmic problems, strategy games, LLM-based agentic system design, and robotic path planning, HERO consistently discovers higher-scoring programs, converges substantially faster than prior LLM-based optimizers, and consumes fewer tokens.
AI.conclusion: Explicit textual gradients are not necessary for effective LLM-based program optimization; a zeroth-order approach with well-managed atomic edit selection and composition can outperform gradient-guided methods across diverse domains while being more token-efficient.

title: CorrelationFlow: A Training-Free Geometric Approach for LiDAR Scene Flow Estimation
summary: LiDAR scene flow estimation has settled into a monoculture: nearly all recent methods share the same feed-forward architecture and the same family of self-supervised losses, inheriting each other's assumptions, and each other's blind spots. When those assumptions fail, as they do for sparse, distant, or fast-moving objects, every method built on them fails together, and adding parameters or simulated training data does not fix what the formulation itself gets wrong. This paper takes the opposite path. We present CorrelationFlow, a training-free geometric framework that reduces scene flow to two textbook operations: connected-component labeling and correlation maximization on bird's-eye-view occupancy images. Objects are isolated as spatio-temporal connected components, their motions recovered as correlation peaks, and the resulting velocities propagated to all member points. However, this dense correlation evaluates every candidate displacement of every cluster and requires a window of past sweeps; therefore, we develop a sparse counterpart that operates on a single sweep pair by matching lightweight occupancy descriptors at boundary key points. Because nothing is trained, nothing is inherited: on the multi-domain test set of the Argoverse 2 2026 Scene Flow Challenge, spanning five datasets with heterogeneous sensors and platforms, CorrelationFlow ranked second among unsupervised methods and degrades most gracefully at long range, where the shared assumptions of learned methods break down. Our results suggest that a substantial share of the scene flow problem is solvable by classical computer vision, and that progress may require questioning the formulation, not scaling it.

AI.tldr: CorrelationFlow is a training-free, classical computer vision framework for LiDAR scene flow estimation that uses connected-component labeling and correlation maximization on bird's-eye-view occupancy images, achieving competitive results (ranked second among unsupervised methods) on the Argoverse 2 2026 Scene Flow Challenge while degrading most gracefully at long range.
AI.motivation: The authors argue that the LiDAR scene flow field has converged on a monoculture of feed-forward architectures and self-supervised losses that share the same assumptions and therefore fail together on sparse, distant, or fast-moving objects. They contend that scaling parameters or adding simulated data cannot fix formulation-level flaws, motivating a fundamentally different, assumption-free approach.
AI.method: CorrelationFlow reduces scene flow to two classical operations: connected-component labeling to isolate spatio-temporal objects, and correlation maximization on bird's-eye-view occupancy images to recover cluster motions, with velocities propagated to all member points. A dense correlation variant uses a window of past sweeps, while a sparse counterpart matches lightweight occupancy descriptors at boundary key points using only a single sweep pair—requiring no training at all.
AI.result: On the multi-domain test set of the Argoverse 2 2026 Scene Flow Challenge (five datasets with heterogeneous sensors and platforms), CorrelationFlow ranked second among unsupervised methods and showed the most graceful degradation at long range, where learned methods' shared assumptions fail.
AI.conclusion: A substantial portion of the scene flow problem is solvable by classical computer vision techniques without training. Progress in the field may require questioning the formulation itself rather than scaling it.

title: When Model Priors Conflict with Visual Evidence: Mitigating Commonsense-Driven Hallucinations by Selective Prior Calibration
summary: In vision--language models, commonsense-driven hallucination (CDH) occurs when a model's commonsense prior overrides clear visual evidence of an atypical state. For example, a model may report that a visibly six-fingered hand has five fingers. We show that these errors are systematically directed: when a model answers a question about a counterfactual (CF) image incorrectly, its answer often coincides with the candidate it prefers without access to the image. Suppressing this prior indiscriminately can repair CF errors, but may also disrupt correct answers on matched commonsense (CS) images, where the same prior is helpful. We therefore propose Selective Prior Calibration (SPC), which subtracts candidate-level prior-preference estimates from image-conditioned scores with an instance-dependent strength and revises the original prediction only when the resulting score pattern strongly supports an alternative. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPC substantially improves accuracy on CF images while largely preserving accuracy on matched CS images. Furthermore, these gains generalize across CDH categories, candidate-answer permutations, and other conflict benchmarks, while SPC rarely alters predictions on benchmarks without such conflicts.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses commonsense-driven hallucination (CDH) in vision-language models, where a model's commonsense prior overrides visual evidence of atypical states (e.g., reporting five fingers on a visibly six-fingered hand). The authors propose Selective Prior Calibration (SPC), which subtracts candidate-level prior-preference estimates from image-conditioned scores with instance-dependent strength and revises predictions only when the score pattern strongly supports an alternative. SPC substantially improves accuracy on counterfactual images while largely preserving accuracy on matched commonsense images, and generalizes across CDH categories, answer permutations, and other conflict benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models systematically hallucinate on counterfactual images because their commonsense priors override clear visual evidence. Existing approaches that suppress the prior indiscriminately repair counterfactual errors but also disrupt correct answers on matched commonsense images where the same prior is helpful. A selective, instance-dependent calibration approach is needed.
AI.method: The paper proposes Selective Prior Calibration (SPC), a post-hoc method that: (1) estimates candidate-level prior-preference scores without image access, (2) subtracts these estimates from image-conditioned scores with an instance-dependent strength, and (3) revises the original prediction only when the resulting score pattern strongly supports an alternative candidate.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show SPC substantially improves accuracy on counterfactual (CF) images while largely preserving accuracy on matched commonsense (CS) images. The gains generalize across CDH categories, candidate-answer permutations, and other conflict benchmarks, while SPC rarely alters predictions on benchmarks without such conflicts.
AI.conclusion: Selective prior calibration effectively mitigates commonsense-driven hallucination by selectively suppressing the commonsense prior only when it conflicts with visual evidence, striking a balance between fixing counterfactual errors and not degrading performance on commonsense-consistent images.

title: Efficient LLM Adversarial Training via Low-Rank Defense and Circuit-Guided Surrogates
summary: Adversarial training is one of the most effective defenses against adversarial attacks, yet the computational cost remains prohibitive at modern scales, especially for large language models (LLMs). While existing mitigation strategies, e.g., latent adversarial training (LAT), have been developed, they still incur a high computational cost. In this work, we comprehensively investigate computation-efficient strategies to speed up LAT from two complementary perspectives: (1) Defense-side optimization: We explore the representation fine-tuning (ReFT) within LAT, and reveal a potential issue if there is a mismatch on which tokens to apply ReFT and the attack. (2) Attack-side optimization: When computing adversarial attacks in each LAT iteration, we extract only the relevant circuits from the LLM to construct a lightweight surrogate model, avoiding the computation in the forward-backward passes through the full model during the attack generation. For both perspectives, we provide theoretical justifications and numerical evidence to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed strategies. Ultimately, compared to standard LAT with full fine-tuning, our method on average reduces per-step adversarial-training FLOPs by 48.1% while requiring only 0.0118% trainable parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates computation-efficient strategies to accelerate latent adversarial training (LAT) for large language models from two perspectives: defense-side optimization using representation fine-tuning (ReFT) and attack-side optimization using lightweight surrogate models built from relevant LLM circuits. The approach reduces per-step adversarial-training FLOPs by 48.1% on average while requiring only 0.0118% trainable parameters compared to standard LAT.
AI.motivation: Adversarial training is effective against adversarial attacks but computationally prohibitive at modern scales, especially for LLMs. Even existing mitigation strategies like latent adversarial training (LAT) remain computationally expensive, motivating the need for efficient acceleration strategies.
AI.method: The paper proposes two complementary optimization strategies: (1) Defense-side: apply representation fine-tuning (ReFT) within LAT, while addressing token-level mismatches between where ReFT is applied and where attacks occur; (2) Attack-side: extract only the relevant circuits from the LLM to build a lightweight surrogate model for adversarial attack generation, avoiding full-model forward-backward passes.
AI.result: The proposed method reduces per-step adversarial-training FLOPs by 48.1% on average while requiring only 0.0118% trainable parameters, compared to standard LAT with full fine-tuning. Both theoretical justifications and numerical evidence support the effectiveness of the proposed strategies.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that LAT can be significantly accelerated through a combination of representation fine-tuning and circuit-based surrogate modeling, offering a practical path toward scalable adversarial training for LLMs with substantial computational savings and parameter efficiency.

title: TAVI-TEC: An AI-Based Tool for Procedural Planning of Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation
summary: Computed tomography angiography (CTA) is crucial for preprocedural TAVI planning, providing the anatomical information required for prosthesis sizing and vascular access assessment. As the volume of TAVI procedure increases, improving efficiency and standardizing annotations is becoming essential in clinical practice. This study presents TAVI-TEC, a fully automated artificial intelligence-based framework integrated into a web based DICOM viewer for routine preoperative TAVI planning. Pre-procedural CTA scans from patients undergoing TAVI with SAPIEN 3 Ultra (S3U) prostheses were processed using a fully automated pipeline. Deep learning-based segmentation of cardiovascular structures, calcification detection, centerline extraction, landmark identification, and annular plane definition was implemented to quantify key annular and aortic root measurements and color-coded maps of lumen reduction and vessel diameter for vascular access. A multilayer perceptron classifier was trained to predict prosthesis size prior to the TAVI procedure. Results revealed that TAVI-TEC enabled pre-procedural measurements in approximately 2-6 min. Strong agreement with clinician-derived measurements was observed for annular area (coefficient of concordance, CCC = 0.934; interclass correlation coefficient, ICC = 0.935; R^2 = 0.881) and perimeter (CCC = 0.909; ICC = 0.909; R^2 = 0.854). The valve-size prediction model achieved 82% overall accuracy, with most misclassifications occurring between adjacent prosthesis sizes. Though further multicenter validation and extension to additional measurements and valve platforms are required, the TAVI-TEC methodology may reduce operator variability in pre-TAVI measurements and streamline the preoperative workflows of the Heart Team for decision-making.

AI.tldr: TAVI-TEC is a fully automated AI-based framework integrated into a web-based DICOM viewer that processes pre-procedural CTA scans for TAVI planning, performing deep learning-based segmentation, calcification detection, centerline extraction, anatomical landmark identification, and annular plane definition. It quantifies key annular and aortic root measurements, generates color-coded maps for vascular access assessment, and predicts prosthesis size using a multilayer perceptron classifier. The system achieves measurements in 2-6 minutes with strong agreement to clinician measurements (annular area CCC=0.934, perimeter CCC=0.909) and 82% overall valve-size prediction accuracy, with misclassifications mostly confined to adjacent sizes.
AI.motivation: As TAVI procedure volumes increase, there is a growing need to improve efficiency and standardize annotations in preprocedural planning. Manual CTA measurements are time-consuming and subject to operator variability, motivating the development of a fully automated AI-based framework to streamline preoperative TAVI workflows and support Heart Team decision-making.
AI.method: The study processes pre-procedural CTA scans from patients undergoing TAVI with S3U prostheses through a fully automated pipeline integrated into a web-based DICOM viewer. The pipeline includes deep learning-based segmentation of cardiovascular structures, calcification detection, centerline extraction, landmark identification, and annular plane definition. It quantifies annular and aortic root measurements, generates color-coded lumen reduction and vessel diameter maps for vascular access, and uses a multilayer perceptron classifier to predict prosthesis size.
AI.result: TAVI-TEC enabled pre-procedural measurements in approximately 2-6 minutes. Strong agreement with clinician measurements was observed for annular area (CCC=0.934, ICC=0.935, R²=0.881) and perimeter (CCC=0.909, ICC=0.909, R²=0.854). The valve-size prediction model achieved 82% overall accuracy, with most misclassifications occurring between adjacent prosthesis sizes.
AI.conclusion: Though further multicenter validation and extension to additional measurements and valve platforms are required, the TAVI-TEC methodology may reduce operator variability in pre-TAVI measurements and streamline preoperative workflows of the Heart Team for decision-making.

title: Beyond Feature and Structure Alignment: Learning Transferable Propagation Knowledge for Graph Foundation Models
summary: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for enabling knowledge transfer across diverse domains. Unlike traditional graph learning methods that are typically designed for in-domain settings, GFMs aim to learn transferable knowledge that can generalize to unseen graph domains. However, unlike language or visual data, graphs lack intrinsic and unified representation units, such as tokens in language and patches in vision, making it challenging to identify transferable knowledge units for building graph foundation models. Existing graph foundation models mainly focus on mitigating domain discrepancies through feature alignment and structure alignment, while overlooking the exploration of transferable knowledge units underlying graph data. Moreover, these methods generally rely on fixed propagation mechanisms during message passing, overlooking the heterogeneity in propagation patterns, as different edges may exhibit distinct propagation patterns for different feature dimensions. To address these limitations, we propose a Propagation-aware Graph Foundation Model (ProGFM), which regards the propagation relationships between edges and feature dimensions as transferable knowledge units. Through a propagation relationship prototype bank, ProGFM learns cross-domain transferable propagation knowledge, enabling adaptive information aggregation in unseen graph domains. Extensive experiments across various cross-domain transfer scenarios demonstrate that ProGFM possesses strong cross-domain knowledge transfer capability and exhibits superior generalization performance compared with existing methods.

AI.tldr: ProGFM is a propagation-aware graph foundation model that treats edge-feature-dimension propagation relationships as transferable knowledge units, using a prototype bank to enable adaptive information aggregation and cross-domain generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing graph foundation models focus on feature/structure alignment to mitigate domain gaps but overlook transferable knowledge units (unlike tokens in language or patches in vision). Additionally, they use fixed propagation mechanisms that fail to account for heterogeneous propagation patterns across edges and feature dimensions.
AI.method: ProGFM regards propagation relationships between edges and feature dimensions as transferable knowledge units, and employs a propagation relationship prototype bank to learn cross-domain transferable propagation knowledge, enabling adaptive information aggregation in unseen graph domains.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across various cross-domain transfer scenarios show that ProGFM possesses strong cross-domain knowledge transfer capability and superior generalization performance compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: ProGFM effectively addresses the lack of intrinsic universal representation units in graphs by leveraging propagation relationship prototypes as transferable knowledge, achieving adaptive aggregation and improved cross-domain generalization.

title: OsteoCAD: A Human-in-the-Loop Cloud-Edge Framework for Bone Tumor Segmentation
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Deep Learning (DL) have notably advanced medical image analysis, yet many health- care organizations struggle to adopt them due to limited com- putational resources and specialized expertise. To address these barriers, we introduce OsteoCAD, a modular eHealth framework that democratizes access to DL tools in clinical practice. Osteo- CAD delivers end-to-end DL capabilities-from dataset creation and preprocessing to model training and inference-through an integrated and user-friendly interface. To mitigate local hardware constraints, the framework securely connects to remote GPU infrastructures. We validate OsteoCAD's feasibility through a real-world case study in Mexico focused on large bone tumor segmentation. The results demonstrate the framework's ability to enable DL-powered eHealth solutions without demanding ad- vanced technical expertise or complex local configurations.

AI.tldr: OsteoCAD is a modular eHealth framework that democratizes access to Deep Learning tools in clinical practice by providing an end-to-end pipeline (from dataset creation to model inference) with a user-friendly interface and secure connection to remote GPU infrastructure, validated through a bone tumor segmentation case study in Mexico.
AI.motivation: Healthcare organizations struggle to adopt AI/DL tools for medical image analysis due to limited computational resources and lack of specialized expertise, creating barriers to leveraging these advanced technologies in clinical settings.
AI.method: The framework is a modular eHealth system providing end-to-end DL capabilities including dataset creation, preprocessing, model training, and inference through an integrated user-friendly interface. It mitigates local hardware constraints by securely connecting to remote GPU infrastructures.
AI.result: Validation through a real-world case study in Mexico focused on large bone tumor segmentation demonstrated the framework's ability to enable DL-powered eHealth solutions without requiring advanced technical expertise or complex local configurations.
AI.conclusion: OsteoCAD successfully lowers the barriers to adopting DL in clinical practice by combining an intuitive interface with remote GPU access, making DL-powered medical imaging accessible to healthcare organizations with limited resources.

authors: Jose Luis Lima de Jesus Silva
title: SILVA Networks as Structured Implicit Layers and Vector Attractors via Dynamic Interaction Fields
summary: Many learning problems require representations that reconcile direct input, nearby structure, and broader context. In implicit neural layers, these influences are usually absorbed into a single fixed-point update, making it hard to identify what enters from the stimulus, what propagates locally, what comes from global context, and what is produced by solver dynamics. Here we introduce SILVA Networks, Structured Implicit Layers and Vector Attractors via Dynamic Interaction Fields. SILVA separates stimulus, local interaction, global interaction, damping, and readout inside one fixed-point architecture. The same template is instantiated for images, molecules, citation networks, and long-range graph benchmarks through domain-specific definitions of nodes, neighborhoods, and global summaries. Experiments and ablations show task-dependent roles for these terms: local interactions are load-bearing in the graph tasks, MNIST gains little from recurrence at the tested capacity, and the clearest global benefit appears in a long-range node-classification benchmark. SILVA therefore provides an implicit representation whose internal interaction dynamics can be trained, ablated, visualized, and diagnosed.

AI.tldr: SILVA Networks introduce structured implicit layers that explicitly separate stimulus, local interaction, global interaction, damping, and readout terms within a single fixed-point architecture, enabling interpretable and diagnosable implicit representations across images, molecules, citation networks, and long-range graph benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Implicit neural layers absorb direct input, nearby structure, and broader context into a single fixed-point update, making it difficult to distinguish what enters from the stimulus, propagates locally, comes from global context, or arises from solver dynamics. The authors aim to disentangle these influences for interpretability and diagnosis.
AI.method: SILVA Networks decompose the fixed-point update into five explicit components: stimulus, local interaction, global interaction, damping, and readout. The same architectural template is instantiated across diverse domains—images, molecules, citation networks, and long-range graphs—by defining domain-specific nodes, neighborhoods, and global summaries.
AI.result: Experiments and ablations reveal task-dependent roles for the interaction terms: local interactions are load-bearing for graph tasks, MNIST shows little benefit from recurrence at tested capacity, and the most significant global-interaction benefit appears in a long-range node-classification benchmark.
AI.conclusion: SILVA provides an implicit representation whose internal interaction dynamics can be trained, ablated, visualized, and diagnosed, offering a more interpretable and structured alternative to opaque implicit neural layers.

title: Training-Free Entity-Level Few-Shot Segmentation of Remote Sensing Images with Advection Refinement
summary: Existing cross-domain few-shot segmentation approaches suffer from high training costs due to source-domain episodic training and pixel-wise dense prediction, while often producing fragmented and noisy predictions. To overcome these issues, we propose a training-free entity-level few-shot segmentation framework for remote sensing images with advection refinement. Specifically, we first leverage SAM3's generic geometric priors to generate category-agnostic entity primitives. By reformulating few-shot inference from pixel-level prediction to entity-level reasoning, foreground and background prototypes are constructed and combined with dense textual semantic responses from SAM3 to build a multi-modal semantic potential field. Furthermore, an advection equation-based semantic refinement mechanism is introduced to propagate category-aware information across both feature and similarity spaces, enhancing semantic continuity and suppressing local texture noise. Extensive experiments on multiple remote sensing datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively mitigates domain shift and local noise, substantially improving SAM3's adaptation capability for remote sensing few-shot segmentation without additional training. Our code will be publicly available at https://github.com/yu-ni1989/ELFSS-AR.

AI.tldr: A training-free, entity-level few-shot segmentation framework for remote sensing images, leveraging SAM3's geometric priors to generate entity primitives, constructing a multi-modal semantic potential field, and using an advection-based refinement mechanism to propagate category-aware information, improving domain adaptation without extra training.
AI.motivation: Existing cross-domain few-shot segmentation methods incur high training costs from source-domain episodic training and pixel-wise dense prediction, and often produce fragmented, noisy predictions. The authors aim to overcome these limitations by proposing a training-free approach.
AI.method: The framework uses SAM3's generic geometric priors to generate category-agnostic entity primitives, reformulating few-shot inference from pixel-level to entity-level reasoning. Foreground/background prototypes are combined with dense textual semantic responses from SAM3 to build a multi-modal semantic potential field. An advection equation-based semantic refinement mechanism propagates category-aware information across feature and similarity spaces to enhance semantic continuity and suppress local texture noise.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple remote sensing datasets demonstrate the framework effectively mitigates domain shift and local noise, substantially improving SAM3's adaptation capability for remote sensing few-shot segmentation without additional training.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training-free entity-level framework with advection refinement offers an efficient and effective solution for cross-domain few-shot segmentation in remote sensing, eliminating training costs while improving segmentation quality.

title: Dynamics-aware identification of governing equations from sparse and noisy data
summary: Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) and PDE functional identification (PDE-FIND) recover parsimonious ordinary and partial differential equations (ODEs and PDEs) from data. However, sparse and noisy temporal measurements can make derivative estimates unreliable. To address this problem, we evaluate Koopman-based upsampling techniques implemented with dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), extended DMD (EDMD), and optimized DMD. These methods learn finite-dimensional approximations of Koopman evolution on selected observables and are used to interpolate and denoise snapshots inside the observed time window before derivative estimation and sparse regression. The empirical benchmark comprises two ODE systems, Lorenz-63 and Van der Pol, and three periodic PDE systems, Burgers, Fisher-Kolmogorov-Petrovskii-Piskunov (Fisher-KPP), and linear advection-diffusion, over sparse and noisy sampling regimes. Polynomial EDMD gives the strongest ODE results, especially in coefficient accuracy. The PDE results are system-dependent: low-rank DMD-assisted reconstructions improve Burgers and advection-diffusion discovery, while the raw baseline (without upsampling) remains competitive for the Fisher-KPP data. A comparison against linear and smoothing-spline interpolation techniques shows that the selected Koopman-based preprocessors provide overall performance gains over these non-dynamical alternatives. We also demonstrate that DMD-assisted upsampling can stabilize Pareto-based non-oracle support-size selection. Overall, Koopman-based upsampling is best viewed as a dynamics-aware preprocessing step that can reduce derivative-estimation error when its observable representation and low-rank structure are appropriate for the data.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates Koopman-based upsampling techniques (DMD, EDMD, and optimized DMD) as preprocessing steps before SINDy/PDE-FIND for identifying ODEs and PDEs from sparse, noisy data. Polynomial EDMD performs best for ODEs, while results for PDEs are system-dependent, with Koopman-based methods generally outperforming non-dynamical interpolation baselines and stabilizing Pareto-based support-size selection.
AI.motivation: Sparse and noisy temporal measurements make derivative estimates unreliable in SINDy and PDE-FIND model discovery. The authors seek a preprocessing approach to improve derivative estimation before sparse regression, motivated by the potential of dynamics-aware Koopman-based upsampling to denoise and interpolate data more effectively than conventional static interpolation techniques.
AI.method: Koopman-based upsampling via dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), extended DMD (EDMD), and optimized DMD is applied. These methods learn finite-dimensional approximations of Koopman evolution on selected observables and are used to interpolate and denoise snapshots within the observed time window prior to derivative estimation and sparse regression. Empirical benchmarks cover two ODE systems (Lorenz-63, Van der Pol) and three periodic PDE systems (Burgers, Fisher-KPP, linear advection-diffusion) under sparse and noisy sampling. Comparisons are made against linear and smoothing-spline interpolation, plus a raw baseline.
AI.result: Polynomial EDMD yielded the strongest ODE results, particularly in coefficient accuracy. PDE results were system-dependent: low-rank DMD-assisted reconstructions improved Burgers and advection-diffusion discovery, while the raw baseline remained competitive for Fisher-KPP. Koopman-based preprocessors outperformed linear and smoothing-spline interpolation overall. DMD-assisted upsampling also stabilized Pareto-based non-oracle support-size selection.
AI.conclusion: Koopman-based upsampling serves as a dynamics-aware preprocessing step that can reduce derivative-estimation error when its observable representation and low-rank structure are well-suited to the data, but its effectiveness is problem-dependent and should be viewed as one tool within a broader preprocessing toolkit.

title: FillGS: Filling Observation Gaps in 4D Gaussian Splatting via Viewpoint-Time Selection and Generative Refinement
summary: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) can render dynamic scenes photorealistically. However, with limited viewpoint coverage, some spatiotemporal regions remain sparsely observed, leading to artifacts, particularly in scenes with large motion. Existing approaches leveraging generative models rely on heuristic virtual-viewpoint selection before refining rendered views. As a result, they cannot actively explore such sparsely observed regions. To address this issue, we propose a pipeline that actively selects spatiotemporal virtual viewpoints to improve 4DGS reconstruction. Our method selects virtual viewpoints for generative enhancement based on the rendering sensitivity and motion-aware observation density of 4D Gaussians, prioritizing views that alleviate observation sparsity. In the refined images, we filter out regions that conflict with captured observations or are likely to contain generative artifacts and then fine-tune 4DGS using only the reliable regions. We evaluate our method on multi-view video benchmarks using new train/test splits designed to induce observation gaps. Results show consistent improvements over prior viewpoint selection strategies and fine-tuning methods in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, while reducing artifacts.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an active spatiotemporal virtual-viewpoint selection pipeline to improve 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) reconstruction in scenes with sparse observation coverage.
