It selects viewpoints based on rendering sensitivity and motion-aware observation density, then fine-tunes 4DGS using only reliable regions from generated images, achieving consistent improvements over prior methods.
AI.motivation: 4DGS can render dynamic scenes photorealistically, but with limited viewpoint coverage, spatiotemporal regions remain sparsely observed, causing artifacts especially in scenes with large motion. Existing generative-model-based approaches use heuristic virtual-viewpoint selection before refining rendered views and cannot actively explore sparsely observed regions.
AI.method: The pipeline actively selects spatiotemporal virtual viewpoints for generative enhancement based on rendering sensitivity and motion-aware observation density of 4D Gaussians, prioritizing views that reduce observation sparsity. In refined images, regions conflicting with captured observations or likely to contain generative artifacts are filtered out, and 4DGS is fine-tuned using only the reliable regions.
AI.result: Evaluated on multi-view video benchmarks with new train/test splits designed to induce observation gaps, the method shows consistent improvements over prior viewpoint selection strategies and fine-tuning methods in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, while reducing artifacts.
AI.conclusion: Active viewpoint selection guided by observation sparsity and rendering sensitivity, combined with reliable-region filtering during fine-tuning, effectively improves 4DGS reconstruction quality in sparsely observed dynamic scenes.

title: DFSC: Error-Controlled Differentiable Mittag-Leffler Propagation for Fractional Scientific Machine Learning
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures. Code and reproducibility materials: https://github.com/hzhooning-art/DFSC and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21588834
summary:
Fractional scientific machine learning requires numerical operators that can be differentiated, batched, accelerated, and composed with neural networks. When the dominant linear fractional evolution is known through a Mittag-Leffler propagator, repeatedly reconstructing that response with a history solver or relearning it from data is unnecessary. We present DFSC, a PyTorch environment organized around the Mittag-Leffler Spectral Layer (MLSL). The layer separates known fractional propagation from data-driven corrections, so neural modules learn only unresolved dynamics while fractional orders and residual-network parameters are optimized jointly. Its adaptive algorithm increases special-function truncation depth or Lanczos dimension until successive differentiable evaluations satisfy a requested tolerance. In the negative-real alternating-series regime, DFSC additionally returns a certified first-omitted-term bound; outside that regime it explicitly labels estimates as empirical.
  DFSC supports dense, sparse, matrix-free, self-adjoint, generalized, and controlled complex operator paths; trainable fractional orders; direct inverse problems; residual neural composition; and CPU/GPU execution. The certified series bound covers all 59 eligible reference cases, with median bound/error effectivity 1.246 for resolved errors. Reusing a prepared batched Lanczos basis gives identical fixed-path values and reduces repeated-query time by 4.61--7.11 times on CPU and 13.07--16.22 times on an RTX 5070, excluding one-time preparation. A 27-case inverse matrix finds full-rank local curvature throughout, while remaining explicitly model-conditional. External solver and mixed real-data results support DFSC as an error-aware optional primitive for matched fractional structure, rather than a general replacement for fractional solvers or neural models.

AI.tldr: DFSC is a PyTorch environment built around a Mittag-Leffler Spectral Layer (MLSL) that separates known fractional propagation from data-driven corrections, enabling differentiable, batched, accelerated neural composition for fractional scientific machine learning with certified error bounds in the negative-real regime.
AI.motivation: Fractional scientific machine learning needs numerical operators that are differentiable, batched, accelerated, and composable with neural networks. When the dominant linear fractional evolution is known via a Mittag-Leffler propagator, repeatedly reconstructing it with history solvers or relearning it from data is wasteful and unnecessary.
AI.method: DFSC organizes computation around the Mittag-Leffler Spectral Layer (MLSL), which separates known fractional propagation from data-driven corrections so neural modules learn only unresolved dynamics. Fractional orders and residual-network parameters are optimized jointly. An adaptive algorithm increases special-function truncation depth or Lanczos dimension until successive differentiable evaluations meet a tolerance; in the negative-real alternating-series regime a certified first-omitted-term bound is returned, otherwise estimates are explicitly labeled empirical. It supports dense, sparse, matrix-free, self-adjoint, generalized, and controlled complex operator paths; trainable fractional orders; direct inverse problems; residual neural composition; and CPU/GPU execution, including a reusable batched Lanczos basis.
AI.result: The certified series bound covers all 59 eligible reference cases with median bound/error effectivity 1.246 for resolved errors. Reusing the prepared batched Lanczos basis gives identical fixed-path values and reduces repeated-query time by 4.61-7.11x on CPU and 13.07-16.22x on an RTX 5070. A 27-case inverse matrix finds full-rank local curvature throughout, while remaining explicitly model-conditional.
AI.conclusion: DFSC serves as an error-aware optional primitive for matched fractional structure rather than a general replacement for fractional solvers or neural models, as supported by external solver and mixed real-data results.

title: CALM-AH: An ABAW11-Calibrated Multimodal Ensemble with Reliability-Gated Multi-Expert Consensus for Video-Level Ambivalence and Hesitancy Recognition
summary: Ambivalence and hesitancy (A/H) are subtle behavioural states that may be expressed through language, voice, facial activity, and other non-verbal cues. The ABAW11 A/H Video Recognition Challenge asks systems to assign a binary A/H label to each naturalistic interview video. Performance is measured using Macro-F1 so that recognition of both A/H and No-A/H samples receives equal importance. We present CALM-AH, a multimodal ensemble that combines textual, acoustic, visual, and derived behavioural-statistical features. We construct 15 non-empty combinations of these feature branches. For each combination, we select the best of three classifier families using validation binary cross-entropy and optimise its decision threshold for validation Macro-F1. The resulting binary decisions are combined using fixed hard-voting weights transferred from BROTHER. We further introduce Reliability-Gated Multi-Expert Consensus(RG-MEC), an anchor-preserving decision-level ensemble that combines an initial prediction with three complementary correction experts: CALM-AH, AffectGPT, and a GPT-based semantic verifier. The initial system provides the default prediction. Its label is overridden only when all three correction experts unanimously support the same alternative class; otherwise, the anchor prediction is retained. This unanimity-gated design limits the influence of isolated expert errors while permitting bidirectional correction when task-specific, multimodal-affective, and semantic-pragmatic evidence are fully consistent. On the participant-disjoint ABAW11 dataset, CALM-AH achieves a Macro-F1 of 0.7525, and the complete RG-MEC system achieves 0.7771.

AI.tldr: The paper presents CALM-AH, a multimodal ensemble for classifying Ambivalence/Hesitancy (A/H) in video interviews, and RG-MEC, a reliability-gated multi-expert decision-level ensemble. CALM-AH combines textual, acoustic, visual, and behavioral-statistical features across 15 feature combinations with three classifier families and hard-voting weights transferred from BROTHER. RG-MEC augments CALM-AH's anchor prediction with three correction experts (CALM-AH itself, AffectGPT, and a GPT-based semantic verifier) using a unanimity-gated rule that only overrides the anchor when all three experts agree on an alternative class. On the participant-disjoint ABAW11 dataset, CALM-AH achieves Macro-F1 of 0.7525 and the full RG-MEC system achieves 0.7771.
AI.motivation: A/H are subtle and challenging behavioural states to recognize automatically. The ABAW11 challenge requires robust multimodal recognition of both A/H and No-A/H classes with equal importance (measured via Macro-F1). The authors aim to improve recognition reliability by combining diverse feature modalities and leveraging multiple complementary expert systems while guarding against isolated expert errors.
AI.method: The system has two components: (1) CALM-AH, a multimodal ensemble that constructs 15 non-empty combinations of textual, acoustic, visual, and behavioral-statistical feature branches, selects the best of three classifier families per combination using validation binary cross-entropy, optimizes decision thresholds for Macro-F1, and combines decisions via fixed hard-voting weights transferred from BROTHER; (2) RG-MEC, an anchor-preserving decision-level ensemble where the initial prediction is overridden only when all three correction experts (CALM-AH, AffectGPT, and a GPT-based semantic verifier) unanimously agree on the alternative class.
AI.result: On the participant-disjoint ABAW11 dataset, CALM-AH achieves a Macro-F1 of 0.7525, while the complete RG-MEC system achieves 0.7771, demonstrating a performance improvement from the multi-expert consensus ensemble.
AI.conclusion: The unanimity-gated multi-expert ensemble (RG-MEC) effectively limits the influence of isolated expert errors while enabling bidirectional correction when multimodal and semantic evidence align. The combination of diverse feature branches in CALM-AH with a consensus-based expert gating mechanism yields strong performance on the A/H recognition task.

title: Learning Lookahead Lemmas for Neural Network Verification
summary: State-of-the-art neural network verifiers use the branch-and-bound procedure as their core solving mechanism. We introduce an inprocessing framework for neural network verification driven by the lookahead procedure. Under this framework, lookahead derives new lemmas over the phases of unstable ReLUs, which are collected into an implication graph that is used to prune the search space and vivify boolean cuts. We instantiate the framework in two state-of-the-art verifiers, Marabou and $α$-$β$-CROWN, and demonstrate that it improves performance in both, proving up to 34% more instances unsatisfiable.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an inprocessing framework for neural network verification that uses a lookahead procedure to derive new lemmas over unstable ReLU phases, collected into an implication graph for search space pruning and boolean cut vivification. The framework is instantiated in Marabou and α-β-CROWN, improving performance and proving up to 34% more instances unsatisfiable.
AI.motivation: Branch-and-bound is the core solving mechanism in state-of-the-art neural network verifiers, but its efficiency is limited by redundant search and weak pruning. The paper aims to improve verification efficiency by introducing an inprocessing framework that leverages lookahead to derive stronger lemmas and prune the search space more effectively.
AI.method: The method introduces a lookahead-based inprocessing framework that derives new lemmas over phases of unstable ReLUs. These lemmas are collected into an implication graph used to (1) prune the search space and (2) vivify boolean cuts. The framework is instantiated in two existing verifiers, Marabou and α-β-CROWN.
AI.result: The framework improves performance in both Marabou and α-β-CROWN, enabling the verifiers to prove up to 34% more instances unsatisfiable compared to baselines without the framework.
AI.conclusion: The lookahead-driven inprocessing framework effectively enhances the branch-and-bound procedure for neural network verification, achieving significant gains in proving unsatisfiability across state-of-the-art verifiers.

title: DualDiT: A Conditional Dual-Output Diffusion Transformer for Joint OCT Image and Segmentation Mask Generation
summary: Background and Objective: Generating realistic medical images with anatomically accurate segmentation masks helps address the shortage of annotated data in medical imaging, particularly in optical coherence tomography (OCT) of mouse eyes, where manual retinal layer delineation is labour-intensive due to tiny structures and required expertise, resulting in scarce datasets. While diffusion models perform well in medical image synthesis, joint image-mask generation has relied mainly on U-Net-based denoisers, leaving diffusion transformers largely unexplored. Methods: We propose a conditional dual-output Diffusion Transformer (DualDiT) for joint synthesis of OCT B-scans and segmentation masks of the upper retinal cell layers in ex vivo mouse retina. DualDiT encodes both modalities into a shared latent space via a pretrained VAE, concatenates their latent representations, and performs conditional diffusion over the joint tensor. We compared DualDiT against two adapted diffusion baselines: DDPM and LDM. Generative quality was assessed via Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and spatial FID (sFID); practical utility via synthetic data augmentation for downstream U-Net segmentation; and perceptual realism via evaluation by three domain experts. Results: DualDiT achieved the best generative quality (FID 56.14, sFID 114.35), outperforming DDPM and LDM. Expert panels misclassified 46% of synthetic samples as real and 42% of real samples as synthetic. Adding DualDiT-generated images and masks improved Dice and IoU scores on a held-out segmentation test set. Conclusions: DualDiT shows that transformer-based diffusion models can effectively learn the joint distribution of OCT images and segmentation masks, surpassing DDPM- and LDM-based baselines in generative fidelity, downstream utility, and perceptual realism, highlighting its potential for data augmentation in annotation-scarce medical imaging.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DualDiT, a conditional dual-output Diffusion Transformer for joint synthesis of OCT B-scans of mouse retina and their segmentation masks. It outperforms DDPM and LDM baselines in generative quality (FID 56.14, sFID 114.35), shows high perceptual realism in expert evaluation, and improves downstream segmentation performance when used for data augmentation.
AI.motivation: Manual retinal layer delineation in OCT of mouse eyes is labour-intensive due to tiny structures and required expertise, leading to scarce annotated datasets. While diffusion models excel at medical image synthesis, joint image-mask generation has predominantly used U-Net denoisers, leaving diffusion transformers unexplored for this task.
AI.method: DualDiT encodes both OCT images and segmentation masks into a shared latent space via a pretrained VAE, concatenates their latent representations, and performs conditional diffusion over the joint tensor using a transformer-based denoiser. It is compared against DDPM and LDM baselines across generative quality (FID, sFID), downstream segmentation utility via data augmentation, and perceptual realism via expert evaluation.
AI.result: DualDiT achieved best generative quality (FID 56.14, sFID 114.35), outperforming DDPM and LDM. Experts misclassified 46% of synthetic samples as real and 42% of real samples as synthetic. Data augmentation with DualDiT-generated images and masks improved Dice and IoU on a held-out segmentation test set.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based diffusion models can effectively learn the joint distribution of OCT images and segmentation masks, surpassing U-Net-based DDPM and LDM baselines in generative fidelity, downstream utility, and perceptual realism, highlighting their potential for data augmentation in annotation-scarce medical imaging.

title: Who Wins Where? Conformal Model Comparison for Local Superiority
summary: Standard model comparison is global, aggregating losses across the covariate space to declare a single winner. This can obscure heterogeneous performance, where different models are preferable in different regions. We introduce conformalized local model comparison, a split-sample framework for constructing calibrated local best-model maps. Given a model comparison score, such as the difference between two squared losses, the method uses three disjoint splits to fit competing models, estimate local centers and scales from out-of-sample scores, and conformally calibrate residual uncertainty. At a target point, the procedure declares a local winner only when a one-sided conformal bound excludes a tie, with the score's sign determining the favored model. We prove finite-sample marginal control for one-sided erroneous declarations on the realized future comparison score, establish pointwise consistency of the localized mean-score estimator away from tie boundaries, show that aggregate comparison can disagree sharply with the prevalence of local superiority, and derive a squared-loss bias--variance decomposition that clarifies how model structure affects local wins. Synthetic and real-data experiments show that the method recovers heterogeneous winner regions, abstains under uncertainty, and yields higher conditional gain than global selection.

AI.tldr: We introduce conformalized local model comparison, a split-sample framework that constructs calibrated local best-model maps, declaring a local winner only when a one-sided conformal bound excludes a tie, with proven finite-sample error control and demonstrated gains over global model selection.
AI.motivation: Standard model comparison aggregates losses across the entire covariate space to declare a single global winner, which obscures heterogeneous performance where different models may be preferable in different regions of the input space.
AI.method: A split-sample framework using three disjoint splits: (1) fitting competing models, (2) estimating local centers and scales from out-of-sample scores, and (3) conformally calibrating residual uncertainty. At a target point, a local winner is declared only when a one-sided conformal bound excludes a tie; the sign of the score determines which model is favored.
AI.result: The method proves finite-sample marginal control for one-sided erroneous declarations on the realized future comparison score, establishes pointwise consistency of the localized mean-score estimator away from tie boundaries, shows aggregate comparison can disagree sharply with the prevalence of local superiority, and derives a squared-loss bias-variance decomposition. Synthetic and real-data experiments confirm accurate recovery of heterogeneous winner regions, appropriate abstention under uncertainty, and higher conditional gain than global selection.
AI.conclusion: Conformalized local model comparison provides a principled, distribution-free framework for identifying where different models win locally, addressing the limitations of global model selection while providing statistical guarantees.

title: SatEdit: Mask-Conditioned Image Editing via VLM-Guided Segment Annotation
summary: Satellite image editing requires spatially precise object-level control, but supervised editing datasets for overhead imagery are costly to build because object masks, semantic labels, and paired edits are rarely available at scale. We introduce SatEdit, a mask-conditioned satellite image editing framework that constructs training supervision from unlabeled imagery. SatEdit proposes object masks with a seg- mentation foundation model, assigns semantic la- bels to sampled segments with a Vision-Language Model, and applies lightweight human verification before generating paired addition and removal exam- ples through mask-guided inpainting. We fine-tune a high-resolution image editing backbone with LoRA on a SODA-A-derived dataset containing 1,014 im- ages and 852 verified object annotations across 91 classes. In controlled comparisons with open- source and proprietary image editing models, SatE- dit achieves the highest aggregate masked-region se- mantic alignment, with a CLIP score of 0.6322 and CLIP delta of 0.0726, while preserving the surround- ing scene qualitatively. These results suggest that VLM-assisted segment annotation is a practical route to data-efficient, spatially controllable satellite image editing.

AI.tldr: SatEdit is a mask-conditioned satellite image editing framework that constructs training supervision from unlabeled imagery using a segmentation foundation model for object masks, a Vision-Language Model for semantic labels, and mask-guided inpainting for paired editing examples. It achieves state-of-the-art masked-region semantic alignment (CLIP score 0.6322, CLIP delta 0.0726) while preserving scene context.
AI.motivation: Satellite image editing requires spatially precise object-level control, but supervised editing datasets for overhead imagery are prohibitively expensive to build because object masks, semantic labels, and paired edits are rarely available at scale.
AI.method: SatEdit constructs training supervision from unlabeled imagery by: (1) proposing object masks with a segmentation foundation model, (2) assigning semantic labels to sampled segments with a Vision-Language Model with lightweight human verification, (3) generating paired addition and removal examples through mask-guided inpainting, and (4) fine-tuning a high-resolution image editing backbone with LoRA on a SODA-A-derived dataset of 1,014 images and 852 verified object annotations across 91 classes.
AI.result: In controlled comparisons with open-source and proprietary image editing models, SatEdit achieves the highest aggregate masked-region semantic alignment with a CLIP score of 0.6322 and CLIP delta of 0.0726, while preserving the surrounding scene qualitatively.
AI.conclusion: VLM-assisted segment annotation is a practical route to data-efficient, spatially controllable satellite image editing.

title: Autonomous Repair for Multi-Agent Systems via Monte-Carlo Tree Search
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) are increasingly deployed to solve complex tasks. In case of incorrect or unsatisfactory outputs, users have to manually locate agent mistakes by inspecting agent trajectories (i.e., {\em failure attribution}) and provide feedback to refine the outputs (i.e., {\em repair}). Despite some recent work in MAS failure attribution, automated mechanisms to recover from such mistakes remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we propose MARS, a search-based framework that formulates MAS repair as a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) process and navigates the vast space of potential repairs via diagnosis-guided expansion with taxonomy-augmented evaluation. Unlike standard MCTS, which evaluates a complete simulation via full rollout, MARS evaluates the agent trajectory using partial rollout to reduce token consumption. Furthermore, we introduce StateMAS, a large-scale MAS repair benchmark with 1,310 replayable multi-agent failure trajectories spanning four types of agent architectures and four LLM backbones. Experiments on StateMAS demonstrate that MARS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an absolute improvement from 3.0\% to 12.1\% across all settings, while maintaining a comparable token consumption cost. The ablation study further confirms that taxonomy-augmented evaluation and diagnosis-guided expansion are critical to achieving these performance gains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MARS, a search-based framework using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for automated repair of multi-agent system failures, and introduces StateMAS, a large-scale benchmark with 1,310 replayable multi-agent failure trajectories across four agent architectures and four LLM backbones. MARS outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 3.0%-12.1% while maintaining comparable token consumption.
AI.motivation: While prior work has addressed failure attribution in multi-agent systems, automated mechanisms to recover from agent mistakes (i.e., repair) remain largely unexplored. Users currently have to manually inspect trajectories and provide feedback, which is inefficient and unscalable.
AI.method: MARS formulates multi-agent system repair as a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) process. It uses diagnosis-guided expansion to navigate the repair space and taxonomy-augmented evaluation to assess repairs. Unlike standard MCTS, it employs partial rollout (rather than full rollout) to evaluate agent trajectories, reducing token consumption.
AI.result: On the StateMAS benchmark, MARS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods with an absolute improvement of 3.0% to 12.1% across all settings, while maintaining comparable token consumption. Ablation studies confirm that taxonomy-augmented evaluation and diagnosis-guided expansion are critical to the performance gains.
AI.conclusion: MARS provides an effective and efficient automated repair mechanism for multi-agent systems, bridging the gap between failure attribution and automated recovery. The StateMAS benchmark offers a reproducible foundation for future research in this area.

title: VFAD: Variational Semantic Prompting Meets Frequency-Adaptive Representation Learning for Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection
summary: Zero-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD) aims to detect and localize anomalies in unseen categories without access to target-specific training data. Although recent CLIP-based methods have demonstrated promising generalization through vision-language alignment, they remain limited in capturing diverse anomaly semantics and subtle local variations. To address these limitations, we propose VFAD, a unified framework that combines variational semantic prompting with frequency-adaptive representation learning. Specifically, we introduce a Variational Semantic Prompt Extractor (VSPE), which adaptively aggregates anomaly-relevant local semantics from dense patch tokens and regularizes them through a variational information bottleneck, thereby incorporating fine-grained visual cues and enabling more precise cross-modal alignment. Furthermore, we develop a Frequency-Adaptive Representation Aggregation (FARA) module that leverages wavelet-based frequency decomposition and frequency-specific expert aggregation to enhance anomaly-discriminative visual representations. By jointly strengthening semantic guidance and visual representation learning, VFAD improves both anomaly discrimination and fine-grained localization. Extensive experiments on 13 industrial and medical benchmarks demonstrate that VFAD consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art ZSAD methods across diverse anomaly scenarios. The code will be publicly available upon publication.

AI.tldr: VFAD is a unified framework for zero-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD) that combines variational semantic prompting with frequency-adaptive representation learning. It introduces a Variational Semantic Prompt Extractor (VSPE) for fine-grained cross-modal alignment and a Frequency-Adaptive Representation Aggregation (FARA) module using wavelet decomposition for enhanced anomaly-discriminative visual features, outperforming state-of-the-art on 13 industrial and medical benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing CLIP-based ZSAD methods via vision-language alignment lack the ability to capture diverse anomaly semantics and subtle local variations, limiting their discrimination and localization performance on unseen categories.
AI.method: VFAD integrates two key components: (1) Variational Semantic Prompt Extractor (VSPE) that adaptively aggregates anomaly-relevant local semantics from dense patch tokens and regularizes them through a variational information bottleneck for precise cross-modal alignment; (2) Frequency-Adaptive Representation Aggregation (FARA) module leveraging wavelet-based frequency decomposition with frequency-specific expert aggregation to strengthen anomaly-discriminative visual representations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 13 industrial and medical benchmarks show VFAD consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art ZSAD methods across diverse anomaly scenarios, with improvements in both anomaly discrimination and fine-grained localization.
AI.conclusion: By jointly strengthening semantic guidance via variational prompting and visual representation learning via frequency adaptation, VFAD effectively addresses the limitations of prior CLIP-based ZSAD approaches, achieving superior performance in both anomaly detection and localization.

title: Benchmarking Frontier Large Language Models Against Official Crash Database Coding Using Police Crash Narratives
summary: Police crash narratives contain information that may supplement structured crash databases, but manual review is labor-intensive and it remains unclear how well large language models (LLMs) reproduce official crash coding. This study benchmarked six frontier LLMs by comparing narrative-derived crash attribute codes with corresponding fields in the Arkansas fatal-crash database. The analysis linked 5,587 fatal-crash narratives with 5,889 structured crash records from Arkansas (2015-2025), yielding 4,194 matched crashes. Six LLMs were evaluated using an identical zero-shot prompt to code crash manner, non-motorist relation, intersection type, work-zone relation, roadway surface condition, and light condition. Performance was evaluated using agreement, macro-averaged F1 score, Cohen's kappa, coverage, selective agreement, and comparisons with always-majority, always-Unknown, and keyword-rule baselines. Repeated-measures analyses and a generalized estimating equations model assessed differences among models and attributes. GPT-5.5 High achieved the highest agreement among the evaluated LLMs, but the always-majority baseline produced higher raw agreement and the keyword-rule baseline achieved macro-averaged F1 score and Cohen's kappa comparable to the best-performing LLM. Agreement was highest for non-motorist relation and crash manner and lowest for light condition, roadway surface condition, and work-zone relation. Differences across crash attributes exceeded differences across models. These results provide a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based crash coding and show that deployment should be evaluated on an attribute-specific basis using transparent baselines and human review.

AI.tldr: This study benchmarks six frontier LLMs against official crash coding by extracting crash attribute codes from Arkansas fatal-crash narratives (4,194 matched crashes, 2015-2025) using identical zero-shot prompts. GPT-5.5 High performed best among LLMs, but simple baselines (always-majority, keyword-rules) matched or exceeded LLM performance, and differences across crash attributes outweighed differences across models.
AI.motivation: Police crash narratives contain valuable supplemental information beyond structured databases, but manual review is labor-intensive, and it is unclear whether LLMs can reliably reproduce official crash coding. A systematic benchmark against ground-truth crash records is needed to evaluate LLM utility in this domain.
AI.method: Linked 5,587 fatal-crash narratives with 5,889 structured crash records from Arkansas (2015-2025), yielding 4,194 matched crashes. Six frontier LLMs were evaluated with an identical zero-shot prompt to code six crash attributes (manner, non-motorist relation, intersection type, work-zone relation, roadway surface condition, light condition). Performance was measured via agreement, macro-F1, Cohen's kappa, coverage, selective agreement, and comparisons against always-majority, always-Unknown, and keyword-rule baselines, with repeated-measures analyses and a generalized estimating equations model.
AI.result: GPT-5.5 High achieved the highest agreement among evaluated LLMs, but the always-majority baseline yielded higher raw agreement and the keyword-rule baseline achieved macro-F1 and kappa comparable to the best LLM. Agreement was highest for non-motorist relation and crash manner, and lowest for light condition, roadway surface condition, and work-zone relation. Differences across crash attributes exceeded differences across models.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based crash coding should be deployed on an attribute-specific basis, benchmarked against transparent baselines, and supplemented with human review. The results provide a benchmark for evaluating future LLM-based crash coding systems.

title: Dense Temporal Contrast Synthesis via Conditioned Latent Transport
summary: Dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) is essential for breast cancer management, but reliance on gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) restricts use in contraindicated populations, prolongs scan protocols, and presents environmental toxicity concerns. Contrast synthesis offers a non-invasive alternative; however, existing approaches struggle to balance spatial realism with temporal continuity, suffer from slow iterative sampling, underutilize structural priors, and lack clinical validation. We propose a novel conditioned latent transport framework that predicts contrast enhancement in a single forward pass. By anchoring the latent trajectory to the pre-contrast anatomy and applying continuous time conditioning, the model synthesizes patient-specific contrast evolution at any acquisition time. The proposed approach outperforms baseline and the state-of-the-art models across spatial, perceptual, temporal, and distributional metrics. Evaluated on an independent external cohort, the method demonstrates robustness to domain shifts induced by scanner noise as well as differing acquisition protocol. Furthermore, our synthetic contrast enhancement significantly improved downstream tumor segmentation performance, yielding a 22.4% relative increase in Dice coefficient (0.60 vs. 0.49 baseline pre-contrast, p < 0.01), reducing boundary segmentation error by over 39%, while outperforming all other generative model baselines. Finally, a reader study involving four breast radiologists evaluated the image quality, kinetic fidelity, and diagnostic viability of our synthesized sequences across 40 randomly selected cases. The results demonstrated that in 70% of cases, synthesized images provided sufficient clinical information to support the same management decisions as real DCE-MRI, suggesting a path toward safer and faster contrast-free or contrast-reduced imaging workflows.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a conditioned latent transport framework for synthesizing DCE-MRI contrast enhancement in a single forward pass, avoiding gadolinium-based contrast agents. The method anchors latent trajectories to pre-contrast anatomy with continuous time conditioning, outperforming baselines across spatial, perceptual, temporal, and distributional metrics. It improves downstream tumor segmentation (22.4% relative Dice increase) and passes reader studies with breast radiologists supporting the same management decisions in 70% of cases.
AI.motivation: DCE-MRI relies on gadolinium-based contrast agents, which are contraindicated in some populations, prolong scan protocols, and raise environmental toxicity concerns. Existing contrast synthesis methods struggle with balancing spatial realism and temporal continuity, suffer from slow iterative sampling, underutilize structural priors, and lack clinical validation.
AI.method: A conditioned latent transport framework that predicts contrast enhancement in a single forward pass. The latent trajectory is anchored to pre-contrast anatomy with continuous time conditioning, enabling patient-specific contrast evolution synthesis at any acquisition time.
AI.result: The method outperforms baseline and state-of-the-art models across spatial, perceptual, temporal, and distributional metrics. It demonstrates robustness to domain shifts on an external cohort. Synthetic contrast enhancement improved downstream tumor segmentation by 22.4% relative Dice increase (0.60 vs. 0.49, p<0.01) and reduced boundary segmentation error by over 39%. A reader study with four radiologists across 40 cases showed 70% of synthesized images supported the same management decisions as real DCE-MRI.
AI.conclusion: The proposed latent transport framework offers a viable path toward safer and faster contrast-free or contrast-reduced breast cancer imaging workflows, with clinical-level diagnostic information preserved in synthesized contrast sequences.

title: Federated Foundation Models Fine-Tuning with Heterogeneous Compressed Clients
summary: Federated learning of foundation models faces a fundamental resource-asymmetry challenge: the institutions holding the most valuable domain-specific data cannot host billion-parameter models. Existing heterogeneous federated approaches attempt to bridge this gap through parameter-efficient tuning, model pruning, or knowledge distillation, yet each trades away a critical property, whether full-model memory reduction, architectural self-containedness, or representational fidelity, leaving the core tension unresolved. We propose FedSLM, a parameter-centric framework for federated fine-tuning with heterogeneous compressed clients. FedSLM uses SVD-based decomposition to produce self-contained client models, whose low-rank subspaces form nested manifolds that are structurally compatible for aggregation. It then applies a two-stage protocol that synchronizes lightweight adapters within compression groups and fuses full-rank reconstructions across groups via structural alignment. Finally, a weak-to-strong elicitation step with auxiliary confidence loss transfers the aggregated knowledge to the full-scale server, while an explicit bias--variance trade-off mitigates compression artifacts. We provide theoretical guarantees for adapter-level aggregation, subspace-alignment bounds for cross-group fusion, and a characterization of how the confidence loss mitigates weak-supervision noise. Experiments on natural language and vision--language benchmarks show that FedSLM outperforms existing federated baselines under both IID and non-IID partitions, while client models operate at roughly 50% of the GPU memory required by the full model.

AI.tldr: FedSLM is a parameter-centric federated fine-tuning framework for heterogeneous compressed clients that uses SVD-based decomposition to create self-contained client models, a two-stage aggregation protocol, and weak-to-strong elicitation to transfer knowledge to a full-scale server, achieving superior performance on NL and VL benchmarks with ~50% GPU memory reduction.
AI.motivation: Federated learning of foundation models suffers from resource asymmetry: institutions with the most valuable domain data cannot host billion-parameter models. Existing heterogeneous federated approaches (PEFT, pruning, distillation) each sacrifice a critical property—full-model memory reduction, architectural self-containedness, or representational fidelity—leaving the core tension unresolved.
AI.method: FedSLM uses SVD-based decomposition to produce self-contained client models whose low-rank subspaces form nested manifolds compatible for aggregation. It employs a two-stage protocol: (1) synchronizing lightweight adapters within compression groups and (2) fusing full-rank reconstructions across groups via structural alignment. A weak-to-strong elicitation step with auxiliary confidence loss transfers aggregated knowledge to the full-scale server, with an explicit bias-variance trade-off to mitigate compression artifacts.
AI.result: Experiments on natural language and vision-language benchmarks show FedSLM outperforms existing federated baselines under both IID and non-IID partitions, while client models operate at roughly 50% of the GPU memory required by the full model.
AI.conclusion: FedSLM resolves the resource-asymmetry challenge in federated foundation model fine-tuning by unifying parameter efficiency, architectural self-containedness, and representational fidelity, with theoretical guarantees for adapter-level aggregation, cross-group fusion bounds, and confidence-loss noise mitigation.

title: OSEF: One-Step Evidence Fusion for Cross-Video Scene Procedure Planning
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, with ancillary technical supplement
summary: Video Scene Procedure Planning (VSPP) supplies the target start-goal observations in advance, leaving open how a planner should act when the evidence must itself be retrieved. We introduce Cross-Video Scene Procedure Planning (CVSPP): given an answer-redacted start-goal query and K candidate videos, a model must retrieve the supporting video, localize the relevant window, and predict the action sequence. Two obstacles couple here. Same-task demonstrations share stages and windows, and an early hard selection passes the wrong scene chain to the planner. We build an eleven-source benchmark with typed negative roles, a fail-closed answer-leakage gate, and separate Evidence- and Plan-axis metrics. On its 14 source-horizon cells we adapt nine planner families against a majority-sequence floor. We then present One-Step Evidence Fusion (OSEF), which scores a query-conditioned cell-and-span lattice over all candidates and feeds the full soft lattice to the planner through a token-global adapter, cropping no window beforehand. OSEF ranks first on all six cells the benchmark certifies as method-rankable. On four matched same-task COIN and CrossTask cells it improves exact-video-and-plan success by 2.9-10.7 points over an enhanced hard-selection SOTA, and a component study assigns the largest single increment to the token-global interface. Five converted-source cells sit at or near the majority-sequence floor, the benchmark's remaining headroom. The supplementary package includes model constructors and evaluation code.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Cross-Video Scene Procedure Planning (CVSPP), a new task where given an answer-redacted start-goal query and K candidate videos, a model must retrieve the supporting video, localize the relevant window, and predict the action sequence. The authors build an eleven-source benchmark with typed negative roles, an answer-leakage gate, and separate Evidence- and Plan-axis metrics. They propose One-Step Evidence Fusion (OSEF), which scores a query-conditioned cell-and-span lattice over all candidates without hard selection and feeds the full soft lattice to the planner through a token-global adapter. OSEF ranks first on all six method-rankable benchmark cells and improves exact-video-and-plan success by 2.9-10.7 points over an enhanced hard-selection SOTA on four matched COIN/CrossTask cells.
AI.motivation: Existing Video Scene Procedure Planning (VSPP) assumes the target start-goal observations are provided in advance, but in real-world settings the supporting evidence must itself be retrieved from candidate videos. The paper addresses the coupled obstacles that retrieval, localization, and planning together pose, where same-task demonstrations share stages/windows and early hard selection can pass the wrong scene chain to the planner.
AI.method: The authors construct an eleven-source benchmark with typed negative roles, a fail-closed answer-leakage gate, and separate Evidence-axis and Plan-axis metrics. They adapt nine planner families against a majority-sequence floor across 14 source-horizon cells, then propose One-Step Evidence Fusion (OSEF), which constructs a query-conditioned cell-and-span lattice over all K candidates and feeds the full soft lattice to the planner through a token-global adapter without cropping any window beforehand.
AI.result: OSEF ranks first on all six benchmark cells certifiable as method-rankable. On four matched same-task COIN and CrossTask cells, it improves exact-video-and-plan success by 2.9-10.7 points over an enhanced hard-selection SOTA. A component study shows the token-global interface contributes the largest single performance increment. Five converted-source cells sit at or near the majority-sequence floor.
AI.conclusion: One-Step Evidence Fusion effectively avoids the compounding errors of hard selection by passing the full soft evidence lattice to the planner, achieving state-of-the-art results across the certifiable benchmark cells. The benchmark's remaining headroom lies in the five converted-source cells near the majority-sequence floor, motivating future work on cross-source generalization.

title: DASH-OPD: Discrepancy-Aware Switching with Hysteresis for On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains student models on their own rollouts to reduce exposure bias. However, in multi-turn agent scenarios, early student errors can lead a trajectory away from the teacher's familiar domain. Existing curriculum learning methods regulate how much teacher support is used according to training progress, but cannot determine when it is needed. In light of this, we propose DASH-OPD, Discrepancy-Aware Switching with Hysteresis for OPD, a new agentic OPD method that can switch executors adaptively and bidirectionally. On each turn, DASH-OPD calculates a mean log-probability ratio between the two executors over action tokens as their discrepancy. Student-to-teacher ratios on student turns form drift signals, while teacher-to-student ratios on teacher turns form recovery signals. These signals are normalized and accumulated over multiple turns into drift and recovery evidence. DASH-OPD switches executors when the evidence exceeds its corresponding switching threshold. This multi turn accumulation makes the switching hysteretic, preventing high-frequency switches caused by transient fluctuations. On ALFWorld, DASH-OPD outperforms all the baselines and demonstrates superior training and deployment efficiency. This paper is a work in progress. Code, training logs, and model checkpoints will be released later.

AI.tldr: DASH-OPD is a new on-policy distillation method for multi-turn agent scenarios that switches between teacher and student executors adaptively using discrepancy-aware evidence accumulation with hysteresis, outperforming baselines on ALFWorld while improving training and deployment efficiency.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation suffers from exposure bias in multi-turn agent scenarios, where early student errors can drift trajectories away from the teacher's familiar domain. Existing curriculum learning methods regulate teacher support based on training progress but cannot determine when support is actually needed at specific turns.
AI.method: DASH-OPD computes a mean log-probability ratio between teacher and student over action tokens each turn, producing drift signals (student-to-teacher ratios) and recovery signals (teacher-to-student ratios). These signals are normalized and accumulated over multiple turns into drift and recovery evidence. Executor switching occurs when accumulated evidence exceeds a corresponding threshold, and this multi-turn accumulation introduces hysteresis to prevent high-frequency switching from transient fluctuations.
AI.result: DASH-OPD outperforms all baselines on the ALFWorld benchmark, demonstrating superior training and deployment efficiency compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The hysteresis-based, bidirectionally adaptive executor switching effectively addresses exposure bias in multi-turn agent on-policy distillation. The paper is a work in progress; code, training logs, and model checkpoints will be released later.

title: Role-Break in Attention Heads: Understanding and Detecting Hallucinations in VLMs
summary: Despite remarkable progress in vision-language generation, Vision-Language Models (VLMs) remain prone to hallucinations, producing content that is inconsistent with or unsupported by the input image. Existing works largely design detection or mitigation methods around one specific hallucination pattern, such as visual-textual imbalance, but real VLM hallucinations arise from a mixture of multiple patterns, so signals bound to a single pattern struggle to remain stable across models and tasks. Under a unified head-level view, we find that hallucination-induced changes manifest as localized deviations from each head's faithful contextual behavior, a phenomenon we term Role-Break. Detailed analysis reveals that these deviations are systematically organized across attention heads, contextual sources, and deviation directions, and that the resulting signal is linearly readable once head identity is preserved. Based on these findings, we build a lightweight linear detector on top of Role-Break that requires no fine-tuning of the VLM, whose feature dimension stays below 5,000 and reaches an average AUROC of 93.23 across six VLMs and four benchmarks. A small-scale intervention experiment further shows that the detected tokens can be directly acted upon in the discriminative setting.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Role-Break, a unified head-level view of VLM hallucinations where hallucination-induced changes appear as localized deviations from each attention head's faithful contextual behavior. These deviations are systematically organized, linearly readable signals, enabling a lightweight linear detector (feature dimension < 5,000, no VLM fine-tuning) that achieves 93.23 average AUROC across six VLMs and four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing hallucination detection/mitigation methods target single hallucination patterns (e.g., visual-textual imbalance), but real VLM hallucinations arise from a mixture of patterns, making pattern-specific signals unstable across models and tasks. A unified framework is needed.
AI.method: The paper introduces Role-Break, a phenomenon where hallucination-induced changes manifest as localized deviations from each attention head's faithful contextual behavior. Analysis reveals these deviations are systematically organized across attention heads, contextual sources, and deviation directions. Leveraging the property that this signal is linearly readable when head identity is preserved, a lightweight linear detector is built on top of Role-Break without VLM fine-tuning.
AI.result: The detector has a feature dimension below 5,000 and achieves an average AUROC of 93.23 across six VLMs and four benchmarks. A small-scale intervention experiment shows detected tokens can be directly acted upon in the discriminative setting.
AI.conclusion: Role-Break provides a unified, cross-pattern explanation of VLM hallucinations at the attention-head level, enabling an efficient and effective linear detection method that generalizes across models and benchmarks without fine-tuning, with potential for direct intervention.

title: What Is Missing in Surgical Risk Stratification and Outcome Prediction: A Scoping Review of End-to-End Machine Learning Approaches
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE JBHI for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Postoperative adverse events, including mortality and morbidity, remain a major global burden, many of which are preventable through early identification of high-risk patients and targeted perioperative care. Accurate risk stratification is therefore essential. With the growing availability of large-scale electronic health records (EHRs), machine learning (ML) provides a data-driven approach to model complex clinical patterns. However, existing studies vary widely in design, and methodological practices remain fragmented. This scoping review characterizes ML pipelines for surgical risk stratification and outcome prediction using EHR data. We reviewed 190 studies covering the ML workflow, including data preprocessing, algorithm selection, model evaluation, and explainability. Most studies relied on single-center private datasets with limited data modalities, while the scarcity of open-access surgical datasets constrained reproducibility and generalizability. Reporting of key preprocessing steps, including missing data handling, feature selection, and class imbalance, was often incomplete. Conventional ML models and simple neural networks predominated, whereas deep learning and multimodal approaches remained uncommon. Benchmark datasets and standardized evaluation protocols were largely absent, hindering cross-study comparisons. Only about one-third of studies incorporated explainability methods. This review identifies methodological gaps limiting clinically robust postoperative ML tools and provides a structured reference to support more rigorous, reproducible, and clinically meaningful ML development for perioperative care.

AI.tldr: This scoping review characterizes machine learning pipelines for surgical risk stratification and outcome prediction using electronic health records, analyzing 190 studies across the full ML workflow from data preprocessing to explainability. It finds that most studies use single-center private datasets with limited data modalities, incomplete reporting of preprocessing steps, and predominantly conventional ML models, while identifying a lack of benchmark datasets, standardized evaluation protocols, and explainability methods as key gaps limiting clinical robustness.
AI.motivation: Postoperative adverse events remain a major preventable global burden, and accurate risk stratification is essential for early identification of high-risk patients. While ML offers a data-driven approach to model complex clinical patterns using large-scale EHRs, existing studies vary widely in design and methodological practices remain fragmented, motivating a systematic characterization of current ML pipelines.
AI.method: The authors conducted a scoping review of 190 studies covering the complete ML workflow for surgical risk stratification, including data preprocessing, algorithm selection, model evaluation, and explainability. They systematically examined dataset characteristics, preprocessing reporting, model types, evaluation protocols, and explainability approaches.
AI.result: Most studies relied on single-center private datasets with limited data modalities. Open-access surgical datasets were scarce, constraining reproducibility and generalizability. Preprocessing steps such as missing data handling, feature selection, and class imbalance were often incompletely reported. Conventional ML models and simple neural networks dominated, while deep learning and multimodal approaches were uncommon. Benchmark datasets and standardized evaluation protocols were largely absent, and only about one-third of studies incorporated explainability methods.
AI.conclusion: The review identifies methodological gaps that limit the clinical robustness of postoperative ML tools and provides a structured reference framework to support more rigorous, reproducible, and clinically meaningful ML development for perioperative care.

title: QR-Structured Thermal Triggers for Targeted Semantic Attacks on Infrared Vision-Language Models
summary: Infrared vision-language models (IR-VLMs) extend thermal perception to open-vocabulary classification, image captioning, and visual question answering. However, their robustness to structured thermal perturbations and the stability of cross-modal semantic alignment remain insufficiently studied. We propose QR-Structured Thermal Triggers (QR-STT), a stealthy, training-free, black-box framework for targeted semantic steering of IR-VLMs. QR-STT preserves the functional regions of a QR pattern while optimizing its internal modules, each of which is assigned a cold, neutral, or hot thermal state. The framework jointly searches module topology and rendering parameters, including position, scale, rotation, intensity, blur, and roundness. A three-stage gradient-free procedure with greedy module-flip refinement efficiently handles the mixed discrete and continuous search space. The objective promotes alignment with an attacker-selected target, suppresses source-class evidence, and regularizes QR structure and visual similarity. Experiments on multiple CLIP-style encoders show that QR-STT consistently redirects image-text alignment toward chosen concepts while maintaining visual stealth. Perturbations optimized for classification also transfer to image captioning and VQA, causing target-consistent semantic drift in generated outputs. These results identify QR-structured thermal patterns as an interpretable attack surface for language-driven infrared perception and highlight the need for robustness evaluation against structured cross-task semantic attacks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes QR-Structured Thermal Triggers (QR-STT), a stealthy, training-free, black-box attack framework that uses QR patterns with optimized thermal states to semantically steer infrared vision-language models (IR-VLMs) toward attacker-chosen targets, with cross-task transfer to captioning and VQA.
AI.motivation: IR-VLMs have extended thermal perception to open-vocabulary tasks but their robustness against structured thermal perturbations and the stability of cross-modal semantic alignment remain understudied. The authors aim to address this gap by identifying and demonstrating an interpretable attack surface for language-driven infrared perception.
AI.method: QR-STT preserves the functional regions of a QR pattern while optimizing its internal modules, each assigned a cold, neutral, or hot thermal state. It jointly searches module topology and rendering parameters (position, scale, rotation, intensity, blur, roundness) using a three-stage gradient-free procedure with greedy module-flip refinement. The objective aligns with an attacker-selected target, suppresses source-class evidence, and regularizes QR structure and visual similarity.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple CLIP-style encoders show QR-STT consistently redirects image-text alignment toward chosen concepts while maintaining visual stealth. Perturbations optimized for classification transfer to image captioning and VQA, causing target-consistent semantic drift in generated outputs.
AI.conclusion: QR-structured thermal patterns represent an interpretable and effective attack surface for IR-VLMs, highlighting the need for robustness evaluation against structured cross-task semantic attacks in infrared perception systems.

title: PiDDM: Physics-Informed Differentiable Degradation Modeling for Lithium-Ion Battery State-of-Health Prediction
summary: Accurate prediction of lithium-ion battery state of health (SOH) is essential for reliable energy storage operation. However, purely data-driven models may generalize poorly across cycling protocols and produce physically implausible behavior during long-term extrapolation. We developed a physics-informed differentiable degradation modeling framework (PiDDM) for battery SOH prediction. PiDDM incorporates empirical Arrhenius degradation kinetics associated with solid electrolyte interphase growth and loss of lithium inventory into the training objective, encouraging physically consistent capacity fade under diverse operating conditions. The framework was evaluated using a public dataset of 55 batteries cycled under six operating protocols. PiDDM achieved the lowest average prediction error among the evaluated models and substantially reduced mean squared error relative to a multilayer perceptron and a baseline physics-informed neural network. For extrapolation, the models were trained on the first 90% of each battery's cycle life and evaluated on the unseen final 10%. PiDDM captured accelerated end-of-life degradation while avoiding the nonphysical capacity regeneration produced by the baseline models. These results show that incorporating degradation physics into neural network training improves predictive accuracy and physical consistency, providing a promising approach for practical battery health monitoring.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PiDDM, a physics-informed differentiable degradation modeling framework for lithium-ion battery state of health (SOH) prediction. It integrates Arrhenius-based SEI growth and lithium inventory loss kinetics into the neural network training objective. Evaluated on 55 batteries across six cycling protocols, PiDDM achieved the lowest prediction error and demonstrated superior extrapolation performance on the unseen final 10% of cycle life, capturing accelerated end-of-life degradation without the nonphysical capacity regeneration seen in baseline models.
AI.motivation: Purely data-driven models generalize poorly across cycling protocols and produce physically implausible behavior (e.g., capacity regeneration) during long-term extrapolation. A physics-informed approach is needed to ensure both predictive accuracy and physical consistency for battery SOH monitoring.
AI.method: PiDDM incorporates empirical Arrhenius degradation kinetics—specifically solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) growth and loss of lithium inventory—directly into the training objective as physics constraints within a differentiable neural network framework. The model was trained and evaluated on a public dataset of 55 lithium-ion batteries cycled under six different operating protocols.
AI.result: PiDDM achieved the lowest average prediction error among evaluated models and substantially reduced mean squared error relative to a multilayer perceptron and a baseline physics-informed neural network. In extrapolation tests (training on first 90% of cycle life, testing on final 10%), PiDDM captured accelerated end-of-life degradation while avoiding the nonphysical capacity regeneration produced by baseline models.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating degradation physics into neural network training improves both predictive accuracy and physical consistency for battery SOH prediction, offering a promising approach for practical battery health monitoring systems.

title: Weight-Space Mixture-of-Experts for Implicit Neural Representation Classification
summary: Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) encode signals as the weights of a coordinate-based neural network and have recently been proposed as an alternative domain for downstream learning. While promising, classification directly in weight space remains challenging due to the high dimensionality and complex structure of INR parameters. Furthermore, the way discriminative information is distributed across INR weights remains poorly understood. We propose a hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts (HMoE) Transformer that processes INR weights using conditional computation aligned with the structure of the underlying implicit network. Coupled with a meta-learning framework that shapes INR parameters for downstream tasks, our model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across standard benchmarks, ranging from low-resolution datasets to high-resolution ImageNet-1K. To gain insight into how INRs encode discriminative information, we develop weight-space attribution and pruning methods that identify parameters most relevant for classification. These analyses reveal how class-specific structure emerges within INR layers and support the suitability of MoE architectures for weight-space learning. Our approach advances both the performance and interpretability of weight-space classifiers.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts (HMoE) Transformer that classifies signals directly in weight space by processing INR parameters with conditional computation aligned to the implicit network's structure. Combined with a meta-learning framework that shapes INR weights for downstream tasks, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy from low-resolution datasets to ImageNet-1K. The paper also develops weight-space attribution and pruning methods to reveal how class-specific discriminative information emerges across INR layers, improving both performance and interpretability.
AI.motivation: Classifying signals directly in INR weight space is challenging due to high dimensionality and complex parameter structure, and there is limited understanding of how discriminative information is distributed across INR weights.
AI.method: (1) A hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts (HMoE) Transformer that processes INR weights using conditional computation aligned with the structure of the underlying implicit network, and (2) a meta-learning framework that shapes INR parameters to facilitate downstream learning tasks. Additionally, weight-space attribution and pruning methods are introduced to identify classification-relevant parameters.
AI.result: State-of-the-art accuracy across standard benchmarks ranging from low-resolution datasets to high-resolution ImageNet-1K. The attribution and pruning analyses reveal how class-specific structure emerges within INR layers, supporting the suitability of MoE architectures for weight-space learning.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical MoE Transformer with meta-learning enhances both performance and interpretability of weight-space classifiers, and the analyses provide insight into how INRs encode discriminative information.

title: StraightDP: Geometry-Aware Differential Privacy for Rectified-Flow Transformers
summary: Differentially private (DP) training of text-conditioned generative models suffers a utility cliff at strong privacy. We revisit this problem through the geometry of rectified flows: along the straight interpolation between noise and data, the Bayes-optimal velocity is governed to leading order at the noise end by a few class-conditional moments, and increasingly sample-specific structure matters toward the data end. StraightDP exploits this heterogeneity end to end. A small budget share releases whitened class-conditional moments once, to be distilled into the weights or injected at sampling time. The rest is spent by pre-declared DP-SGD toward the data end, beyond the moments' reach. At $\varepsilon=1$ on MNIST, the released moments alone already attain $0.76$ downstream accuracy with prototype-like samples and an FID of $237$, and uniform DP-SGD attains $0.21$. The pipeline built on the release reaches $0.81$ accuracy at FID $56$ in a public latent space. Constraining per-token stream norms of the multimodal backbone leaves the pretraining loss unchanged yet improves downstream accuracy in the extreme-noise pixel-space regime, and its accuracy effect becomes monotonically more favorable as privacy strengthens. The released moments also port to frozen SD3-medium, where sampling-time injection beats DP-LoRA training at a fraction of the budget.

AI.tldr: StraightDP addresses the utility cliff in differentially private training of generative models by exploiting the geometry of rectified flows: releasing whitened class-conditional moments with a small privacy budget share, then spending the rest on pre-declared DP-SGD toward the data end. This achieves 0.81 accuracy at FID 56 on MNIST at ε=1, and the released moments transfer to frozen SD3-medium via sampling-time injection, beating DP-LoRA at a fraction of the budget.
AI.motivation: Differentially private training of text-conditioned generative models suffers a severe utility cliff at strong privacy (small ε), where existing approaches produce poor-quality outputs.
AI.method: The method, StraightDP, leverages the geometry of rectified flows: along the straight noise-to-data interpolation, the Bayes-optimal velocity at the noise end is governed by a few class-conditional moments, while sample-specific structure matters toward the data end. It releases whitened class-conditional moments once using a small budget share (injected at sampling or distilled into weights), then spends the remaining budget on pre-declared DP-SGD toward the data end. It also constrains per-token stream norms of the multimodal backbone.
AI.result: At ε=1 on MNIST: released moments alone achieve 0.76 downstream accuracy with prototype-like samples and FID 237 (vs 0.21 for uniform DP-SGD); the full pipeline reaches 0.81 accuracy at FID 56 in a public latent space. Constraining per-token stream norms preserves pretraining loss yet improves downstream accuracy in the extreme-noise regime, with effects becoming monotonically more favorable as privacy strengthens. Released moments transfer to frozen SD3-medium where sampling-time injection beats DP-LoRA at a fraction of budget.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the heterogeneous geometry of rectified flows—spending privacy budget where sample-specific structure matters most—substantially mitigates the DP utility cliff in generative model training.

title: Lightweight Neural Networks for Affordance Segmentation: Enhancement of the Decoder Module
summary: The deployment of deep neural networks for visual affordance segmentation on wearable robots poses may prove critical, due to some conflicting aspects of the problem. On one hand, affordance segmentation requires high-level abstraction capabilities, that typically involve large-size models. On the other hand, computing resources hosted on wearable robots prevent to run large-size models in real-time. The paper presents an analysis of the role of the segmentation head in the trade-off between generalization performance and compute cost. The obtained models outperform modern baseline solutions in well-known, real-world datasets while meeting low computing requirements.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how the segmentation head design affects the trade-off between generalization performance and computational cost for visual affordance segmentation on wearable robots, achieving models that outperform modern baselines while meeting low compute requirements.
AI.motivation: Affordance segmentation on wearable robots faces a conflict: it requires high-level abstraction (typically needing large models) but wearable robots have limited computing resources that prevent real-time execution of large models.
AI.method: The paper analyzes the role of the segmentation head in balancing generalization performance versus compute cost, presumably evaluating different head architectures under constrained conditions.
AI.result: The obtained models outperform modern baseline solutions on well-known real-world datasets while simultaneously meeting low computing requirements.
AI.conclusion: A well-designed segmentation head can effectively mitigate the trade-off between generalization and computational efficiency, enabling high-quality affordance segmentation on resource-constrained wearable robots.

title: Curriculum Matters: Data-Efficient Relational PFN Pretraining with Synthetic Data
comment: Accepted to the International Conference on Very Large Databases (VLDB 2026), Tabular Data Analysis (TaDA)
summary: Relational Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) such as RDB-PFN approximate Bayesian inference over multi-table relational databases by pretraining on millions of synthetic tasks. We investigate three intertwined questions about this paradigm. First, can a structurally different synthetic generator PluRel substitute for RDB-PFN's prior? Second, how much does the order in which synthetic data is presented to the PFN affect downstream performance? Third, how much relational reasoning can a PFN acquire from single-table synthetic pretraining alone, before any relational data is introduced? Using PluRel as the sole synthetic data source across all experiments, we find: (i) a progressive single-table curriculum that gradually widens schema complexity from 7 to 17 columns reaches 0.703 average ROC-AUC on the 23-task tabular benchmark using only approximately 13,300 synthetic tables (approximately 45x fewer single-table datasets than RDB-PFN's reported warm-up recipe), while the same data trained all-at-once collapses to 0.541 ROC-AUC; (ii) a relational curriculum trained from scratch on only approximately 5,500 PluRel databases reaches 0.638 average ROC-AUC on the 19-task RelBench/4DBInfer benchmark, recovering 88% of RDB-PFN's reported performance with approximately 220x less relational synthetic data; and (iii) the single-table curriculum model, evaluated directly on the relational benchmark without any relational adaptation, achieves 0.631, nearly matching the dedicated relational pipeline. Together, these findings suggest that curriculum design and synthetic data diversity may matter more for relational PFN pretraining than the specific relational generator or raw synthetic scale alone.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether a structurally different synthetic data generator (PluRel) can substitute for RDB-PFN's prior in relational Prior-Data Fitted Networks, examining the effects of data ordering, synthetic data amount, and whether single-table pretraining alone can acquire relational reasoning.
AI.motivation: RDB-PFN approximates Bayesian inference over multi-table relational databases via pretraining on synthetic tasks. Three interconnected questions are explored: (1) can a different synthetic generator (PluRel) substitute for RDB-PFN's prior, (2) how much does data presentation order affect performance, and (3) how much relational reasoning can be acquired from single-table synthetic pretraining alone.
AI.method: Experiments use PluRel as the sole synthetic data source. Three settings are evaluated: (i) a progressive single-table curriculum widening schema complexity from 7 to 17 columns, (ii) a relational curriculum trained from scratch, and (iii) direct evaluation of the single-table curriculum model on relational benchmarks. Results are compared against RDB-PFN's reported baselines on tabular (23-task) and relational (19-task RelBench/4DBInfer) benchmarks.
AI.result: (i) The single-table curriculum reaches 0.703 average ROC-AUC on the 23-task tabular benchmark with only ~13,300 synthetic tables (45x fewer than RDB-PFN's warm-up), while all-at-once training collapses to 0.541. (ii) A relational curriculum with only ~5,500 PluRel databases reaches 0.638 ROC-AUC on RelBench/4DBInfer, recovering 88% of RDB-PFN's performance with ~220x less data. (iii) The single-table curriculum model evaluated directly on relational benchmarks achieves 0.631, nearly matching the dedicated relational pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Curriculum design and synthetic data diversity matter more for relational PFN pretraining than the specific relational generator or raw synthetic data scale alone. PluRel can effectively substitute for RDB-PFN's prior, and surprisingly, single-table pretraining alone can achieve relational reasoning performance close to dedicated relational pipelines.

title: Leveraging Transfer Learning with Class-Specific Decoders for Laparoscopic Segmentation
comment: Paper already Published in IEEE Big data 2025
summary: Effective multi-organ segmentation in surgical data requires learning the intricate anatomical features and alleviating the challenge of class imbalance, which results from relatively lower proportions of small and limitedly exposed structures. Recent works on laparoscopic multi-organ segmentation focus on learning structure-specific features through class-specific decoder architectures and report favorable results. This work extends the decoder-focused architectures to investigate knowledge sharing in the cross-surgical domain. We utilize two datasets representing different surgical domains, rectal and cholecystectomy surgeries, to explore how surgical conceptual knowledge transfers under partially common anatomical representations. Additionally, we compare the feature adaptation for the encoder and decoder at different training stages to analyse the knowledge adaptation and retention in the network. Our results corroborate previous findings on decoder-specific architectures and demonstrate that the organ-specific decoder model (CEMD), fully fine-tuned after cross-domain pre-training, achieves the highest segmentation performance (62.4\% dice) while converging substantially faster than training from scratch. However, we also find that class imbalance in surgical data remains a persistent challenge that transfer learning does not fully resolve for underrepresented anatomical structures.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates cross-domain knowledge transfer for multi-organ segmentation in laparoscopic surgery using decoder-specific architectures (CEMD), across rectal and cholecystectomy datasets, achieving 62.4% dice with faster convergence after fine-tuning but finding that class imbalance remains unresolved.
AI.motivation: Multi-organ segmentation in surgical data faces challenges of learning intricate anatomical features and class imbalance. Prior work focused on class-specific decoder architectures. This work extends that to investigate knowledge sharing across surgical domains under partially common anatomical representations.
AI.method: Uses two datasets from different surgical domains (rectal and cholecystectomy) to explore cross-domain transfer. Compares feature adaptation of encoder and decoder at different training stages; evaluates the organ-specific decoder model (CEMD) with full fine-tuning after cross-domain pre-training versus training from scratch.
AI.result: The fully fine-tuned CEMD after cross-domain pre-training achieves highest segmentation performance (62.4% dice) and converges substantially faster than training from scratch. However, class imbalance for underrepresented anatomical structures remains a persistent challenge not fully resolved by transfer learning.
AI.conclusion: Decoder-specific architectures with cross-domain pre-training improve segmentation performance and convergence speed for multi-organ laparoscopic segmentation, but class imbalance remains an open challenge that transfer learning alone cannot fully address.

title: PluRel-to-RDB-PFN: Schema-Guided Synthetic Relational Pretraining
comment: Proceedings of the 2nd ICML on Foundation Models for Structured Data
summary:
Relational Foundation Models (RFMs) require large-scale synthetic relational databases for pretraining, but existing approaches tightly couple data generation with the model training pipeline. We study whether PluRel, a general-purpose synthetic relational database generator, can serve as an external data source for RDB-PFN, a relational in-context learner originally pretrained with a 600K-task single-table warm-up followed by an approximately 1.8M-task adaptation stage.
  We build a conversion pipeline that maps PluRel-generated databases, including externally constructed binary prediction tasks, into the RDB-PFN training format and evaluate three curriculum strategies: SCHEMA-GUIDED FIRST (real-world schema then fully synthetic), FULLY SYNTHETIC (diverse synthetic schemas throughout), and SCHEMA-GUIDED LAST (fully synthetic then real-world schema). Using only approximately 5,500 relational databases (approximately 33K tasks), roughly 55x fewer tasks than the original protocol, and no single-table warm-up, our best curriculum (SCHEMA-GUIDED FIRST) achieves 0.6346 average ROC-AUC across 19 real benchmark tasks at 1024-shot context, recovering 87.6% of the published RDB-PFN performance (0.7245). At 64-shot context, the gap narrows to 93.8% (0.6116 vs. 0.6517). Our results demonstrate that external synthetic generators can provide useful pretraining signals for RFMs when combined with appropriate curriculum design and that exposure to a real-world schema early in training is substantially more effective than late-stage schema adaptation.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that PluRel, an external general-purpose synthetic relational database generator, can effectively pretrain RDB-PFN (a relational in-context learner) using roughly 55x fewer tasks (33K vs 1.8M+) than the original protocol.
