The best curriculum, SCHEMA-GUIDED FIRST (real-world schema before fully synthetic data), recovers 87.6% of published RDB-PFN performance at 1024-shot context and 93.8% at 64-shot context.
AI.motivation: Relational Foundation Models (RFMs) require massive synthetic relational databases for pretraining, but existing approaches tightly couple data generation with the model training pipeline, limiting flexibility and external reusability. The authors investigate whether a general-purpose synthetic data generator can serve as an independent, external data source for pretraining an RFM.
AI.method: The authors build a conversion pipeline that maps PluRel-generated databases (including externally constructed binary prediction tasks) into RDB-PFN's training format. They evaluate three curriculum strategies: SCHEMA-GUIDED FIRST (real-world schema then fully synthetic), FULLY SYNTHETIC (diverse synthetic schemas throughout), and SCHEMA-GUIDED LAST (fully synthetic then real-world schema). Training uses only ~5,500 relational databases (~33K tasks) with no single-table warm-up.
AI.result: The best curriculum (SCHEMA-GUIDED FIRST) achieves 0.6346 average ROC-AUC across 19 real benchmark tasks at 1024-shot context, recovering 87.6% of published RDB-PFN performance (0.7245). At 64-shot context, it achieves 0.6116 vs 0.6517, recovering 93.8% of performance.
AI.conclusion: External synthetic generators can provide useful pretraining signals for RFMs when combined with appropriate curriculum design. Exposure to a real-world schema early in training is substantially more effective than late-stage schema adaptation, suggesting curriculum ordering is critical for effective pretraining with external data.

title: Multi-Source Multi-View Graph Domain Adaptation with Hyperbolic Residual Encoding for Cross-Site MDD Identification from rs-fMRI
summary: Cross-site identification of major depressive disorder (MDD) from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) is hindered by inter-site distribution shifts and heterogeneous functional connectivity (FC) views. These views capture complementary neural relationships but exhibit distinct site biases and graph topologies, complicating alignment without sacrificing disease-relevant information or cross-view consistency. Existing studies largely treat multi-view connectome learning and cross-site adaptation separately. To the best of our knowledge, few studies have jointly modeled multiple FC views under multi-source unsupervised domain adaptation for cross-site rs-fMRI-based MDD classification. We construct Pearson correlation, sparse representation, and Granger causality graphs, each encoded by a view-specific graph attention network. Dual-stream adaptive fusion explicitly integrates pairwise cross-view interactions, followed by lightweight hyperbolic residual encoding for curvature-aware representation refinement. Class-wise Cauchy--Schwarz alignment reduces inter-source and source-target discrepancies, complemented by adversarial learning, information maximization, and confidence-aware pseudo-labeling. Across seven unlabeled target domains, our framework achieves 73.60% mean accuracy and 71.90% AUC, demonstrating effective generalization under heterogeneous acquisition conditions. These results highlight the effectiveness of unified heterogeneous-view modeling, curvature-aware refinement, and multi-source domain adaptation for cross-site MDD identification.The source code is at https://github.com/OPUS-Lightphenexx/MM-HyperGDA

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a multi-view graph adaptation framework (MM-HyperGDA) that jointly models three functional connectivity views (Pearson correlation, sparse representation, Granger causality) using view-specific graph attention networks, with dual-stream adaptive fusion and hyperbolic residual encoding, plus class-wise Cauchy-Schwarz alignment for multi-source unsupervised domain adaptation. It achieves 73.60% mean accuracy and 71.90% AUC across seven unlabeled target domains for cross-site MDD classification.
AI.motivation: Cross-site MDD identification from rs-fMRI is challenging due to inter-site distribution shifts and heterogeneous functional connectivity views. Existing approaches treat multi-view connectome learning and cross-site adaptation separately, and few studies jointly model multiple FC views under multi-source unsupervised domain adaptation for cross-site rs-fMRI-based MDD classification.
AI.method: The framework constructs three FC graphs (Pearson correlation, sparse representation, Granger causality), each encoded by a view-specific graph attention network. Dual-stream adaptive fusion explicitly integrates pairwise cross-view interactions, followed by lightweight hyperbolic residual encoding for curvature-aware representation refinement. Class-wise Cauchy-Schwarz alignment reduces inter-source and source-target discrepancies, complemented by adversarial learning, information maximization, and confidence-aware pseudo-labeling.
AI.result: Across seven unlabeled target domains, the framework achieves 73.60% mean accuracy and 71.90% AUC, demonstrating effective generalization under heterogeneous acquisition conditions.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight the effectiveness of unified heterogeneous-view modeling, curvature-aware refinement, and multi-source domain adaptation for cross-site MDD identification. Source code is publicly available.

title: HERO: History-Enriched Rollout Training for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Neural Operators
summary: Neural operators provide fast surrogates for time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) by applying a learned evolution operator recursively to its own predictions, but this autoregressive rollout feeds every prediction error back as input, so local errors accumulate. Existing rollout-training strategies reduce the mismatch between training inputs and self-generated states, yet their supervision still measures only the absolute discrepancy from the ground-truth trajectory. Such supervision is therefore uninformative about whether the operator has overcome the long-horizon failure behaviors it exhibited earlier during optimization. We propose history-enriched rollout training (HERO), which augments conventional absolute trajectory supervision with relative supervision derived from the model's optimization history. HERO ranks detached candidate rollouts from a periodically refreshed lagged operator, the current model, and a perturbed input by rollout error, spectral discrepancy, energy drift, and error growth, and selects the strongest failure trajectory as reference. This reference enters a margin-based objective as a fixed comparison baseline, inducing a bounded, sample-dependent reweighting of the ground-truth rollout gradient rather than an independent gradient direction, which we further analyze theoretically. Experiments on nine PDE benchmarks with spectral and attention-based backbones show that HERO consistently improves long-horizon accuracy, stable rollout length, and out-of-distribution robustness at no inference-time cost. These results indicate that history-enriched relative supervision is effective for stabilizing long-horizon autoregressive prediction.

AI.tldr: HERO (history-enriched rollout training) is a training strategy for neural operator surrogates of time-dependent PDEs that augments conventional absolute trajectory supervision with relative supervision derived from the model's optimization history, selecting the strongest failure trajectory as a margin-based comparison baseline to improve long-horizon autoregressive stability.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive rollout in neural operators feeds every prediction error back as input, causing local errors to accumulate over long horizons. Existing rollout-training strategies reduce input distribution mismatch but their supervision only measures absolute discrepancy from ground truth, which is uninformative about whether the operator has overcome the long-horizon failure behaviors it exhibited earlier during optimization.
AI.method: HERO augments conventional absolute trajectory supervision with relative supervision from the model's optimization history. It ranks detached candidate rollouts—from a periodically refreshed lagged operator, the current model, and a perturbed input—by rollout error, spectral discrepancy, energy drift, and error growth, then selects the strongest failure trajectory as a reference. This reference enters a margin-based objective as a fixed comparison baseline, inducing a bounded, sample-dependent reweighting of the ground-truth rollout gradient rather than an independent gradient direction. The approach is also analyzed theoretically.
AI.result: Experiments on nine PDE benchmarks with spectral and attention-based backbones show that HERO consistently improves long-horizon accuracy, stable rollout length, and out-of-distribution robustness at no inference-time cost.
AI.conclusion: History-enriched relative supervision is effective for stabilizing long-horizon autoregressive prediction in neural operators for time-dependent PDEs.

title: OSAGEN: Object-Aware Mask Priors and Multistage Decoupled Diffusion for Industrial Anomaly Generation
summary: Industrial anomaly detection and localization are limited by scarce real anomalies and pixel-level annotations, a bottleneck that synthetic image-mask pairs can alleviate. However, existing few-shot mask-guided generation may over-follow mask geometry, produce weak anomalies, or use condition masks incompatible with the current object instance. We propose OSAGEN, which combines object-aware mask priors with multistage decoupled diffusion. Its three-stage adaptation sequentially learns normal appearance, defect appearance under coarse conditions, and fine-grained mask calibration, improving defect realization and local control. QBG injects object structure from a matched normal image into mask diffusion to produce object-aware priors, while ISC restricts anomaly propagation and preserves normal content during sampling. A lightweight materialization step recovers pixel-level labels aligned with the realized defects. On MVTec AD and VisA, OSAGEN achieves AP-P/F1-P scores of 88.1/82.2 and 68.5/66.1, respectively, under a unified downstream localization protocol. The code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: OSAGEN is a synthetic anomaly generation framework that combines object-aware mask priors with multistage decoupled diffusion to produce realistic image-mask pairs for industrial anomaly detection and localization.
AI.motivation: Industrial anomaly detection is bottlenecked by scarce real anomalies and expensive pixel-level annotations. Existing few-shot mask-guided generation methods suffer from over-following mask geometry, generating weak anomalies, or using condition masks incompatible with the current object instance.
AI.method: OSAGEN uses three-stage adaptation that sequentially learns normal appearance, defect appearance under coarse conditions, and fine-grained mask calibration. It incorporates QBG (Query-Based Generation?) which injects object structure from a matched normal image into mask diffusion to produce object-aware priors, and ISC which restricts anomaly propagation and preserves normal content during sampling. A lightweight materialization step recovers pixel-level labels aligned with realized defects.
AI.result: On MVTec AD and VisA, OSAGEN achieves AP-P/F1-P scores of 88.1/82.2 and 68.5/66.1 respectively under a unified downstream localization protocol.
AI.conclusion: OSAGEN effectively improves defect realization and local control through object-aware mask priors and multistage decoupled diffusion, achieving strong performance on standard industrial anomaly benchmarks.

title: Implicit Machine Learning Force Fields Accelerate Molecular Dynamics Simulations
summary: We introduce implicit machine learning force fields (I-MLFFs), which replace explicit stacks of neural network layers with self-consistent fixed-point equations. In molecular simulations, this formulation enables intermediate representations to be reused across successive timesteps, thereby warm-starting force evaluation. The resulting models effectively combine the computational footprint of a shallow, single-layer MLFF with the representational capacity and accuracy of a deep neural network. Our approach unlocks architecture-agnostic efficiency gains that are inaccessible when force prediction and trajectory integration are considered separately. We demonstrate this across three major classes of graph neural networks: invariant, equivariant Cartesian tensor, and SO(3)-equivariant spherical-tensor architectures. Each yields a two- to five-fold reduction in compute and memory footprint. Crucially, these gains are achieved while retaining full atomistic resolution and the original integration timestep, avoiding spatial or temporal coarse graining. Our contribution therefore advances the scaling frontier of quantum-mechanically faithful molecular simulation, enabling longer trajectories and larger atomistic systems within fixed GPU memory and compute budgets, and thereby opening access to new insights across biomolecular and material systems.

AI.tldr: I-MLFFs replace explicit neural network layer stacks with self-consistent fixed-point equations, enabling intermediate representations to be warm-started across timesteps. This yields a 2-5x reduction in compute and memory across invariant, equivariant Cartesian tensor, and SO(3)-equivariant architectures while retaining full atomistic resolution and the original integration timestep.
AI.motivation: Deep neural network force fields are computationally expensive for molecular simulations due to explicit feedforward passes at every timestep. The authors seek to decouple the representational capacity of deep networks from their per-timestep computational cost by leveraging the temporal reuse of intermediate representations that become possible when force prediction and trajectory integration are treated jointly rather than separately.
AI.method: Implicit machine learning force fields (I-MLFFs) formulate force prediction as a fixed-point iteration rather than an explicit stack of layers. Intermediate representations computed at one timestep are reused (warm-started) at subsequent timesteps, effectively giving the computational cost of a shallow single-layer model while retaining the expressive capacity of a deep network. The approach is architecture-agnostic and demonstrated on three classes of GNNs: invariant, equivariant Cartesian tensor, and SO(3)-equivariant spherical-tensor architectures.
AI.result: Across all three graph neural network architecture classes, the method yields a two- to five-fold reduction in both compute and memory footprint, without spatial or temporal coarse graining—full atomistic resolution and the original integration timestep are preserved.
AI.conclusion: I-MLFFs advance the scaling frontier of quantum-mechanically faithful molecular simulation, enabling longer trajectories and larger atomistic systems within fixed compute and memory budgets, thereby opening new avenues for studying biomolecular and material systems.

title: The K-Space Signature: Frequency-Domain Representation Learning for Medical Deepfake Detection
summary: In medical imaging, generative models are increasingly deployed to synthesize realistic data and augment limited datasets. Unfortunately, while beneficial for privacy-preserving data sharing, these synthesized images can be repurposed for malicious intents, threatening public health through the creation of Medical Deepfakes. To address this threat, we introduce the K-Space Signature (KSS), a novel forensic framework that isolates hardware and generative traces within the spectral domain. By shifting analysis to the frequency domain, the KSS suppresses macroscopic anatomical variance by subtracting an empirical global anatomical prior computed in the Logarithmic Power Spectral Density (Log-PSD) space. To effectively process these globally distributed spectral artifacts without the local spatial bias inherent to Convolutional Neural Networks, we pair the KSS representation with a novel 3D MLP-Mixer architecture equipped with an ArcFace metric-learning head. Extensive experiments on multi-center 3D MRI datasets demonstrate that this combined approach achieves exceptional detection performance, exceeding 0.99 Accuracy and ROC-AUC on multi-generator synthetic datasets. Furthermore, the framework exhibits robust zero-shot generalization, maintaining strong discriminative power (up to 0.93 Accuracy) on independent datasets acquired from entirely unseen scanners. To ensure full reproducibility, the complete source code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the K-Space Signature (KSS), a forensic framework for detecting Medical Deepfakes in 3D MRI images by analyzing hardware and generative traces in the spectral (frequency) domain. It combines a global anatomical prior subtraction in Log-PSD space with a novel 3D MLP-Mixer architecture using ArcFace metric learning, achieving >0.99 Accuracy/ROC-AUC on multi-generator datasets and up to 0.93 Accuracy on unseen scanners via zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: While generative models are beneficial for augmenting limited medical imaging datasets and enabling privacy-preserving data sharing, they can also be maliciously repurposed to create Medical Deepfakes that threaten public health. A forensic framework is needed to detect such synthetic medical images.
AI.method: The KSS framework shifts analysis to the frequency (K-space) domain, computing Logarithmic Power Spectral Density (Log-PSD) representations and subtracting an empirical global anatomical prior to suppress macroscopic anatomical variance. The resulting K-Space Signature is processed by a novel 3D MLP-Mixer architecture that avoids the local spatial bias of CNNs, paired with an ArcFace metric-learning head for effective discrimination of globally distributed spectral artifacts.
AI.result: The framework achieves exceptional detection performance exceeding 0.99 Accuracy and ROC-AUC on multi-generator synthetic 3D MRI datasets. It also demonstrates robust zero-shot generalization, maintaining up to 0.93 Accuracy on independent datasets from entirely unseen scanners. Source code and pre-trained models will be released for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: The K-Space Signature framework with its 3D MLP-Mixer architecture provides a powerful, generalizable solution for Medical Deepfake detection in 3D MRI, effectively leveraging spectral-domain traces of hardware and generative processes while generalizing to unseen acquisition settings.

title: MBDiff: Multi-view Behavior-aware Diffusion Model for Probabilistic Utility Data Imputation
summary: Utility data (e.g., electricity, water, and gas consumption), collected by ubiquitous sensors and embedded devices, often contains substantial missing values due to various factors such as device failures and data transmission issues. The data missingness can severely impact utility billing accuracy, hinder demand forecasting, and disrupt efficient utility supply management. As a result, utility data imputation has attracted much interest from both industry and academia. While many studies have attempted to address this issue, most of them rely on aggregated datasets for training, overlooking rich user behavior information, which could provide valuable insights for more accurate imputation. However, learning comprehensive user behavior from long-term, diverse, and incomplete utility data remains a significant challenge. Moreover, leveraging user behavior information to guide imputation is nontrivial due to the indirect nature of the correlations. To address these challenges, we propose MBDiff, a Multi-view Behavior-aware Diffusion Model for Probabilistic Utility Data Imputation. MBDiff incorporates two key technical components: (i) a multi-view User Behavior Extraction module that learns comprehensive user behavior from multiple perspectives, including global, local, and instance-level views; and (ii) a behavior-aware conditional diffusion model consisting of a reference selection module and a conditional attentional denoising network to impute utility data in a computationally efficient manner. We implement and evaluate MBDiff by collaborating with one of the largest municipal utility providers in Florida. Experimental results demonstrate our proposed MBDiff effectively outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, e.g., it improves 7.04% and 29.1% on the electricity and water usage datasets for block missingness imputation, respectively.

AI.tldr: MBDiff is a multi-view behavior-aware diffusion model for probabilistic utility data imputation that learns comprehensive user behavior from global, local, and instance-level views, then uses a conditional diffusion framework with reference selection and attentional denoising to impute missing utility data. Evaluated with a major Florida utility provider, it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by improving imputation by 7.04% and 29.1% on electricity and water datasets for block missingness.
AI.motivation: Utility data collected by sensors often contains substantial missing values due to device failures and transmission issues, which harms billing accuracy, demand forecasting, and supply management. Existing imputation methods largely rely on aggregated datasets and overlook rich user behavior information that could provide valuable insights for more accurate imputation. Learning comprehensive user behavior from long-term, diverse, incomplete data and leveraging it to guide imputation is challenging due to the indirect nature of behavior-imputation correlations.
AI.method: MBDiff consists of two key components: (i) a multi-view User Behavior Extraction module that learns user behavior from three complementary perspectives—global, local, and instance-level views; and (ii) a behavior-aware conditional diffusion model comprising a reference selection module and a conditional attentional denoising network for computationally efficient probabilistic imputation.
AI.result: Experiments conducted in collaboration with one of the largest municipal utility providers in Florida show that MBDiff outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving imputation accuracy by 7.04% on the electricity dataset and 29.1% on the water usage dataset for block missingness.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating multi-view user behavior information into a conditional diffusion framework effectively improves utility data imputation accuracy, demonstrating the value of behavior-aware modeling for handling missing data in real-world utility systems.

title: MoRoute: Dynamic Routing for In-Context Multimodal Video Generation
summary: Multimodal video generation aims to generate and edit videos conditioned on arbitrary combinations of text, images, and videos within a single model, allowing diverse tasks to share complementary data and generative priors. Unifying these tasks requires multimodal understanding of diverse conditions, which is typically provided by a pretrained vision-language model (VLM). A key challenge is how to connect the VLM's hierarchical multimodal representations with a pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT). Existing methods either inject features from only the final or a few manually selected VLM layers, or jointly train architecture-matched understanding and generation streams, making it difficult to reuse heterogeneous pretrained backbones. We introduce MoRoute, a unified multimodal video generation framework that formulates a frozen VLM and a pretrained video DiT with different architectures as heterogeneous experts connected through dynamic layer routing. For each input, a lightweight block-wise router enables every DiT block to select the VLM layer most relevant to its generation stage, thereby learning an adaptive correspondence between multimodal understanding and video synthesis. MoRoute further incorporates reference images and source videos directly into the DiT token sequence through unified in-context conditioning, preserving fine-grained visual details across diverse generation and editing tasks. Experiments on IntelligentVBench, OpenVE-Bench, and RefVIE-Bench show that MoRoute consistently surpasses the best competing method on each benchmark, improving the average score by 0.15, 0.18, and 0.34 on a 1-5 scale, respectively.

AI.tldr: MoRoute is a unified multimodal video generation framework that connects a frozen VLM and a pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT) through dynamic layer routing. A lightweight block-wise router enables each DiT block to select the most relevant VLM layer adaptively, and reference images/videos are incorporated via unified in-context conditioning. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods on IntelligentVBench, OpenVE-Bench, and RefVIE-Bench.
AI.motivation: The key challenge is connecting a pretrained VLM's hierarchical multimodal representations to a pretrained video DiT with different architectures. Existing methods either inject features from only final or few manually selected VLM layers, or jointly train architecture-matched streams, making it difficult to reuse heterogeneous pretrained backbones.
AI.method: MoRoute treats a frozen VLM and a pretrained video DiT as heterogeneous experts connected via dynamic layer routing. A lightweight block-wise router lets every DiT block select the most relevant VLM layer for its generation stage, learning an adaptive correspondence between understanding and synthesis. Reference images and source videos are included directly in the DiT token sequence via unified in-context conditioning.
AI.result: On IntelligentVBench, OpenVE-Bench, and RefVIE-Bench, MoRoute consistently surpasses the best competing method, improving average scores by 0.15, 0.18, and 0.34 respectively on a 1-5 scale.
AI.conclusion: MoRoute demonstrates that dynamic layer routing between a frozen VLM and a pretrained video DiT enables effective reuse of heterogeneous pretrained backbones, achieving superior performance across diverse multimodal video generation and editing tasks.

title: SERUM: State Extraction and Refinement for User Modeling
summary: Agentic assistants capable of proactive, personalized interactions require structured models of user intent and workflow. However, building these models from raw, unstructured screen activity remains an open challenge. We present SERUM, a multi-pass framework that extracts finite-state behavioral models directly from unstructured egocentric video using hierarchical VLM annotation. Processing screen recordings through a sliding window, SERUM alternates between activity-recognition and intent-inference passes, with each pass refining labels using accumulated prior context to reduce hallucination and temporal conflation seen in single-pass annotation. Synonymous states are then merged via sentence embeddings and human-calibrated thresholds into a compact, coherent taxonomy. We evaluate behavioral structure by fitting first-order Markov models over the resulting label sequences (both actions and intents) and measuring predictive accuracy against frequency baselines. Across 61 egocentric videos in four domains (coding, cooking, physical activities, and daily life), we find: (1) iterative label refinement converges to a stable state vocabulary, which we term schematic equilibrium, after several passes; (2) normalized Markov models achieve substantially lower perplexity and higher action predictions than frequency baselines, with the largest gains on structured tasks like coding; and (3) human annotators rate final-pass labels as accurate and meaningfully improved over first-pass labels. To our knowledge, SERUM is the first system to produce interpretable process models from unstructured egocentric screen video without manual annotation, opening a scalable pathway for user modeling and behavioral understanding in the wild. Our demo, code, and results are publicly available

AI.tldr: SERUM is a multi-pass framework that extracts finite-state behavioral models (taxonomies of actions and intents) from unstructured egocentric screen video using hierarchical VLM annotation with iterative label refinement, merging synonymous states via sentence embeddings and human-calibrated thresholds. Evaluated on 61 videos across four domains, it achieves lower perplexity and higher predictive accuracy than frequency baselines, converges to a stable "schematic equilibrium" vocabulary, and produces labels rated more accurate than single-pass annotations—claiming to be the first system to derive interpretable process models from unstructured egocentric screen video without manual annotation.
AI.motivation: Agentic assistants need structured models of user intent and workflow, but building these models from raw, unstructured screen activity remains an open challenge. Existing single-pass annotation approaches suffer from hallucination and temporal conflation, and no system has yet produced interpretable process models from unstructured egocentric screen video without manual annotation.
AI.method: SERUM processes screen recordings through a sliding window using hierarchical VLM annotation, alternating between activity-recognition and intent-inference passes. Each pass refines labels using accumulated prior context to reduce hallucination and temporal conflation. Synonymous states are merged via sentence embeddings and human-calibrated thresholds into a compact taxonomy. Behavioral structure is evaluated by fitting first-order Markov models over label sequences and measuring predictive accuracy against frequency baselines.
AI.result: Across 61 egocentric videos in coding, cooking, physical activities, and daily life: (1) iterative label refinement converges to a stable state vocabulary ("schematic equilibrium") after several passes; (2) normalized Markov models achieve substantially lower perplexity and higher action prediction than frequency baselines, with largest gains on structured tasks like coding; (3) human annotators rate final-pass labels as accurate and meaningfully improved over first-pass labels.
AI.conclusion: SERUM is the first system to produce interpretable process models from unstructured egocentric screen video without manual annotation, opening a scalable pathway for user modeling and behavioral understanding in the wild. Its code, demo, and results are made publicly available.

title: DynoDINO: Harnessing Dynamic Latent Information from DINO Features for Multi-Phase Medical Image Segmentation
summary:
Multi-phase Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography (CECT) plays a central role in the diagnosis and characterization of focal lesions by capturing temporal enhancement patterns across multiple acquisition phases. Accurate lesion segmentation from such data remains challenging because clinically relevant contrast kinetics are distributed across phases, while anatomical inconsistencies, respiratory motion, and incomplete acquisitions often lead to inter-phase misalignment and interrupted temporal information. Conventional segmentation frameworks typically process each phase independently or rely on simple fusion strategies, limiting their temporal reasoning capability.
  To address these challenges, we propose DynoDINO, a unified framework tailored to address the core challenges of multi-phase medical image segmentation. DynoDINO first performs slice-level alignment to establish inter-phase anatomical correspondence and then employs a Multi-phase Fusion Model to jointly enhance temporal correlations across phases. Our fusion model incorporates a Mix-attention (MA) mechanism for efficient multi-phase feature calibration and an Adaptive Gating Mechanism with difference-based residual learning to selectively preserve diagnostically relevant contrast variations while suppressing artifacts caused by residual misalignment. In addition, the adaptive gating mechanism improves training stability by preventing feature degradation caused by unguided subtraction operations.
  Experiments on three large-scale datasets, including LiTS, PLC-CECT, and WAW-TACE, demonstrate that DynoDINO consistently improves boundary delineation and structural fidelity under standard, shifted, and missing-phase conditions.

AI.tldr: DynoDINO is a unified framework for multi-phase CECT lesion segmentation that performs slice-level alignment followed by a Multi-phase Fusion Model with Mix-attention and an adaptive gating mechanism with difference-based residual learning, achieving consistent improvements over baselines on three large-scale datasets.
AI.motivation: Multi-phase CECT segmentation is challenging because contrast kinetics are distributed across phases while inter-phase misalignment from motion and incomplete acquisitions disrupt temporal information. Existing frameworks process phases independently or use simple fusion, limiting temporal reasoning.
AI.method: DynoDINO first performs slice-level alignment to establish inter-phase anatomical correspondence, then employs a Multi-phase Fusion Model that uses a Mix-attention (MA) mechanism for efficient multi-phase feature calibration and an Adaptive Gating Mechanism with difference-based residual learning to preserve diagnostically relevant contrast variations while suppressing residual misalignment artifacts. The gating mechanism also improves training stability.
AI.result: Experiments on three large-scale datasets (LiTS, PLC-CECT, and WAW-TACE) show DynoDINO consistently improves boundary delineation and structural fidelity under standard, shifted, and missing-phase conditions.
AI.conclusion: DynoDINO effectively addresses multi-phase medical image segmentation challenges through alignment and adaptive fusion, demonstrating robust performance across diverse datasets and challenging conditions such as phase shifts and missing phases.

title: SAF-OPD: Stable Advantage Fusion for On-Policy Distillation
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) broadcasts a single response-level reward to every token, while on-policy distillation (OPD) scores each token against a stronger teacher for a dense advantage but caps performance at teacher quality and discourages exploration beyond it. Their complementarity makes combining RLVR and OPD promising, but we find that fusing the two advantages with a fixed coefficient triggers entropy collapse from two miscalibrations: a magnitude mismatch, where token-level OPD advantages can spike far beyond the bounded RLVR advantage and erase its signal, and a temporal mismatch, where sustained full-strength OPD keeps pulling the student toward the teacher and limits exploration needed to surpass it. We propose SAF, a Stable Advantage Fusion framework that resolves both issues via a lightweight, four-stage pipeline applied only to the OPD advantage: a sparsify-then-compress mechanism for magnitude control paired with a warm-up-then-anneal mechanism for temporal control, with each stage independently switchable and adding negligible overhead. Instantiating RLVR with GRPO, we evaluate SAF across seven mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks with Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B: SAF avoids entropy collapse and consistently outperforms fixed-coefficient GRPO+OPD fusion, improving the aggregate score by 0.51-2.70% across all six model-domain settings while achieving more stable training.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SAF (Stable Advantage Fusion), a framework that combines reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and on-policy distillation (OPD) by addressing two miscalibrations—magnitude mismatch and temporal mismatch—in the OPD advantage signal via a lightweight four-stage pipeline (sparsify-then-compress for magnitude control, warm-up-then-anneal for temporal control), improving performance by 0.51-2.70% across seven math/code benchmarks with three Qwen3 model sizes.
AI.motivation: RLVR broadcasts a single response-level reward to all tokens while OPD provides dense token-level advantages but caps performance at teacher quality and discourages exploration. Combining them is promising but naively fusing with a fixed coefficient causes entropy collapse due to magnitude mismatch (OPD advantages spiking beyond RLVR's bounded signal) and temporal mismatch (sustained OPD pulls toward teacher, limiting exploration needed to surpass it).
AI.method: SAF applies a lightweight four-stage pipeline only to the OPD advantage: (1) sparsify-then-compress for magnitude control of OPD advantages, and (2) warm-up-then-anneal for temporal control of the OPD contribution. Each stage is independently switchable and adds negligible overhead. RLVR is instantiated using GRPO as the base algorithm.
AI.result: SAF avoids entropy collapse and consistently outperforms fixed-coefficient GRPO+OPD fusion across seven mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks using Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B, improving aggregate scores by 0.51-2.70% across all six model-domain settings while achieving more stable training.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SAF framework effectively resolves the two miscalibration issues in RLVR+OPD fusion, enabling stable training that benefits from both dense teacher-guided advantages and verifiable reward signals, consistently exceeding fixed-coefficient fusion baselines.

title: Explaining AI-Image Detection: What the Heatmap Actually Shows
comment: 8 pages of main text; 27 pages including references and appendix. 9 figures, 21 tables
summary: A marketplace review photograph is a document: platforms approve refunds on it, and generative models drove the cost of forging one to zero. We study that detection problem, so we build a detector and attach an attribution map as its evidence, then measure what that pair delivers on 186,527 images under controls designed to change our conclusions when something is wrong. Compression history, not synthesis, drives naive evaluation: our strongest model reaches 0.9999 PR-AUC (area under the precision-recall curve) on a product-disjoint split, yet falls to 0.7254 once we re-encode synthetics into the real class's format, while five public detectors move by at most 0.07. Aligning one class relocates the cue rather than removing it, and the repaired model then assigns native files a median probability of synthesis of 0.0004. One identical final encode for both classes repairs that, and a three-seed factorial credits the encoding change with the whole gain (+0.176 +- 0.009 PR-AUC). That encode equalises the last stage only: forensic features alone still separate the classes at 0.7145 against a base rate of 0.254. For evidence we test maps causally, against controls that never consult the detector. Whether an attribution ranking exists at all depends on whether the detector reacts to the image. On our first-fix detector, which calls 96 of 100 edited frames real, no map beats a random one. On the detector we selected, twelve of seventeen maps clear that control on edited images and eight on generated ones; perturbation leads both axes and no gradient-CAM variant shows a positive advantage. The trivial controls never clear it, and on generated images the centre prior is worse than random. Our ensembled regional map clears both axes and takes the top pixel AP at 12.4 s per map against 44.9 for occlusion. Clearing a detector-blind control is not yet a faithful explanation, and we demonstrate none.

AI.tldr: A marketplace review photograph is treated as a document whose authenticity must be verified against forged generative content. The authors build a detector with attribution maps as evidence, evaluating on 186,527 images with carefully designed controls. They find naive evaluation is driven by compression history rather than synthesis (0.9999 PR-AUC drops to 0.7254 after re-encoding), that alignment shifts rather than removes the discriminative cue, and that casual attribution maps are tested against detector-blind controls—revealing that no tested method produces a faithful explanation, though an ensembled regional map clears the control on both edited and generated axes.
AI.motivation: Generative models have driven the cost of forging marketplace review photographs to zero, making detection a pressing problem. Platforms approve refunds based on such images, so reliable detection with interpretable evidence is needed.
AI.method: A detector is built on 186,527 images with an attribution map as evidence. Evaluation is controlled to expose confounds: re-encoding synthetics into the real class's format, aligning classes, applying an identical final encode to both classes, and testing attribution maps causally against controls that never consult the detector. A three-seed factorial design credits gains to specific processing changes.
AI.result: The strongest model hits 0.9999 PR-AUC on a product-disjoint split but falls to 0.7254 after re-encoding. An identical final encode for both classes repairs the gap (+0.176±0.009 PR-AUC credited to encoding via three-seed factorial). Forensic features alone still separate classes at 0.7145 vs. 0.254 base rate. Twelve of seventeen maps beat random controls on edited images, eight on generated ones; perturbation leads both axes, no gradient-CAM variant shows positive advantage, and the central prior is worse than random on generated images. No faithful explanation is demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: Compression history, not synthesis, drives naive detector evaluation; alignment relocates rather than removes the cue. Attribution maps must pass detector-blind causal controls to be meaningful, but passing such a control is not yet sufficient for a faithful explanation—none of the tested methods achieves that.

title: Frugal Bayesian Optimization: Scalable Surrogates for Data- and Resource-Limited Discovery
summary: Bayesian Optimization (BO) is widely adopted for data-efficient optimization in scientific and engineering applications, yet its computational cost is rarely evaluated alongside optimization performance. Here we present a systematic, compute-aware study of BO that evaluates surrogate models along two axes: optimization quality and computational frugality. Across eight benchmark functions and nine real-world datasets spanning materials science, mechanics, robotics, chemistry, and machine learning, we benchmark four surrogate models: Gaussian Processes, Random Forests, NGBoost, and Bayesian Adaptive Spline Surfaces. We show that Gaussian Process-based BO consistently incurs the highest time and memory overhead without delivering superior optimization or sample efficiency. In contrast, scalable alternatives achieve equal or better performance at a fraction of the computational cost. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a surrogate-recommendation framework that predicts the most suitable BO surrogate from inexpensive dataset characteristics. Together, these results establish FruBO as a reproducible, compute-aware baseline for Bayesian Optimization and provide practical guidance for surrogate selection under limited computational and experimental budgets.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic, compute-aware study of Bayesian Optimization (BO), evaluating four surrogate models across benchmarks. It finds GP-based BO incurs the highest computational cost without superior performance, motivates the FruBO framework that recommends surrogates based on dataset characteristics, and establishes a reproducible compute-aware baseline for BO.
AI.motivation: Bayesian Optimization is widely used but its computational cost is rarely evaluated alongside optimization performance. The paper aims to fill this gap by systematically assessing both optimization quality and computational frugality of surrogate models.
AI.method: Benchmarks four surrogate models (Gaussian Processes, Random Forests, NGBoost, and Bayesian Adaptive Spline Surfaces) across eight benchmark functions and nine real-world datasets spanning multiple domains. Introduces a surrogate-recommendation framework predicting the most suitable surrogate from inexpensive dataset characteristics.
AI.result: Gaussian Process-based BO consistently incurs the highest time and memory overhead without delivering superior optimization or sample efficiency. Scalable alternatives achieve equal or better performance at a fraction of the computational cost.
AI.conclusion: The authors establish FruBO as a reproducible, compute-aware baseline for Bayesian Optimization and provide practical guidance for surrogate selection under limited computational and experimental budgets.

title: TraceViT: Grounded Trace Supervision for Visual Abstract Reasoning
summary: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) tests whether a model can infer an unseen transformation from a few input-output examples and apply it to a new grid. Looped visual reasoners refine predictions over multiple iterations, but conventional training constrains only the final output, leaving intermediate refinements unconstrained. We propose that these refinements should instead follow the transformation step by step. We introduce TraceViT, a looped visual reasoner trained with semantically monotonic transformation chains. We obtain these chains by rewriting and verifying programmatic task implementations, decomposing each solution into intermediate grid states. Each iteration is grounded by a task reference derived from the few-shot demonstrations and an object workspace representing the current grid state. Because these chains may differ in length from the loop, soft trace alignment enforces only their ordering, letting the model allocate iterations freely. TraceViT achieves 67.8% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-1 and 24.3% on ARC-AGI-2. Controlled ablations on ARC-AGI-1 show that trace supervision becomes beneficial only when paired with grounding. Code and data will be available at https://github.com/LiuBinnan/TraceViT.

AI.tldr: TraceViT is a looped visual reasoner for the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus, trained with semantically monotonic transformation chains derived from decomposed programmatic solutions. It achieves 67.8% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-1 and 24.3% on ARC-AGI-2, with ablations showing trace supervision is only beneficial when paired with grounding.
AI.motivation: Looped visual reasoners refine predictions over multiple iterations, but conventional training only constrains the final output, leaving intermediate refinements unconstrained. The paper proposes that these refinements should follow the transformation step by step to better guide the model's reasoning process.
AI.method: TraceViT decomposes programmatic task implementations into intermediate grid states via rewriting and verification, producing semantically monotonic transformation chains. Each iteration is grounded by a task reference from few-shot demonstrations and an object workspace representing the current grid state. Soft trace alignment enforces only the ordering of chains, allowing flexible allocation of iterations since chain length may differ from loop length.
AI.result: TraceViT achieves 67.8% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-1 and 24.3% on ARC-AGI-2. Controlled ablations on ARC-AGI-1 show that trace supervision becomes beneficial only when paired with grounding.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that grounding intermediate transformations with task references and object workspaces is essential for trace supervision to improve looped visual reasoning performance, and soft trace alignment effectively handles the mismatch between chain lengths and loop iterations.

title: UniPolymer: A Unified Framework for Property Prediction, Structure Recommendation, and Evaluation in Polyimide Design
summary: Designing polyimide structures with specific glass transition temperatures (Tg) is highly challenging. Existing methods primarily focus on target-conditioned generation, lacking an assessment of the consistency between the generated structure and the target properties. This leads to low-quality candidates deviating from the design objective entering subsequent processes, increasing invalid experiments and prolonging the development cycle. To address this issue, we propose UniPolymer, a unified framework for property prediction, target-conditioned generation, candidate evaluation, and structure recommendation in polyimide design and a dataset containing 10066 deduplicated polyimide repeating units with Tg tags (PITg-Curated) was constructed. To improve the consistency between generated candidate structures and the target Tg, UniPolymer first establishes a reliable structure-property relationship mapping through self-supervised chemical semantic learning, structural consistency enhancement, and multi-scale information fusion. Subsequently, the model employs a continuous-discrete joint Tg representation to guide the autoregressive generation of SELFIES. The generated candidate structures are further evaluated using a frozen property predictor and polyimide-specific structural constraints, and ranked according to their deviation from the target Tg, thereby preventing structures deviating from the target from entering the subsequent validation stage. Experimental results show that UniPolymer achieved a property prediction accuracy of R^2=0.93 and a candidate structure evaluation pass rate of 73.79%, which are 2% and 1.21% higher than the best baseline, respectively. Meanwhile, the predicted Tg values of the recommended candidates are in high agreement with the results of molecular dynamics simulations, thereby reducing the number of candidates that enter the high-cost experimental stage.

AI.tldr: UniPolymer is a unified framework integrating property prediction, target-conditioned generation, candidate evaluation, and structure recommendation for polyimide design with specific glass transition temperatures (Tg). It leverages self-supervised chemical semantic learning, structural consistency enhancement, multi-scale information fusion, and a continuous-discrete joint Tg representation to guide SELFIES-based autoregressive generation. The framework achieves R²=0.93 in property prediction and a 73.79% candidate evaluation pass rate, outperforming the best baseline by 2% and 1.21% respectively, while recommended candidates show high agreement with molecular dynamics simulations.
AI.motivation: Designing polyimide structures with specific Tg values is highly challenging. Existing target-conditioned generation methods lack assessment of consistency between generated structures and target properties, leading to low-quality candidates deviating from design objectives entering downstream processes—increasing invalid experiments and prolonging development cycles.
AI.method: UniPolymer unifies property prediction, target-conditioned generation, candidate evaluation, and structure recommendation in one framework. It constructs a dataset PITg-Curated with 10,066 deduplicated polyimide repeating units with Tg labels. The model builds a reliable structure-property mapping via self-supervised chemical semantic learning, structural consistency enhancement, and multi-scale information fusion. A continuous-discrete joint Tg representation guides autoregressive SELFIES generation, and candidates are evaluated using a frozen property predictor plus polyimide-specific structural constraints, then ranked by deviation from target Tg.
AI.result: UniPolymer achieves a property prediction accuracy of R²=0.93 and a candidate evaluation pass rate of 73.79%, surpassing the best baseline by 2% and 1.21% respectively. Predicted Tg values of recommended candidates align closely with molecular dynamics simulation results, reducing the number of candidates entering high-cost experimental validation.
AI.conclusion: By integrating generation with consistency evaluation, UniPolymer effectively filters out low-quality candidates that deviate from target Tg, improving the efficiency of polyimide design and reducing the cost associated with invalid experiments and slow development cycles.

title: TOOD: Task-Aware Out-of-Distribution Score Calibration for Continual Learners
comment: 21 pages, 9 figures, and 4 tables. Accepted for oral presentation at the Conference on Lifelong Learning Agents (CoLLAs 2026)
summary: The primary challenge of continual learning (CL) systems is to learn new tasks while remaining performant on previously learned tasks. A similarly important though less well-studied aspect of CL systems is their ability to distinguish inputs that are unlikely to come from within the set of tasks the system has already encountered, often called out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. This paper presents several findings related to the dynamics of OOD detection in CL systems, causes of performance degradation over time which we call OOD forgetting (OODF), and proposed mitigation strategies for this degradation. Chiefly, we find the unintuitive result that OODF is only weakly anti-correlated with classification performance on previous tasks, suggesting that the underlying mechanisms producing OODF are distinct. Moreover, this effect is observed for both energy-based and feature-based OOD detection methods. Energy-based detectors suffer a drop in logit scale as additional tasks are learned, which we term the Confidence Gap, while feature-based detectors also degrade under a complementary effect we call Manifold Crowding. Motivated by these observations, we propose TOOD, a training-free post-hoc method that decomposes logits into per-task energy scores and re-calibrates them using replay-buffer statistics. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and a 100-task ImageNet-1K stream show that TOOD improves OOD detection performance over uncalibrated energy in most settings and ranks first or second in nine of ten CIFAR configurations, with the largest gains when the confidence gap is most severe. These results suggest that a substantial portion of OOD deterioration in continual learning arises from score miscalibration rather than from a complete loss of discriminative structure.

AI.tldr: This paper studies out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in continual learning (CL) systems, identifying a phenomenon called OOD forgetting (OODF) that is only weakly anti-correlated with classification performance. The authors identify two complementary causes—Confidence Gap (logit scale drop in energy-based detectors) and Manifold Crowding (degradation in feature-based detectors)—and propose TOOD, a training-free post-hoc method that decomposes logits into per-task energy scores and re-calibrates them using replay-buffer statistics. TOOD improves OOD detection across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and a 100-task ImageNet-1K stream, demonstrating that much OOD deterioration stems from score miscalibration rather than loss of discriminative structure.
AI.motivation: While continual learning primarily focuses on learning new tasks without forgetting old ones, the ability to detect out-of-distribution inputs—inputs unlikely to belong to any seen task—is equally important but understudied. This paper aims to characterize the dynamics of OOD detection degradation in CL systems, understand its underlying causes, and propose effective mitigation strategies.
AI.method: The authors first empirically characterize OOD forgetting (OODF) in CL systems, finding it is only weakly anti-correlated with task classification performance. They identify two distinct degradation mechanisms: the Confidence Gap, where energy-based detectors suffer a drop in logit scale as tasks accumulate, and Manifold Crowding, where feature-based detectors degrade via a complementary effect. Based on these insights, they propose TOOD, a training-free post-hoc method that decomposes logits into per-task energy scores and recalibrates them using statistics from the replay buffer.
AI.result: Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and a 100-task ImageNet-1K stream show that TOOD improves OOD detection over uncalibrated energy in most settings, ranking first or second in nine of ten CIFAR configurations, with the largest gains when the confidence gap is most severe.
AI.conclusion: A substantial portion of OOD deterioration in continual learning arises from score miscalibration rather than a complete loss of discriminative structure, indicating that effective post-hoc calibration can recover much of the lost OOD detection performance without additional training.

title: Assessing the Generalization of Graph Neural Networks for Fault Location Across Increasing Distributed Energy Resource Penetration Levels
comment: Accepted to IEEE SmartGridComm 2026. Copyright 2026 IEEE
summary: Accurate fault location is critical for distribution network reliability. However, increasing distributed energy resource (DER) penetration complicates fault location due to intermittent generation and bidirectional power flows that reshape fault signatures. Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks (STGNNs) have shown promise by jointly modeling spatial and temporal dependencies, but their behavior under increasing DER penetration has not been studied rigorously. In this paper, we (i) systematically benchmark spatio-temporal graph attention network (STGATv2) against purely temporal (gated recurrent unit, GRU), purely spatial (GATv2) and traditional machine learning baselines, and (ii) evaluate how well models generalize across increasing DER penetration levels (10%, 25%, 50%) on a reconfigured IEEE 123-bus feeder with multiple DER injection points and moderate-to-high impedance faults. Results show that STGATv2 consistently outperforms neural baselines, achieving 92-94% macro F1 in-distribution. Notably, generalization across penetration levels is asymmetric: training at 50% penetration retains near in-distribution F1 score at lower levels, whereas training at 10% degrades considerably at 50% - with STGATv2 retaining 81-84% F1 under these drastic shifts, substantially higher than GATv2 and GRU which drop to 69-74% F1 and 73-75% F1 respectively. Under realistic measurement noise, STGATv2 maintains > 85% F1, while GRU drops as low as 33.5% F1, highlighting the critical role of topological awareness for robust fault location in active distribution networks.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks a Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Network (STGATv2) against purely temporal (GRU), purely spatial (GATv2), and traditional ML baselines for fault location in active distribution networks with increasing DER penetration. STGATv2 consistently outperforms baselines (92-94% macro F1 in-distribution), shows asymmetric generalization across DER penetration levels, and maintains robust performance under measurement noise (>85% F1), highlighting the value of topological awareness.
AI.motivation: Fault location in distribution networks is critical for reliability, but increasing DER penetration reshapes fault signatures due to intermittent generation and bidirectional power flows, complicating fault location. While STGNNs have shown promise for modeling spatial-temporal dependencies, their behavior under increasing DER penetration has not been rigorously studied.
AI.method: Systematically benchmarks STGATv2 against GRU (temporal-only), GATv2 (spatial-only), and traditional ML baselines. Evaluates generalization across increasing DER penetration levels (10%, 25%, 50%) on a reconfigured IEEE 123-bus feeder with multiple DER injection points and moderate-to-high impedance faults.
AI.result: STGATv2 achieves 92-94% macro F1 in-distribution, outperforming neural baselines. Generalization across DER penetration is asymmetric: training at 50% retains near in-distribution F1 at lower levels, but training at 10% degrades considerably at 50%. STGATv2 retains 81-84% F1 under drastic shifts versus 69-74% for GATv2 and 73-75% for GRU. Under measurement noise, STGATv2 maintains >85% F1 while GRU drops to 33.5% F1.
AI.conclusion: Topological awareness provided by STGATv2 is critical for robust fault location in active distribution networks, enabling resilience to DER penetration shifts and measurement noise that purely temporal or spatial models cannot achieve.

title: CoDe-SSM: Context-Detail Decoupled State Space Model for Efficient UHD Image Restoration
summary: Ultra-high-definition (UHD) image restoration must balance the aggregation of spatially recurring degradation cues with the preservation of localized image structures. Compact aggregation can reduce redundant processing but may attenuate edges, textures, and other fine structures. Existing approaches manage UHD restoration cost through downsampling, window partitioning, or cluster-based token reduction; yet many of them do not explicitly retain information that is poorly represented by shared aggregation. In this study, we propose a Context-Detail Decoupled State Space Model (CoDe-SSM) for UHD restoration, which processes aggregated context and clustering residuals in separate pathways. The context modeling pathway, implemented by the Global Cluster Scan Module (GCSM), aggregates features into $K$ input-dependent cluster centers and applies selective SSM reasoning over the resulting fixed-order sequence, enabling cross-region context sharing while decoupling computational cost from spatial resolution. The detail recovery pathway, implemented by the Local High-Frequency Module (LHFM), processes the clustering residual with an input-derived high-frequency mask and a sparse mixture of convolutional experts. Extensive experiments on five UHD benchmarks and five degradation types demonstrate that our explicit context-detail decoupling strategy yields substantial gains in restoration quality while maintaining desirable efficiency.

AI.tldr: CoDe-SSM is a Context-Detail Decoupled State Space Model for ultra-high-definition image restoration that separates aggregated context modeling from detail recovery into two parallel pathways, achieving substantial restoration quality gains across five UHD benchmarks and five degradation types while maintaining efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing UHD restoration methods reduce computational cost via downsampling, window partitioning, or cluster-based token reduction, but most do not explicitly preserve information that is poorly represented by shared/aggregated representations—leading to loss of fine structures like edges and textures.
AI.method: CoDe-SSM processes context and detail in separate pathways. The Global Cluster Scan Module (GCSM) aggregates features into K input-dependent cluster centers and applies selective SSM reasoning over the fixed-order sequence for cross-region context sharing while decoupling cost from spatial resolution. The Local High-Frequency Module (LHFM) processes the clustering residual using an input-derived high-frequency mask and a sparse mixture of convolutional experts.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on five UHD benchmarks and five degradation types demonstrate substantial gains in restoration quality while maintaining desirable efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly decoupling context from detail in UHD restoration yields substantial quality improvements without sacrificing efficiency, validating the effectiveness of the proposed two-pathway architecture.

title: Sample Efficient Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning via Best Policy Identification
summary: We present HBPI-UCRL, a model-based algorithm for hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) that learns high-level and low-level policies in parallel. HBPI-UCRL exploits the fact that a high-level transition corresponds to a multi-step transition at the low level. We introduce two conditions on the low-level dynamics that are sufficient to make parallel HRL learnable. When these conditions hold, we prove that HBPI-UCRL has a polynomial sample complexity in the problem parameters. In the sparse-reward, goal-directed setting, our sample complexity upper bound for HBPI-UCRL is strictly lower than that of its non-hierarchical counterpart, providing theoretical justification for the empirical success of HRL.

AI.tldr: HBPI-UCRL is a model-based hierarchical reinforcement learning algorithm that learns high-level and low-level policies in parallel, leveraging the multi-step nature of high-level transitions. It achieves polynomial sample complexity under two sufficient conditions on low-level dynamics, and in sparse-reward goal-directed settings, its sample complexity is strictly lower than non-hierarchical RL, theoretically justifying HRL's empirical advantages.
AI.motivation: While hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) has shown empirical success, there is a lack of theoretical guarantees explaining why and when HRL outperforms flat RL. This paper aims to provide a rigorous theoretical framework demonstrating when parallel hierarchical learning is sample-efficient and provably better than non-hierarchical approaches.
AI.method: The paper introduces HBPI-UCRL, a model-based optimistic algorithm that learns high-level and low-level policies simultaneously. It identifies two sufficient conditions on low-level dynamics that make parallel HRL learnable, and provides a theoretical sample complexity analysis for the algorithm.
AI.result: HBPI-UCRL achieves polynomial sample complexity in the problem parameters when the two structural conditions hold. In sparse-reward, goal-directed settings, the sample complexity upper bound is strictly lower than the non-hierarchical counterpart, providing the first theoretical justification for HRL's empirical success.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a theoretical foundation for when and why hierarchical RL can achieve better sample efficiency than flat RL, demonstrating that structural properties of low-level dynamics can make parallel HRL provably learnable and advantageous in goal-directed sparse-reward settings.

title: FlexComposer: Unified Video Compositing from Images to Dynamic Footage with Flexible Trajectory Control
summary: Generative video compositing, which involves inserting external assets seamlessly into existing video sequences, is essential for content creation and visual effects. However, existing approaches suffer from a control-fidelity trade-off: they either hallucinate motion from static images, failing to preserve the dynamics of pre-animated assets, or lack fine-grained spatial control for precise asset placement along user-defined trajectories. We propose FlexComposer, a unified framework that standardizes video compositing as a trajectory-guided conditional generation task, enabling the seamless integration of both static images and dynamic footage. Our approach introduces three key designs: (1) a Unified Canonical Foreground Representation that decouples an object's intrinsic motion from its global displacement, standardizing heterogeneous inputs into a stabilized, centered latent space; (2) a Spatial-Aware Latent Injection strategy that exploits the translation equivariance of VAE latent spaces to transport canonical features onto target trajectories via a parameter-free mechanism; and (3) a Hybrid Dataset and Synthetic-to-Real Curriculum that synergizes procedural simulation, real-world cinematic footage, and generative data to implicitly learn physically plausible illumination and shadow harmonization. This unified design handles diverse inputs from product photos to dynamic subjects achieving high-fidelity motion control and environmental integration without the need for explicit 3D reconstruction or auxiliary learnable adapters. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlexComposer outperforms state-of-the-art methods in visual quality, temporal consistency, and trajectory adherence.

AI.tldr: FlexComposer is a unified framework for generative video compositing that standardizes the task as trajectory-guided conditional generation, enabling seamless insertion of both static images and dynamic footage into videos with high-fidelity motion control and spatial precision, without requiring 3D reconstruction or learnable adapters.
AI.motivation: Existing video compositing approaches suffer from a control-fidelity trade-off: they either hallucinate motion from static images (losing the dynamics of pre-animated assets) or lack fine-grained spatial control for precise asset placement along user-defined trajectories.
AI.method: FlexComposer introduces three key designs: (1) a Unified Canonical Foreground Representation that decouples an object's intrinsic motion from its global displacement, standardizing heterogeneous inputs into a stabilized latent space; (2) a Spatial-Aware Latent Injection strategy exploiting VAE latent space translation equivariance to transport canonical features onto target trajectories via a parameter-free mechanism; and (3) a Hybrid Dataset and Synthetic-to-Real Curriculum combining procedural simulation, real-world cinematic footage, and generative data to implicitly learn physically plausible illumination and shadow harmonization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlexComposer outperforms state-of-the-art methods in visual quality, temporal consistency, and trajectory adherence across diverse inputs ranging from product photos to dynamic subjects.
AI.conclusion: A unified trajectory-guided formulation can overcome the control-fidelity trade-off in video compositing, achieving high-fidelity motion control and environmental integration without explicit 3D reconstruction or auxiliary learnable adapters.

title: Analysing User Reviews to Identify User Concerns Around Permissions in AI Apps
summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in everyday software, making its integration into mobile apps inevitable. However, AI mobile app developers are not always versed in security and privacy best practices, leaving users to monitor their own security and understand how apps use their data. App reviews capture real user experiences, helping others make informed decisions before downloading. This paper presents a machine learning model for classifying AI app reviews into permission-related categories. Because user reviews are unstructured, assembling a conventional labeled training set is difficult. To address this, AI-generated security and permission reviews are used to identify relevant training examples from a large corpus of human-written reviews, eliminating the need for manual annotation. The proposed approach classified permission reviews with an accuracy of 82%. Analysis shows that users organise their concerns by sentiment toward the requesting app rather than specific permission types, with implications for users, developers, and platform administrators.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a machine learning model that classifies AI mobile app reviews into permission-related categories without manual annotation, achieving 82% accuracy by using AI-generated reviews to identify relevant training examples from a large corpus of human-written reviews. Analysis reveals users organize their concerns by sentiment toward the app rather than specific permission types.
AI.motivation: AI mobile app developers often lack security and privacy expertise, leaving users to self-monitor their security. App reviews contain valuable user experiences but are unstructured, making conventional labeled training set assembly difficult. There is a need for an automated approach to classify permission-related reviews to help users make informed decisions and understand how apps use their data.
AI.method: The proposed approach uses AI-generated security and permission reviews to identify relevant training examples from a large corpus of human-written reviews, eliminating the need for manual annotation. A machine learning model is then built to classify AI app reviews into permission-related categories.
AI.result: The proposed approach classified permission reviews with an accuracy of 82%. Analysis of the classified reviews shows that users organize their concerns by sentiment toward the requesting app rather than specific permission types.
AI.conclusion: The findings have implications for users, developers, and platform administrators. The work demonstrates that AI-assisted training data generation can effectively replace manual annotation for review classification in the AI app security/privacy domain, and reveals user sentiment patterns that can inform better app design and platform policies.

title: OASIS: Occlusion-aware Single-image Hand Avatar Reconstruction via 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: Accepted to ACM Multimedia 2026. Project page: https://mova-hand.github.io/MOVA/. Code repository: https://github.com/ivyyy77/OASIS
summary: Single-image 3D hand avatar reconstruction is fundamentally ill-posed and particularly challenging due to limited visual evidence under severe self-occlusion and the complex pose-dependent deformation of highly articulated hands. Existing methods predominantly rely on implicit NeRF-style representations, whose volumetric fitting is computationally expensive and often struggles to preserve fine-grained hand details. In this work, we present OASIS, a tailored 3D Gaussian Splatting framework for single-image hand avatar reconstruction. To faithfully encode sparse image-specific appearance cues in single-view reconstruction, we construct geometry-aligned visual evidence tokens by explicitly aligning input image observations with 3D hand geometry and context-adaptively tokenizing the resulting visual evidence. Since severe self-occlusion makes the reliability of image evidence inherently visibility-dependent, we introduce a visibility-conditioned point-image attention to reliably transfer visual evidence to geometric tokens, yielding occlusion-aware Gaussian features for faithful and robust reconstruction. To further capture non-rigid deformation of articulated hands, we introduce a Feature-on-Mesh representation to enable Gaussian deformation to be guided by local surface stretching. Under this framework, we adopt a one-shot adaptation scheme that learns a shared hand prior from multi-identity training data and then fits it to a target image for target-specific reconstruction. Extensive experiments show that OASIS outperforms existing baselines in both visual fidelity and efficiency across challenging poses and in-the-wild scenarios, and further demonstrates strong versatility in downstream applications such as text-to-avatar generation and texture editing.

AI.tldr: OASIS is a tailored 3D Gaussian Splatting framework for single-image 3D hand avatar reconstruction that uses geometry-aligned visual evidence tokens, visibility-conditioned point-image attention for occlusion-aware Gaussian features, and a Feature-on-Mesh representation to handle pose-dependent deformation, achieving superior visual fidelity and efficiency over existing baselines.
AI.motivation: Single-image 3D hand avatar reconstruction is fundamentally ill-posed due to severe self-occlusion and complex pose-dependent deformation of articulated hands. Existing NeRF-style implicit methods are computationally expensive and struggle to preserve fine-grained hand details, motivating a more efficient and detail-preserving approach.
AI.method: OASIS employs a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework with three key components: (1) geometry-aligned visual evidence tokens that align input image observations with 3D hand geometry and context-adaptively tokenize visual evidence; (2) a visibility-conditioned point-image attention mechanism that transfers visual evidence to geometric tokens in an occlusion-aware manner; and (3) a Feature-on-Mesh representation that guides Gaussian deformation via local surface stretching. A one-shot adaptation scheme learns a shared hand prior from multi-identity data and fits it to a target image.
AI.result: OASIS outperforms existing baselines in both visual fidelity and efficiency across challenging poses and in-the-wild scenarios, and demonstrates strong versatility in downstream applications such as text-to-avatar generation and texture editing.
AI.conclusion: The proposed 3D Gaussian Splatting-based framework with occlusion-aware feature encoding and mesh-guided deformation provides an effective and efficient solution for single-image hand avatar reconstruction, with broad applicability to downstream tasks.

title: Versatile On-device Adaptation at the Edge by Unifying Few-shot, Zero-shot, Continual, and In-context Learning
summary: With the ever-increasing pervasiveness of smart edge devices, the demand is growing for applications that can be tailored to users (e.g., custom keyword spotting) or patients (e.g., adaptive health monitoring). Yet, most edge devices rely on fixed inference algorithms and thus cannot learn on-device to personalize predictions. When they can, devices typically support only a specific learning scenario, such as few-shot learning (FSL): going beyond this requires resorting either to another specialized device or to cloud-based retraining, which implies significant energy and latency overheads, a lack of real-time capabilities, and privacy concerns. In this work, we introduce embedder-centric learning (ECL), a framework that unifies four different online learning scenarios: FSL for on-the-fly customization, continual learning (CL) for knowledge accumulation, zero-shot learning (ZSL) for leveraging semantic data, and in-context learning (ICL) for adapting beyond classification. We demonstrate in silicon that ECL can be deployed on resource-constrained devices across four real-world use cases representative of the aforementioned learning scenarios. Our approach establishes a new state-of-the-art performance for FSL character recognition (Omniglot: 96.8% for 5-way 1-shot, 83.3% for 32-way 1-shot), and the first hardware baseline for CL in keyword spotting (NeuroBench keyword FSCIL: 71.8% for 200-way 5-shot). Moreover, we present the first hardware demonstrations of ZSL with semantic data (60.6% for 5-way spoken sentence classification) and ICL (46.2% at the 500th token of RegBench) operating at micro-to-milliwatt power budgets. Therefore, by unifying multiple learning scenarios, we pave the way for smart and versatile devices that can adapt right at the edge, without reliance on the cloud.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces embedder-centric learning (ECL), a unified framework enabling four online learning scenarios (FSL, CL, ZSL, ICL) on resource-constrained edge devices. Demonstrated in silicon across four real-world use cases, ECL achieves state-of-the-art FSL results, the first hardware baseline for CL in keyword spotting, and first hardware demonstrations of ZSL and ICL—all within micro-to-milliwatt power budgets.
AI.motivation: Edge devices typically run fixed inference algorithms and cannot learn on-device to personalize predictions. When learning is possible, devices support only a single scenario (e.g., FSL), requiring specialized hardware or cloud retraining—incurring energy/latency overheads, lacking real-time capabilities, and raising privacy concerns. A unified framework supporting multiple learning scenarios at the edge is needed.
AI.method: The paper proposes embedder-centric learning (ECL), a framework that unifies four online learning scenarios—FSL for customization, CL for knowledge accumulation, ZSL for semantic data usage, and ICL for adaptation beyond classification. ECL is deployed in silicon on resource-constrained devices and evaluated across four real-world use cases representing each scenario.
AI.result: ECL achieves SOTA FSL on Omniglot (96.8% for 5-way 1-shot, 83.3% for 32-way 1-shot); first hardware CL baseline for keyword spotting (NeuroBench FSCIL: 71.8% for 200-way 5-shot); first hardware demonstrations of ZSL (60.6% for 5-way spoken sentence classification) and ICL (46.2% at 500th token of RegBench), all at micro-to-milliwatt power budgets.
