AI.conclusion: By unifying multiple learning scenarios under one framework, ECL enables smart, versatile edge devices that can adapt locally without cloud reliance, paving the way for personalized, real-time, and privacy-preserving on-device learning.

title: Cross-Resolution Semantic Learning for Graph Domain Adaptation
summary: Graph Domain Adaptation (GDA) transfers predictive knowledge from labeled source graphs to unlabeled target graphs under distribution shift. Existing methods align representations or regularize graph structures, but do not explicitly model how class-discriminative knowledge learned at different source neighborhood ranges should be routed across target ranges. We call the neighborhood range encoded by a graph representation its propagation resolution and define semantic resolution shift as a cross-domain change in the propagation resolutions at which class-discriminative evidence is strongest. Such shifts can make fixed same-resolution pairing suboptimal and increase the risk of negative transfer. To address this issue, we propose Cross-Resolution Semantic Learning (CReSL), a GDA method that learns soft sourceto-target resolution correspondence from cross-domain class structure. First, CReSL constructs a multi-resolution representation bank using a shared Graph Neural Network and learnable resolution embeddings, with a resolution-indexed expert for each source resolution. Second, CReSL introduces Cross-Resolution Prototype Transport, which constructs class-resolution prototypes from source labels and soft target posteriors and converts cross-domain prototype discrepancies into expert-specific routing over target resolutions. Third, CReSL introduces Cross-Resolution Target Grafting, which constructs posterior-weighted target-to-source prototype displacements and enforces correspondence-weighted prediction consistency for instance-level adaptation under class uncertainty. Extensive experiments on graph benchmarks under diverse domain shifts show that CReSL outperforms strong representative baselines across most settings.

AI.tldr: CReSL is a Graph Domain Adaptation method that addresses semantic resolution shift—where the neighborhood range carrying class-discriminative evidence changes across domains—by learning soft source-to-target resolution correspondences via multi-resolution representation banks, prototype transport, and target grafting, outperforming strong baselines on graph benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing GDA methods align representations or regularize graph structures but fail to explicitly model how class-discriminative knowledge at different source neighborhood ranges (propagation resolutions) should be routed to target ranges. Fixed same-resolution pairing becomes suboptimal under cross-domain resolution shifts, increasing the risk of negative transfer.
AI.method: CReSL consists of three components: (1) a multi-resolution representation bank built with a shared GNN and learnable resolution embeddings, plus a resolution-indexed expert per source resolution; (2) Cross-Resolution Prototype Transport, which builds class-resolution prototypes from source labels and soft target posteriors, converting cross-domain prototype discrepancies into expert-specific routing over target resolutions; (3) Cross-Resolution Target Grafting, which constructs posterior-weighted target-to-source prototype displacements and enforces correspondence-weighted prediction consistency for instance-level adaptation under class uncertainty.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on graph benchmarks under diverse domain shifts show that CReSL outperforms strong representative baselines across most settings.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling and routing across propagation-resolutions addresses semantic resolution shift in GDA, yielding superior adaptation performance compared to prior alignment/regularization approaches.

title: HierDoc: Hierarchical Page-to-Region Evidence Routing for Long-Document Visual Question Answering
summary: Multi-page document visual question answering requires locating sparse evidence at both the page and region levels. Existing approaches typically emphasize one level over the other: page-centric methods focus on page acquisition, with region operations serving mainly as navigation aids, whereas region-centric methods assume that the relevant pages have already been supplied. Consequently, page and region selection remain disconnected rather than forming successive evidence decisions. We propose HierDoc, a hierarchical evidence-routing framework that formulates long-document evidence acquisition as two-stage set prediction from pages to regions. A page policy selects evidence pages from the full document; these pages are then parsed for semantic elements, after which a region policy selects the elements passed to a downstream answer model. Both answer-agnostic policies are optimized with stage-wise GRPO using granularity-specific structured-set rewards. The answer model receives selected full pages together with selected region crops and OCR or table text, preserving global context while emphasizing fine-grained evidence. Across the evaluated benchmarks, HierDoc achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance among open-weight systems, improving LongDocURL by 16.87% relative to the strongest reported open-weight baseline. Controlled ablations further show that selected regional evidence improves the page-only system in accuracy and F1 by 5.51% and 4.82%, respectively. These results demonstrate the benefit of organizing coarse page routing and fine-grained region routing as successive, separately optimized stages of a unified evidence-acquisition process.

AI.tldr: HierDoc is a hierarchical evidence-routing framework for multi-page document VQA that formulates long-document evidence acquisition as a two-stage set prediction from pages to regions. It uses a page policy to select evidence pages, then a region policy to select fine-grained semantic elements within those pages, with both optimized via stage-wise GRPO. It achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance among open-weight systems, improving LongDocURL by 16.87% over the strongest reported open-weight baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-page document VQA approaches treat page and region evidence selection as disconnected, with page-centric methods treating region operations as navigation aids and region-centric methods assuming relevant pages are already supplied. The authors argue these levels should form successive, unified evidence decisions rather than separate concerns.
AI.method: HierDoc formulates evidence acquisition as a two-stage set prediction problem. A page policy selects evidence pages from the full document; these pages are then parsed into semantic elements, and a region policy selects the relevant elements to pass to the downstream answer model. Both answer-agnostic policies are trained with stage-wise GRPO using granularity-specific structured-set rewards. The final answer model receives selected full pages alongside selected region crops and OCR/table text to preserve global context while emphasizing fine-grained evidence.
AI.result: HierDoc achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance among open-weight systems across evaluated benchmarks, improving LongDocURL by 16.87% relative to the strongest reported open-weight baseline. Controlled ablations show that adding selected regional evidence to the page-only system improves accuracy by 5.51% and F1 by 4.82%.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the benefit of organizing coarse page routing and fine-grained region routing as successive, separately optimized stages of a unified evidence-acquisition process, confirming that hierarchical evidence routing improves multi-page document VQA performance.

title: Scaling Properties of Text Conditioning in Visual Generation
comment: Code: https://github.com/heheyas/context-scaling Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/heheyas/context-scaling Demo: https://heheyas-context-scaling.hf.space/ Project page: https://heheyas.github.io/context-scaling
summary: We study empirical scaling properties for text conditioning in visual generation. Such properties have rarely been measured because diffusion loss does not scale with the number of tokens in natural-language prompts. Surprisingly, we find that the converged diffusion loss scales with the amount of structured language in the prompt. To quantify structured language, we adapt two complementary measures: a white-box likelihood metric (GPG) and a black-box attribute metric (ED). Across controlled training runs, the converged diffusion loss decreases approximately linearly with GPG and follows a power law with ED. Guided by these scaling properties, we improve \emph{diffusability} by constructing structured prompts with semantic and geometric annotations derived from images, and improve \emph{promptability} by training a prompter through supervised fine-tuning, cold-start, and verifier-gated on-policy distillation. The resulting system outperforms all evaluated open-weight models on nearly every compositional, reasoning, and world-knowledge benchmark, while matching or surpassing the strongest closed-weight models on most evaluations.

AI.tldr: This paper studies empirical scaling properties of text conditioning in visual generation, finding that converged diffusion loss scales with the amount of structured language in prompts (linearly with GPG and as a power law with ED). Based on these properties, the authors improve "diffusability" via structured prompts with semantic/geometric annotations and "promptability" via a trained prompter, achieving state-of-the-art performance across compositional, reasoning, and world-knowledge benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Diffusion loss in visual generation does not scale with prompt token count in natural language, making it difficult to predict or optimize text-conditioning performance. The authors aim to identify what property of prompts does drive scaling and leverage it to improve both the conditioning quality and the prompt-generation capability.
AI.method: (1) Quantify structured language in prompts using two complementary measures: a white-box likelihood metric (GPG) and a black-box attribute metric (ED). (2) Conduct controlled training runs to establish scaling laws between converged diffusion loss and these metrics. (3) Improve diffusability by constructing structured prompts with semantic and geometric annotations derived from images. (4) Improve promptability by training a prompter through supervised fine-tuning, cold-start, and verifier-gated on-policy distillation.
AI.result: The converged diffusion loss decreases approximately linearly with GPG and follows a power law with ED. The resulting system outperforms all evaluated open-weight models on nearly every compositional, reasoning, and world-knowledge benchmark, and matches or surpasses the strongest closed-weight models on most evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Text conditioning in visual generation follows predictable scaling laws tied to structured language in prompts, not just token counts. These findings enable principled improvements in both prompt construction (diffusability) and prompt generation (promptability), yielding a system competitive with or superior to the state of the art.

title: Toward Robust and 3D-Aware RGB-NIR Imaging in the Dark
comment: ACM Multimedia 2026, Codes and Models: https://github.com/MyNiuuu/3DarkFusion
summary: Robust low-light imaging remains challenging for the community. Recent studies have explored fusing Near-Infrared (NIR) with noisy RGB to achieve improved enhancement, yet most methods depend on carefully curated training data pairs, with limited robustness under different scenarios. This paper offers a new perspective for RGB-NIR low-light imaging by incorporating 3D-aware neural modeling. Without using clean RGB supervision, a powerful model can be optimized to implicitly fuse extremely noisy RGB observations with NIR cues in 3D space, effectively recovering clean RGB images. The proposed model obviates the requirement for clean RGB data collection, generalizes across different noise levels. Extensive evaluations on synthetic and real data demonstrate its superiority. Codes available: https://github.com/MyNiuuu/3DarkFusion

AI.tldr: This paper presents a 3D-aware neural modeling approach for robust RGB-NIR low-light imaging that fuses extremely noisy RGB with NIR cues in 3D space without requiring clean RGB supervision, achieving generalization across noise levels and outperforming prior methods on synthetic and real data.
AI.motivation: Existing RGB-NIR fusion methods for low-light enhancement depend on carefully curated training data pairs with clean RGB supervision, limiting their robustness across different scenarios and noise levels.
AI.method: The proposed model leverages 3D-aware neural modeling to implicitly fuse extremely noisy RGB observations with NIR cues in 3D space. It is optimized without clean RGB supervision and can generalize across different noise levels.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on both synthetic and real data demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing approaches, with generalization across different noise levels.
AI.conclusion: The 3D-aware fusion approach eliminates the need for clean RGB data collection and provides robust low-light image enhancement across varied noise conditions, with code made publicly available.

title: OnlineCache: Learning Dynamic Caching Policies with Error Correction for Efficient Diffusion Inference
comment: Dynamic timestep-level cache method for diffusion acceleration via policy gradient
summary: Diffusion models have revolutionized generative tasks but incur high latency due to iterative denoising. While cache-based strategies accelerate inference by reusing intermediate features, they largely rely on static, sample-agnostic schedules. We argue that this rigidity overlooks two facts empirically validated in this paper: (i) generation difficulty varies across prompts, requiring adaptive resource allocation--complex inputs demand more computation while simpler ones require less; (ii) error sensitivity fluctuates across timesteps, where static policies may cache high-error steps or waste computation on low-error ones. We therefore propose OnlineCache, a dynamic caching framework that jointly learns when to cache and how to correct approximation errors. We leverage policy gradient to train a lightweight network for adaptive speed-quality trade-offs, and incorporate a learnable corrector to mitigate caching-induced errors. Both modules are jointly optimized under a bilevel optimization framework, with the policy targeting global generation quality and the corrector minimizing local errors. Our method automatically allocates computational resources across both samples and timesteps, improving overall generation quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate clear superiority. On FLUX.1-dev model, OnlineCache achieves nearly 3 speedup while preserving generation fidelity. On DiT and CogVideoX, it similarly delivers competitive acceleration without compromising quality; across all scenarios, it consistently outperforms existing cache-based acceleration baselines.

AI.tldr: OnlineCache is a dynamic caching framework for diffusion model acceleration that jointly learns when to cache intermediate features and how to correct caching-induced errors via a policy gradient-based lightweight network and a learnable corrector, optimized under a bilevel framework. It adaptively allocates computation across both samples and timesteps, achieving ~3x speedup on FLUX.1-dev and competitive acceleration on DiT and CogVideoX while outperforming existing cache-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing cache-based acceleration strategies for diffusion models rely on static, sample-agnostic schedules, overlooking two key empirical facts: (i) generation difficulty varies across prompts, requiring adaptive resource allocation, and (ii) error sensitivity fluctuates across timesteps, where static policies may cache high-error steps or waste computation on low-error ones.
AI.method: OnlineCache learns when to cache (via a lightweight policy network trained with policy gradient for adaptive speed-quality trade-offs) and how to correct approximation errors (via a learnable corrector module). Both are jointly optimized under a bilevel optimization framework: the policy targets global generation quality while the corrector minimizes local errors, enabling automatic resource allocation across both samples and timesteps.
AI.result: On FLUX.1-dev, OnlineCache achieves nearly 3x speedup while preserving generation fidelity. On DiT and CogVideoX, it delivers competitive acceleration without compromising quality, and consistently outperforms existing cache-based acceleration baselines across all scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Dynamically allocating computational resources jointly across samples and timesteps, combined with learned error correction, yields superior speed-quality trade-offs for diffusion model inference compared to static cache-based schedules.

title: ALIVE: Warnings Before Exclusion in Budgeted Multi-Source Learning
summary: A routing decision can be revised at the next transaction, but a latched source exclusion persists across later decisions. We ask what evidence should authorize these unequal-persistence actions when finite-population auditing and learning share a budget. ALIVE (Action-Layered Intervention via Evidence) is an auditable control layer: one randomized without-replacement prefix supplies cached evidence, heuristic warnings drive non-latching floor-bounded routing, and only two fresh simultaneous certificate separations may latch an exclusion request subject to capacity-feasible activation. Conditional on fixed support and labels under an ideal uniform audit permutation, any predictable controller preserving this interface inherits an anytime familywise bound of δon acting against a source that fails the pre-fixed absolute or relative strict-majority-disagreement predicate. With a published known-size, all-strict-majority PPR engine, median evidence count fell from 304 to 96 identities in e40 and from 171 to 62 in e60, while both engines used 48 in e80. In the matched CIFAR controller, the persistent-action layer added +0.1935 accuracy-AUBC percentage points over routing-only in all ten paired seed clusters. The +0.1954-point full-system contrast against CBR was also positive but did not meet the predeclared multiplicity-adjusted criterion (conditional Holm-adjusted sign-flip reference value =.097656). On a fixed natural panel, exploratory PPR used a median closure prefix of 95 rather than 105 for exploratory Serfling/FPC, but still exposed 88.0% of the panel and had no downstream task. Together these results map a restraint--power--cost--utility boundary: the action contract controls a defined persistent decision, while net value depends on evidence margin, audit cost, and budget regime.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ALIVE, an auditable control layer for decision-making systems that distinguishes between non-latching routing decisions (revisable) and latched source exclusions (persistent). It establishes an evidence-authorization framework where only two fresh simultaneous certificate separations can latch an exclusion, while heuristic warnings drive floor-bounded routing. Under an ideal uniform audit permutation, the framework guarantees an anytime familywise error bound of δ against sources failing a strict-majority-disagreement predicate. Empirically, ALIVE reduces median evidence count from 304→96 (e40) and 171→62 (e60) identities in a PPR engine, adds +0.1935 accuracy-AUBC points over routing-only across all ten seed clusters in CIFAR, and maps a restraint-power-cost-utility boundary for persistent decisions.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the asymmetry between routing decisions (revisable at next transaction) and latched source exclusions (persisting across decisions). The key question is what evidence should authorize these unequal-persistence actions when finite-population auditing and learning share a constrained budget, since prior frameworks do not properly distinguish evidentiary requirements for reversible versus irreversible actions.
AI.method: ALIVE (Action-Layered Intervention via Evidence) consists of three components: (1) one randomized without-replacement prefix supplying cached evidence, (2) heuristic warnings driving non-latching floor-bounded routing, and (3) two fresh simultaneous certificate separations that may latch an exclusion request subject to capacity-feasible activation. The theoretical guarantee is proven conditional on fixed support and labels under an ideal uniform audit permutation, ensuring an anytime familywise bound of δ against sources failing pre-fixed absolute or relative strict-majority-disagreement predicates.
AI.result: With a published known-size, all-strict-majority PPR engine, median evidence count fell from 304 to 96 identities in e40 and 171 to 62 in e60, while both engines used 48 in e80. On the matched CIFAR controller, the persistent-action layer added +0.1935 accuracy-AUBC percentage points over routing-only across all ten paired seed clusters. The full-system +0.1954-point contrast against CBR was directionally positive but failed the predeclared multiplicity-adjusted criterion (Holm-adjusted sign-flip reference value = 0.097656). On a fixed natural panel, exploratory PPR used a median closure prefix of 95 versus 105 for exploratory Serfling/FPC but exposed 88.0% of the panel.
AI.conclusion: The results map a restraint-power-cost-utility boundary: the action contract successfully controls a defined persistent decision with guaranteed familywise error control, but net value depends on evidence margin, audit cost, and budget regime. The framework demonstrates that latching persistent exclusions requires stronger evidentiary standards (two simultaneous certificate separations) than revisable routing, and this asymmetry yields measurable efficiency gains in evidence consumption while preserving statistical guarantees.

title: Explore Beyond the Boundary Using Entropic Information
summary: In reinforcement learning, exploration with sparse and delayed rewards presents a significant challenge due to the limited feedback available for guiding the learning process. Addressing this issue requires extensive exploration in the state space to discover valuable reward signals. In this paper, we propose Entropic Information for Exploration (ENTINEX), a novel method that enhances exploration by incentivizing agents to explore beyond the boundaries of the state distribution. ENTINEX achieves this by assigning intrinsic rewards to these boundaries, leveraging entropic information to identify them effectively. Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate that ENTINEX consistently improves exploration performance in environments characterized by sparse and delayed rewards. Our experimental results show that ENTINEX outperforms existing exploration methods, highlighting its effectiveness in both sparse and delayed reward scenarios.

AI.tldr: ENTINEX is a novel reinforcement learning exploration method that assigns intrinsic rewards to states beyond the boundaries of the current state distribution using entropic information, improving performance in sparse and delayed reward environments.
AI.motivation: Exploration with sparse and delayed rewards is challenging due to limited feedback, requiring extensive state-space exploration to discover valuable reward signals.
AI.method: ENTINEX incentivizes agents to explore beyond the boundaries of the state distribution by assigning intrinsic rewards to these boundary regions, using entropic information to identify them.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show ENTINEX consistently improves exploration performance and outperforms existing exploration methods in environments with sparse and delayed rewards.
AI.conclusion: ENTINEX effectively addresses sparse and delayed reward exploration challenges by leveraging entropic information to drive boundary exploration, outperforming prior methods.

title: End-to-End Fairness Optimization with Fair Decision-Focused Learning
summary: Many real-world systems rely on predictive models to inform decisions, and fairness concerns arise in both the prediction and decision stages. We introduce end-to-end fairness optimization (E2EFO) as a unifying framework that integrates fairness across the prediction-to-decision pipeline. We focus on resource allocation with group-based fairness: the prediction task estimates allocation impacts while limiting accuracy disparity across groups, and the decision task distributes those impacts equitably by optimizing a group-based alpha-fairness measure. Within this framework, we propose fair decision-focused learning (FDFL), a training paradigm that jointly accounts for prediction accuracy, prediction fairness, and decision regret -- the loss in decision fairness due to imperfect predictions. FDFL trains the predictor by gradient descent, combining the objective gradients through multi-task learning techniques. The core computational challenge is the decision Jacobian with respect to the predictor parameters: we derive exact closed-form formulas for a tractable class of fair allocation and apply a differentiable optimization layer in the general case. We further establish a finite-sample generalization bound for the scalarized FDFL objective. Numerical experiments on a healthcare-based single resource allocation and a synthetic multiple resource allocation illustrate the value of jointly accounting for prediction fairness and decision fairness in prediction-informed decision-making.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces end-to-end fairness optimization (E2EFO), a unifying framework integrating fairness across prediction-to-decision pipelines for resource allocation. It proposes fair decision-focused learning (FDFL), a training paradigm jointly optimizing prediction accuracy, prediction fairness, and decision regret, with exact closed-form decision Jacobians for tractable allocations and a differentiable optimization layer for general cases, plus a finite-sample generalization bound.
AI.motivation: Real-world systems rely on predictive models for decisions, but fairness concerns exist in both prediction and decision stages. Existing approaches typically address fairness separately in these stages, lacking a unified treatment that accounts for how prediction errors propagate and affect final decision fairness.
AI.method: FDFL trains the predictor via gradient descent, combining gradients from prediction accuracy, prediction fairness, and decision regret objectives through multi-task learning. The decision Jacobian is computed via exact closed-form formulas for a tractable class of fair allocation problems, and a differentiable optimization layer is used for general cases. A finite-sample generalization bound is established for the scalarized FDFL objective.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on a healthcare-based single-resource allocation task and a synthetic multiple-resource allocation task demonstrate that jointly accounting for prediction fairness and decision fairness improves prediction-informed decision-making compared to approaches that treat these stages separately.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end fairness optimization is valuable for prediction-informed decision-making, and FDFL provides a principled training paradigm that balances prediction quality, prediction equity, and downstream decision fairness in resource allocation settings.

title: TFGformer: Multivariate Time Series Forecasting via Time-Frequency Graph Learning and Covariate Fusion
summary: Large-scale multivariate time series from heterogeneous IoT sensors demand accurate long-term forecasting for resource scheduling and predictive maintenance. While recent time series foundation models exhibit strong generalization, they rely on static parametric knowledge and lack dynamic access to external historical patterns during inference. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) offers a potential remedy, yet its application to time series forecasting is challenged by magnitude variations across heterogeneous sources and the mismatch between historical similarity and future consistency. We propose CrossRAG, a retrieval-augmented forecasting framework that integrates Shape-Aware Memory (SAM) with RevIN normalization for magnitude-robust shape-level retrieval, Future-Consistent Contrastive (FCC) learning to distinguish informative references from hard negatives with similar history but divergent futures, and Cross-Attention Temporal Fusion (CATF) to fuse retrieved historical--future reference pairs into the backbone's representations at the representation level. Experiments on seven public benchmarks show that CrossRAG consistently outperforms both parametric-only baselines and existing retrieval-augmented forecasting methods.

AI.tldr: CrossRAG is a retrieval-augmented forecasting framework for large-scale heterogeneous IoT time series that combines Shape-Aware Memory with RevIN normalization for magnitude-robust retrieval, Future-Consistent Contrastive learning to filter informative references, and Cross-Attention Temporal Fusion to integrate historical-future reference pairs into backbone representations, outperforming parametric-only and existing retrieval-augmented baselines on seven benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Time series foundation models rely on static parametric knowledge and lack dynamic access to external historical patterns during inference. While RAG could address this, its application to time series is challenged by magnitude variations across heterogeneous sources and the mismatch between historical similarity and future consistency.
AI.method: CrossRAG integrates three components: (1) Shape-Aware Memory with RevIN normalization for magnitude-robust shape-level retrieval, (2) Future-Consistent Contrastive learning to distinguish informative references from hard negatives (similar history but divergent futures), and (3) Cross-Attention Temporal Fusion to fuse retrieved historical-future reference pairs into the backbone's representations at the representation level.
AI.result: Experiments on seven public benchmarks show CrossRAG consistently outperforms both parametric-only baselines and existing retrieval-augmented forecasting methods.
AI.conclusion: The dynamic retrieval of relevant historical patterns, made robust to magnitude differences and future inconsistency across heterogeneous IoT data, yields superior long-term forecasting performance compared to purely parametric models and prior retrieval-augmented approaches.

title: Parameter-Free Heavy-Tailed Bandits
summary:
Heavy-tailed distributions arise naturally in sequential decision-making problems such as financial investment, online advertising, and network management, where rare but extreme outcomes can dominate performance. Heavy-tailed bandits model online decision-making in these settings by assuming only that rewards $X$ satisfy $\mathbb{E}[|X|^{1+ε}]\leq u$, for some tail exponent $ε\in(0,1]$ and moment bound $u<+\infty$. However, most existing regret minimization algorithms require these parameters to be known. This assumption is particularly restrictive in practice: $ε$ and $u$ govern the frequency and magnitude of rare events and are therefore precisely the quantities that are hardest to infer reliably from limited observations.
  Motivated by an open problem posed by Genalti and Metelli at COLT 2025, we resolve the assumption-free adaptation problem for heavy-tailed bandits and characterize the price in the regret of not knowing the tail parameters. We first study adaptation to the moment bound $u$ for a fixed tail exponent $ε$. We prove that every algorithm unaware of $u$, or of any upper bound on it, must obey a sharp trade-off between its distribution-dependent and distribution-free regret guarantees. We then introduce a scheduled-exploration algorithm that requires no knowledge of $u$ and matches the resulting adaptation frontier up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we show that the same algorithm can be instanced without knowing $ε$ by calibrating its exploration schedule to the endpoint $ε=1$. It achieves sublinear regret for every fixed $ε>0$, while no algorithm can guarantee sublinear regret uniformly over all $ε\in(0,1]$. Altogether, our results resolve the COLT open problem without additional distributional assumptions and provide a sharp characterization of the statistical cost of adapting to unknown heavy tails.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves the COLT 2025 open problem on assumption-free adaptation for heavy-tailed bandits, where the tail exponent ε and moment bound u are unknown. It characterizes the regret price of not knowing these tail parameters, proves a sharp trade-off between distribution-dependent and distribution-free regret for algorithms unaware of u, and introduces a scheduled-exploration algorithm that achieves the adaptation frontier up to logarithmic factors without knowing u or ε.
AI.motivation: Heavy-tailed distributions naturally model sequential decision-making problems (finance, advertising, networks) where rare extreme outcomes dominate performance. Existing regret minimization algorithms for heavy-tailed bandits require knowledge of the tail parameters ε and u, which are precisely the quantities hardest to estimate from limited data. This parametrization dependence is practically restrictive, motivating the need to solve the assumption-free adaptation problem posed by Genalti and Metelli at COLT 2025.
AI.method: The paper first analyzes adaptation to the moment bound u for a fixed tail exponent ε, proving a sharp trade-off lower bound that every algorithm unaware of u (or any upper bound on it) must satisfy between its distribution-dependent and distribution-free regret. It then designs a scheduled-exploration algorithm requiring no knowledge of u that matches the resulting adaptation frontier up to logarithmic factors. Finally, the same algorithm is instanced without knowing ε by calibrating its exploration schedule to the endpoint ε=1, and an impossibility result is established showing no algorithm can guarantee sublinear regret uniformly over all ε∈(0,1].
AI.result: The paper provides a sharp characterization of the adaptation frontier for unknown moment bound u, a scheduled-exploration algorithm matching this frontier up to logarithmic factors, and demonstrates sublinear regret for every fixed ε>0 even when ε is unknown. It also proves a lower bound that no algorithm can achieve sublinear regret uniformly over all ε∈(0,1], resolving the COLT open problem without additional distributional assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The work fully resolves the assumption-free adaptation problem for heavy-tailed bandits, characterizing the statistical cost of adapting to unknown heavy tails and providing a near-optimal algorithm. It shows that adaptation to unknown u and ε is achievable with sublinear (though costlier) regret, with the caveat that uniform guarantees across all tail exponents are impossible, thereby giving a complete picture of the regret landscape for parameter-free heavy-tailed bandits.

title: MolGVR: A Chemistry-Grounded Framework for Text-to-Molecule Generation
summary: Text-to-molecule generation is typically formulated as a one-shot sequence generation problem, where a model directly maps target descriptions to molecular representations. However, molecular descriptions often contain informative structural constraints, and violating such constraints can change the molecular identity. This makes chemical verification and error correction important but underexplored. To fill this gap, we propose MolGVR, a chemistry-grounded Generator--Verifier--Refiner framework. The Generator infers structural evidence and generates candidate molecules. The Verifier addresses the lack of chemical validation by converting descriptions into chemical constraints and checking candidates against them. The Refiner addresses generation failures by revising candidates rejected by the Verifier. Experiments on ChEBI-20 and PCDes show that MolGVR improves exact-match performance. These results suggest that coupling generation with executable verification and feedback-guided refinement is an effective way to improve text-to-molecule generation.

AI.tldr: MolGVR is a chemistry-grounded Generator-Verifier-Refiner framework for text-to-molecule generation that extracts structural constraints from descriptions, verifies candidate molecules against these constraints, and refines rejected candidates, improving exact-match performance on ChEBI-20 and PCDes benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Text-to-molecule generation is typically treated as one-shot sequence generation, but molecular descriptions often contain informative structural constraints. Violating these constraints can alter molecular identity, yet chemical verification and error correction remain underexplored in this task.
AI.method: MolGVR consists of three components: (1) a Generator that infers structural evidence and generates candidate molecules; (2) a Verifier that converts descriptions into chemical constraints and checks candidate molecules against them; and (3) a Refiner that revises candidates rejected by the Verifier in a feedback-guided loop.
AI.result: Experiments on ChEBI-20 and PCDes demonstrate that MolGVR improves exact-match performance over baseline text-to-molecule generation approaches.
AI.conclusion: Coupling generation with executable verification and feedback-guided refinement is an effective paradigm for improving text-to-molecule generation, addressing the gap in chemical validation during the generation process.

title: DreamQAS: Learning a Decision-Useful World Model for VQE-Efficient Quantum Architecture Search
summary: Reinforcement-learning-based quantum architecture search (RL-QAS) repeatedly optimizes a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) after extending a circuit, although circuit construction and action legality are deterministic and known. We introduce DreamQAS, a model-based RL framework that preserves these exact circuit dynamics and learns only the expensive post-VQE feedback. A recurrent randomized-prior ensemble predicts an oracle-free score relative to an empirical energy frontier and supports multi-step imagined policy learning over explicit legal circuits. Ranking-based activation, uncertainty-aware pessimism and truncation, and selective real-VQE verification form a reliability-controlled learning loop. Under a common 15,000-episode budget and frozen evaluation for the RL methods, DreamQAS has the lowest mean frozen-policy energy error on four of five molecular tasks and the second-lowest on one. At fine-error targets reached by all seeds of both methods, it uses 1.6x to 2.0x fewer real VQE calls on four tasks and 10.6x fewer on BeH2-8q. Counterfactual action-ranking utility increases across all five tasks, with a mean increase of 0.346 and a 95 percent confidence interval of [0.185, 0.507], while direct greedy and beam use of the same model does not recover the gains of imagined policy learning. Ensemble disagreement also improves risk-coverage over random rejection on all three probed tasks. These results establish a world-model design for QAS whose value lies in decision-useful feedback rather than exact energy prediction.

AI.tldr: DreamQAS is a model-based reinforcement learning framework for quantum architecture search that replaces expensive real VQE computations with a recurrent randomized-prior ensemble predictor, preserving exact circuit dynamics while learning only the post-VQE feedback. It achieves the lowest mean frozen-policy energy error on four of five molecular tasks and reduces real VQE calls by 1.6x-10.6x while improving counterfactual action-ranking utility.
AI.motivation: Standard RL-based quantum architecture search (RL-QAS) repeatedly runs a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) after extending circuits, which is computationally expensive. However, circuit construction and action legality are deterministic and known, so only the post-VQE feedback is truly costly to obtain. The authors seek to exploit this structure by learning only the expensive feedback while preserving exact circuit dynamics, rather than modeling the entire environment.
AI.method: DreamQAS uses a model-based RL framework with: (1) exact circuit dynamics preserved while learning only post-VQE feedback via a recurrent randomized-prior ensemble predictor; (2) oracle-free score prediction relative to an empirical energy frontier; (3) multi-step imagined policy learning over explicit legal circuits; (4) ranking-based activation, uncertainty-aware pessimism and truncation; and (5) selective real-VQE verification forming a reliability-controlled learning loop.
AI.result: Under a 15,000-episode budget with frozen evaluation, DreamQAS achieves the lowest mean frozen-policy energy error on four of five molecular tasks and second-lowest on one. At fine-error targets, it uses 1.6x-2.0x fewer real VQE calls on four tasks and 10.6x fewer on BeH2-8q. Counterfactual action-ranking utility increases across all five tasks with mean increase 0.346 (95% CI [0.185, 0.507]). Ensemble disagreement improves risk-coverage over random rejection on all three probed tasks.
AI.conclusion: DreamQAS establishes that a world-model design for quantum architecture search is valuable for decision-useful feedback rather than exact energy prediction. The imagined policy learning and reliability-controlled learning loop deliver significant efficiency gains in real VQE calls while maintaining or improving solution quality, demonstrating that separating known circuit dynamics from expensive learned feedback is a powerful design principle for RL-QAS.

title: Adaptive FastOPD: Progress-Aware Rollout Horizon Expansion for Efficient On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense teacher supervision along student-generated trajectories, but its online rollout process incurs substantial computational cost, particularly when a few long responses delay batch completion. Existing acceleration methods typically control rollout length using fixed budgets or absolute teacher--student agreement thresholds, which may not reflect learning progress across different models and training stages. We propose Adaptive FastOPD, a progress-aware strategy that expands the rollout horizon only when learning near the current boundary region has plateaued and the current horizon is sufficiently utilized. The former is determined from four teacher--student signals measured relative to their values upon entering each horizon, making expansion responsive to stage-specific progress rather than a predefined step interval or an absolute threshold on the raw agreement signals, while the latter prevents a small number of long responses from triggering increases in rollout cost. Across two teacher--student pairs, Adaptive FastOPD achieves the highest average performance while reducing training time by 49.1--71.2\% relative to OPD 15K, and remains robust across a range of hyperparameter settings.

AI.tldr: Adaptive FastOPD is a progress-aware strategy for on-policy distillation that adaptively expands the rollout horizon only when learning near the current boundary has plateaued and the current horizon is sufficiently utilized, achieving the highest average performance while reducing training time by 49.1-71.2% relative to OPD 15K.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation provides dense teacher supervision but incurs substantial computational cost due to online rollout, especially when a few long responses delay batch completion. Existing acceleration methods use fixed budgets or absolute agreement thresholds that fail to reflect learning progress across different models and training stages.
AI.method: Adaptive FastOPD expands the rollout horizon only when: (1) learning near the current boundary region has plateaued, determined from four teacher-student signals measured relative to their values upon entering each horizon (making expansion responsive to stage-specific progress rather than predefined intervals or absolute thresholds), and (2) the current horizon is sufficiently utilized, preventing a few long responses from triggering rollout cost increases.
AI.result: Across two teacher-student pairs, Adaptive FastOPD achieves the highest average performance while reducing training time by 49.1-71.2% relative to OPD 15K, and remains robust across a range of hyperparameter settings.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive FastOPD demonstrates that progress-aware, stage-relative rollout horizon expansion is a more effective and efficient acceleration strategy for on-policy distillation than fixed-budget or absolute-threshold approaches.

title: A Human-Centered Validation of the Explainability-Performance Coefficient
summary: The rapid adoption of deep learning models in high-risk domains has intensified the need for trustworthy Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). However, objectively evaluating explanation fidelity and aligning XAI metrics with human-centered understanding remain critical open challenges. In this work, we propose a model-agnostic metric, the EPC score, which is an extension of the Explainability-Performance Coefficient (EPC), that quantifies explanation quality by explicitly balancing the trade-off between feature selection sparsity and preserved model performance. Through an empirical validation across tabular, text, and image modalities, we show that the EPC score effectively uncovers operational dependencies among network activations, data dimensionality, and explainer performance. Furthermore, we validate the EPC score against independent human-based explanations, proving that higher EPC scores strongly align with human lexical sentiment judgments and spatial visual annotations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the EPC score, a model-agnostic metric extending the Explainability-Performance Coefficient to quantify explanation quality by balancing feature selection sparsity with preserved model performance, validated across tabular, text, and image modalities and aligned with human-level explanations.
AI.motivation: Despite the rapid adoption of deep learning in high-risk domains, objectively evaluating explanation fidelity and aligning XAI metrics with human-centered understanding remain unresolved challenges.
AI.method: The EPC score is a model-agnostic metric that extends the Explainability-Performance Coefficient (EPC) by explicitly balancing the trade-off between feature selection sparsity and preserved model performance. It is empirically validated across tabular, text, and image modalities.
AI.result: The EPC score effectively uncovers operational dependencies among network activations, data dimensionality, and explainer performance. It also strongly aligns with human lexical sentiment judgments and spatial visual annotations, with higher EPC scores corresponding to better human-aligned explanations.
AI.conclusion: The EPC score provides a robust, model-agnostic, and human-validated metric for evaluating explanation quality in XAI, addressing the need for trustworthy and interpretable AI systems.

title: Transcript-Managed Transformers: Monotone Multi-Agent Collapse and Universality with Two Pop-Enabled Transcripts
comment: 14 pages, 2 tables, 0 figures. Theoretical results on transcript management for fixed-precision Transformers: monotone multi-agent collapse to finite-state transducers, and universality with two pop-enabled transcript channels
summary:
We study transcript management for fixed, finite-precision causal Transformers. A transcript is partitioned into channels of bounded blocks. Each transition consults a fixed visible suffix and may append one block, leaving the model, weights, and token protocol unchanged. The operation $P_c:=\PopContext(c)$ deletes the newest block on channel $c$ and exposes its predecessor.
  We model the layer by the Transcript-Managed Transducer $\TMTn{k}$: one finite controller, $k$ channels, and per-round actions from stay, push, and pop under a caller-driven status map. Fixed visible windows encode as finite symbols. The pop-free Restricted Transcript-Managed Transducer $\RTMTn{k}$ is the standard append-only layer and, for every fixed $k$, realizes exactly the deterministic finite-state transductions. The same holds for every fixed finite agent population under a monotone protocol that appends, routes, and copies visible blocks.
  Admitting $\{P_c\}_{c=1}^k$ restores pop. Newest-first, a pop-enabled channel is a stack; compiling to the Hopcroft--Ullman presentation transfers the classical hierarchy: $\DCFL$ for $k=1$ and $\RE$ for every $k\ge2$. Orchestrated one-channel agents match one controller with $k$ channels, so two pop-enabled transcripts---in one agent or two---suffice for universality. Simulation costs and invariance to fixed block size and visible radius are stated. The bounds fix precision, alphabets, blocks, visibility, controller state, and population; growing exact context, hidden-block access, writable stores, and unbounded \textbf{Spawn} add further state.

AI.tldr: This paper studies transcript management in fixed finite-precision causal Transformers, where a transcript is partitioned into channels of bounded blocks. The proposed Transcript-Managed Transducer (TMT^k) models the layer with one finite controller, k channels, and per-round actions (stay, push, pop) under a caller-driven status map. Pop-free restricted variants realize exactly deterministic finite-state transductions, while admitting pop operations restores classical hierarchy: DCFL for k=1 and RE for k≥2.
AI.motivation: To understand the computational power of fixed finite-precision causal Transformers when managing transcripts (memory) across bounded blocks and channels, and to characterize what automata-theoretic classes such systems can realize.
AI.method: The authors define the Transcript-Managed Transducer TMT^k: one finite controller, k channels, bounded blocks, and per-round actions (stay, push, pop) under a caller-driven status map. They analyze both pop-free Restricted Transcript-Managed Transducers (RTMT^k) and pop-enabled variants. For pop-enabled systems, they compile to the Hopcroft–Ullman presentation to transfer classical hierarchy results (DCFL for k=1, RE for k≥2). They also consider orchestrated one-channel agents.
AI.result: The pop-free RTMT^k realizes exactly the deterministic finite-state transductions for every fixed k, and the same holds for every fixed finite agent population under monotone appending/routing/copying protocols. Pop-enabled transcripts behave as stacks when viewed newest-first: k=1 captures DCFL, while k≥2 captures RE. Two pop-enabled transcripts (one agent or two) suffice for universality. Simulation costs and invariance to fixed block size/visible radius are established, with bounds fixed for precision, alphabets, blocks, visibility, controller state, and population.
AI.conclusion: The transcript-management framework precisely characterizes Transformer memory: append-only channels yield only finite-state behavior, while pop-enabled channels (acting as stacks) recover the full classical hierarchy—DCFL with one channel and universal computation (RE) with two or more, whether in one agent or distributed across a population.

title: The Grokked Illusion: True Equilibrium Mitigates Catastrophic Forgetting
summary: While neural networks are typically evaluated by their training and test performance, these metrics do not reveal how robust a learned representation is. Recent studies have shown that solutions occupying larger volumes in parameter space, as quantified by Boltzmann entropy, often exhibit superior generalizability compared to those reached by conventional optimization, a phenomenon known as the high entropy advantage. Here we ask whether this advantage persists beyond generalization. Specifically, we investigate models' robustness, the ability to retain the learned knowledge when the model is subsequently trained to acquire new information. Using grokking in modular arithmetic as a controlled setting, we design a noise injection experiment to evaluate the robustness difference between AdamW-trained transformers and high-entropy model sampled from Wang-Landau Molecular Dynamics with identical saturated performance. By forcing both models to fully remember new data with random labels, we find that AdamW-trained models suffer from catastrophic forgetting, with original task test accuracy dropping from 100% to below 75%, whereas the high-entropy models maintain approximately 95% test accuracy. We term this hidden fragility behind apparent generalization the "grokked illusion." Through singular value decomposition of the neural network weights, we discover that high-entropy neural networks possess significantly higher effective rank in attention and MLP layers both before and after noise injection, indicating richer feature representations can serve as a buffer against catastrophic forgetting. Our findings demonstrate that perfect generalization does not imply equal robustness, offering a new perspective on what makes a trained model robust to interference.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that models achieving identical generalization performance can differ dramatically in robustness. Using modular arithmetic grokking as a controlled setting, the authors find that AdamW-trained transformers suffer catastrophic forgetting (accuracy dropping from 100% to below 75%) when forced to learn new random-label data, while high-entropy models sampled from Wang-Landau Molecular Dynamics retain ~95% accuracy. The key mechanism is that high-entropy networks possess significantly higher effective rank in attention and MLP layers, providing richer feature representations that act as a buffer against catastrophic forgetting—a phenomenon the authors term the "grokked illusion."
AI.motivation: Standard training and test metrics do not reveal how robust a learned representation is. While recent work has shown that high-entropy solutions exhibit superior generalizability (the high entropy advantage), the authors ask whether this advantage extends beyond generalization to robustness—the ability to retain knowledge when a model is subsequently trained on new information.
AI.method: The authors use grokking in modular arithmetic as a controlled setting and design a noise injection experiment. They compare two types of transformer models with identical saturated performance: (1) AdamW-trained transformers and (2) high-entropy models sampled from Wang-Landau Molecular Dynamics. Both models are then forced to fully memorize new data with random labels, and their original task accuracy is measured. Additionally, singular value decomposition (SVD) of network weights is used to analyze effective rank in attention and MLP layers before and after noise injection.
AI.result: AdamW-trained models suffer catastrophic forgetting, with original task test accuracy dropping from 100% to below 75%, while high-entropy models maintain approximately 95% test accuracy. SVD analysis reveals that high-entropy neural networks have significantly higher effective rank in both attention and MLP layers, both before and after noise injection.
AI.conclusion: Perfect generalization does not imply equal robustness. The high entropy advantage extends beyond generalization to robustness, where richer feature representations (as reflected by higher effective rank) serve as a buffer against catastrophic forgetting. This reveals a "grokked illusion"—the hidden fragility behind apparent generalization—and offers a new perspective on what makes a trained model robust to interference.

title: TerraNova: A Foundation Model for the Anthropocene
comment: 32 pages, 16 figures. Supplementary Information (full methodological specification, ablation programme, extended results, computational cost; 157 pages) available at the project page: https://carlosrodriguezpardo.es/projects/TerraNova/
summary: A defining problem of the Anthropocene is to model the physical Earth and human societies as one coupled system, yet no learned representation spans their observational breadth. We argue the obstacle is geometric: the physical Earth is measured as continuous fields that ignore political borders, whereas societies are reported for administrative units. Earth-system foundation models serve the first geometry; coupling it to the second has required lossy averaging over borders. We introduce TerraNova, a foundation model trained on 1,024 physical and societal records in their native geometries: 512 gridded Earth-system fields and 512 national indicators. Dedicated encoders represent location, country, time and task, cross-modal transformers fuse them into a shared spatiotemporal state, and a hypernetwork generates a per-query decoder whose evidential head returns a predictive distribution. Two contrastive objectives couple the representation: a population-weighted alignment between each country and coordinates in its territory, and one to pretrained geospatial embeddings carrying image-derived semantics. Read out through that decoder, the representation is competitive with purpose-built geospatial encoders while spanning axes they do not represent (time, oceans and uncertainty) and supporting country-level capabilities. The frozen backbone reconstructs dense fields from sparse observations and adapts to unseen variables in minutes on consumer hardware.

AI.tldr: TerraNova is a foundation model that jointly models physical Earth fields (gridded, continuous) and societal indicators (national, discrete) in their native geometries, using cross-modal transformers with dedicated encoders, a hypernetwork-based per-query decoder with evidential heads, and contrastive objectives that align countries with their territory and with pretrained geospatial embeddings. It matches purpose-built geospatial encoders while also supporting time, oceans, uncertainty, and country-level predictions, and adapts to unseen tasks quickly on consumer hardware.
AI.motivation: Modeling the Anthropocene requires a unified representation of physical Earth and human societies as one coupled system, but no learned representation spans both. The obstacle is geometric: Earth data are continuous gridded fields ignored by political borders, while societal data are reported for administrative units. Prior coupling required lossy averaging over borders.
AI.method: TerraNova is trained on 1,024 physical and societal records in native geometries: 512 gridded Earth-system fields and 512 national indicators. It uses dedicated encoders for location, country, time, and task; cross-modal transformers fuse these into a shared spatiotemporal state; and a hypernetwork generates a per-query decoder whose evidential head returns a predictive distribution. Two contrastive objectives couple the representation: population-weighted alignment between each country and its territorial coordinates, and alignment to pretrained geospatial embeddings with image-derived semantics.
AI.result: The learned representation is competitive with purpose-built geospatial encoders while additionally spanning time, oceans, and uncertainty, and supporting country-level capabilities. The frozen backbone reconstructs dense fields from sparse observations and adapts to unseen variables within minutes on consumer hardware.
AI.conclusion: A single shared geometry-agnostic representation can bridge continuous Earth-system fields and discrete societal indicators without lossy border averaging, enabling joint modeling of the coupled physical–human system and rapid adaptation to new variables.

title: A Neurosymbolic Approach for Explainable Early Diagnosis of Alzheimer's Disease
summary: Identifying reliable Alzheimer's disease (AD) markers typically requires manual, labor-intensive transcription and expert analysis, limiting its scale. We introduce an automated pipeline that extracts qualitative knowledge about potential AD progression indicators directly from audio recordings of verbal fluency tests. Our method uses pretrained foundation models to process raw audio and extract clinically relevant variables to construct a Bayesian Network (BN); this BN is used to reason about the AD progression markers and infer their qualitative relationships. Our system successfully recovers known clinical knowledge and identifies novel relationships between linguistic markers.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an automated pipeline that extracts qualitative knowledge about Alzheimer's disease progression indicators from audio recordings of verbal fluency tests, using pretrained foundation models to construct a Bayesian Network that recovers known clinical knowledge and identifies novel relationships between linguistic markers.
AI.motivation: Manual transcription and expert analysis for identifying Alzheimer's disease markers is labor-intensive and limits scalability, motivating the need for an automated approach.
AI.method: The pipeline processes raw audio from verbal fluency tests using pretrained foundation models to extract clinically relevant variables, then constructs a Bayesian Network to reason about AD progression markers and infer their qualitative relationships.
AI.result: The system successfully recovers known clinical knowledge about AD markers and identifies novel relationships between linguistic markers.
AI.conclusion: An automated, scalable pipeline using foundation models and Bayesian Networks can effectively extract and reason about Alzheimer's disease progression indicators directly from audio recordings.

title: Pyramidal Width Can Increase Under Vertex Insertion
summary: Lacoste-Julien and Jaggi conjectured in 2015 that the pyramidal width of a polytope cannot increase when a vertex is added, provided that every old point remains a vertex. We give an exact counterexample with six integer points in $\R^3$. For \[ P=\conv\{v_0,\ldots,v_4\},\qquad Q=\conv\{v_0,\ldots,v_5\}, \] where \[ \begin{aligned} v_0&=(-1,-3,-1), & v_1&=(3,2,-2), & v_2&=(0,2,1),\\ v_3&=(-1,-3,3), & v_4&=(-2,0,1), & v_5&=(-1,0,-2), \end{aligned} \] all five vertices of $P$ remain vertices of $Q$, but \[ \PWidth(P)^2=\frac{48}{353} \quad\text{and}\quad \PWidth(Q)^2=\frac{36}{133}. \] Thus vertex insertion increases pyramidal width by the factor $\sqrt{1059/532}\approx 1.410886779$. The proof uses the equivalence between pyramidal width and facial distance, certifies both face lattices by integer supporting hyperplanes, and evaluates every facial distance by a finite rational calculation. A dependency-free exact verifier accompanies the paper.

AI.tldr: This paper provides an exact counterexample to the 2015 Lacoste-Julien and Jaggi conjecture that pyramidal width of a polytope cannot increase when a vertex is added (with all old points remaining vertices). A polytope P with 5 vertices in R^3 and a polytope Q with 6 vertices (adding one point) are constructed such that all vertices of P remain vertices of Q, yet the squared pyramidal width increases from 48/353 to 36/133, a factor of approximately 1.41.
AI.motivation: Lacoste-Julien and Jaggi conjectured in 2015 that pyramidal width, an important quantity in understanding Frank-Wolfe algorithm convergence, cannot increase under vertex insertion when all old vertices are preserved. Disproving or proving this conjecture is significant for understanding the behavior and convergence guarantees of conditional gradient methods.
AI.method: The paper constructs explicit polytopes P and Q in R^3 with six integer points, where P = conv{v0,...,v4} and Q = conv{v0,...,v5}. The proof leverages the equivalence between pyramidal width and facial distance, certifies both face lattices via integer supporting hyperplanes, and evaluates every facial distance through a finite rational computation. A dependency-free exact verifier accompanies the paper to confirm the results.
AI.result: The counterexample shows PWidth(P)^2 = 48/353 and PWidth(Q)^2 = 36/133, meaning vertex insertion increases pyramidal width by the factor sqrt(1059/532) ≈ 1.410886779. This directly disproves the Lacoste-Julien and Jaggi conjecture.
AI.conclusion: The Lacoste-Julien and Jaggi conjecture is false. Pyramidal width can increase when a vertex is added to a polytope, even when all existing vertices remain vertices. The counterexample is exact, supported by a reproducible dependency-free verification.

title: MOT-SR: Multi-Objective Tool-Augmented Scientific Equation Discovery with Large Language Models
summary: Symbolic Regression (SR) aims to discover analytical equations from observational data and plays a central role in scientific modeling. While recent Large Language Model (LLM) based approaches show promise, they face two limitations. First, they lack data analysis mechanisms for uncovering variable dependencies, which reduces the efficiency of equation discovery. Second, most methods rely on single-objective evaluation focused solely on fitting error. This neglect of structural complexity and generalization often causes models to converge prematurely to local optima, limiting their ability to explore the broader equation space. We propose Multi-Objective Tool-augmented Symbolic Regression (MOT-SR), a unified framework that integrates external analytical tools to extract structural priors and guide equation generation, while jointly optimizing for accuracy, complexity, and generalization via a multi-objective evaluation module that maintains a dynamic Pareto front. MOT-SR employs two collaborative LLM modules: a Meta Strategy Generator, which selects tools and synthesizes structural optimization strategies based on Pareto-optimal equations, and an Equation Generator, which produces new candidate equations accordingly. The system operates in a closed-loop manner, continuously refining both strategies and equation structures. Across 40 standard tasks, MOT-SR outperforms existing SR methods in accuracy, generalization, and efficiency. We further validate MOT-SR on extreme mass-ratio inspiral (EMRI) orbital modeling, an important problem in space-based gravitational-wave astronomy where small local errors can accumulate substantially over long-term evolution. The discovered interpretable correction achieves the lowest trajectory-level integration error on held-out configurations. These results demonstrate the potential of MOT-SR to enable reliable modeling of long-horizon scientific dynamics.

AI.tldr: MOT-SR is a multi-objective, tool-augmented symbolic regression framework that uses LLMs with external analytical tools and Pareto-front optimization to discover equations balancing accuracy, complexity, and generalization, outperforming existing methods on 40 standard tasks and achieving state-of-the-art trajectory-level accuracy on EMRI orbital modeling.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based symbolic regression methods lack data analysis mechanisms for uncovering variable dependencies and rely on single-objective evaluation focused only on fitting error. This neglect of structural complexity and generalization causes premature convergence to local optima, limiting exploration of the broader equation space.
AI.method: MOT-SR integrates external analytical tools to extract structural priors and guide equation generation, while jointly optimizing accuracy, complexity, and generalization via a multi-objective evaluation module that maintains a dynamic Pareto front. It employs two collaborative LLM modules: a Meta Strategy Generator that selects tools and synthesizes structural optimization strategies, and an Equation Generator that produces candidate equations. The system operates in a closed loop, continuously refining strategies and equation structures.
AI.result: Across 40 standard tasks, MOT-SR outperforms existing SR methods in accuracy, generalization, and efficiency. On extreme mass-ratio inspiral (EMRI) orbital modeling, the discovered interpretable correction achieves the lowest trajectory-level integration error on held-out configurations.
AI.conclusion: MOT-SR demonstrates strong potential for reliable symbolic regression and modeling of long-horizon scientific dynamics, particularly in domains where small local errors can accumulate substantially over extended time evolution, such as space-based gravitational-wave astronomy.

title: Convergence and Regret of the Policy Gradient for Multi-Armed Bandits in Diffusion Environment
summary: This paper studies the policy gradient update for a multi-arm bandit problem in diffusion environment that is described by a stochastic differential equation (SDE) under the continuous-time reinforcement learning framework by Wang et al. (2020), Jia and Zhou (2022b). With the logit parameterization for the stochastic policy, we show that it converges almost surely to the optimal arm under an arbitrary constant learning rate. Furthermore, we derive the non-asymptotic regret upper bound when the constant learning rate is below a time-invariant threshold; and the regret bound has order $O(\log T)$. We improve the analysis in Lattimore (2026a) for the same SDE by constructing a novel Lyapunov function and demonstrate the transparency of analyzing policy gradient using the tools in SDEs. In addition, the same Lyapunov function is also helpful in analyzing the discrete-time policy gradient algorithm.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the policy gradient update for a multi-arm bandit problem in a diffusion environment modeled by an SDE under the continuous-time reinforcement learning framework. The authors show almost sure convergence to the optimal arm with a constant learning rate and derive an O(log T) non-asymptotic regret bound using a novel Lyapunov function.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to improve the analysis of policy gradient methods in continuous-time bandit problems (following Wang et al. 2020, Jia and Zhou 2022b) and to improve upon the previous analysis by Lattimore (2026a) for the same SDE, demonstrating that SDE-based tools provide transparency in analyzing policy gradient algorithms.
AI.method: The paper uses logit parameterization for the stochastic policy in a multi-arm bandit modeled by an SDE. It constructs a novel Lyapunov function to analyze the policy gradient dynamics, proving almost sure convergence under arbitrary constant learning rates and deriving non-asymptotic regret bounds. The same Lyapunov function is also applied to analyze the discrete-time policy gradient algorithm.
AI.result: The policy gradient update converges almost surely to the optimal arm under an arbitrary constant learning rate. The non-asymptotic regret upper bound is of order O(log T) when the constant learning rate is below a time-invariant threshold. The novel Lyapunov function improves upon the analysis in Lattimore (2026a).
AI.conclusion: The novel Lyapunov function provides a cleaner and more transparent analysis of policy gradient methods in both continuous-time (SDE) and discrete-time settings, yielding strong convergence guarantees and logarithmic regret bounds.

title: The Parts Are Greater Than the Sum: Automated Task Sequencing for Efficient Training of Multi-Policy LLMs
summary: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) commonly adapts large language models using a single shared Low-Rank Adapter (LoRA). This shared optimization space often suffers from interference when adapting heterogeneous task sequences, leading to poor transfer and catastrophic forgetting. Existing approaches mainly improve adapter expressiveness by increasing parameter capacity or composing multiple adapters, yet they still rely on a shared optimization path. In this paper, we propose an optimization-path organization framework for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models, implemented as an automatic multi-policy PEFT architecture. Specifically, optimization-compatible adaptation paths are automatically organized through task grouping and task sequencing under a fixed parameter budget. The organized optimization paths are implemented as independent Quantized Low-Rank Adapters (QLoRA), enabling heterogeneous tasks to be optimized in decoupled adaptation spaces while preserving positive transfer among compatible tasks. Experiments on the TRACE benchmark demonstrate that performance consistently improves from conventional single-policy PEFT to multi-policy PEFT, with the proposed automatic multi-policy framework achieving the best performance of 44.78 under the same trainable capacity. This suggests that optimization-path organization is more effective than simply increasing adapter capacity for heterogeneous parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an automatic multi-policy PEFT framework that organizes optimization paths for LLM fine-tuning by grouping and sequencing tasks into independent QLoRA adapters under a fixed parameter budget, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the TRACE benchmark (44.78) by decoupling heterogeneous task optimization while preserving positive transfer among compatible tasks.
AI.motivation: Traditional PEFT using a single shared LoRA suffers from optimization interference when adapting heterogeneous task sequences, leading to poor transfer and catastrophic forgetting. Existing approaches either increase adapter capacity or compose multiple adapters but still rely on a single shared optimization path, which does not fundamentally address the interference problem.
AI.method: The proposed framework automatically organizes optimization paths through task grouping and task sequencing under a fixed parameter budget. These organized paths are implemented as independent Quantized Low-Rank Adapters (QLoRA), allowing heterogeneous tasks to be optimized in decoupled adaptation spaces while maintaining positive transfer among compatible tasks via task grouping.
AI.result: On the TRACE benchmark, performance consistently improves from conventional single-policy PEFT to multi-policy PEFT, with the proposed automatic multi-policy framework achieving the best performance of 44.78 under the same trainable capacity.
AI.conclusion: Optimization-path organization is more effective than simply increasing adapter capacity for heterogeneous parameter-efficient fine-tuning, suggesting that how adaptation paths are organized matters more than how much parameter capacity is allocated.

title: When Does On-Policy Interaction Help? Representational Tradeoffs in Value-Based Imitation Learning
summary:
Imitation learning (IL)---training an agent to replicate expert behavior from demonstrations---underpins applications from robotics to language model training. Standard approaches such as Behavior Cloning (BC) are known to suffer from compounding errors and performance plateaus, particularly when the learner cannot perfectly represent the expert's policy (as is typical, e.g., in distillation). Two interventions are widely understood empirically to improve performance: querying the expert interactively along the learner's own trajectories, and using value function estimation en route to generating a policy rather than directly fitting the expert's full action distribution.
  We investigate the nature of these improvements and their potentially surprising interplay. Our main finding is that expert interaction relaxes the representational demands on the learner: one only needs a model capable of realizing the expert's value function, bypassing the (often stricter) requirement of realizing the expert's policy itself. Concretely, we introduce OVI, an interactive on-policy IL algorithm that is statistically efficient whenever the learner can represent the expert's value function and computationally efficient given access to a linear maximization oracle. We complement this with a negative result showing that interaction is necessary. Namely, without stronger assumptions beyond expert-value realizability alone, any offline IL algorithm must scale with the complexity of the expert policy class. Our findings bear out empirically. OVI outperforms offline policy-based (BC), interactive policy-based (DAgger), and offline value-based IL methods, with the largest gains when the learner network is substantially less expressive than the expert's.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OVI, an interactive on-policy imitation learning algorithm that achieves statistical efficiency whenever the learner can represent the expert's value function rather than the expert's policy itself. It also proves a negative result showing that interaction is necessary: without expert-value realizability and without interaction, any offline IL algorithm must scale with expert policy class complexity.
AI.motivation: Standard imitation learning approaches like Behavior Cloning suffer from compounding errors and performance plateaus, especially when the learner cannot perfectly represent the expert's policy (common in distillation). Two known empirical improvements are interactive expert querying along learner trajectories and value-function-based policy generation. The authors aim to understand the nature of these improvements and their interplay.
AI.method: The authors introduce OVI (presumably "On-policy Value Imitation"), an interactive on-policy IL algorithm that is statistically efficient when the learner can represent the expert's value function, and computationally efficient given a linear maximization oracle. They also present a theoretical negative result establishing that interaction is necessary when only expert-value realizability holds (no stronger assumptions), and validate their findings empirically against BC, DAgger, and offline value-based IL methods.
AI.result: OVI outperforms offline policy-based (BC), interactive policy-based (DAgger), and offline value-based IL baselines, with the largest gains when the learner network is substantially less expressive than the expert's. The theoretical results show expert interaction relaxes representational demands from expert policy realizability to expert value realizability, and that interaction is provably necessary to escape expert policy class complexity scaling in offline settings.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes that the key benefit of interactive expert querying in imitation learning is reducing the representational burden from realizing the expert's policy to realizing only its value function. Interaction is provably necessary for this benefit, and the proposed OVI algorithm demonstrates the practical value of this insight, particularly under model capacity mismatch.

title: CENDRe: Concept Extraction with Natural Domain Representations
summary: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are widely used for time-series classification, but their deployment in critical domains requires understanding the temporal and spectral patterns that drive their predictions. Concept extraction (CE) methods identify such patterns by analyzing representations within the models' latent space. However, existing time-series CE methods have three limitations: they operate only in the time domain and overlook frequency features, predefine the number of concepts, and produce localizations misaligned with the regions the model uses. We address these limitations by proposing CENDRe, a concept extraction method for CNNs. It first discovers concepts by clustering per-timestep latent representations in two stages, where silhouette-guided aggregation selects the number of concepts automatically.
