Then, it localizes each concept through gradients of a presence score that contrasts the latent representations with their prototypes, producing masks that concentrate on the regions driving the concept. These gradients, propagated through a differentiable invertible mapping of the input such as a Fourier transform, yield localizations for the same concepts in the frequency domain. Finally, each concept receives a relevance score that quantifies its contribution to each class. On synthetic benchmarks, CENDRe achieves representation correctness comparable to state-of-the-art CE methods and significantly higher importance correctness. On real bearing-fault data, CENDRe extracts the frequency bands driving the model's predictions, located in regions commonly inspected for fault diagnosis, producing evidence to assess the model that time-domain CE methods cannot.

AI.tldr: CENDRe is a novel concept extraction method for CNNs in time-series classification that discovers concepts via two-stage silhouette-guided clustering in latent space, localizes them in both time and frequency domains through gradient-based contrast with prototypes, and assigns relevance scores per class. It outperforms state-of-the-art CE methods on synthetic benchmarks and extracts interpretable frequency bands on real bearing-fault data.
AI.motivation: Existing time-series concept extraction methods have three key limitations: they only operate in the time domain and ignore frequency features; they require the number of concepts to be predefined; and they produce localizations that are misaligned with the regions the model actually uses. This hampers trustworthy deployment of CNNs in critical domains.
AI.method: CENDRe first discovers concepts by clustering per-timestep latent representations in two stages, using silhouette-guided aggregation to automatically determine the number of concepts. It then localizes concepts via gradients of a presence score contrasting latent representations with their prototypes, producing masks focused on driving regions. These gradients are propagated through a differentiable invertible mapping (e.g., Fourier transform) to yield frequency-domain localizations. Finally, each concept receives a per-class relevance score.
AI.result: On synthetic benchmarks, CENDRe achieves representation correctness comparable to state-of-the-art CE methods and significantly higher importance correctness. On real bearing-fault data, CENDRe extracts the frequency bands driving model predictions in regions commonly inspected for fault diagnosis, producing evidence time-domain CE methods cannot provide.
AI.conclusion: CENDRe addresses all three limitations of existing time-series CE methods by enabling both time- and frequency-domain concept localization, automatic concept number selection, and well-aligned localizations. It provides richer, more accurate interpretability evidence for CNNs in critical time-series classification applications.

title: GQ-FSL: Green Quantized Federated Split Learning
comment: To appear in IEEE 27th International Workshop on Signal Processing Advances in Wireless Communications (SPAWC), 2026
summary: Deploying state-of-the-art deep neural networks (DNNs) at the wireless edge is severely bottlenecked by the strict energy and resource constraints of mobile devices. While federated split learning (FSL) mitigates on-device computation by offloading workloads to an edge server, this may introduce systemic overheads, while the continuous exchange of cut-layer data, and submodels still incurs significant energy consumption (EC). To address this, we propose a green quantized FSL (GQ-FSL) framework that incorporates stochastic quantization for both local collaborative training and wireless transmissions. Notably, GQ-FSL supports asymmetric precision levels for the client- and server-side submodels, effectively decoupling device energy constraints from global convergence degradation. To quantify these tradeoffs, we develop parameterized energy models for the split architecture and derive a theoretical convergence bound under statistically heterogeneous data. Building on that, we formulate a joint optimization problem to configure the DNN split point and precision levels, minimizing the total system EC while satisfying a strict target accuracy constraint. Ultimately, we demonstrate that GQ-FSL enables large-scale DNN deployment on resource-constrained devices, achieving superior energy efficiency compared to quantized federated learning and full-precision FSL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GQ-FSL, a green quantized federated split learning framework that employs stochastic quantization for both local training and wireless transmissions, with asymmetric precision levels for client- and server-side submodels. It jointly optimizes the DNN split point and precision levels to minimize total system energy consumption while satisfying a target accuracy constraint, demonstrating superior energy efficiency over quantized FL and full-precision FSL.
AI.motivation: Deploying state-of-the-art DNNs at the wireless edge is bottlenecked by strict energy and resource constraints of mobile devices. While federated split learning (FSL) offloads computation to edge servers, it introduces systemic overheads and continuous exchange of cut-layer data/submodels that incur significant energy consumption, motivating the need for a more energy-efficient framework.
AI.method: GQ-FSL incorporates stochastic quantization for both local collaborative training and wireless transmissions, supporting asymmetric precision levels for client- and server-side submodels. The authors develop parameterized energy models for the split architecture and derive a theoretical convergence bound under statistically heterogeneous data. They formulate a joint optimization problem to configure the DNN split point and precision levels, minimizing total system EC under a strict accuracy constraint.
AI.result: GQ-FSL enables large-scale DNN deployment on resource-constrained devices, achieving superior energy efficiency compared to quantized federated learning and full-precision federated split learning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed GQ-FSL framework effectively decouples device energy constraints from global convergence degradation via asymmetric precision levels, and the joint optimization of split point and precision levels yields significant energy savings while meeting accuracy targets, making edge DNN deployment feasible on resource-constrained devices.

title: Freeze, Then Select: Structured Field Adapters and Stability-Validated Weak Selection for PDE Discovery from Sparse Observations
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, and 17 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: PDE discovery from sparse observations requires reconstructing a continuous field and selecting the correct differential terms. Our analysis of optimization paths in coupled neural PDE discovery reveals three behaviors: the exact support can persist to the end of training, appear only transiently, or fail to emerge. To decouple equation selection from neural optimization, we develop a freeze-then-select method combining a structured field adapter with Stability-Validated Weak Selection (SVWS). Trained from observations without a PDE residual, the adapter factorizes the field into learned spatial features and temporal coefficients represented by cubic splines. After freezing the field, SVWS identifies recurrent terms across independent weak-form systems, refits candidate supports, and selects the final equation on held-out weak-form systems. Beyond fixed libraries, we apply the same principle to expressions generated by genetic programming and recover the power-law form of an unknown nonlinear diffusion function from sparse, noisy observations. Across all six sparse MDBench regimes, our method attains the highest exact support recovery rate, with its clearest gains over classical and neural baselines on challenging Kuramoto-Sivashinsky dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses PDE discovery from sparse observations by analyzing optimization dynamics in coupled neural approaches, revealing three support-selection behaviors, and proposing a freeze-then-select method (structured field adapter + Stability-Validated Weak Selection) that decouples equation selection from neural optimization. It achieves state-of-the-art exact support recovery across all six sparse MDBench regimes and extends to genetic-expression-based libraries, recovering power-law nonlinear diffusion.
AI.motivation: Coupled neural PDE discovery methods suffer from a fundamental coupling between field reconstruction and equation selection, making it unclear whether correct differential terms (support) can be reliably recovered. Analysis reveals that exact support can persist, appear transiently, or fail to emerge during optimization, motivating a decoupled design where equation selection is performed independently from neural field fitting.
AI.method: The method (freeze-then-select) first trains a structured field adapter from sparse observations without a PDE residual, factorizing the field into learned spatial features and cubic-spline temporal coefficients. After freezing the field, SVWS identifies recurrent terms across independent weak-form systems, refits candidate supports, and selects the final equation on held-out weak-form systems. The same principle is applied to genetic-programming-generated expression libraries in addition to fixed dictionaries.
AI.result: Across all six sparse MDBench regimes, the method achieves the highest exact support recovery rate, with clearest gains over classical and neural baselines on challenging Kuramoto-Sivashinsky dynamics. It also successfully recovers the power-law form of an unknown nonlinear diffusion function from sparse, noisy observations.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling PDE support selection from neural field optimization is key to robust PDE discovery under sparse, noisy observations. The freeze-then-select paradigm with weak-form validation outperforms coupled neural and classical baselines, and generalizes beyond fixed libraries to expression-space search.

title: SVR: Self-Verifying Refinement via Joint Verdict-Confidence Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Test-Time Compute
summary: Scaling test-time computation can improve language-model reasoning, but uniform budgets waste computation on easy inputs, while verifier-guided refinement relies on external feedback. We introduce Self-Verifying Refinement (SVR), an oracle-free multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that learns to use self-verification as a compute-control policy. At each turn, the model produces a solution together with a discrete correctness verdict and a confidence score; it retains the current answer only when the verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold, and otherwise continues refinement using its own self-verification. Ground-truth correctness is used only to construct training rewards and is never exposed to the policy through refinement prompts or required at inference. SVR is trained with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories using rewards that promote solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states; adaptive stopping is activated only at inference. On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves a macro-average accuracy of 0.563 with only 2.99 inference turns on average. In the evaluated complete-system comparison, it exceeds standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference while requiring substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference. These results demonstrate that learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation.

AI.tldr: SVR is an oracle-free multi-turn RL framework that learns to use self-verification as a compute-control policy, achieving 0.563 macro-average accuracy with only 2.99 inference turns on seven math benchmarks, outperforming standard GRPO and strong baselines while using fewer turns.
AI.motivation: Scaling test-time computation can improve reasoning but uniform budgets waste compute on easy inputs, while verifier-guided refinement relies on external feedback. The authors aim to enable adaptive compute allocation using internal self-verification signals rather than external oracles.
AI.method: SVR is trained with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories. At each turn the model produces a solution with a correctness verdict and confidence score. The model retains the answer only if verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold, otherwise it refines. Ground-truth is used only for training rewards (solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, stop-ready correct states), never exposed to the policy. Adaptive stopping is applied only at inference.
AI.result: On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves 0.563 macro-average accuracy with only 2.99 average inference turns, exceeding standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference, while using substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference.
AI.conclusion: Learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation, eliminating the need for external verifiers or ground-truth feedback at inference.
